en: *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*, Book 1, *Pauroḍāśika* Book, Chapter 1, Section 1: The Establishment of the Fires (*Agnnyādhāna*). Unite the Brahman; quicken that for me! Unite the Kṣatra; quicken that for me! Unite food (*iṣ*); quicken that for me! Unite strength (*ūrj*); quicken that for me! Unite wealth (*rayi*); quicken that for me! Unite prosperity (*puṣṭi*); quicken that for me! Unite progeny (*prajā*); quicken that for me!

Unite the cattle; quicken them for me! You are praised, O bestower of people. May the gods who drink the *śukra* lead you forward. Producing offspring rich in heroes, go around! O *śukra*, with the brilliance of the *śukra*. You are praised, O bestower of people. May the gods who drink the *manthin* lead you forward. Producing offspring rich in progeny, go around! O *manthin*, with the brilliance of the *manthin*. Meeting together from heaven and earth, unite life; quicken that for me! Unite the out-breath (*prāṇa*); quicken it for me! Unite the in-breath (*apāna*); quicken it for me!

Join the pervasive breath (vyāna); quicken that for me. Join the eye; quicken that for me. Join the ear; quicken that for me. Join the mind; quicken that for me. Join the speech; quicken that for me. You two are life; bestow life upon me. Bestow life upon the sacrifice. Bestow life upon the lord of the sacrifice. You two are the out-breath (prāṇa); bestow the out-breath upon me. Bestow the out-breath upon the sacrifice.

{1.1.1.4} Bestow breath upon the lord of the sacrifice! You two are sight; bestow sight upon me. Bestow sight upon the sacrifice. Bestow sight upon the lord of the sacrifice! You two are hearing; bestow hearing upon me. Bestow hearing upon the sacrifice. Bestow hearing upon the lord of the sacrifice! You two are the gods Śukra and Manthin; arrange the divine clans; arrange the human clans.

Bestow nourishment and vigor upon us; bestow vital breaths upon the cattle; bestow progeny upon me and upon the sacrificer. Śaṇḍa is cast out; Marka is cast out. Śaṇḍa and Marka are driven away together with that [enemy]. You are the kindling-stick of the *śukra* cup; you are the kindling-stick of the *manthin* cup. He is the first creator, Viśvakarman; he is the first Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni; he is the first Bṛhaspati, the wise. To that Indra I offer the pressed soma.

1.1.2 Anuvāka 2: The Establishment of the Sacred Fires {1.1.2.1} One should establish the sacred fires under the Kṛttikās. The Kṛttikās are indeed the lunar mansion of Agni. Having established him in his own deity, he becomes endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*). The Kṛttikās are indeed the mouth of the lunar mansions. He who establishes the fires under the Kṛttikās becomes preeminent. Moreover, furthermore...

{1.1.2.2} They honor [the constellation] Agni-nakṣatra; for it becomes a burner of one's house. Prajāpati created Agni under Rohiṇī. The gods established him under Rohiṇī; from that, they indeed ascended all heights. That is the reason for Rohiṇī’s name "Rohiṇī" (the Ascending One). He who establishes the fire under Rohiṇī prospers indeed; he ascends all heights. The gods, being auspicious, desired to establish the fire.

{1.1.2.3} Their fire had not been established. Then desirable wealth departed from them. They established the fire under the two *punarvasū* constellations; thereupon, indeed, desirable wealth returned to them. He who, having previously been prosperous, should become more wretched, should establish his fire under the *punarvasū*; verily, desirable wealth returns to him once again, and he becomes prosperous. He who should desire, "May my offspring be inclined toward giving," should establish his fire under the two former *phalgunī*s.

{1.1.2.4} The Pūrva-phalgunīs are indeed the lunar mansion of Aryaman; for they call him Aryaman who bestows gifts. His offspring become desirous of giving. He who should desire, "May I be fortunate," should establish his sacred fires under the two Uttara-phalgunīs. The Uttara-phalgunīs are indeed the lunar mansion of Bhaga; he becomes truly fortunate. There were, indeed, Asuras named Kālakañjas.

They piled the fire-altar for the sake of the heavenly world. One man placed a brick; another man placed a brick. Indra, calling himself a Brāhmaṇa, placed a brick, saying, "This one of mine is named Citrā. They ascended to the heavenly world. Indra pulled out that brick; they were scattered. Those who were scattered became the *ūrṇāvabhya* plants. Two [bricks] flew away.

{1.1.2.6} Those two became divine dogs. He who has rivals should establish the sacred fires under the Citrā constellation; he thus scatters his rivals and places vigor, strength, sensory power, and heroism within himself. A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires in spring; for spring is indeed the season of the Brāhmaṇa. Having established them in its own season, he becomes endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*). This [spring] is indeed the mouth of the seasons.

{1.1.2.7} As for the spring: he who establishes the sacred fires in the spring becomes preeminent; moreover, he establishes them as something born from a womb. A Rājanya should establish the fires in the summer; the summer is indeed the season of the Rājanya. Having established them in his own season, he becomes possessed of power. A Vaiśya should establish the fires in the autumn; the autumn is indeed the season of the Vaiśya.

Having established him in his own proper season, he becomes possessed of cattle. One should not establish the sacred fire during the two former *phalgunī* constellations; for these are the last night of the year. By establishing the fire at the very end of the year, one becomes worse off. One should establish it during the two latter *phalgunī* constellations; for these are the first night of the year. By establishing the fire at the very beginning of the year, [one prospers].

He becomes more prosperous. Furthermore, when the sacrifice approaches him, then he should establish the fires; that indeed is his prosperity. 1.1.3 Anuvāka 3: The Establishment of the Fires {1.1.3.1} He digs up [the ground], thereby removing whatever in it is impure. He sprinkles water for the sake of pacification. He scatters sand; this is indeed the form of Agni Vaiśvānara; by means of its very form, he wins Vaiśvānara. He scatters saline soil; for saline soil is nourishment and procreation.

{1.1.3.2} He establishes the fire for the sake of nourishment and procreation; moreover, it is for the sake of recognition, for salt-earth (ūṣas) is indeed the means of recognizing cattle. Heaven and Earth were together; as they were separating, they said, "Let there be that which is worthy of sacrifice common to us both. That which was worthy of sacrifice in yonder [heaven], he placed in this [earth]; those became the salt-earth.

{1.1.3.3} Whatever of this [earth] was fit for sacrifice, he placed that in yonder [heaven]. That is the black spot in the moon. While scattering the saline soil (*ūṣān*), he should meditate on that. Verily, he establishes the fire in the sacrificial portion of both heaven and earth. Agni hid himself from the gods; having assumed the form of a mole (*ākhu*), he entered the earth. Making mounds (*ūtīḥ*) as he went, he moved along the earth. That became mole-hill soil (*ākhukarīṣa*).

{1.1.3.4} When rat-dung is the material, he secures whatever of it is hidden there. Ants indeed dig out this strength and sap from the earth; that is the anthill. When an anthill mound is the material, he secures the very strength and sap of the earth; moreover, it is the sense of hearing itself, for the anthill is the sense of hearing of the earth.

{1.1.3.5} He who knows thus becomes free from deafness. Prajāpati created offspring; their food was exhausted. For them, he produced broth (*sūda*). Thereupon, indeed, their food was not exhausted. For whomsoever broth is the sacrificial material (*saṃbhāra*), food is not exhausted in his house. In the beginning, this world was water, a mere ocean. Because of that, Prajāpati exerted himself.

"How could this be? he wondered. He saw a lotus leaf lying there. He thought, "There must indeed be that upon which this rests. Having assumed the form of a boar, he dived down. He reached the earth below; having struck it, he emerged. There he spread it out upon the lotus leaf. That which he spread out—

That is the earth-nature (*pṛthivītva*) of the earth. "This indeed has come into being" (*abhūt*); that is the ground-nature (*bhūmitva*) of the ground. The wind blew toward it from all directions; he made it firm with pebbles (*śarkarā*). "It has become auspicious for us" (*śam naḥ abhūt*); that is the pebble-nature (*śarkaratva*) of the pebbles. In that there is a preparation of earth dug up by a boar, he establishes the fire on this very [earth] so as not to fail. There are pebbles for the sake of stability.

{1.1.3.8} Moreover, for the sake of well-being: "Agni should be established with seed," they say. The waters were the wives of Varuṇa. Agni desired them; he united with them. His seed fell away; it became gold. When one places gold [on the altar], one establishes Agni with his seed. "Indeed, a man is loathsome to his own seed," they say.

He places it on the north side for the sake of freedom from loathing. He hands it over; he thus hands over misfortune itself. Agni hid himself from the gods, having assumed the form of a horse. He remained in the *aśvattha* tree for a year; that is why the *aśvattha* is called *aśvattha*. In that the *aśvattha* is used as a ritual material, he thereby secures whatever in him was hidden there.

{ 1.1.3.10} The gods, indeed, divided among themselves the vital energy (*ūrj*). From that, the *udumbara* tree arose. The *udumbara* is indeed vital energy. In that there is a supporting material (*saṃbhāra*) made of *udumbara*, one secures vital energy for oneself. Soma was in the third heaven from here. Gāyatrī brought him down. A leaf of his was torn off; that became the *parṇa* tree. That is the origin of the name *parṇa*.

{1.1.3.11} He whose sacrificial equipment consists of *parṇa* wood attains the very drinking of Soma. The gods indeed conversed regarding the Brahman; the *parṇa* tree overheard it. Therefore, its name is "Suśravas" (the well-hearing). When the sacrificial equipment consists of *parṇa* wood, one attains spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Prajāpati created Agni; he was afraid, thinking, "He will burn me. He quieted him with the *śamyā*.

{1.1.3.12} That [is] for peace, for the state of being pacified. In that the ritual material (*saṃbhāra*) consists of *śamī* wood, it is for the sake of peace and to prevent burning. Since the splendor (*bhās*) reached the *vikaṅkata* tree when Agni was created, in that the ritual material consists of *vikaṅkata* wood, he indeed secures splendor. "Agni should be established with his heart intact," they say. The Maruts extinguished Agni with water; they cut out the heart of him who was exhausted, and it became a thunderbolt (*aśani*). In that the ritual material consists of a tree struck by lightning, he establishes Agni with his heart intact.

Anuvāka 4: The Establishment of the Fires {1.1.4.1} One should establish the fire at twelve paces. Twelve months are a year; verily, having won it from the year, he establishes it. If he were to establish it at twelve paces, he would win only what is limited. He should establish it where the eye is fixed, thinking, "This much is twelve paces. Thus he wins both the limited and the unlimited. Verily, one speaks untruth with speech; one thinks untruth with the mind.

The eye is indeed truth. One says, "I have seen," and [the other replies], "I saw. That is truth. He who establishes the sacred fires when the eye is established establishes them in truth itself. Therefore, one who has established the fires should not speak untruth; no Brahmin should dwell in his house without having eaten. For his fire is established in truth. Indeed, the night belongs to Agni.

{1.1.4.3} The sacrificial animals belong to Agni; the day belongs to Indra. He establishes the *gārhapatya* fire at night; verily, he wins cattle. He establishes the *āhavanīya* fire by day; verily, he wins power (*indriya*). He establishes the *āhavanīya* fire when the sun has half-risen. For it was in this very world that Prajāpati created offspring. Thereby the sacrificer creates offspring. Moreover, he wins both the past and the future.

Iḍā, the daughter of Manu, was the one who perceived the sacrifices. She heard that the Asuras were establishing their fires. She went there; they first established the Āhavanīya fire, then the Gārhapatya, and then the Anvāhāryapacana. She said, "Their prosperity has gone backward; having been auspicious, they shall now perish."

{1.1.4.5} For whomsoever the fire is established in this manner, his prosperity turns away from him; having been fortunate, he comes to ruin. She heard it said, "The gods are establishing the fire. She went there. They first established the Anvāhāryapacana fire, then the Gārhapatya, and then the Āhavanīya. She said:

"Their prosperity has gone to the east; having become auspicious, they will go to the heavenly world, but they will not obtain offspring"—so it is said of him for whom the fire is thus established. His prosperity goes to the east; having become auspicious, he goes to the heavenly world, but he does not obtain offspring. Iḍā said to Manu: "In such a way indeed shall I establish your fire, so that you will propagate with offspring, cattle, and pairs."

"You shall stand firm in this world; you shall conquer the heavenly world," [he says]. He places the *gārhapatya* fire first. Indeed, offspring and cattle are born after the *gārhapatya*; by means of the *gārhapatya*, he thus brought forth for him offspring and cattle. Then the *anvāhāryapacana* fire: this world is, as it were, horizontal; by that, he established himself firmly in this very world. Then the *āhavanīya* fire: by that, he conquered the heavenly world.

{1.1.4.8} For whomsoever the fire is established in this manner, he is propagated with offspring, cattle, and pairs; he stands firm in this world and conquers the heavenly world. But for whomsoever the fire is established contrary to the deities, he is cut off from the deities and becomes worse off. For whomsoever it is established according to the deities, he is not cut off from the deities and becomes more prosperous.

{1.1.4.9} "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases," [with these words] he should establish [the fire] for those of the Bhṛgu and Aṅgira lineages. "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of the Ādityas, the gods," [with these words] for other Brāhmaṇa lineages. "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of King Varuṇa," [with these words] for a king. "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the power of Indra," [with these words] for a Rājanya.

"O Manas, lord of the village, O lord of vows, I establish thee with the vow"—thus for a Vaiśya. "O Ṛbhus, lords of the gods, O lord of vows, I establish thee with the vow"—thus for a chariot-maker. Agni is established according to the respective deity; he is not cut off from the deities; he becomes more prosperous.

Anuvāka 5: The Establishment of the Fire {1.1.5.1} Prajāpati beheld the truth of speech. With it, he established the fire; with it, indeed, he prospered. He says, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar. This, indeed, is the truth of speech. He who establishes the fire with this [formula] prospers. Moreover, he becomes one who attains the truth. Furthermore, if one who knows thus practices sorcery against another, he surely lays him low.

He says, "Bhūḥ. By this, the sacrificer creates progeny. He says, "Bhuvaḥ. By this, he becomes firmly established in this very world. He says, "Svaḥ. By this, he becomes firmly established in the heavenly world. With three syllables he establishes the *gārhapatya* fire; these worlds are three. Thus, he establishes it so that it is firmly rooted in these very worlds. With all five [syllables] together, he establishes the *āhavanīya* fire.

{1.1.5.3} Indeed, this Āhavanīya fire is established for the sake of the heavenly world. In that very heavenly world, he attains all the truth of speech. He establishes the Gārhapatya fire with three verses and the Āhavanīya fire with five; thus they amount to eight. The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī. Thus, he establishes Agni in his full extent.

Prajāpati created offspring. Once created, they moved away from him. He drew forth light for them. Beholding that light, the offspring turned back toward him. When he draws [the fire] out, he should draw it up as if holding it aloft like a fire; thus the offspring, beholding the light, turn back toward the sacrificer. The eye of Prajāpati swelled; it fell away and became a horse. That is the reason for the horse's name, *aśva*.

{1.1.5.5} This Agni is indeed Prajāpati; the horse is of Prajāpati. In that he leads the horse in front, Prajāpati follows along, seeing his own eye. The horse is indeed a thunderbolt. In that he leads the horse in front, he drives away his born rivals. He turns it back again.

{1.1.5.6} He repels those who are yet to be born. The Āhavanīya fire desired the Gārhapatya; the Gārhapatya desired the Āhavanīya. He was unable to separate them. He became a horse that leads from the front (*pūrvavāṭ*) and carried the former forward. That is why the one who leads from the front is called *pūrvavāṭ*. In that he leads the horse in front, it serves as the separator between these two; moreover, he thereby makes them possessed of distinct powers.

If he were to carry [the fire] higher and higher with the head, he would cut off the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). He carries it lower and lower with the head for the protection of the vital breaths. At first he carries it this much; then this much; then this much. These are the three worlds; thus he establishes it firmly within these very worlds. Prajāpati created Agni. He was afraid, thinking, "He will burn me up."

{1.1.5.8} He divided his greatness threefold, for the sake of peace and to prevent burning. In that the fire is established threefold, he thereby divides its greatness for the sake of peace and to prevent burning. He brings it back again; he thereby reunites its greatness. This horse is indeed an animal; this [horse] is Rudra.

{1.1.5.9} As for the fire: if one were to place the fire in the footprint of the horse, he would consign the cattle to Rudra; the sacrificer would be left without cattle. If, on the other hand, he were not to step upon it, his cattle would remain unappropriated. He should step upon it from the side, so that the embers of the established fire might roll back toward him. Thus his cattle become appropriated, and he does not consign them to Rudra.

{1.1.5.10} He offers three oblations. The sacrificer strides after the stride of the Virāj itself. [The offerings are] to Agni Pavamāna, to Agni Pāvaka, and to Agni Śuci. In that he offers to Agni Pavamāna, he purifies him. In that [he offers] to Agni Pāvaka, he bestows food upon him once he is purified. In that [he offers] to Agni Śuci, he bestows spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) upon him from above.

Anuvāka 6: The Establishment of the Fires {1.1.6.1} The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. As the gods were about to achieve victory, they deposited their precious wealth in Agni, thinking: "This shall be ours if they should defeat us. Agni was unable to endure that; he distributed it in three parts: one third among the cattle, one third in the waters, and one third in the sun.

{1.1.6.2} Having won that [victory], the gods sought to recover it. They offered a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna. Agni Pavamāna is indeed cattle; whatever was in the cattle, they recovered that by means of this offering. They [offered] to Agni Pāvaka. Agni Pāvaka is indeed water; whatever was in the waters, they recovered that by means of this offering.

{1.1.6.3} These [oblations] are for Agni Śuci. Indeed, that sun is Agni Śuci. Whatever was in the sun, that they thereby obtained. The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "These are indeed the bodies of the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*); the cake on eight potsherds for Agni is the establishment of the fires. If one were to offer that [cake], these [other oblations] would not exist; it would be as if there were only the self.

{1.1.6.4} It is not the limbs; it is just like that. If one were to offer these [limbs] separately, they would not be limbs, nor would it be the self; it is just like that. Both must be offered together for the sake of the sacrifice’s possession of a self. Indeed, both his sensory power and his vigor are thereby obtained.

{1.1.6.5} He who establishes the sacred fires should subsequently offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni, and a pap to Aditi. Indra and Agni are indeed the two gods among the deities who are untiring; by means of those very two deities who are untiring, he secures for himself sensory power and vigor. There is a pap for Aditi; Aditi is indeed this earth; verily, he finds firm support upon her. This is indeed the seed of the cow.

{1.1.6.6} That which is the clarified butter, the rice grains of the ox—verily he wins a pair. It is in ghee; this is for the sake of the sacrifice’s lack of harshness. Four *ārṣeya* priests consume it; verily he offers in the light of the quarters. These oblations are indeed cattle; Agni is Rudra.

{1.1.6.7} If he were to offer these oblations immediately, he would hand over his cattle to Rudra; the sacrificer would become destitute of cattle. If he were not to offer them subsequently, his cattle would remain unsecured. He should offer them subsequently after twelve nights. For the twelve nights are indeed the counterpart of the year. Having thus appeased Rudra for him by means of the year, he secures cattle. If he were to offer these oblations one by one, [the same fault would occur].

{1.1.6.8} It is just as if one were to fill three receptacles: such is that [act]. One should not leave behind the means of procreation. Having set aside one [portion], he should combine the two remaining. He leaves behind the third world for him, for the sake of procreation; he is subsequently reproduced with offspring and cattle. Moreover, this is the overcoming of the sacrifice itself. He sets the chariot wheel in motion; by means of a human chariot, he thus descends upon the divine chariot.

{1.1.6.9} The exponents of Brahman say: "Should the Agnihotra be offered, or should it not be offered? If one were to offer it with a sacrificial formula (*yajus*), one would offer the oblations out of their proper sequence. If one were not to offer it, Agni would perish. It should be offered silently; thus one offers the oblations in their proper sequence, and Agni does not perish. One gives [a gift] to the Āgnīdhra."

He gratifies the seasons, whose mouth is Agni. He gives a cushion; this is for the attainment of forms. He gives a horse to the Brahman priest; thus he attains sensory power (*indriya*). He gives a milch cow to the Hotṛ priest; thus he attains blessings (*āśis*). He gives an ox to the Adhvaryu priest; for the ox is a carrier, and the Adhvaryu is a carrier.

{1.1.6.11} By means of fire itself, he wins the fire of the sacrifice. He gives a pair of cattle for the attainment of a pair. He gives a garment; for a garment belongs to all the deities; thus he gratifies all the deities. He gives up to twelve; for twelve months are a year; he finds firm support in the year itself. One may give more at will, for the attainment of the unlimited.

Anuvāka 7: The Establishment of the Fire {1.1.7.1} The Gharma is the head; may this Agni here become dear to the cattle. Grant protection to our children and descendants. The vital breath is Vāta; may this Agni here become dear to the cattle. Cook well-ripened food for our children and descendants. Go forward, O wise one, along the eastern direction. O Agni, be the fire in front of Agni here. Shining forth, illumine all the quarters. Bestow strength upon us, upon our bipeds and quadrupeds.

The *arka* is the eye; that is yonder sun, and that is this fire. May he be well-beloved by the cattle. O bright one, that which is your bright luster, your bright body, your bright, unaging light—with that shine for me; with that I establish you. O Agni, through Agni, through the sacred word (*brahman*), I have attained; I have pervaded; I have pervaded a full span of life. Those two auspicious bodies of yours, O Agni—the *virāj* and the *svarāj*—may they enter me; may they quicken me.

O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Sovereign and the Overpowering—may they enter me; may they quicken me. O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Pervasive and the Encompassing—may they enter me; may they quicken me. O Agni, those two auspicious bodies of yours, the Mighty and the Abundant—may they enter me; may they quicken me. Those auspicious bodies of yours, O Agni—with them I establish you. Those terrible bodies of yours, O Agni—with them go to that [enemy].

Anuvāka 8: The Establishment of the Fires {1.1.8.1} These worlds, indeed, are the fires. If they were established without being separated [from one another], they would consume the sacrificer. He establishes the Gārhapatya fire with the words, "The Gharma is the head"; the Anvāhāryapacana with, "Vāta is the breath"; and the Āhavanīya with, "Arka is the eye. By this very means he separates them; thus they do not consume the sacrificer. When the Gārhapatya is being established, the Rathantara is sung; for this world is indeed related to the Rathantara.

{1.1.8.2} He establishes him (Agni) firmly established in this very world. While the fire is being lifted up, he should sing the Vāmadevya; the Vāmadevya is indeed the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); thus he establishes him firmly established in the intermediate space itself. Moreover, the Vāmadevya is indeed peace (*śānti*); he lifts him up as peaceful and favorable to cattle. While the Āhavanīya fire is being established, he should sing the Bṛhat; yonder world is indeed of the Bṛhat; thus he establishes him firmly established in yonder world itself. Prajāpati created Agni.

{1.1.8.3} That horse, having become a stallion (*vāra*), went away. He restrained it with the *Vāravantīya* [Sāman]; that is the reason for the name of the *Vāravantīya*. With the *Śyaita*, he made it white (*śyeta*); that is the reason for the name of the *Śyaita*. When the *Vāravantīya* is sung over [the fire], having restrained it, he establishes it firmly. With the *Śyaita*, he makes it white. With the words "The Gharma is the head," he establishes the Gārhapatya fire; thus he establishes it together with its head.

{1.1.8.4} The subsequent sacrifice inclines toward him. This Agni is indeed Rudra; when he is being established, he is capable of harming the cattle of the sacrificer. "May he be well-beloved by the cattle," he says; he thus makes him well-beloved by the cattle for the sake of non-injury to the cattle. "Grant protection to our children and offspring," he says; he thereby invokes this very blessing. "The wind is the breath," [he says] regarding the Anvāhāryapacana fire.

{1.1.8.5} He establishes it with breath. "Cook the food, savory for our children and descendants," he says; verily, he makes food savory for him. "Go forward, knowing, along the eastern quarter," he says; this is their differentiation, and thus he makes them of distinct power. "Bestow strength upon us, bipeds and quadrupeds," he says; verily, he invokes this blessing. "The Arka is the eye," he says regarding the Āhavanīya fire; the Arka is indeed the food of the gods.

He wins food itself. "Shine for me with that," he says; thus he kindles it. "Thou hast reached, thou hast pervaded," he says three times while tossing it upward. These worlds are three; he thus establishes it in these very worlds. That should not be done in such a way. He would establish what has been tossed and is thus unstable. Having lifted it up and established it, he should then recite the consecration formula. Thus he establishes it so that it is not tossed and is firmly established.

"Thou art the sovereign and the self-ruler; those auspicious bodies of thine, O Agni, with them I enkindle thee," he says. These indeed are the auspicious bodies of Agni; with these very ones he causes him to prosper. "Those terrible bodies of thine, O Agni, with them go to so-and-so," he should say of whomsoever he hates; with those very ones he causes him to perish.

Anuvāka 9: The Establishment of the Sacred Fires {1.1.9.1} He churns the fire from the heart of a *śamī* tree. This, indeed, is the sacrificial body of Agni; verily, he thus generates it for him. Aditi, desiring sons, cooked a *brahmaudana* (a porridge of sacred food) for the Sādhyas, the gods. They gave her the remnants. She ate it, and she conceived seed. Dhātṛ and Aryaman were born from her. She cooked a second [portion].

They gave her the remnants. She ate that; she conceived seed, and from her Mitra and Varuṇa were born. She cooked a third [cake]. They gave her the remnants. She ate that; she conceived seed, and from her Aṃśa and Bhaga were born. She cooked a fourth.

They gave her the remnants; she ate it, and she conceived seed. From that, Indra and Vivasvat were born. He cooks the *brahmaudana* (sacrificial rice for the Brahman); thus he deposits seed. The Brahmins eat the rice. With whatever clarified butter remains, he anoints the fuel-sticks and places them on the fire. Indeed, from the remnants Aditi conceived seed.

{1.1.9.4} From the very remains he deposits that seed. The fuel-sticks are indeed bone; the clarified butter is seed. When he places the fuel-sticks on the fire after anointing them with clarified butter, he thus places bone within the seed. He places three [fuel-sticks], for the sake of pairing. There are this many, being commensurate with Prajāpati, the mouth of the sacrifice.

There are this many; they are commensurate with the joints of the sacrifice. There are this many; for there is just this much vigor in a man; they are commensurate with vigor. They are moist; for semen is poured out as if it were moist. He establishes [the fires] from a variegated *aśvattha* tree; thus it becomes variegated. He establishes them with verses containing the word "ghee."

This, indeed, is the dear abode of Agni: namely, clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Verily, he causes him to prosper with his own dear abode; and also with splendor. For a Brāhmaṇa, one should place [the fire] with *gāyatrī* verses. The Brāhmaṇa has the *gāyatrī* as his meter; this is for the sake of restoring his own meter. For a Rājanya, one should place it with *triṣṭubh* verses. The Rājanya has the *triṣṭubh* as his meter; this is for the sake of restoring his own meter.

{1.1.9.7} For a Vaiśya, [the initiation is] with *jagatī* verses. The Vaiśya has the *jagatī* as his meter; this is for the sake of establishing him in his own meter. He should guard it for a year, for semen, once deposited, increases for a year. If it should not come to him within a year, he should add fuel again; thus the semen, being deposited, continues to increase. He should not eat meat; he should not approach a woman. (He should approach her.)

{1.1.9.8} If he were to eat meat or approach a woman, he would be deprived of virility; Agni would not come to him. On the day before he is to establish the fires, he cooks the *brahmaudana* (the Brahmin’s rice-mess). It was the Ādityas who first went from here to the heavenly world, and they indeed push back anyone departing from here. These Brahmins are truly those very Ādityas; through them alone he attains companionship.

They do not push him away. The exponents of the Veda say: "Where is that fire to be prepared which procreates offspring and cattle for him? He should kindle the fire with wood-shavings on that night. At the break of dawn, he should heat the two churning-sticks over it; it is just as when a cow in heat approaches a bull. Having removed the ashes, he churns the fire.

That indeed is the continuity of the fire. Having churned it, he draws it out toward the east. Thus, he causes that deposited seed to be born after a year. "His fire has not been established," they say, of one who establishes the fire without having first laid the kindling-sticks. He should lay those down a year beforehand; having thus secured him through the year, he establishes the fire. If he does not lay them down within a year—

One should install [the fires] twelve days before [the full moon]; for the twelve nights are indeed the image of the year; thus, the fires are truly installed for him throughout the year. If one should not install them on the twelfth day, one should install them three days before; they are indeed installed for him.

Anuvāka 10: The Establishment of the Fires {1.1.10.1} Prajāpati created living beings. He felt himself depleted. He performed austerity. He beheld vigor within himself. That grew; it was emitted from him upward by force. It became Virāj. The gods and the Asuras seized her. Prajāpati said: "She is mine indeed."

"O Dohās, yours alone [are they]," he said. Thereupon she stepped forth toward the east. Prajāpati grasped it: "O Atharvan, guard my food. She stepped forth a second time. Prajāpati grasped it: "O Narya, guard my offspring. She stepped forth a third time. Prajāpati grasped it: "O Śaṃsya, guard my cattle."

She stepped forth a fourth time. Prajāpati grasped it: "O wide-extending one, guard my assembly! She stepped forth a fifth time. Prajāpati grasped it: "O thou dwelling in the depths, guard my mantra! Indeed, she strode out those fires; Prajāpati grasped them, and thus the *paṅkti* itself. For this *paṅkti* has entered into the Brāhmaṇa.

He fashions that [fire-altar] from out of himself when the fire is established. Therefore, just so many fires are established. For all this is fivefold; verily by means of the fivefold he preserves the fivefold. "O Atharvan, protect my food," he says; verily by this he preserves food. "O Narya, protect my offspring," he says; verily by this he preserves offspring. "O Śaṃsya, protect my cattle," he says.

By this [rite], he wins cattle. "O wide-extending one, protect my assembly," he says; by this, he wins power (*indriya*) for the assembly. "O Ahi Budhnya, protect my counsel (*mantra*)," he says; by this, he wins glory (*śrī*) for the counsel. In that they cook the *anvāhārya* mess on the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, thereby that [fire] is gratified and pleased for him. In that they place the clarified butter (*ājya*) upon the *gārhapatya* fire and perform the sacrifice for the wives, thereby that [fire] is gratified and pleased for him.
In that they offer oblations in the *āhavanīya* fire...

By that, he is pleased and gratified with him when they are victorious in the assembly hall. By that, he is pleased and gratified with him when food is brought into the dwelling. By that, he is pleased and gratified with him. Thus, all of them, being pleased and gratified, are established for him. When about to go on a journey, one should worship each [deity] individually, just as one departs from home after entrusting it to a Brahmin residing there; such indeed is that. Having returned, one worships again.

That was indeed their misfortune. She ascended upwards from there; she became Rohiṇī. That is the reason for Rohiṇī’s name. One should install the sacred fire in Rohiṇī. He installs it in its own womb; he prospers by means of it.

Prapāṭhaka 2: The Remainder of the Gavāmayana; Anuvāka 1: The Remainder of the Gavāmayana {1.2.1.1} What is impure in her is being cleared away. May it strike away the evil of the sacrificer. May the four quarters be auspicious to us. May Mother Earth be propitious for the winning of offspring. May the divine Waters be for our aid. May they be for our drinking. May they flow toward us with health and well-being. They are the form of Vaiśvānara, flowing around upon the earth. May they enter into us with comfort.

{1.2.1.2} That which is here from heaven, that which is there from earth—the two worlds, being born together, came into being as one. May the red soil protect the black, and may the black protect the red. May you come most readily here to the sacrificial portion of both. When you moved across the earth performing your protections, having assumed the form of a mole and made yourself a burrow—that which was hidden of yours, we now gather here; may we live a hundred autumns with our heroes. Bringing hither the vigor of the earth and its essence, may we live a hundred wide-reaching autumns.

{1.2.1.3} Discovered by ants in their hiding places—may we, with your broad hearing, be free from deafness. For the offspring created by Prajāpati, may there be well-being for us against the onslaught of hunger. I bring forth food and vigor for the creatures; I bring broth for the houses and essence. Carrying this which he discovered while assuming its form—hidden within the midst of the flood—we shall worship it here without failure. May we perform our service toward it without mishap.

{1.2.1.4} That which he beheld in the midst of the body, that broad foundation of the world which he saw—he brings forth that leaf of the earth, the expansion [of the world], born indeed from the abode of the lotus. Those [waters] by which he made firm this broad foundation of the world, the sustainer of all people—may they all be auspicious pebbles for us. Golden, the seed of Agni, born from the waters, immortal among living beings—that, gathering together and placing to the north, [he sets down].

{1.2.1.5} By giving [this] away, may I cross over misfortune. When you, having assumed the form of a horse, stood upon the *aśvattha* tree, having hidden yourself from the gods for a year—that which was concealed in you, we now gather here. May we live a hundred autumns with our heroes. You have arisen from the strength of the earth; O Lord of the Forest, grow forth with a hundred branches. Rejoicing in food and strength through you, may we rejoice in the increase of wealth and in nourishment. That which belongs to you as you were being carried away by the *gāyatrī*...

A leaf fell from the third heaven; that is this very leaf, for it was born from the leaf of Soma. From that I take it, for the attainment of the drinking of Soma. That which you overheard when the gods were uttering the discourse of Brahman—you are indeed heard as Suśravas (the Well-Hearing). May spiritual luster enter me from that! Gathering it together, may I directly attain that. With that [leaf] by which Prajāpati quenched the flame of the Agni who had been created—[I take] this [leaf] for the sake of non-burning.

{1.2.1.7} I bring the *śamī* wood for the sake of peace. That splendor of yours which, when you were created and set forth, reached the *vikaṅkata* tree, O Jātavedas—measured by that splendor, shine forth after a wide world for us. That heart of yours, O Jātavedas, which they cut out while you were exhausted, having moistened it with water, O Maruts—I gather that together for you from the thunderbolt. Be here, O Agni, with your body whole and with your heart. These great [flames] have been gathered from the variegated *aśvattha* tree.

{1.2.1.8} You have been consecrated for the body; you are commensurate with Prajāpati, the mouth of the sacrifice. Three [of you] are tripartite, forming a pair for the sake of procreation. Born from the *aśvattha* tree that carries the oblation, I gather together the sacrificial body of Agni. [I gather] her whose womb is peaceful, who is the embryo of the *śamī* tree, for the sake of generating Agni. That *aśvattha* tree which has grown up together with the *śamī*—that I bring for you with a sacred prayer (*brahman*).

{1.2.1.9} Together with the sacrificial signs—O Jātavedas, you whom they gathered together, as you were latent within the beings according to their respective bodies—being thus assembled, sit down, auspicious to all creatures. As one who knows, lead us toward a wide world. To the wise seer, the holy one, the bull, the vigorous one, let there be speech that offers praise. May that from which fear arises become for us freedom from fear. I sacrifice to the gods who are to be appeased. Serve Agni with the fuel-stick.

{1.2.1.10} Awaken the guest with clarified butters; pour the oblations into him. O Agni, may the ladles dripping with clarified butter approach you, O beloved one. Accept my fuel-sticks. We strengthen you, O Aṅgiras, with fuel-sticks and clarified butter. Blaze forth mightily, O youngest one! Being kindled, you are the first sacred law (dharma). He who possesses all boons is anointed with unguents.

{1.2.1.11} Agni, whose hair is flame, whose cleansing is clarified butter, the purifier; he is the perfect sacrificer for the gods’ sacrifice. Agni has clarified butter as his womb; kindled with clarified butter, clarified butter is his food. Rivers carry you, dripping with clarified butter. Drinking the clarified butter, perform the sacrifice well for the gods. O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation, be one whose face is clarified butter and whose womb is clarified butter. Having drunk the clarified butter and the sweet, pleasant milk of the cow, protect this [sacrificer] as a father protects his son.

{ 1.2.1.12} O Agni, most youthful one, when you are kindled, the gods have made you their messenger, the bearer of oblations; you who possess wide-reaching paths, whose source is clarified butter, and who are invoked with offerings. They have established you as a brilliant eye among those who impel [the sacrifice]. O Agni, from of old, seeking favor, they have kindled you with excellent fuel when you are invoked with clarified butter. Increasing and nourished by the plants, you spread yourself across the wide expanses of the earth. With clarified butter as your face, seated at the pole of the cosmic order (*ṛta*), men strive toward Agni as they kindle him like a friend.

{1.2.1.13} Kindling you, O Agni, shining in the assemblies, may he raise up for us a prayer of brilliant color. O Agni, cause the progeny to dwell together; [cause] the quarters of space along with the cattle to dwell together. Bestow upon him the kingdoms that were in the impulsion of Savitṛ. The two great queens of the people at the seat of Order—come hither, you who are the support of riches. You two, pregnant with the kinsman, Jātavedas, bring forth as the leader of the sacrifices.

{1.2.1.14} Ascend, mount, my *śakvarī* verses! Through cosmic order (*ṛta*), O Agni, together with long life and splendor, may we live long through each succeeding year, so that I may perform the sacrifice at every new moon and full moon. You two are possessed of the seasons and have Agni as your seed; receive the embryo, for I bestow it upon you both. This is the truth: that you shall bear a hero, and you shall bring forth a hero. Through me, you two shall procreate in the morning; once procreated, you shall cause me to procreate.

{1.2.1.15} Through offspring, cattle, and spiritual luster, may I attain the heavenly world. From untruth I go to truth; from the human I go to the divine. I restrain my speech for the sake of the divine. Kindling the fire with wood-shavings, may I win both worlds. Having prospered in both worlds, may I cross beyond death. O Jātavedas, sprinkle here the seed of the universe—that which shall be born from austerity.

{ 1.2.1.16} Producing from the aśvattha tree Agni, the bearer of oblations, who was born from the womb of the śamī and is the source of bliss—this is your seasonal birthplace, from which, once born, you shone forth. Knowing this, O Agni, ascend it, and then increase our wealth. Depart, go away, and creep away from here—ye who are here, both those of old and those who are new. Yama has given this dwelling-place on earth; the ancestors have prepared this world for him.

{1.2.1.17} You are the ash of Agni; you are the soil of Agni. You are consciousness, the sustainer of desire. May your sustaining of desire be in me. I unite your hearts; may your minds be united; may your breaths be united. Those bodies of yours which are dear, may your dear hearts be united; may your self be dear to you, and may your dear bodies be mine.

May heaven and earth be favorable; may the waters and the plants be favorable; may the fires, being of one accord, be favorable separately for my preeminence. May those fires that are of one mind between heaven and earth, conforming to the two spring seasons, enter together as the gods enter Indra. By the vigor of heaven, by the greatness of earth.

{1.2.1.19} With the nourishment of the intermediate space, I establish [the fire] that possesses all cattle. Mortals have brought forth the immortal one—him who is unwearied, the crosser [of difficulties], whose jaws are firm. Let the ten sisters, the maidens moving together, take hold of him at birth as he becomes a man. By the breath of Prajāpati, I breathe upon you; by the nourishment of Pūṣan, for me, for long life lasting a hundred autumns. For a hundred autumns, for life and for luster.

For life and for merit. I am yours; you are mine. This [is our bond]. You are my source; I am your source. Being mine alone, O Agni, carry the oblations—O Jātavedas, the son who makes the world for his father. I place you, the immortal, in breath; the eater of food for the sake of food; the protector for the sake of protection. With a good household-fire, burning away enemies, bringing forth each dawn more auspicious than the last.

O Agni, driving away our rivals, bestow upon us abundance of wealth, food, and vigor. May these riches attend me; may I dwell here with these offspring. May the multiform Iḍā abide here; shine forth, O Jātavedas, in the midst of wealth. I lift you up for strength and power, for virility, for breath, and for splendor. You are the overcomer of rivals, the overcomer of Vṛtra. That majesty of yours which is among the gods and leads to heaven—[may it be ours].

{1.2.1.22} That Self of yours which has entered into the cattle, that nourishment of yours which has spread among men—with that [joy], O Agni, come to us with pleasure. From heaven, from earth, from the intermediate space, from the wind, from the cattle, and from the plants—wheresoever you have come into being, O Jātavedas—from there, O Agni, come to us with pleasure. Proceeding toward the eastern quarter, go forth as one who knows; O Agni, be here the foremost fire of Agni. Shining brightly, illumine all the quarters.

{1.2.1.23} Bestow strength upon us, both bipeds and quadrupeds. Agni has looked along the vanguard of the dawns; the first Jātavedas has looked along the days. He has looked along the many rays of the sun; he has stretched himself along heaven and earth. Step forth, for you are great! O possessor of the altar, [be] for the sake of men. Be watchful in the three worlds. That which is here from heaven and that which is there from earth—the two world-halves (rodasī), being in agreement, have come together.

{ 1.2.1.24} May Jātavedas sit upon the backs of those two, bringing welfare to offspring and being pleasant to the body. I place you, the breath, in the immortal; as an eater of food for the sake of food, as a protector for the sake of protection. O bright one, that which is your bright luster, your bright body, your bright, unceasing light—with that shine for me; with that I establish you. By Agni, O Agni, through the sacred word (brahman), I have attained; I have pervaded; I have pervaded a full lifespan.

O Narya, protect my offspring for the sake of immortality and life—those already born and those yet to be born, established in immortality and truth. O Atharvan, protect my food, the essence and the nourishment here for the sake of long life; O inviolable one, O you of cool body, make our food free from poison. O Praiseworthy One, protect my cattle, both those that are two-footed and those that are four-footed.

{1.2.1.26} And those here, O Agni, that have eight hooves, and those that have one hoof and move swiftly—protect my assembly, O wide-extending one! And those who are members of the assembly, the sitters in the hall—make them endowed with sensory power; let them attain a full lifespan. O Ahi Budhnya, protect my mantra, which the seers who know the three Vedas know: the Ṛg-verses, the Sāman-chants, and the Yajus-formulas; for that is the immortal glory of the virtuous.

{1.2.1.27} The young woman with four tufts of hair, well-formed, her face anointed with ghee, in the midst of the world—being cleansed for great good fortune, milk for me, for the sacrificer, all desires. Being right here, O Agnis, I sustain you who are there with breath, speech, and mind. May life not abandon me while I am hidden. I worship you with the Vaiśvānara light. Prajāpati’s Virāj stepped forth fivefold; the Rohiṇī rose upward, the womb and the foundation of Agni.

Anuvāka 2: Supplement to the Gavāmayana {1.2.2.1} These days are nine in number. There are indeed nine heavenly worlds. In that they undertake these days, the performers of the sacrificial session (*satrin*) proceed while firmly established in those very nine heavenly worlds. "The *agniṣṭoma* [sacrifices] should be performed as the *paraḥsāman* [days]," they say; "for the heavenly world is commensurate with the *agniṣṭoma*. There are twelve stotras of the *agniṣṭoma*, and twelve months are a year. Therefore, one should not heed that.
The *ukthya* sacrifices alone, characterized by the seventeen-fold chant (*saptadaśa*), should be performed as the *paraḥsāman* days.

The *ukthas* are indeed cattle; they serve for the acquisition of cattle. The *viśvajit* and *abhijit* are *agniṣṭomas*; the subsequent *paraḥsāman* days are *ukthyas* with seventeen-fold stomas. When these are chanted together, they amount to the *virāj*. Two verses remain over: by one the *go* is in excess, and by one the *āyus* is deficient. The world of heaven is indeed light; the *virāj* is nourishment.

{1.2.2.3} By means of that, they indeed conquer the world of heaven. That which is the *rāthaṃtara* [sāman] beyond [the others] should be performed on the first day; the *bṛhat* on the second; the *vairūpa* on the third; the *vairāja* on the fourth; the *śākvara* on the fifth; and the *raivata* on the sixth. They lead those [sāmans] away from the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]. These cups are drawn as a continuous succession.

{1.2.2.4} The *atigrāhya* cups are drawn during the *paraḥsāman* chants. By means of these, they extend these very worlds. These cups are drawn in pairs; the *atigrāhya* cups are drawn during the *paraḥsāman* chants. By means of them, the sacrificers obtain a mate. The *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant. The *bṛhat* is indeed the world of heaven. By the *bṛhat* itself, they go to the world of heaven. There is a *sāman* named *trayastriṃśin*; it occurs during the midday *pavamāna*.

There are indeed thirty-three deities; they thus win the deities themselves. Those who approach the year from here toward the future do not attain well-being for themselves. But those who approach it from there toward the present, they indeed attain well-being for themselves. It is in this way that they approach it from there toward the present. Prajāpati is indeed he who is Indra; that [sacrifice] leads him to the gods.

Anuvāka 3: Supplement to the Gavamayana [1.2.3.1] These cups are indeed a continuous succession: namely, the Paraḥsāman cups and the Viṣūvat day with its Divākīrtya chant. Just as there are two sides to a house, so there are two sides to the year. If these cups were not drawn, the two sides of the year would fall apart in opposite directions, and they would meet with ruin. Since these cups are drawn, it is as when one fastens the two sides of a house together toward the central beam.

{1.2.3.2} In this way, they extend the two wings of the year up to the Divākīrtya day; they do not come to ruin. There is a twenty-one-fold day; the cups are drawn with the Śukra cup first, for the sake of support and stability. On this day, an animal dedicated to Sūrya is sacrificed; a supplementary cup for Sūrya is drawn. They thus bring the day into harmony with its own form; moreover, this offering is brought as a tribute to the day itself. On this day, seven supplementary cups are drawn.

There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head; yonder sun is the head of creatures. Verily, he places the vital breaths in the head of creatures; therefore there are seven vital breaths in the head. Indra, having slain Vṛtra and defeated the Asuras, conquered these worlds. Of him, that world [the zenith] remained unconquered. Becoming Viśvakarman, he conquered it. In that the cup for Viśvakarman is drawn, [it is for the conquest of that world].

{1.2.3.4} For the conquest of the world of heaven. Indeed, those who draw the Vaiśvakarman cup fall away from this world. The Āditya cup is drawn on the following day; Aditi is indeed this earth. Thus they find firm support upon her. They are drawn alternately: by one, they proceed performing all ritual acts; by the other, they find support upon this earth. These two are drawn alternately during the latter half of the year. Both of them are drawn together at the Mahāvrata rite.
Having reached the very end of the sacrifice, they become firmly established in both worlds. The *uktha* becomes the *arkya*, for the attainment of food.

Anuvāka 4: The Remainder of the Gavamayana [1.2.4.1] This [sacrifice] consists of twenty-one [parts]. By means of this very twenty-one-fold [stoma], the gods caused Āditya to ascend from here to the highest world of heaven. Indeed, this [sacrifice] is twenty-one-fold from here. Of it, there are ten days below and ten above. This very [sacrifice] is established on both sides within the Virāj; for it is indeed established on both sides within the Virāj. Therefore, moving between these two worlds, it proceeds heating all the worlds of heaven.

{1.2.4.2} The gods were afraid that the sun, the world of heaven, would slip away beyond their reach. They made it firm with the meters for the sake of support. The gods were afraid that the sun, the world of heaven, would fall down from above. They raised it up with five rays. Therefore, on the twenty-first day, five *divākīrtya* hymns are performed; for the *divākīrtyas* are indeed the rays. Those which are in the *gāyatra* [meter] are placed in the *gāyatrī* verses of the two subsequent *pavamāna* chants.

The *mahādivākīrtya* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant of the Hotṛ; the *vikarṇa* is the *brahmasāman*; the *bhāsa* is the *agniṣṭoma*. Now, these are the *paras*. By means of the *paras*, the gods caused the Āditya to reach the heavenly world. Because they caused him to reach it (*apārayan*), that is the "parahood" of the *paras*. The *paras* cause him who knows this to reach [the goal]. Now, these are the *sparas*. By means of the *sparas*, the gods caused the Āditya to support himself in the heavenly world. Because they caused him to support himself (*aspārayan*), that is the "sparahood" of the *sparas*. The *sparas* cause him who knows this to support himself.

Anuvāka 5: Supplement to the Gavāmayana {1.2.5.1} Those for whom the year has not been completed when the Ekādaśinī is reached go to a lack of support. They sacrifice a dwarf animal dedicated to Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; they thus sacrifice the sacrifice itself for the sake of support. They sacrifice [an animal] dedicated to Indra and Agni. Indra and Agni are indeed among the gods those whose vigor is undiminished. Those two deities who are undiminished in vigor—those very ones they sacrifice to.

{1.2.5.2} They sacrifice a victim for the Viśve Devas; thus they win the deities themselves. They sacrifice a milch-cow to Heaven and Earth; thus they find firm support in Heaven and Earth. They sacrifice a calf to Vāyu; Vāyu himself wins the deities from their respective abodes for them. They sacrifice a barren ewe to Aditi; Aditi is indeed this earth; thus they find firm support in her. They sacrifice [a cow] to Mitra and Varuṇa.

{1.2.5.3} By means of Mitra alone they pacify the well-offered part of the sacrifice; by means of Varuṇa, the ill-offered part. They immolate a hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati at the Mahāvrata rite. An additional draught for Prajāpati is drawn. They thus bring the day into harmony with its proper form; moreover, this offering is presented as a tribute to the day itself. They immolate a victim for Agni for the sake of clear discernment. Indeed, during the preceding months, they have secured only goats; now, these bovine animals are immolated.

It is for the acquisition of both kinds of cattle. If they were to sacrifice an extra set of eleven animals, their enemy would be left over. If they were to combine the animals in pairs, they would make their own life-span shorter. Since these animals are sacrificed according to the Brāhmaṇa injunctions, the enemy is not left over, nor do they make their own life-span shorter.

Anuvāka 6: The Remainder of the Gavāmayana {1.2.6.1} Prajāpati, having created living beings, lay down exhausted. The gods, having gathered together the essence and the vital energy of all beings, healed him with it. Because [he] "turned back" (avavarti) as one who was great (mahān), that is the reason for the Mahāvrata’s name "Mahāvrata. Because it is a "great vow" (mahad vratam), that is the reason for the Mahāvrata’s name "Mahāvrata. Because it is "the vow of the great one" (mahato vratam), that is the reason for the Mahāvrata’s name "Mahāvrata. The Stoma consists of twenty-five parts.

The year consists of twenty-four half-months. Whatever was produced within this year became the twenty-fifth [stoma], the food. It is performed in the middle; for food, when eaten in the middle, satisfies. Thus, strength (*ūrj*) is placed in the very midst of creatures. Now, as to why it is performed at the end: therefore, at the end of the year, creatures flourish. It is performed at the end for the sake of procreation alone. The *trivṛt* becomes the head.

For the head is indeed threefold: hair, skin, and bone. They chant with [the verses] directed away; therefore it remains exactly the same. It does not become fat when [the body] becomes fat, nor does it become thin when [the body] becomes thin. One wing consists of fifteen [verses], the other of seventeen. Therefore birds turn toward one half [of their body]; for that [wing] is made heavier on one side.

The self consists of twenty-five parts; therefore, cattle are most excellent in their middle part. The tail consists of twenty-one parts. They chant in *dvipadā* verses for the sake of stability. They chant with everything together, for one who possesses a self is complete through his entire self. They fly up together; they leave one verse remaining for each, for the limbs are bound to the self. Indeed, not every man is complete by means of this alone.

Whatever body hair, teeth, or nails are trimmed away from here and there, they are thereby restored. There is a couch made of Udumbara wood; the Udumbara is indeed vigor and food. It serves for the attainment of vigor and the eating of food. He whose right to sit upon the couch has not been won should ascend the couch and chant the *udgītha*, thinking, "May I win my right to sit upon the couch among the gods. Thus he wins his right to sit upon the couch.

{1.2.6.6} He whose claim to the seat on the couch (*talpasadya*) has been won should mount the couch and chant the *udgītha*, saying: "May you not lose your right to the seat on the couch among the gods. Thus he does not lose his right to the seat on the couch. He recites the *śastra* on the swing (*pleṅkha*). The swing is indeed greatness; it is for the attainment of great food. The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. They contended for the sun. The gods won it.

A Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra strive together at the leather-worker's trade. The Brāhmaṇa is indeed the divine caste; the Śūdra is the demonic. One of them should say, "These have succeeded; these have brought about prosperity. The other should say, "These are makers of ruin; these have brought about misfortune. Whatever good deed they perform, whatever success they achieve—that one of them consecrates. Whatever evil deed they perform, whatever failure they suffer—that the other strikes away.
The Brāhmaṇa wins. They thus appropriate for themselves that very sun, the adversary.

Prapāṭhaka 3: Vājapeya; Anuvāka 1: Vājapeya {1.3.1.1} The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. As the gods were about to achieve victory, they deposited their radiant bodies within Agni and Soma, thinking, "This shall be ours if they should conquer us. Because of that, Agni and Soma departed. Having won the victory, the gods sought after Agni and Soma. They found Agni lying hidden in the seasons; with the case-endings (*vibhakti*), they recovered his radiant bodies.

{1.3.1.2} They found Soma; they slew him. According to his characteristic marks, they divided his body; those became the *grahas* (libation cups). That is why the *grahas* have their name. For one who knows thus, when the *grahas* are drawn, they are truly drawn for him. One should not perform anything that does not pertain to Agni at the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*). If one were to perform something that does not pertain to Agni at the re-establishment of the fires, it would be unsuccessful—that indeed would be [the case].

{1.3.1.3} This [portion] is indeed performed as not pertaining to Agni: namely, when one offers to the *samidhs*, to Tanūnapāt, to the *iḍas*, and to the *barhis*. Both *ājyabhāgas* (butter-portions) should belong to Agni. "They say that they do not become *ājyabhāgas*," because both belong to Agni and follow one after the other. The latter [of the two] should be for Agni Pavamāna. Insofar as it is for Pavamāna, by that it becomes an *ājyabhāga*; by that it becomes [connected with] Soma. The *puro'nuvākyā* of the *ājyabhāga* belonging to Agni is the verse containing the word *budhnavat*.

{1.3.1.4} It is just as when one awakens a sleeping person; such indeed is that [case]. The verses for the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings should be those dedicated to Agni. By this, everything becomes dedicated to Agni. "He approaches the radiant deity all at once," they say. "She is liable to burn him up," they say. He should reply, "No. For Agni is procreation; thus he approaches procreation itself. "The *yajus* formulas have been performed and the sacrificial materials gathered," they say.

"The materials are not to be collected; the *yajus* formula is not to be performed," so it is said. But indeed, the materials are to be collected and the *yajus* is to be performed, for the successful completion of the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*). Therefore, he proceeds with the formulas in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). For this re-establishment is, as it were, like one who is about to depart; just as one searches for something lost in a low voice.

{1.3.1.6} It is exactly like that. He offers the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation loudly, just as if one had found something lost and said, "Here it is! It is exactly like that. They say, "He approaches the radiant deity all at once; she is liable to burn him up. One should not approach it in that manner. One should employ the case-endings (*vibhakti*) only in the *prayāja* and *anūyāja* offerings. The two *ājyabhāga* offerings should remain as they were before. The same applies to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

"One approaches that which is like the Vaiśvānara [offering], yet more productive. Regarding this, they say: "This is indeed deficient; it is not performed as being dedicated to Agni. One should say: "No. He offers to Agni first among the *vibhaktis*, and to Agni last among the *patnīsaṃyājas*. Therefore it is dedicated to Agni; therefore it is performed in a complete and successful manner."

Anuvāka 2: The Vājapeya Sacrifice {1.3.2.1} The gods indeed brought forth the sacrifices according to their respective visions: one the Agniṣṭoma, another the Ukthya, and another the Atirātra. They all saw the Vājapeya together; yet they did not yield to one another, each saying, "I shall sacrifice with this. They said, "Let us run a race for it."

{1.3.2.2} They ran a race for it. Bṛhaspati won it. He sacrificed with it. He attained self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). Indra said to him, "Let me sacrifice with this. He sacrificed with it for Indra. He went to the forefront of the deities. He attained self-sovereignty. They stood firm for his preeminence.

He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Vājapeya, goes to self-sovereignty (*svārājya*); he attains the pre-eminence among his equals; they stand for his leadership. This sacrifice indeed belongs to both the Brāhmaṇa and the Rājanya. They call this very sacrifice the Vājapeya. For it is a seeker of strength (*vāja*); for by means of it the gods desired to obtain strength. Soma, indeed, is the Vājapeya. He who knows Soma as the Vājapeya—

Having drunk it, he himself becomes a *vājī* (a prize-winner); a *vājī* is born from him. The *Vājapeya* is indeed food; he who knows thus eats food, and an eater of food is born from him. The *Vājapeya* is indeed the *brahman*; he who knows thus eats food through the *brahman*, and a *brahman* is born from him.

{1.3.2.12} Speech indeed is the production of strength (*vāja*). He who knows thus performs his heroic power through speech; speech comes to him. He speaks speech that has drunk [the essence]. Prajāpati assigned the sacrifices to the gods; he kept the Vājapeya for himself. The gods said to him: "This indeed is the sacrifice, namely the Vājapeya."

"May this indeed be ours here," they said. To them he gave these *ujjiti* (verses of victory). These *ujjitayaḥ* are now explained for the sake of the completeness of the sacrifice and so that the deities may not be excluded from their share. The gods, indeed, struck away the impurity (*śamala*) of both the sacred formulation (*brahman*) and the food. That which was the impurity of the sacred formulation became the *gāthā* and the *nārāśaṃsī*; that which was the impurity of the food became *surā* (fermented liquor).

Therefore, one should not accept [gifts] from one who is singing or from one who is intoxicated; for were he to accept them, he would accept impurity. All speech is indeed mastered by him who performs the Vājapeya sacrifice: that which is on earth, that which is in Agni, that which is in the Rathantara; that which is in the intermediate space, that which is in Vāyu, that which is in the Vāmadevya; that which is in heaven, that which is in Āditya, that which is in the Bṛhat; that which is in the waters, that which is in the plants, and that which is in the trees. Therefore, the officiating priest of the Vājapeya is worthy of honor, for all speech has been mastered by him.

Anuvāka 3: The Vājapeya Sacrifice {1.3.3.1} The gods, indeed, could not win over that part of the sacrifice which they had not won by means of other cups (*graha*). They won it over by means of the *atigrāhya* cups; hence the name *atigrāhya* (exceeding-cups) for them. When the *atigrāhya* cups are drawn, whatever part of the sacrifice they had not won by means of other cups, that very part they win over by exceeding [the others]. Five are drawn; the sacrifice is fivefold. Having obtained the sacrifice in its entirety, he wins it.

{1.3.3.2} All [the cups] belong to Indra; thus, in a single way, they bestow sensory power upon the sacrificer. Seventeen cups for Prajāpati are drawn; Prajāpati is seventeenfold—for the attainment of Prajāpati. He draws [each cup] with a single verse; thus, in a single way, he bestows vigor upon the sacrificer. He draws both the Soma-cups and the Surā-cups; for Soma is indeed the supreme food of the gods.

{1.3.3.3} This belongs to human beings: that which is *surā* (fermented liquor). By means of the highest food, he secures for himself lower food. He draws the *soma*-cups. Soma is indeed the splendor of the *brahman*. By means of the splendor of the *brahman*, he places splendor in the sacrificer. He draws the *surā*-cups. *Surā* is indeed the impurity of food.

{1.3.3.4} By means of the very dross of food, he removes the dross from the sacrificer. He draws both the Soma-cups and the Surā-cups. Soma is indeed male; Surā is female. That is a pair. Thus he creates a pair for him at the sacrifice for the sake of procreation. By the Soma-cups, he wins over his own self; by the Surā-cups, his wife. Therefore, one who has performed the Vājapeya obtains a wife in that world, for he has conquered through the Vājapeya.

The Soma cups are drawn first; the Surā cups are drawn afterwards. He sets down the Soma cups to the east of the axle and the Surā cups to the west of the axle, for the sake of distinguishing between the superior and the inferior. The Soma is indeed the sacrificer, and the Surā is food. He interlinks the Soma cups and the Surā cups; verily, he interlinks him with food.

"You are mingled; mingle me with prosperity," he says. Prosperity, indeed, is food. Thus, he unites him with the eating of food. Now, surā is the impurity of food. Impurity, indeed, is evil. He thus intermingles him with evil, with impurity, when he intermingles the soma-cups and the surā-cups. "You are separated; separate me from evil," he says. Thus, he turns him away from evil, from impurity.

Therefore, one who has performed the Vājapeya sacrifice is purified, fit for sacrifice, and worthy of sacrificial gifts. He runs forward with the Soma-cups; by them he conquers that world (the heavenly world). He runs backward with the Surā-cups; by them he conquers this world (the earthly world). They stand firm with the Soma-cups; by means of truth alone he is consecrated. They carry the Surā-cups to the Vājasṛt priests; by means of untruth alone he unites the common people. He gives a golden vessel full of honey, thinking, "May I become worthy of honey."

He offers to Brahman in a single manner; thus, in one way, he bestows life-span and splendor upon the sacrificer. Anuvāka 4: The Vājapeya. The exponents of sacred knowledge say: "It is neither an Agniṣṭoma, nor an Ukthya, nor a Ṣoḍaśin, nor an Atirātra. Then why are all the sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) included within the Vājapeya? One should reply: "By means of the animal sacrifices. He immolates an animal for Agni; thereby he secures the Agniṣṭoma. With the animal for Indra and Agni, he secures the Ukthya. With the animal for Indra, the Ṣoḍaśin chant. With the animal for Sarasvatī, the Atirātra.

The chant for the Bṛhat [Sāman] dedicated to the Maruts: there are indeed as many forms of sacrifice as these; it is by means of the animal sacrifices that he wins them. He preserves his own self by means of the Agniṣṭoma; the out-breath and in-breath by means of the Ukthya; virility by means of the chant of the Ṣoḍaśin; speech by means of the Atirātra; and offspring by means of the chant of the Bṛhat. He conquers this very world by means of the Agniṣṭoma; the intermediate space by means of the Ukthya.

{1.3.4.3} By means of the *ṣoḍaśin* chant, he ascends to the heavenly world; by means of the *atirātra*, he ascends the very paths traveled by the gods. By means of the *bṛhat* chant, he ascends the firmament (*nāka*). He bestows brilliance upon himself with the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni; vigor and strength with that dedicated to Indra and Agni; sensory power with that dedicated to Indra; and speech with that dedicated to Sarasvatī. By means of the barren cow dedicated to the Maruts, he conquers both the world of the gods and the world of men. He immolates seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati; Prajāpati is seventeenfold.

{1.3.4.4} For the attainment of Prajāpati, there are black, uniform [animals]. For Prajāpati is indeed thus; it is for the sake of prosperity. Having carried fire around them, he releases them. The Maruts sought to destroy the sacrifice of Prajāpati; for them he offered this barren cow to the Maruts. By means of her, he pacified them. Having performed the rite with the offering to the Maruts, he should cause these [other animals] to be immolated. Thus, having pacified the Maruts themselves—

{1.3.4.5} He proceeds with these for the non-spoiling of the sacrifice. He offers the omentum all at once, for these [deities] have but a single deity; thus he places vigor in the sacrificer all at once. Now he proceeds with the *naivāra* (wild rice) offering in seventeen bowls; for these are indeed sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*). Moreover, he thereby closes up the breach in the cattle. He proceeds with the final offering to Sarasvatī; Sarasvatī is indeed speech. Therefore, among the vital breaths, speech is the last.
Thus, he establishes the sacrifice in Prajāpati himself; for Prajāpati is speech. She has no teeth; therefore, human beings speak all forms of speech.

Anuvāka 5: The Vājapeya Sacrifice {1.3.5.1} He offers an oblation to Savitṛ before each and every ritual act. "Who knows that? they say—"that which is prior to the Vājapeya and that which is subsequent to it. Thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he performs the rites in their proper order. He offers at each pressing (*savana*). Thereby the sacrificer constructs a bridge as a means of ascent for the attainment of the heavenly world. "May the Lord of Speech make our speech sweet today," he says. In ancient times, speech was indeed the food of the gods. Verily, he makes speech itself into food for him.

{1.3.5.2} With the words, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra," he brings down the chariot for the sake of victory. He says, "Now at the impulse of strength, the great mother... By this, he obtains both that which is on this earth and that which is upon it; moreover, he is consecrated in both of them. With the words, "In the waters is immortality, in the waters is healing," he washes the horses. Indeed, a third part of the horse has entered into the waters; by washing them in the waters, he causes that part to float up after him.

Whatever part of it has entered into the waters, that very part he secures. Indeed, a horse frequently comes into contact with what is impure; when he cleanses it in the waters, he makes it pure. "Vāyu has harnessed you, or Manu has harnessed you," he says. These deities indeed harnessed the horse in the beginning; by means of them, he harnesses it. This is for the sake of winning the sacrifice. He harnesses it with a *yajus* formula for the sake of distinction.

He cleanses [the chariot] with the words, "Apāṃnapāt, the swift-racer. Verily, he makes them pure; furthermore, he praises those who are about to run the race. He strides the Viṣṇu-steps; having become Viṣṇu himself, he conquers these worlds. The chariot belongs to the All-gods (Vaiśvadeva). He says, "The two hooks, the two side-hooks, on both sides of the chariot. Verily, he pays homage to those very deities who have entered into the chariot, for his own safety. The chariot of one who knows thus becomes one that never falters.

Anuvāka 6: The Vājapeya Sacrifice {1.3.6.1} "Under the impulse of the god Savitṛ, through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize, may I win the prize," he says. Thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he wins the prize through the sacred word (brahman). "Under the impulse of the god Savitṛ, through Bṛhaspati, the winner of the prize, may I ascend to the highest firmament (nāka)," he says. Thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he ascends to the highest firmament through the sacred word. He ascends onto a chariot wheel fixed in the Cātvāla pit.

From this, indeed, the Aṅgirasas went to the highest world; the sacrificer goes directly to the heavenly world. He encircles [the chariot]. The chariot is indeed a thunderbolt; by the thunderbolt itself he conquers the quarters.

{1.3.6.2} He sings the *vājina* chant. *Vāja* is indeed food; verily, he secures food for himself. The height of speech departed from the gods; it entered the trees. That same speech which is in the drum speaks among the trees. Therefore, the drum speaks beyond all other voices. They beat the drums; for this is the highest speech.

{1.3.6.3} That [sound] which is in the drum—by means of the highest speech, he wins the lower speech. Moreover, the sacrificer wins the very height of speech. "Speak speech for Indra! Make Indra win the prize! Indra has won the prize! so he says. For he who sacrifices is indeed Indra at this time. It is the sacrificer himself who wins the prize. Seventeen archers run the race. There is a seventeen-fold hymn of praise (*stotra*). Seventeen [gifts] are given each time.

Prajāpati is seventeenfold; [it serves] for the attainment of Prajāpati. "Thou art a courser, thou art a steed, thou art a racer," he says. Agni indeed is the courser, Vāyu is the steed, and Āditya is the racer. By means of these very deities, he yokes the divine chariot for him. He yokes one that is drawn by side-horses; for the divine chariot is indeed drawn by side-horses. Verily, he yokes the divine chariot for him.

"O prize-winners, run for the prize; go to the goal! he says. The world of heaven is indeed the goal; thus they go to the world of heaven. For those who run the race, they indeed go to the world of heaven. They run facing eastward, for the world of heaven is, as it were, in the eastern direction. He consecrates them with four verses. There are four meters; by means of the meters, he causes them to go to the world of heaven.

{1.3.6.6} Verily, those who run the race fall away from this world; they turn back toward the north. By that very act, they lead them from this world. He offers the oblation for unyoking the chariot for the sake of stability. "May the impulse of strength come to me," he says. Strength (*vāja*) is indeed food; verily, he secures food for himself. Those who run the race win according to their respective worlds.

He gives a *kṛṣṇala* seed to each of the *vājasṛt* priests. Whatever strength and world they win, that he purchases and secures for himself. He presents [the offering] all at once to the Brahman priest; thus he bestows vigor upon the sacrificer in a single mass. The gods indeed ran a race for the plants; Bṛhaspati won them. He chose the wild rice (*nīvāra*) as his prize; that is why wild rice is called *nīvāra*. There is a sacrificial pap made of wild rice.

This, indeed, is the supreme food of the gods: namely, wild rice (*nīvāra*). By means of this supreme food, he secures for himself inferior food. It consists of seventeen bowls; Prajāpati is seventeenfold, for the attainment of Prajāpati. It is prepared with milk; he thereby bestows radiance upon him. It is mixed with clarified butter for the sake of purity. This [oblation] has Bṛhaspati as its deity.

{1.3.6.9} He who sacrifices with the Vājapeya: this is a *caru* offering for Bṛhaspati. He causes the horses that are about to run and those that have already run to smell it. Whatever strength (*vāja*) and world they win, that very thing he secures for himself. With the words, "O trees, you have caused Indra to win; be unyoked," he unyokes the drums. Whatever strength, world, and power (*indriya*) those drums win, that very thing he secures for himself.

Anuvāka 7: The Vājapeya Sacrifice {1.3.7.1} He causes the sacrificer to put on a garment of *tārpya* silk. The *tārpya* is indeed the sacrifice; verily, by means of the sacrifice, he causes him to prosper. He causes him to put on one made of *darbha* grass. *Darbha* grasses are indeed a means of purification; verily, he purifies him. He who sacrifices with the Vājapeya seeks to win strength (*vāja*).
