Plants, indeed, are strength. In that he causes him to put on one made of *darbha*, [he wins it].

{1.3.7.2} For the attainment of strength. "O wife, come; let us two ascend to heaven," he says. This is the taking hold of the sacrifice by the wife for the sake of non-interruption. The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is seventeen *aratnis* in height. Prajāpati is seventeenfold; it is for the attainment of Prajāpati. It is hornless and four-cornered. The top-ring (*caṣāla*) is made of wheat. These are neither rice nor barley; they are wheat.

For in this very way Prajāpati [acted] for prosperity; moreover, he makes that world full of food for him. He wraps it with garments. The sacrificial post is indeed the sacrificer. The garment belongs to all the deities. Verily, he causes him to prosper through all the deities. Moreover, the sacrificer thereby constructs a bridge as a means of ascent for the attainment of the heavenly world. He offers twelve Vājaprasavīya oblations.

Twelve months are a year; verily he gratifies the year. Moreover, he places the year itself upon him for the attainment of the heavenly world. He ascends by means of ten ritual arrangements (*kalpa*). There are indeed nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, with the navel as the tenth. Having thus arranged the vital breaths according to their proper places, he goes to the heavenly world. So much, indeed, is the property of a person.

{1.3.7.5} As long as his vital breaths last, and for as much as he possesses, with that he goes to the heavenly world. "We have gone to the light of heaven," he says; thus he indeed goes to the heavenly world. "We have become immortal," he says; for the heavenly world is, as it were, immortality. "We have become the offspring of Prajāpati," he says; for this world belongs to Prajāpati. By this [formula], he does not depart from this very world.

"May I be united with offspring; may offspring be united with me," he says. Thus he invokes this very blessing. They strike [the ground] with handfuls of earth. This [earth] is indeed food; verily, they endow him with the eating of food. They strike it with saline soil. For saline soil is food manifest; verily, they endow him directly with the eating of food. They strike it from the east toward the west.

For food is eaten from the front toward the back; they strike it at the head, for food is eaten from the head. They strike it from all directions; verily, they secure food for him from every direction. He who climbs the sacrificial post is liable to burn away from this world. He descends upon gold; gold is indeed immortality, and the heavenly world is immortality. Verily, he finds firm support in the immortal heavenly world. It is one hundred mānas in weight.

A man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers; he thus becomes firmly established in life-span and power. The goat is indeed the form of nourishment (*puṣṭi*); for three times a year it brings forth offspring other than itself. He descends onto the skin of a ram; he thus becomes firmly established in nourishment and procreation.

Anuvāka 8: The Vājapeya Sacrifice {1.3.8.1} He offers seven oblations of food. There are indeed seven kinds of food; as many kinds of food as there are, those very ones he secures. There are seven cultivated plants and seven wild plants; it is for the securing of both types. He offers of each kind of food, for the securing of each kind of food. If one who has performed the Vājapeya sacrifice were to eat anything not secured [by the ritual], [it would be improper].

{1.3.8.2} One would be deprived of what has been acquired. He offers after taking portions from everything, for the sake of acquiring what has not yet been acquired. He offers with a ladle made of *udumbara* wood; the *udumbara* is indeed strength and food—for the sake of acquiring strength and food. He says, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ"; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he consecrates him with the sacred word (*brahman*) and with the deities. He consecrates him with every kind of food—for the sake of acquiring every kind of food.

He sprinkles him from the front, facing westward; for food is eaten from the front, facing westward. He sprinkles him from the head; for food is eaten from the head. He lets it flow down as far as the mouth; thus he bestows upon him the enjoyment of food from the very mouth. "With the sovereignty of Agni, I sprinkle thee," he says; this indeed is the impulse of Agni; with that very impulse he sprinkles him. "With the sovereignty of Indra, I sprinkle thee," he says.

{1.3.8.4} By this [rite], he bestows sensory power (*indriya*) upon him. "With the sovereignty of Bṛhaspati, I consecrate you," he says. Bṛhaspati is indeed the sacred formulation (*brahman*) of the gods; with the sacred formulation itself, he consecrates him. They present the Soma-cups and the portions to be cut off to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); by these, he makes that world possessed of food. They present the Surā-cups and the portions not to be cut off to the Vājasṛts; by these, he makes this world possessed of food. Thus, he is consecrated in both worlds. The Vājasṛts engage in a contest for victory.

{1.3.8.52} For the sake of securing the senses, they chant at the morning pressing with verses that are undefined (*anirukta*). Prajāpati is undefined; [this serves] for the attainment of Prajāpati. At the midday pressing, they chant with verses containing the word *vāja*. *Vāja* is indeed food; verily, he secures food. At the third pressing, they chant with verses containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*. Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; *śipi* is cattle. Verily, he establishes himself in the sacrifice and in cattle. The *Bṛhat* [Sāman] is the final one; verily, he leads him to the end for the sake of glory.

Anuvāka 9: The Vājapeya Sacrifice {1.3.9.1} "Seated among men (nṛṣadam) thee," he says. Men are indeed offspring; verily, by this he is consecrated for offspring. "Seated in wood (druṣadam)" he says. Trees are indeed wood; verily, by this he is consecrated for trees. "Seated in the world (bhuvanasadam)" he says. When one becomes more prosperous, they say of him, "He has gone to the world (bhuvanam agan). Verily, by this he goes to the world.

"Seated in the waters, seated in the clarified butter," he says; by this, he is consecrated for the waters and the clarified butter. "Seated in the sky," he says; when one indeed becomes more prosperous, they say of him, "He has gone to the sky"; by this, he goes to the sky itself. "Seated on the earth, seated in the intermediate space," he says; by this, he is consecrated for these very worlds. Therefore, the sacrificer of the Vājapeya does not descend to anyone else, for he is as if consecrated among the deities themselves.

"He sits upon the firmament," he says; for when one becomes more prosperous, they say of him, "He has gone to the firmament. By this, he indeed goes to the firmament. "The cups belonging to the five peoples," he says; by this, he is consecrated for the sake of the five peoples. "The essence of the waters, the vigor of the plants," he says; by this, he is consecrated for the sake of the essence of the waters. "The ray of the sun, brought together," he says, for the sake of its brilliance.

Anuvāka 10: The Vājapeya Sacrifice {1.3.10.1} Indra, having slain Vṛtra and defeated the Asuras, returned on the day of the new moon (Amāvāsyā). The ancestors (Pitṛs) arrived on the previous day. The sacrifice went to the ancestors. The gods asked for it back; they did not give it back to them. They said, "Let us choose a boon; then we shall give it back to you. Let the sacrifice be performed for us alone on the previous day."

They gave him back to them. Therefore, the rite for the ancestors is performed on the previous day. In that he performs [the rite] for the ancestors on the previous day, the sacrificer, having redeemed the sacrifice from the ancestors, extends it. He says, "Svadhā! Adoration to Soma, drunk by the ancestors! Thus, he secures for himself the drinking of Soma from his father; for a father who is dying does not say, "This is the drinking of Soma. The drinking of Soma is indeed vital power (*indriya*); thus he secures for himself the drinking of Soma as vital power. By that vital power, he obtains a second wife.

{1.3.10.3} Indeed, the Vājaśravasas of old knew this *brāhmaṇa* passage; therefore, they each obtained two wives. He who knows thus obtains a second wife. "To Agni Kavyavāhana, *svadhā*, homage! he says. He thereby gratifies that Agni who belongs to the ancestors. He offers three oblations; he deposits [the remains] three times; thus they amount to six.

There are six seasons; he thus gratifies the seasons. He places the stirring-stick silently, for there either is or is not a sixth season. When the gods and the ancestors have been gratified, human ancestors follow after them. He offers three oblations and deposits [the remains] three times; they amount to six. There are indeed six seasons.

The seasons are indeed the divine ancestors. He thus gratifies the seasons, the divine ancestors. When they are gratified, the human ancestors follow after them in being satisfied. The sacrificial grass (barhis) is cut in a single stroke; for the ancestors are, as it were, singular. He places [the offerings] three times; for the ancestors are in the third world from here. He thus gratifies them. He turns away his face.

The ancestors are indeed bashful; he waits until the heat has subsided. For the ancestors partake of the heat. The exponents of sacred knowledge say: "Should one eat, or should one not eat? If he were to eat, he would be eating food belonging to others and would be liable to die prematurely. If he were not to eat, it would not be an offering.

He would be cut off from the ancestors. It should indeed be smelled; it is neither eaten nor uneaten. For when the ancestors depart, they take away a hero, or they bestow a hero. He cuts the fringe [of his garment], for the ancestors have a share in the taking away. Thus he satisfies the ancestors. He should cut his hair in the latter part of life, for at that time he is closer to the ancestors.

He pays homage; for homage belongs to the ancestors. "Homage to you, O ancestors, for your essence! Homage to you, O ancestors, for your vigor! Homage to you, O ancestors, for your life-force! Homage to you, O ancestors, for your *svadhā*! Homage to you, O ancestors, for your wrath! Homage to you, O ancestors, for your terrible power! O ancestors, homage to you who abide in this world!"

"May those who are in this world follow you; may those who are in this world follow me. May you be the most excellent among them who are in this world; may I be the most excellent among them who are in this world," he says. He becomes the most excellent among his equals, who, knowing thus, performs [the rite] for the ancestors. This indeed is the sacrifice of human beings.

The other sacrifices belong to the gods; therefore, he who performs [rites] for the ancestors moves about in the world of the fathers. He is liable to perish. By means of a verse addressed to Prajāpati, he returns again. Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice; thus he returns together with the sacrifice itself. He does not become subject to death. When he performs [rites] for the ancestors, the sacrificer moves about in the world of the fathers; he is liable to meet with misfortune.
"Prajāpati alone is able to lead you up from there," they say; because he returns with a verse addressed to Prajāpati, Prajāpati himself leads him up from there. The sacrificer does not come to ruin.

Chapter 4, Section 1: The Cups (Grahas) Both these, the gods and the asuras, were created from Prajāpati. He did not distinguish between them, [thinking], "These are one group, those are another. He made stalks for the gods; he pressed them, purified them with a strainer, and drew them out on the far side of the strainer. They became the cups (*grahas*). That is the reason for the name of the cups.

{1.4.1.2} These cups (grahas) that are drawn in the house of the sacrificer are indeed deities. The gods know him for whom these cups are drawn while he possesses such knowledge. This Upāṃśu cup is indeed an oblation to Soma. "I shall satisfy the gods with Soma"—with this very thought one sacrifices with Soma when he offers the Upāṃśu; by means of Soma itself he thus satisfies the gods. And when he offers the other cups (grahas), [he satisfies them likewise].

{1.4.1.3} The gods themselves go to the gods when he offers from the cups; by that very correspondence, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world. They say: "What was this in the beginning?"—"The vessels," they say. This earth, indeed, was this in the beginning; these [vessels] were made of clay. By means of them, the gods did not attain distinction. They saw these wooden vessels; they made them.

{1.4.1.4} By means of those [vessels], they indeed attained distinction. In that the vessels are made of wood, the sacrificer attains distinction by means of them. Those which are made of wood—by means of them he conquers yonder world. Those which are made of clay—by means of them he conquers this world. The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "Which are the four bowls for Vāyu, the Soma-drawing vessels? The gods, indeed, milked the speckled cow (*pṛśni*).

These were her udders. This earth, indeed, is *pṛśni*. Into her, the Ādityas milked four-footed cattle by means of the *ādityasthālī* (the Āditya-vessel). In that there is an *ādityasthālī*, the sacrificer thereby milks these four-footed cattle from this [earth]. Into her, Indra milked vital power (*indriya*) by means of the *ukthyasthālī*. In that there is an *ukthyasthālī*, the sacrificer thereby milks vital power from this [earth]. Into her, the Viśve Devas milked vigor (*ūrj*) by means of the *āgrayaṇasthālī*. In that there is an *āgrayaṇasthālī*, [the sacrificer thereby milks vigor from this earth].

{1.4.1.6} By means of that [vessel], the sacrificer milks this [earth] for vigor (*ūrj*). Men milked longevity (*āyus*) from that [earth] by means of the *dhruva* vessel. In that there is a *dhruva* vessel, the sacrificer thereby milks this [earth] for longevity. He takes [the portion] with a vessel; he offers it with a *vāyavya* cup. Therefore, people milk cattle with one vessel and receive [the milk] with another. Thus, the sacrificer attains distinction.

Anuvāka 2: Mantras Remaining from the Sautrāmaṇī Sacrifice {1.4.2.1} O Aśvins, you two, together with Namuci the Asura, drinking the *surā* liquor, O lords of splendor, have aided Indra in his deeds. Like parents aiding their son, both Aśvins, O Indra, have aided you through your deed with wondrous powers. When you drank the *surā* liquor with your mighty acts, O Maghavan, Sarasvatī attended upon you constantly. O Agni, the oblation has been poured into your mouth like clarified butter into a ladle, like Soma into the sacrificial cup.

Bestow upon us wealth that wins the prize, rich in heroes, praiseworthy, glorious, and vast—that wealth in which horses, bulls, oxen, barren cows, and rams are released and offered as oblations. O Knower, who drinks the sweet juice and whose back is sprinkled with Soma, generate a lovely hymn from your heart for Agni. For your two seats, ordained by the gods, are measured out separately; do not come into contact with one another in the highest heaven. You are the spirited Surā, and this is Soma; do not harm me as you enter your own womb.

{1.4.2.3} What remains here of the pressed juice, what Indra drank with his powers—that I consume here as King Soma, with a gracious mind. I have heard of two paths of the fathers: one of the gods and one of mortals. By these two, this entire world comes together, between the former and the latter signpost. O God Varuṇa, that bond of yours which is in the *gāyatrī* meter—that I release for you with this [offering].

{1.4.2.4} O God Varuṇa, that bond of yours which has the *triṣṭubh* as its meter—by this [offering], I release it from you. O God Varuṇa, that bond of yours which has the *jagatī* as its meter—by this [offering], I release it from you. Soma indeed seizes the sovereignty of him who, being a king or one entitled to kingship, sacrifices with Soma. These oblations belong to the *devasū*. So many indeed are the consecrations (*sava*) of the gods; they themselves bestow those consecrations upon him. They consecrate him again for sovereignty. Thus, through the *devasū*, he becomes a king.

Anuvāka 3: Expiation concerning the milking for the Agnihotra {1.4.3.1} "Up has risen the goddess Aditi, she of all forms; she has bestowed long life upon the lord of the sacrifice, preparing a portion for Indra, for Mitra, and for Varuṇa. This Agnihotra-cow is indeed this [earth]. She sits down for him whose Agnihotra-cow sits down. One should make her rise with the verse: "Up has risen the goddess Aditi. This earth, indeed, is the goddess Aditi.

{1.4.3.2} He raises this very cow for him. "He has placed life in the lord of the sacrifice," he says; verily, he bestows life upon him. "Making a portion for Indra, and for Mitra and Varuṇa," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula itself. Indeed, she sits down having perceived misfortune and the evil of that man whose *agnihotra* cow, when let loose, sits down. Having milked her, he should give her to a Brahmin, or to one who would not eat his food. Thus he releases misfortune and evil upon him.

Having milked, he gives [the gift]. For a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is not given that has not been seen [to be produced]. Indeed, the milk of one whose *agnihotra* spills while being milked enters the earth. He says: "That milk which today has clung to the earth, which has flowed into the plants, and which has entered the waters—may there be milk in my houses, milk in the cows, milk in the calves; may there be that milk in me! Thus he places the milk within himself, in his house, and among his cattle. He pours water [into the vessel].

{1.4.3.4} By means of water alone he recovers it. For whoever mixes that which is unimpaired with that which is impaired in the sacrifice—both of them then become impaired. Indeed, this Agnihotra becomes impaired when, while being milked, it spills. If one were to milk over it again, he would mix the unimpaired part of the sacrifice with the impaired. Therefore, however it may be, it must be offered as it is. Then, having milked another cow, it should be offered again; thus, by means of the unimpaired, he repairs the impaired part of the sacrifice.

{1.4.3.15} If [the oblation] should spill while being carried forward, were he to go back again without having offered it from that point, he would cut the sacrifice asunder. Wherever it spills, sitting down there, he should take it up again. Right where it spills, from that very spot he takes it up again. It should be offered exactly as it was, however it may have been; then, having milked another cow, he should offer again. By means of the uninjured, he repairs the injured part of the sacrifice.

{1.4.3.6} The sacrifice of one whose dog runs between while the *agnihotra* oblation is placed on the fire is indeed torn asunder. This Agni is indeed Rudra. If he were to turn back toward the cow, he would deliver the cattle over to Rudra, and the sacrificer would become destitute of cattle. If he were to sprinkle water [toward it], the water is the food of Agni; he would thus deliver what is not fit for food to both of them. Therefore, having taken ashes from the *gārhapatya* fire...

With the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, "Viṣṇu strode through this," he should run out from the Āhavanīya fire while scattering [the ashes]. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus, by means of the sacrifice itself, he continues the sacrifice. He scatters ashes over the footprint for the sake of pacification.

Anuvāka 4: Expiation concerning the fire in the Agnihotra {1.4.4.1} The Āhavanīya fire indeed desires to swallow the Gārhapatya, and the Gārhapatya desires to swallow the Āhavanīya, for him whose fire the sun sets upon while it has not yet been carried forth. He should carry gold tied with a blade of Darbha grass in front; then the fire; then the Agnihotra offering. In that he carries the gold in front—the gold is indeed light; verily, seeing the light, he carries the fire forth. In that he carries the fire first and then the Agnihotra offering...

{1.4.4.2} He leads him forward with his own share. A Brāhmaṇa of Ṛṣi lineage should lift him up. The Brāhmaṇa indeed is all the deities; verily he lifts him up with all the deities. Having set down the Agnihotra, he should remain seated until the sun sets. He truly dies following the vow that has been violated. He reaches the end of himself who faints. He reaches the end of the sacrifice for whom the sun sets while the fire has not yet been lifted up.

{1.4.4.3} Again he offers with the *samanya* verse. By means of the end, he indeed recovers the end of the sacrifice. Varuna seizes the sacrifice of him whose fire is not yet carried forward when the sun sets upon it. He should offer a *caru* oblation to Varuna; by that very act, he ransoms the sacrifice. Indeed, the *āhavanīya* fire desires to go down into the *gārhapatya*, and the *gārhapatya* desires to go down into the *āhavanīya*, of him whose fire is not yet carried forward when the sun rises upon it. He should carry forth four ladlings of clarified butter first.

{1.4.4.4} Now as for the fire, and then the *agnihotra*: when he brings the clarified butter (*ājya*) first, this indeed is the beloved abode of Agni; that which is the clarified butter—verily, he causes him to prosper with his own beloved abode. When he carries the fire forward first and then the *agnihotra*, he leads it forth with its own share. A Brahmin of noble lineage (*ārṣeya*) should carry it forward; for the Brahmin is indeed all the deities.

{1.4.4.5} He raises him up by means of all the deities indeed. For him whose fire has not been raised when the sun rises over it, the dawn dawns away from him, as it were, turning its back. "May Dawn with her banner rejoice in the sacrifice invited by the gods; to the gods, the most honey-sweet, Svāhā!"—sitting facing west, he should offer with clarified butter. Thus he causes the dawn to shine toward him. Having set down the Agnihotra oblation, he should remain seated until the breath ceases. He dies following his violated vow; he reaches the very end of himself.

{1.4.4.6} He who suffers [from this] reaches the end of the sacrifice. If the sun rises while his *āhavanīya* fire has not yet been carried forward, he should kindle it again and offer the oblation; by means of the very end, he repairs the end of the sacrifice. Mitra indeed seizes the sacrifice of him whose *āhavanīya* fire has not been carried forward when the sun rises. He should offer a *caru* of rice for Mitra; by that very act, he redeems the sacrifice. If the *gārhapatya* fire should go out while the *āhavanīya* has not yet gone out...

If one were to churn the *gārhapatya* fire without having extinguished the *āhavanīya*, he would cause a break in the ritual continuity and produce a rival for himself. Whatever in the sacrifice is performed in a domestic or worldly manner, Rudra follows after it. If he were to settle [the new fire] before [extinguishing the old], he would be worshipping a worldly fire; Rudra would be likely to destroy his cattle. Therefore, having extinguished the *āhavanīya*, he should churn the *gārhapatya*.

{1.4.4.8} "From here Agni was first born, Jātavedas from his own womb; may he, knowing [the way], carry the oblation to the gods by means of the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī. Verily, by means of the meters he causes him to be born from his own womb. He churns the Gārhapatya fire. Indeed, cattle attend upon the one who has established the Gārhapatya fire. When that fire goes out, the cattle depart after it. "Rejoice for the sake of food and wealth! [he says].

"For power, for glory, for nourishment, for lordship," he says. Wealth, indeed, is cattle; verily, he causes cattle to rest for him. "May the two springs of Sarasvatī enkindle thee," he says. The *ṛc* and the *sāman* are indeed the two springs of Sarasvatī; verily, by means of the *ṛc* and the *sāman*, he enkindles him. "Thou art the sovereign (*samrāj*), thou art the far-shining (*virāj*)," he says. The *rathantara* is indeed the sovereign; the *bṛhat* is the far-shining.

{1.4.4.10} With those two very [fires] he kindles him. The wheel is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*). The thunderbolt cuts off the sacrifice of one whose cart or chariot passes between the two fires. Having extinguished the Āhavanīya fire, he should draw it out from the Gārhapatya with [the verse]: "O Agni, that place which was formerly established for you has extended along the rays of the sun; bring this back to us, abiding in wealth; unite us with a favor that brings strength."

{1.4.4.9} By means of this very sacrifice, he continues the sacrifice from the preceding one. "Thou, O Agni, art far-extending," he says; Agni is all the deities. Thus, by means of the deities, he continues the sacrifice. He should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt (the path-maker). Verily, he has recourse to Agni Pathikṛt with his own share. He leads him along the path that is fit for sacrifice. An ox is the sacrificial fee; for it is a carrier, and [this serves] for prosperity.

Anuvāka 5: Expiation for the Excess of Soma {1.4.5.1} If at the morning pressing the soma is left over, being left over while desiring the midday pressing, they perform the rite with the *dhayadvatī* verses, beginning with "The cow yields milk for the Maruts. Indeed, that which is studied out of its proper sequence destroys; and this [excess] is indeed like a joint (*sandhi*). When there is an excess of the pressing, they perform the rite with the *dhayadvatī* verses for the pacification of the joint.
The *gāyatra* chant is used and the fifteenfold hymn-form (*pañcadaśa-stoma*) is employed; by means of these, they do not depart from the morning pressing.

They perform [the rites] with the *marutvatīya* verses; thus they do not depart from the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*). They fill the cups following that of the Hotṛ. The Hotṛ recites the *anuśaṃsa*. He thereby restores the sacrifice from its very center. For him whose Soma is left over at the midday pressing, it is left over as he desires the third pressing for the Ādityas. The *gaurīvita* Sāman is used; the *gaurīvita* is indeed redundant. That which is redundant in the pressing is what is left over.

{1.4.5.2} For the pacification of what is excessive, they perform [the rite] with the verse, "O Sūrya, you are truly great. Whatever desire for the *āditya* pressing was exceeded, by that very desire they bring it to fulfillment. The *gaurivīta* *sāman* is used; by means of it, they do not depart from the midday pressing. The *stoma* is the seventeenfold (*saptadaśa*); by means of it, they do not depart from the third pressing. They fill the cups following the cup of the *hotṛ*; the *hotṛ* recites the *anuśaṃsa*.

{1.4.5.4} He thus restores the sacrifice from its very center. If at the third pressing the Soma should be left over, he should perform an Ukthya. If at the Ukthya it should be left over, he should perform an Atirātra. If at the Atirātra it should be left over—that indeed is difficult to discern. For the cattle are about to overcome the sacrificer. The Bṛhat-sāman is used; for the Bṛhat indeed supported these worlds, and cattle are related to the Bṛhat. By means of the Bṛhat, he thus supports cattle for him.

They perform [the rites] with verses containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*; for Śipiviṣṭa is indeed the prosperity of the gods; verily, they cause him to prosper through prosperity. They fill the cups following the cup of the Hotṛ; the Hotṛ recites the *anuśaṃsa*; thus he establishes the sacrifice from its very center.

Anuvāka 6: A specific type of many Soma sacrifices performed in a single village. {1.4.6.1} In every community, there is indeed an Indra. Two who press [Soma] together press toward that same one Indra. This sacrifice is indeed extended as Prajāpati; its pressing-stones are its teeth. Of these two who press together, they crush one or the other. "The deities approach from the front," they say; for he who approaches first becomes superior.
There are as many *ājya* offerings as there are [verses], for the sake of victory.

{1.4.6.2} The opening verses (*pratipad*) contain the word "Maruts. The Maruts are indeed the unconquered abode of the gods; he thus strives in the very unconquered abode of the gods. Both the *Bṛhat* and the *Rathaṃtara* Sāmans are employed. This [earth] is indeed the *Rathaṃtara*, and yonder [sky] is the *Bṛhat*. By means of these two, he passes between them: between speech and mind, between out-breath and in-breath, and between heaven and earth.

{ 1.4.6.3} From all wealth that is to be known, the *abhivarta* becomes the *brahmasāman*, for the purpose of ascending to the world of heaven. The *abhijit* occurs, for the purpose of conquering the world of heaven. The *viśvajit* occurs, for the conquest of all. Regarding this they say: "He whose sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) are more numerous appropriates the deities. If the *agniṣṭoma* soma sacrifice should follow after [these].

{1.4.6.4} He should perform the Ukthya sacrifice if it is an Ukthya. He should perform the Atirātra sacrifice; for by means of the sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*), he appropriates the deity of his rival. Whoever overcomes [the opponent] by means of the meters (*chandas*) overcomes him who is pressing the Soma together. "For the settling, for the reclining," he says; for the settling and the reclining are indeed the meters. By means of the meters, he thus overcomes the opponent's meters. The Adhvaryu is indeed the impeller (*iṣṭarga*) of the officiating priests.

{1.4.6.36} Indeed, the merit of one who has sacrificed perishes before that of one who has not sacrificed. He says, "O out-breath and in-breath, protect me from death! Thus he takes refuge in out-breath and in-breath. He says, "O out-breath and in-breath, do not abandon me! Out-breath and in-breath do not leave him before his full span of life. Those among the consecrated (*dīkṣita*) for whom someone dies bring misfortune upon themselves. If they were to cast him away, their world would become like that of those who commit cruel deeds. He should say, "Bring him! Burn him!"

Having placed it to the south of the altar, they should praise it with the verses of the Serpent Queen (*sarparājñī*). For she is indeed the queen of all that creeps; thus they entrust him to her. "That is unsuccessful," they say, "that which is praised but not recited. The Hotṛ, first among them, wearing his sacred cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), should go around the Mārjālīya fire while reciting the *yāmī* verses; he should mention the verses of the Serpent Queen. Thus they entrust him to both worlds.

{1.4.6.7} Moreover, they indeed shake him; moreover, others indeed deny him. They go around three times. These worlds are three; it is from these very worlds that they shake him. They go around three times again. This makes six. The seasons are six; it is by means of the seasons that they shake him. They should take "O Agni, you purify the lifespans" as the introductory verse (*pratipad*). Their Soma sacrifice should have the *Rathantara* as its *sāman*. Thus, they place life within themselves; moreover, they go away having cast off evil.

Anuvāka 7: Expiations for the Sprouting of the Sacrificial Post, etc. {1.4.7.1} Verily, from him whose sacrificial post sprouts, the cattle and his virility depart after having made his color that of the Asuras. He should offer a multi-colored animal to Tvaṣṭṛ. Tvaṣṭṛ indeed is the lord of forms; he who is the lord of forms bestows cattle and virility upon this man. Cattle and virility do not depart from him. Verily, those for whom the consecrated fire goes out go toward ruin.

{1.4.7.2} If the Āhavanīya fire should go out, if one were to churn it [from scratch], he would cause a break in continuity and would produce a rival for himself. If the Āhavanīya should go out, he should take it from the Āgnīdhra fire. If the Āgnīdhra should go out, he should take it from the Gārhapatya fire. If the Gārhapatya should go out, he should churn it again from that very same place.

{1.4.7.3} Here indeed he lies hidden. For wherever they see him hidden, there they seek him. From whatever piece of wood the fire should fly up, from that one he should make the two kindling sticks (*araṇī*). He should also make a *krumuka* stick. This *krumuka* is indeed the dear body of Agni; with his own dear body he thus endows him. He churns the Gārhapatya fire.

The *gārhapatya* fire is indeed the womb of Agni. He thus generates him from his own womb; he does not generate a rival for him. If one's *soma* should run out, he should divide a piece of gold into two parts. He should shake one part over the *ṛjīṣa* and offer the other as a libation. Thus he presses *soma* itself and offers *soma* itself. Indeed, when the *soma* was being pressed, its beloved body departed.

That became gold, the *hiraṇya*. When they make it into gold, they endow him with his own dear body. If they should carry off one's un-purchased Soma, he should simply purchase [another]; that is the expiation for that. If they should carry off one's purchased [Soma], he should press out *ādāra* plants and *phālguna* plants. That stalk of the Soma which Gāyatrī brought away fell down.

They became *ādāra* plants. Indra slew Vṛtra; his bark fell away, and it became the *phālguna* plants. The *phālgunas* are indeed cattle; King Soma is cattle. When he presses both the *ādāras* and the *phālgunas*, he is pressing King Soma himself. He should mix [the soma] with boiled milk at the morning pressing, and with curds at the midday pressing.

{1.4.7.7} At the third pressing, with the *nītamiśra* [oblation], there should be an *agniṣṭoma* Soma sacrifice with the *rathantara* as its *sāman*. Whatever officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) have been chosen, they alone should perform the sacrifice for him. He should give one cow as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to them alone. He should purchase Soma again; by means of the sacrifice itself, he seeks to recover the sacrifice. That indeed is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*) for that. For he who pledges himself to a *sattra* (sacrificial session) pledges himself to all the deities and to all the *pṛṣṭha* chants.

A person indeed consists of only this much: as much as his wealth is. He should sacrifice with all his possessions. His Soma sacrifice should have all the *pṛṣṭha* chants. Thus he ransoms himself from all the deities and from all the *pṛṣṭha* chants.

Anuvāka 8: Mantras for the Cause of Purification {1.4.8.1} Pavamāna, who dwells in the light, the observer of all people, with his purifying filter—may he, the Purifier, cleanse me. May the divine folk cleanse me; may the sages cleanse me with their wisdom; may all living beings cleanse me. O Jātavedas, possessed of the purifier, with that purifier, O radiant God, shine with your bright luster; O Agni, according to your power, follow after my powers.

{1.4.8.2} That purifier of yours which is spread within your flame, O Agni—by means of that we purify our *brahman*. With both, O divine Savitṛ—the purifier and the impulse—we purify this *brahman*. The purifying goddess, belonging to all the gods, has come; she whose many forms have smooth backs. Rejoicing with her in our common feasts, may we be masters of riches.

May Vaiśvānara purify me with his rays; may Vāta, the swift and bliss-bringing, purify me with his breath; may Heaven and Earth, the righteous and worthy of sacrifice, purify me with their milk and waters. O Savitṛ, purify me with great, triple-layered, and most exalted divine thoughts. O Agni, purify me with your skills—that by which the gods purified themselves, that by which the waters [purified] the heavenly Kaśa—with that divine *brahman*.

{1.4.8.4} We purify this sacred knowledge (*brahman*). He who studies the *pāvamānī* hymns partakes of the entire purified essence gathered by the seers (*ṛṣi*), which has been made savory by Mātariśvan. He who studies the *pāvamānī* hymns—the essence gathered by the seers—for him Sarasvatī milks forth milk, clarified butter, honey, and water. The *pāvamānī* hymns are the bringers of well-being.

For they are easy to milk and full of milk; their essence was gathered by the seers. Immortality is placed within the Brāhmaṇas. May the Pāvamānī verses point out to us this world and that one beyond. May they fulfill all our desires—these divine verses, brought together with the gods, the Pāvamānīs which bring well-being. For they are easy to milk and drip with clarity; their essence was gathered by the seers.

Amṛta is placed within the Brāhmaṇas, by which means the gods always purify themselves with the filter. With that thousand-streamed [filter], may the Pāvamānī verses purify me. The filter belonging to Prajāpati has a hundred supports and is golden. By means of it, we who know Brahman purify the purified Brahman. May Indra purify me with good guidance; may Soma with well-being, and Varuṇa with concord. May King Yama purify me with his crushing powers; may Jātavedas purify me with strengthening power.

Anuvāka 9: The Remainder of the Cāturmāsya within the Rājasūya {1.4.9.1} The progeny indeed performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*), practicing austerity while not offering oblations. The gods saw a ladle full of clarified butter, a self-offering (*svadhā*). As it rose up, they offered it; by means of that, they secured nourishment (*ūrj*) for every half-month. Therefore, the gods are sacrificed to every half-month. The ancestors saw a ladle full of clarified butter, a self-offering (*svadhā*). As it rose up, they offered it.
By means of that, they secured strength for themselves month by month; therefore, it is performed for the ancestors month by month. Men saw a ladle full of clarified butter, the *svadhā* offering.

As he was rising up, they offered oblations to him. By that, they won two-fold nourishment (*ūrj*). Therefore, twice a day it is brought to men: in the morning and in the evening. The cattle saw a cup full of clarified butter, a self-sustaining power (*svadhā*). As it was rising up, they offered oblations to it. By that, they won three-fold nourishment. Therefore, thrice a day the cattle move forth: in the morning, at the time of the *saṃgava* (the mid-morning gathering), and in the evening. The Asuras saw a cup full of clarified butter, a self-sustaining power.

As he was rising up toward them, they offered oblations. By that means, they secured nourishment (*ūrj*) for a year. Those gods thought: "Those [Asuras] have indeed become what we once were. They perceived these Cāturmāsya sacrifices; they performed them. By means of those very sacrifices, they wrested that nourishment away from them. Thereupon, the gods prospered, and the Asuras were defeated.

In that he sacrifices, he thereby wins the very strength (*ūrj*) which the gods won for themselves. In that he makes offerings to the ancestors, he thereby wins the very strength which the ancestors won for themselves. In that they bring food to the guest-house, he thereby wins the very strength which human beings won for themselves. In that he gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), [he wins the strength which the Ṛṣis won].

{1.4.9.5} Whatever nourishment (*ūrj*) the cattle won for themselves, that he wins for himself by means of this, when he sacrifices with the *Cāturmāsya* offerings. Whatever nourishment the Asuras won for themselves, that he wins for himself by means of this; he prospers in his own person, and his rival is defeated. These *Cāturmāsya* rites are indeed the stride of the *Virāj*. By the *Vaiśvadeva*, he established himself in this world; by the *Varuṇapraghāsas*, in the intermediate space; by the *Sākamedhas*, in yonder world.
He who, knowing this, performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, indeed slays all that [evil] and becomes [the whole].

Anuvāka 10: The Remainder of the Cāturmāsya within the Rājasūya {1.4.10.1} Agni, indeed, is the *saṃvatsara*; Āditya is the *parivatsara*; Candramas is the *idāvatsara*; Vāyu is the *anuvatsara*. In that one sacrifices with the Vaiśvadeva, one thereby attains Agni as the *saṃvatsara*. Therefore, when sacrificing with the Vaiśvadeva, one should make this aspiration: "May I attain prosperity for a full year. In that one sacrifices with the Varuṇapraghāsas, one thereby attains Āditya as the *parivatsara*.

Therefore, when the sacrificer performs the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings, he should pray: "May I attain well-being for the Parivatsara year. In that he sacrifices with the Sākamedha offerings, he thereby attains the Idāvatsara year, which is the moon itself. Therefore, when the sacrificer performs the Sākamedha offerings, he should pray: "May I attain well-being for the Idāvatsara year. In that he sacrifices with the Pitṛyajña, he thereby comes to rest among the gods; otherwise, Vāyu and the Anuvatsara year would remain unsatisfied for him. In that he sacrifices with the Śunāsīrīya offering...

{1.4.10.3} Thus he attains Vāyu for the duration of a year. Therefore, at the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice, the sacrificer should pray: "May I obtain well-being for the duration of a year. For they say, "He who sacrifices with the Cāturmāsyas desires to attain the year. Indeed, he who, knowing this, sacrifices with the Cāturmāsyas, attains the year. The All-gods sacrificed together; they sacrificed to Agni alone. They conquered this world.

{1.4.10.4} In that [world] where Agni dwells; when he sacrifices with the Vaiśvadeva, he conquers that very world. In that [world] where Agni dwells; he attains union (*sāyujya*) with Agni himself. When he sacrifices with the Vaiśvadeva, then he attains the lordship of the year (*saṃvatsara*). When he attains the lordship of the year, then he attains the status of one who has sacrificed a thousand times (*sahasrayājin*). When he attains the status of one who has sacrificed a thousand times...

{1.4.10.5} Then he attains the householder. When he attains the householder, then he becomes fire. When he becomes fire, then he becomes a cow. This indeed is the measure of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice; this is their lowest [stage]. From here on, each subsequent stage becomes more excellent. Because the All-Gods (Viśve Devāḥ) sacrificed together, that is the reason for the Vaiśvadeva’s name as "belonging to the All-Gods."

{1.4.10.6} Now, Āditya sacrificed to King Varuṇa with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings. He won this world in which Āditya dwells. When one sacrifices with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings, one wins that very world in which Āditya dwells; one attains union with Āditya himself. Because Āditya sacrificed to King Varuṇa with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings, that is the reason for the name "Varuṇapraghāsas. Then King Soma sacrificed to the *chandases* (metres) with the Sākamedha offerings.

He conquered this world in which the moon shines; when he sacrifices with the Sākamedha offerings, he conquers that very world in which the moon shines. He attains union with the moon itself. The moon is indeed Soma; he who, knowing this, sacrifices with the Sākamedhas, truly consumes Soma directly. When King Soma and the meters came together...

{1.4.10.8} That is why the Sākamedha offerings are called Sākamedhas. Now, the Seasons, acting as fathers, worshipped Prajāpati, their father, with the Pitṛyajña. They won this world in which the Seasons dwell. When one sacrifices with the Pitṛyajña, he wins that very world in which the Seasons dwell. He attains union with the Seasons themselves. Because the Seasons, acting as fathers, worshipped Prajāpati, their father, with the Pitṛyajña, that is why the Pitṛyajña is called Pitṛyajña.

{1.4.10.9} Then the plants sacrificed to this god with the Tryambaka offerings, thinking, "May we spread forth. Thereupon they indeed spread forth. He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Tryambaka offerings, spreads forth with offspring and cattle. Then Vāyu sacrificed to Parameṣṭhin with the Śunāsīrīya offering. He won that world in which Vāyu dwells. When one sacrifices with the Śunāsīrīya, he wins that very world in which Vāyu dwells.

He attains union with Vāyu itself. The exponents of Brahman say: "Does the performer of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices perish? Or does he not perish? Indeed, while living, he enters the seasons. If he dies in spring, he becomes spring; if in summer, he becomes summer; if in the rains, he becomes the rains; if in autumn, he becomes autumn; if in winter, he becomes winter. Having become a season, he enters the year. The year is Prajāpati; indeed, he is Prajāpati himself.

Prapāṭhaka 5: Nakṣatreṣṭakā; Anuvāka 1: Mantras for the Vaikṛta Nakṣatreṣṭakās. {1.5.1.1} The Kṛttikās belong to Agni. The bright [light] is above; the luminous is below. Rohiṇī belongs to Prajāpati. The waters are above; the plants are below. The Ārdrā belongs to Soma. The outspread [heavens] are above; those who weave are below. The Bāhū belong to Rudra. The hunters are above; the scattering [of arrows] is below. The Punarvasū belong to Aditi. The wind is above; the moist is below.

{1.5.1.2} Tiṣya belongs to Bṛhaspati. The sacrificers are above, while those performing the oblation are below. The Āśleṣās belong to the serpents; those approaching are above, while those dancing toward [them] are below. The Maghās belong to the Fathers; weeping is above, while falling away is below. The former Phalgunīs belong to Aryaman; the wife is above, while the bull is below. The latter [Phalgunīs] belong to Bhaga; those being carried are above, while those carrying are below.

{1.5.1.3} The hand of the god Savitṛ; impulsion from above, acquisition from below. Of Indra, Citrā; cosmic order from above, truth from below. Of Vāyu, Niṣṭyā; the creeper from above, non-accomplishment from below. Of Indra and Agni, Viśākhā; the yokes from above, those being drawn from below. Of Mitra, Anūrādhā; the ascending from above, the ascended from below.

{1.5.1.4} Rohiṇī belongs to Indra. Hearing from above, she hears back from below. Mūlavarhaṇī belongs to Nirṛti. Breaking down from above, they hear back from below. The first Aṣāḍhās belong to the Waters. Splendor from above, assembly from below. The later [Aṣāḍhās] belong to the Viśve Devas. Complete victory from above, the conquest from below. Śroṇā belongs to Viṣṇu. Inquiring from above, the path from below.

{1.5.1.5} Śraviṣṭhās belong to the Vasus. That which is beyond is existence; that which is below is prosperity. Śatabhiṣaj belongs to Indra. Viśvavyacas is beyond; Viśvakṣiti is below. The former Proṣṭhapadas belong to Aja Ekapād. Vaiśvānara is beyond; Vaiśvāvasava is below. The latter [Proṣṭhapadas] belong to Ahi Budhnya. Abhiṣiñcantas is beyond; Abhiṣuṇvantas is below. Revatī belongs to Pūṣan. Cows are beyond; calves are below. The Aśvayujas belong to the Aśvins.
The village is on the far side, the army on the near side; Apabharaṇī belongs to Yama. Drawing away on the far side, carrying off on the near side—the full [vessel] which the gods placed behind you.

Anuvāka 2: The Auspicious Time for the Performance of Rites {1.5.2.1} One should perform [the rite] at whatever constellation is auspicious, even until near dawn. For when the sun rises, then the constellation disappears. One should perform whatever rite one intends to do at such a time that the sun has traveled as far as it can go and one can still see the last glimmer of the stars; thus one performs it on an auspicious day. In this very way, Mātsya caused both Śatadyumna and Yajñasena to be defeated.

{1.5.2.2} Verily, he who knows Prajāpati as consisting of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) is known in both worlds. His hand is indeed Hasta; his head is Citrā; his heart is Niṣṭyā; his two thighs are Viśākhā; his support is Anūrādhā. He who knows thus is indeed Prajāpati as consisting of the lunar mansions; he is known in both worlds.

{1.5.2.3} "In this world and in that world. If he should desire a daughter who shall be beloved, he should give her away under the constellation *niṣṭyā*. She indeed becomes beloved, and she never returns [to her father's house]. There is a lunar mansion named *abhijit*, situated above the *aṣāḍhās* and below the *śroṇā*. The gods and the Asuras were engaged in battle; the gods conquered in that lunar mansion.

{1.5.2.4} Because they conquered by means of it, that is the reason for the name of the Abhijit [sacrifice]. If one should desire of someone, "May he conquer unconquerably," one should cause him to sacrifice under this lunar mansion (nakṣatra). He conquers indeed unconquerably; yet, it is as if he is conquered by evil. Prajāpati created cattle. They approached every lunar mansion, and they became exactly equal. Then they approached the Revatī [mansion].

{1.5.2.10} They prevailed upon the Revatī [nakṣatra]. Therefore, one should perform rites for cattle under the Revatī. Whatever is subsequent to the Soma sacrifice, they truly prevail upon it. This world was indeed water in the beginning; because they crossed over it, that is the "star-like" (*tāraka*) nature of the stars (*tārakā*). Whoever sacrifices here reaches that world; that is the "reaching" (*nakṣatra*) nature of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).

The stars are indeed the dwellings of the gods; he who knows this becomes possessed of a dwelling. Whatever wonderful things there are upon this earth, these are the stars. Therefore, one should not utter an improper name for a wonderful thing, nor should one dwell [there] or sacrifice [under it], for that would be exactly as if one were acting on an evil day. Other [stars] are indeed the stars of the gods.

{1.5.2.7} The other [set] are the *yama*-constellations. *Kṛttikā* is the first; *viśākhe* is the last. These are the divine (*deva*) constellations. *Anūrādhā* is the first; *apabharaṇī* is the last. These are the *yama* constellations. Those which are the divine constellations move to the south; those which are the *yama* constellations [move to the north].

{1.5.2.8} "We have succeeded after them"—thus [they were called] Anūrādhās. "We have struck down their eldest"—thus [they were called] Jyeṣṭhaghnī. "We have torn out their root"—thus [they were called] Mūlabarhaṇī (or Mūlavarhaṇī). Because they did not withstand [them], [they were called] Aṣāḍhās. Because they became lame, [they were called] Śroṇās.

Because she heard [the sound], that is Śroṇā. Because she heard [it] most clearly, those are Śraviṣṭhās. Because they healed [him] by the hundreds, that is Śatabhiṣaj. They raised him up under the Proṣṭhapadas; they cried out at Revatī; they yoked [the horses] under the Aśvayujas; they carried him away under the Apabharaṇīs. These, indeed, are the Nakṣatras of Yama. One should perform whatever rite he intends to do under those very Nakṣatras which belong to the gods; thus he performs it on an auspicious day.

Anuvāka 3: The Auspicious Time through Subsistence on the Day’s Portions {1.5.3.1} The morning breath of the god Savitṛ is his exhalation; the evening breath of Varuṇa is his inhalation. That which is subsequent to the morning [breath] and prior to the time when the cattle are gathered (saṃgava) is from that the gods fashioned the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. That is the "scouring" (*nirmārga*), wherein strength has been taken away. The time of Mitrā is the gathering of the cattle; that day is auspicious and full of splendor. Therefore, at that time, the cattle come together. That which is subsequent to the gathering of the cattle...

{1.5.3.2} That which is prior to midday—from that the gods fashioned the Ukthya; that is its loss of vigor, its exhaustion. Midday belongs to Bṛhaspati; that is a meritorious and brilliant day; therefore, at that time, it burns most intensely. That which is subsequent to midday and prior to afternoon—from that the gods fashioned the Ṣoḍaśin; that is its loss of vigor, its exhaustion.

The afternoon belongs to Bhaga; it is an auspicious and radiant day. Therefore, in the afternoon, young women wander about seeking Bhaga. That which is after the afternoon and before the evening belongs to Varuṇa. From that, the gods fashioned the Atirātra sacrifice. That [time] is one whose vigor has been taken away; it is a time for cleansing. The evening belongs to Varuṇa; it is an auspicious and radiant day. Therefore, at that time, one should not speak untruth.

The Brāhmaṇa is indeed the twenty-eighth among the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). On a single day, there are five auspicious lunar mansions and four inauspicious ones; these make nine. Those that are beyond the lunar mansions and those that are below them make eleven. The Brāhmaṇa is the twelfth. He who, knowing this, observes the vow for a year—by means of the year itself, his vow becomes protected. On a single day, there are five auspicious lunar mansions and four inauspicious ones.

These are nine: the night belongs to Agni; the day belongs to Indra. These make eleven; the sun is the twelfth. He who, knowing this, observes the vow for a year—by means of the year itself, his vow becomes protected.

Anuvāka 4: Praise of the Vessels Constituting the Remnants of Soma {1.5.4.1} The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "How many vessels carry the sacrifice? One should reply: "Thirteen. If he should ask, "Who fashioned them?", one should reply: "Prajāpati. If he should ask, "From what did he fashion them?", one should reply: "From his own self. From the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the in-breath (*apāna*) alone, he fashioned the *upāṃśu* and *antaryāma* [vessels].

{1.5.4.2} From the *vyāna* [breath] he fashioned the *upāṃśusavana* stone; from speech, the *aindravāyava* cup; from strength and will (*dakṣa-kratu*), the *maitrāvaruṇa* cup; from hearing, the *āśvina* cup; from sight, the *śukra* and *manthin* cups; from the self (*ātman*), the *āgrayaṇa* cup; from the limbs, the *ukthya* cup; from life-force (*āyus*), the *dhruva* cup; and from the foundation, the two *ṛtupātra* vessels. Prajāpati indeed fashioned that sacrifice. Once fashioned, it did not stand firm; it collapsed. Then Prajāpati saw these fillings (*apivāpa*); he scattered them.
With these he indeed sows the sacrifice; in that there are sowing [verses], it is for the support of the sacrifice and to prevent its collapse.

*Anuvāka 5: The Sowing Mantras, remnants of the Cāturmāsya.* Truth alone is the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*). Nothing whatsoever transcends Truth. Upon Truth the ocean is set; upon Truth this earth is supported. With a sharp flame, Agni has overcome the heat; with the *uṣṇih* meter, the head is placed upon the heat. By the splendor of Vaiśvānara, by Truth I turn him downward; by Truth I turn him around.

{1.5.5.2} I follow after him with fervor (*tapas*). I turn toward him with auspiciousness (*śiva*). I turn toward him with vigor (*śagma*). That is the Eternal Law (*ṛta*), that is the Truth (*satya*); that is the Vow (*vrata*), may I be able to fulfill it. Through that may I be able; through that may I prosper. That which the Gharma has turned around—the boundaries of the earth and of heaven—Agni, ruling with might, and Varuṇa together with his holy thoughts.

Indra, together with his friends the Maruts; Agni, with his sharp flame; the heat pervaded by the *uṣṇih* meter; the head placed upon the heat—with the splendor of Vaiśvānara, with *ṛta*, I turn it back for him; with *satya*, I turn it around for him; with heat, I follow it for him; with what is auspicious, I bring it near for him; with what is efficacious, I turn it toward him for him.

That is the cosmic order (*ṛta*); that is the truth (*satya*). That is the vow; may I be able to fulfill it. Through that may I be able; through that may I prosper. He who upon the skin of this earth causes the plants to turn back—Agni, ruling with might, Varuṇa together with his prayers, Indra with his friends the Maruts, and Agni with his sharp flame—the heat has overcome the *uṣṇihā*.

The head has been placed upon austerity; by the splendor of Vaiśvānara. By the *ṛta* I turn it back; by the *satya* I turn it around; by austerity I follow it; by the auspicious I turn it toward me; by the powerful I turn it hither. That is the *ṛta*, that is the *satya*; that is the vow, may I be able to fulfill it. By that may I be able; by that may I prosper.

{1.5.5.6} He released one month for the sake of creatures; through it, he brought greatness to them, and immortality to mortals. "You are born after offspring; that indeed is your immortal [portion], by which months, half-months, seasons, and years [are formed]. By this, O Prajāpati, they turned back for you as you were sacrificing.

By this sacred word (*brahman*), I turn back [the heat] for his life. Agni with his sharp flame, the *uṣṇih* meter, and the heat that has overcome [him]—the head is placed within the heat. By the splendor of Vaiśvānara, by *ṛta*, I turn it back; by *satya*, I turn it around; by *tapas*, I follow it; by the auspicious, I bring it near; by the powerful, I turn it toward him. That is *ṛta*, that is *satya*; that is the vow, may I be able to fulfill it. By that may I be able; by that may I succeed.

Anuvāka 6: The Ritual for Shaving as a Remnant of the Cāturmāsya Sacrifice {1.5.6.1} Whatever the gods did at the sacrifice, the Asuras did likewise. Those Asuras, however, could not see [the way] above their backs. First they shaved their hair, then their beards, then their armpits; thereupon they went downward and were defeated. For whomsoever they shave in this manner, he goes downward.

{1.5.6.2} Moreover, he becomes as if turned away. Then the gods beheld [the body] above the backs. They shaved first the armpits, then the beard, then the hair. Thereupon they became successful; they went to the heavenly world. He for whom they shave in this manner prospers in his own person and goes to the heavenly world.

{1.5.6.3} Now, Manu saw this pair in the shaver. He shaved his beard first, then his armpits, then his hair. Thereby he indeed procreated with offspring and cattle. For whomsoever they shave in this manner, he procreates with offspring, cattle, and pairs. The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. They contended for a year. The gods then overcame them by means of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices alone.

{1.5.6.4} By means of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, those whose king was Indra won four months; they turned them toward the head and turned them around. By means of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, those whose king was Varuṇa won four months; they turned them toward the head and turned them around. By means of the Sākamedha sacrifices, those whose king was Soma won four months; they turned them toward the head and turned them around. Whatever sustenance there was in the year, that they won from them. Thereupon the gods prospered, and the Asuras were defeated.

He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the Cāturmāsya offerings, having cut off the month of his rival, turns it both downward and around. That which is the means of subsistence for the year—he deprives his rival of that. His rival perishes through hunger. He turns [the earth] over with red-hot iron; for when the season arrives, Agni turns this earth over. Having assumed this very form, he turns it over. From then on, day by day, it becomes more abundant.

{1.5.6.6} He procreates. He who, knowing thus, causes [the hair] to be removed with red iron—having assumed this very form—he causes it to be removed. From that time on, becoming greater day by day, he goes forth; he truly procreates. One should cause it to be removed with a three-striped porcupine quill. For the prosperities of the gods are threefold: there are three meters, three pressings, and these three worlds.

{1.5.6.7} By means of the two *ṛc*s, he establishes that vigor in these worlds. If one who performs the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices were not to offer a portion from himself, he would be cut off from the gods; he would have to turn back every four months. However, by offering it in secret, he offers a portion from himself to the gods so as not to be cut off. He who performs the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifice is indeed brought near to the gods. He who, knowing this, both turns [the sacrifice] toward them and turns away from them, approaches the deities themselves. Rudra does not take ill-will toward his offspring or his cattle.

Anuvāka 7: Mantras for the Bricks called Saṃtata (Continuous). Continue life from breath; continue out-breath from in-breath; continue diffused breath from out-breath; continue sight from diffused breath; continue hearing from sight; continue mind from hearing; continue speech from mind; continue the self from speech; continue the earth from the self; continue the intermediate space from the earth; continue heaven from the intermediate space; continue the world of light (*suvar*) from heaven.

Anuvāka 8: Mantras for the Bricks Named after the *Atharvaśiras* Indra, with the bones of Dadhyañc, unopposed, struck down ninety-nine Vṛtras. Seeking the horse’s head which was hidden in the mountains, he found it at Śaryaṇāvat. There they recognized the secret name of Tvaṣṭṛ belonging to the cow, even as it was in the house of the moon. To Indra alone do the singers sing aloud.

{1.5.8.2} Indra with hymns by the chanters; Indra the voices have sung aloud. Indra indeed is with the two bay steeds, mingled with the one yoked by speech. Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, is golden-hued. Indra, for far-reaching vision, caused the sun to ascend to heaven. He split the mountain asunder with the cattle. O Indra, protect us in battles for booty and in contests for a thousandfold gain.

Fierce with his fierce aids, that Indra we impel for strength; for the slaying of the great Vṛtra, he has become the bull, the showerer of benefits. That Indra was made for the giving of gifts; he is the most powerful, established in might. Radiant, worthy of praise, and beloved by Soma, he is like a thunderbolt fashioned by song. Strong and unshakable, the fierce and unconquerable one has grown great.

Anuvāka 9: The Soma-offering subsidiaries beginning with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and ending with the commencement of the *bahiṣpavamāna*. {1.5.9.1} The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. Prajāpati set aside his eldest son, Indra, thinking, "Lest the more powerful Asuras slay him. Prahrāda Kāyādhava, indeed, set aside his own son Virocana, thinking, "Lest the gods slay him. Those gods, having approached Prajāpati, said:
"There is no war for one who is without a king. 'Let us seek Indra,' they said; so they sought him through sacrificial rites."

{1.5.9.2} They did not find him by means of the sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*). They sought him by means of the *iṣṭi* offerings; they found him by means of the *iṣṭi* offerings. That is why the *iṣṭis* have their name: they are indeed called *eṣṭayas*. They call them *iṣṭis* cryptically, for the gods are fond of the cryptic. For him, they offered this consecration-offering (*dīkṣaṇīya*) on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni and Viṣṇu. Having fled from that, they performed [the sacrifice]. They brought those *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings to them.

Having performed that very rite as its conclusion, they ran away. They ascended toward the *prāyaṇīya* [opening-offering]; having run away from that, they performed it. He brought them back at the conclusion of the *śaṃyu*-formula. Having performed that very rite as its conclusion, they ran away. They ascended toward the *ātithya* [guest-offering]; having run away from that, they performed it. He brought them back at the conclusion of the *iḍā*-invocation. Having performed that very rite as its conclusion, they ran away. Therefore, these sacrifices are completed with those respective conclusions.

{1.5.9.4} For thus did the gods act. "The gods acted thus," so indeed do men act. Those gods said, "In that we perform this sacrifice loudly, the Asuras find our evil. Let us perform the Upasad with a low voice; then the Asuras will not find our evil. They performed the Upasad with a low voice. Having recited only three *sāmidhenī* verses—

{1.5.9.5} Having poured the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* ladle and having offered three oblations directed forward, they performed the *upasad* offering with the *sruva* ladle, saying: "I have struck down the fierce word; I have struck down the terrible word, svāhā! Hunger and thirst are indeed the fierce word; sin and the killing of a kinsman are the terrible word. By this means, the gods indeed struck away that fourfold evil. And so does the sacrificer who knows thus. Having recited three *sāmidhenī* verses and having poured the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* ladle...

Having offered three oblations directed forward, he offers the *upasat* with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), saying: "I have struck down fierce speech; I have struck down dazzling speech, svāhā! Hunger and thirst are indeed fierce speech; sin and the killing of a kinsman are dazzling speech. By this, the sacrificer strikes away that evil which is fourfold. Having led the animal forward, they immolate it on the very day [of the *upasat*]. On that very day, the gods struck away misfortune, evil, and death.
Having led [the sacrifice] forward, they proceeded at the beginning of the night. By means of that very night, the gods struck away misfortune, evil, and death.

Therefore, one should immolate the animal after having extended [the ritual] through the day. By that, the sacrificer drives away misfortune, evil, and rivals from the very day. He should proceed with the night after having likewise extended it. By that, the sacrificer drives away misfortune, evil, and rivals from the very night. This animal dedicated to two deities is immolated on the Upavasatha day. For in this world, the sacrificer consists of two things: bone and flesh.

By this, the sacrificer prepares both the bone and the flesh. These, indeed, are the five deities: Agni and Soma, Agni, Mitra and Varuṇa. The sacrificer is fivefold: skin, flesh, sinew, bone, and marrow. By this, he releases his self—which is thus divided fivefold—from the noose of Varuṇa, for the sake of healing and freedom from Varuṇa’s grasp. They summoned him in the morning with seven meters.

Therefore, seven meters, each increasing by four syllables, are recited in the Prātaranuvāka. They approached him with this [verse] and waited upon him, saying, "Sing unto him, O men! Therefore, the Bahiṣpavamāna stotra is to be performed while sitting near it.

Anuvāka 10: The *stomas* beginning with the *trivṛt* {1.5.10.1}. That ocean blazed up from the north toward the edge of the earth. This, indeed, is that ocean: namely, the *cātvāla* pit. And this, indeed, is that edge of the earth: namely, the edge of the *vedī*. Thus, this [fire] has three corners and extends over three generations; therefore, they dig it three spans deep. It was enclosed by two rings of gold and silver. Because they generated it from above this [earth], it is therefore called *āditya*.

{1.5.10.2} Now, as for the fact that he was held by two handles made of gold and silver: that is his "Kauśika" nature. They praised him with the *Trivṛt* [Stoma]; they took him up with the *Trivṛt*; they brought him forward with the *Trivṛt*. Such is the measure of the *Trivṛt*. They praised him with the *Pañcadaśa* [Stoma]; they took him up with the *Pañcadaśa*; they brought him forward with the *Pañcadaśa*. Such is the measure of the *Pañcadaśa*.

{1.5.10.3} They praised him with the seventeenfold [Stoma]. They took him up with the seventeenfold. They brought him with the seventeenfold. As great as was the measure of the seventeenfold, so much of his splendor fell away while he was being brought. They praised him with the twenty-onefold. They took him up with the twenty-onefold. They brought him with the twenty-onefold. As great as was the measure of the twenty-onefold—when they praise him with the ninefold (trivṛt)—it is for this reason.

{1.5.10.4} By means of the *trivṛt* they thus take up the sacrificer; by means of the *trivṛt* they carry him away. As great as is the measure of the *trivṛt*, Agni indeed is the *trivṛt*. As much smoke as rises from the burning fire and spreads abroad, so great is the measure of the *trivṛt*. It is by this that they cause him to attain the measure, the union (*sāyujya*), and the same world (*salokatā*) as Agni. Furthermore, when they praise with the *pañcadaśa*, it is by means of the *pañcadaśa* that they take up the sacrificer.

{1.5.10.5} They carry him away with the fifteen-fold hymn alone, for as great as is the measure of the fifteen-fold hymn—Candramas (the Moon) indeed is the fifteen-fold; for he wanes on the fifteenth day and waxes on the fifteenth day. It is thus that they cause him to attain union and co-residence with Candramas. Now, when they praise with the seventeen-fold hymn, they take hold of the sacrificer with the seventeen-fold hymn itself; they carry him away with the seventeen-fold hymn itself.

{1.5.10.6} As great as is the measure of the seventeenfold [stoma], Prajāpati indeed is the seventeenfold; thus they cause him to attain the measure, the union, and the same world as Prajāpati. Now, when they praise with the twenty-onefold [stoma], they take up the sacrificer by means of that very twenty-onefold; they lead him away by means of that very twenty-onefold. As great as is the measure of the twenty-onefold, yonder sun indeed is the twenty-onefold; thus they cause him to attain the measure, the union, and the same world as the sun.

They lead one to union (*sāyujya*), to co-residence (*salokatā*), or to proximity (*sāmīpya*). These two were the *kuśī* (earthenware bowls). They struck [them] apart; they became day and night. Day became golden, and night silver. When the sun rises, it follows along this very golden *kuśī*. And when it sets, it enters into this very silver *kuśī*. Prahrāda Kāyādhava indeed cast out his own son Virocana; he became a cleft. Therefore, one should not sip water from a cleft.

Anuvāka 11: The Savanīya Puroḍāśas {1.5.11.1} Those which are the four *stomas* are indeed the *kṛta* [age]. Now, those which are five are the *kali* [age]. Therefore, it is the *catuṣṭoma*. That is the reason for the *catuṣṭoma*'s name as *catuṣṭoma*. Regarding this, they say: "Which are those lights (*jyotis*) that are its *stomas*? They are the *trivṛt*, the *pañcadaśa*, the *saptadaśa*, and the *ekaviṃśa*.

{1.5.11.2} These, indeed, are those lights which are its *stomas*. He said: "Being carried by the seventeen-fold hymn, I was distressed; heal me! The Aśvins healed him with parched grains (*dhānā*), Pūṣan with groats (*karambha*), Bhāratī with the *parivāpa* (fried barley), and Mitra and Varuṇa with curd-mixture (*payasyā*). Regarding this, they say:

{1.5.11.3} As for the grains for the Aśvins, the groats for Pūṣan, the parched barley for Bhāratī, and the curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa—why is it that they sacrifice these oblations to Indra alone? He should say: "Because these deities healed him by means of these oblations; therefore [they are offered to him]. At the morning pressing, the Vasus healed him with a cake on eight potsherds; at the midday pressing, the Rudras with a cake on eleven potsherds;
and at the third pressing, the Viśve Devas with a cake on twelve potsherds.

If he were to offer cakes on eight potsherds at the morning pressing, on eleven potsherds at the midday pressing, and on twelve potsherds at the third pressing, that would be a reversal of the sacrifice. He should offer cakes on eleven potsherds at the morning pressing, on eleven potsherds at the midday pressing, and on eleven potsherds at the third pressing, for the sake of the regularity of the sacrifice. Regarding this they say: "The morning pressing belongs to the Vasus."

The midday pressing belongs to the Rudras; the third pressing belongs to the Viśvedevas. Now, why do they sacrifice to Indra alone with these oblations? One should say: "Because these deities healed him with these oblations; therefore [they sacrifice to him]."

Anuvāka 12: The Seven Metres {1.5.12.1}. They were afraid of the stumbling of that Speech. They supported it upon these seven metres. Because they supported it (*aśrayan*), that is the reason for the name *Śrāyantīya* of the *Śrāyantīya*. Because they warded it off (*avārayan*), that is the reason for the name *Vāravantīya* of the *Vāravantīya*. They were afraid of the very stumbling of that Speech. For it, they placed these seven metres, each increasing by four syllables. Of them, three remained in excess; three did not suffice.

He touched the *bṛhatī* itself with two syllables—namely, with day and night. Regarding this, they say: "Which is that divine-syllabled *bṛhatī* upon which it rested? There are twelve full-moon nights, twelve *aṣṭakā*s, and twelve new-moon nights. This indeed is that divine-syllabled *bṛhatī*.

{1.5.12.3} "In which [metre] did that find support? Those metres which exceeded [the norm] and those which did not arise—these they considered to be powerless and deficient. Bṛhatī said, "Becoming me alone, take refuge in me. Anuṣṭubh arose as Bṛhatī by means of four syllables; Paṅkti exceeded Bṛhatī by four syllables. Having cut off these four syllables from it (Paṅkti), he placed them [into Anuṣṭubh].

Having become *bṛhatī*s themselves, they both took refuge in the *bṛhatī*. With eight syllables, the *uṣṇih* did not rise up to the level of the *bṛhatī*; with eight syllables, the *triṣṭubh* exceeded the *bṛhatī*. From that [excess], he cut off these eight syllables and added them [to the *uṣṇih*]. Having become *bṛhatī*s themselves, they both took refuge in the *bṛhatī*. With twelve syllables, the *gāyatrī* did not rise up to the level of the *bṛhatī*.
The *jagatī* exceeded the *bṛhatī* by twelve syllables; having cut off these twelve syllables from it, he placed them [into the *bṛhatī*].

{1.5.12.5} Having become two *bṛhatī*s, they took refuge in the *bṛhatī*. Prajāpati said: "O meters, let my chariot be yours; with you, may I traverse this path. Of that [chariot], the *gāyatrī* and the *jagatī* became the two wings; the *uṣṇih* and the *triṣṭubh* became the two side-poles (*praṣṭya*); the *anuṣṭubh* and the *paṅkti* became the two shafts (*dhur*); and the *bṛhatī* itself became the seat (*uddhi*). Having mounted this chariot of meters, he—
He traversed this path. Indeed, having mounted this chariot of the meters, he traverses this very path by which he now moves—both he who, knowing thus, sacrifices with Soma, and he who knows it thus.

Prapāṭhaka 6: The Rājasūya, Anuvāka 1. He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Anumati. Those [sparks] which fall westward from the *śamyā*—that is for Nirṛti on one potsherd. This earth is indeed Anumati; this earth is Nirṛti. He proceeds first with the offering to Nirṛti. Thus he expiates the evil, Nirṛti, first. It is on one potsherd; he thus expiates Nirṛti all at once. If they were to go toward the Gārhapatya fire without having made the offering, [the following would occur].

Having become Rudra, Agni rises up after [the fire] and might slay both the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer. He says, "Eat, svāhā! Rejoice in the oblation!"—verily, by means of the oblation he pacifies him. Neither the *adhvaryu* nor the sacrificer comes to ruin. They proceed with a single fire-brand; for that is the portion belonging to Nirṛti. He leads [it] toward this direction; for this is indeed the direction of Nirṛti. Verily, in its own direction he causes Nirṛti to be appeased.

{1.6.1.3} He offers on a self-made salt-flat or in a cleft. This, indeed, is the abode of Nirṛti; he thus propitiates Nirṛti in her own abode. "This is thy portion, O Nirṛti," he says; he thus points her out. "Thou art possessed of oblation at the being," he says; he thus turns toward prosperity. "Release him from distress," he says; he thus releases him from distress. He offers with his two thumbs.

{1.6.1.4} In the end, he indeed expiates Nirṛti. A black garment with a black fringe is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). This, indeed, is the form of Nirṛti. By means of her very form, he expiates Nirṛti. They return without looking back, for the sake of concealment from Nirṛti. Having returned, he offers an oblation on the Gārhapatya fire with the words: "Svāhā! Adoration to him who has done this! Thus, paying homage by means of the oblation, they turn toward the Gārhapatya. He proceeds with the rite accompanied by Anumati; for this earth, indeed, is Anumati.

{1.6.1.5} This very [earth] grants her approval for his kingship. A cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). He makes this very earth his cow. He offers a *caru* oblation to Āditya. He is consecrated over both kinds of subjects: the divine and the human. A choice boon (*vara*) is the sacrificial fee; for a choice boon is the perfection of kingship. He offers an eleven-potherd cake to Agni and Viṣṇu. Agni is all the deities.

Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; he thus wins both the deities and the sacrifice. A dwarf (*vāmana*) is the draft-animal as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). In that it is a draft-animal, it belongs to Agni; in that it is a dwarf, it belongs to Viṣṇu—for the sake of prosperity. He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma. "By means of Agni and Soma, Indra slew Vṛtra"—in that he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma.

{1.6.1.7} [The offering] for Vṛtra-slaying is indeed for the sake of victory. Gold is the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity. Having slain Vṛtra, Indra was deprived of both the deities and his own power (*indriya*). He beheld this cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni; he offered it. By that, indeed, he regained both the deities and his power. In that he offers a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni, the sacrificer thereby regains both the deities and his power. A draft-bull is the sacrificial fee.

{1.6.1.8} Because it is a bull, it belongs to Agni; because it is a bull, it belongs to Indra—for prosperity. He offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni and curds for Indra. In that there is an offering for Agni—Agni, indeed, is the mouth of the sacrifice—he places prosperity at the very front of the sacrifice. In that there is curds for Indra...

He wins the very sense-faculties (*indriya*). A draft-bull is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). In that it is a draft-animal, it belongs to Agni; in that it is a bull, it belongs to Indra—for the sake of prosperity. As many creatures as ate the plants before they were offered, they perished. There is the *Āgrayaṇa* offering for the eating of what has been offered, so that the sacrificer may not perish.

{1.6.1.10} The gods indeed ran a race for the plants; Indra and Agni won them. They two offered this cake on twelve potsherds to Indra and Agni. In that there is an offering to Indra and Agni, it is for victory. It consists of twelve potsherds; the year has twelve months. Verily, by means of the year, he secures food for him. There is a pap for the Viśve Devas; food belongs to the Viśve Devas. Verily, he makes the food palatable for him.

The first-born calf is the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity. He offers a pap of *śyāmāka* grain to Soma. Soma is indeed the king of that which ripens without being ploughed; he thus makes that which ripens without being ploughed palatable for him. A garment is the sacrificial fee.
