For a garment has Soma as its deity; it is for the sake of prosperity. He offers a pap to Sarasvatī and a pap to Sarasvant. Thus he obtains a pair. A pair of cattle is the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity.

He indeed departs from the prosperity of the mouth of the sacrifice who departs from Agni as the deity. There are eight of these oblations; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and Agni is of the Gāyatrī nature. Thus, by that very means, he does not depart from the prosperity of the mouth of the sacrifice nor from Agni as the deity.

Anuvāka 2: The Vaiśvadeva Section in the Rājasūya {1.6.2.1} By means of the Vaiśvadeva [sacrifice], Prajāpati created offspring. Once created, they did not propagate. Agni desired, "May I procreate these [beings]. He bestowed grief upon Prajāpati. He grieved, desiring offspring. Therefore, both he whom the offspring consume and he whom they do not—both of them grieve, desiring offspring. Into those [beings], he emitted Agni. Agni entered into them.

Soma deposited the seed; Savitṛ brought it forth; Sarasvatī bestowed speech; Pūṣan nourished it. These very [deities] are employed three times a year. These gods are the lords of prosperity. Prajāpati is indeed the year. By means of the year itself, he brought forth offspring for him. Those offspring, once born, the Maruts struck down, thinking, "They have not employed us as well."

Prajāpati saw this oblation to the Maruts on seven potsherds; he offered it. Thereupon, he indeed became fit for his subjects. In that the offering to the Maruts is made, it is for the success of the sacrifice and for the non-destruction of the subjects. It consists of seven potsherds, for the Maruts consist of seven groups; verily, he arranges the people for him group by group. That Prajāpati grieved.

{1.6.2.4} "The Maruts have destroyed those offspring whom I previously created. How shall I create others?"—thus [he thought]. His vital energy (*śuṣma*) became an egg and emerged. He drew it apart; he nourished it; it was born. This is indeed the form of the egg: that which is the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture). In that he draws it apart...

{1.6.2.5} By this, the sacrificer nourishes offspring. There is curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for the Viśvedevas; for offspring belong to the Viśvedevas. He thus procreates offspring for him. He brings the whey (*vājina*); he thus places seed in the offspring once they have been born. There is a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth; he thus encloses the offspring, once born, on both sides with Heaven and Earth. The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. Then Agni said:

"Worship me first; with me as your mouth, you shall conquer the Asuras," so [Agni] said. "Me as the second," said Soma, "with me as king, you shall conquer. "Me as the third," said Savitṛ, "impelled by me, you shall conquer. "Me as the fourth," said Sarasvatī, "I shall bestow sensory power upon you. "Me as the fifth," said Pūṣan, "with me as your foundation, you shall conquer."

{1.6.2.7} They conquered the Asuras with Agni as their mouth, with Soma as their king, impelled by Savitṛ; Sarasvatī bestowed sensory power (*indriya*), and Pūṣan was their foundation. Thereby, indeed, the gods were victorious. When these oblations are offered, it is for the sake of victory. He does not throw up the *uttaravedi* (high altar); for the *uttaravedi* is cattle, and at this time cattle are as if yet unborn.

Anuvāka 3: The Vaiśvadeva section of the Rājasūya {1.6.3.1}. The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is threefold: the mother, the father, and the son; that indeed constitutes a pair. The caul, the embryo, and the placenta; that indeed constitutes a pair. The sacrificial grass is tied together in three parts; these are the three worlds; he thus finds firm support in these very worlds. It is then tied together again as one; for this world is, as it were, one.

In this very world he finds firm support through that. There are *prasuva* offerings; verily, he wins the first-born prosperity. A first-born calf is the sacrificial fee for the sake of success. He takes speckled butter; speckled butter is indeed cattle; verily, he wins cattle. It consists of five portions, for cattle are fivefold. It is of many forms.

{1.6.3.3} For cattle are multiform; [this serves] for prosperity. They churn the fire. Prajāpati, having Agni as his mouth, indeed created offspring. In that they churn the fire, the sacrificer creates offspring with Agni as their mouth. Nine fore-offerings (prayāja) are offered; nine after-offerings (anūyāja); eight oblations (havīṃṣi); two libations of ghee (āghāra); and two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga).

They amount to thirty. The Virāj consists of thirty syllables; the Virāj is food. Verily, by means of the Virāj, he secures for himself the eating of food. The sacrificer is the cake on one potsherd; the clarified butter is brilliance. In that he pours the clarified butter over the cake on one potsherd, he endows the sacrificer with brilliance. The sacrificer is the cake on one potsherd; the clarified butter is cattle.

{1.6.3.5} In that he pours clarified butter onto the cake on one potsherd, he causes the sacrificer himself to prosper with cattle. If he were to pour a small amount, few cattle would attend upon him while providing for him. If he were to pour a large amount, many cattle would attend upon him while providing for him. Having poured a large amount, he should make the back of the cake visible; thus many cattle indeed attend upon him while providing for him. The cake on one potsherd is the sacrificer himself. If he were to cut off a portion from the cake on one potsherd...

{1.6.3.6} He should cut the portion for the sacrificer; otherwise, the sacrificer might become intoxicated or perish. It should be offered only once, for the world of heaven is, as it were, a single unit. Having made the offering, he offers over it again; having caused the sacrificer to go to the world of heaven, he thus endows him with splendor. The one-potsherd cake is indeed the sacrificer, and the Āhavanīya fire is the world of heaven.

{1.6.3.7} In that he offers the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) upon the Āhavanīya fire, he causes the sacrificer himself to go to the heavenly world. If he were to offer with his hand, he would strike the sacrificer away from the heavenly world. He offers with a ladle (*sruk*) for the attainment of the heavenly world. If he were to step forward (to the east), he would conquer the world of the gods; if to the south, the world of the fathers; if to the west.

The *rakṣas* would destroy the sacrifice if [the offering] were made facing north; for by facing north, one would conquer the world of men. It should be offered while firmly established. Indeed, when the cake on one potsherd is firmly established, Heaven and Earth become established after it. Heaven and Earth are the seasons, and the sacrifice follows the seasons; the sacrificer follows the sacrifice, and offspring follow the sacrificer. Therefore, it should be offered while firmly established.

He sacrifices to the *vājins*. They are Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya; these indeed are the *vājins*, and it is them he sacrifices to. Now, moreover, they say: "The meters are the *vājins*"; it is them he sacrifices to. The *ṛc* and the *sāman* are Indra’s two bay steeds (*harī*), the drinkers of Soma; the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are their support, and the *vājina* offering is their portion.

If one were to offer the oblation without having cast the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) into the fire, he would be offering fodder to two animals that have not been driven away. He offers after having cast the enclosing sticks; thus he offers fodder to two animals that have indeed been driven away. He pours the whey (*vājina*) over the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). The sacrificial grass is indeed offspring, and the whey is seed; thus he places seed within the offspring. They consume it after having invited one another, for these [priests] partake of the Soma-drink; moreover, they place seed within their own selves.
The sacrificer eats last. The whey is indeed cattle; thus they establish the sacrificer in cattle.

Anuvāka 4: The Varuṇapraghāsa in the Rājasūya. {1.6.4.1} Prajāpati, having become Savitṛ, created offspring. They disregarded him; they departed from him. Having become Varuṇa, he seized those offspring with Varuṇa’s noose. Those offspring were seized by Varuṇa. Seeking protection, they ran back again to Prajāpati. Prajāpati saw these Varuṇapraghāsa offerings; he offered them. By means of them, he indeed released the offspring from Varuṇa’s noose. Therefore, the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings are offered.

{1.6.4.2} [He did this] so that the offspring would not be seized by Varuṇa. Their right arm was bent downward and their left was extended. He dug out this second altar on the south side. Thereby, he extended the right arm of the offspring. Because they dig out a second altar on the south side, therefore the performer of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices has both arms extended in yonder world, for he has conquered through the sacrifice. The two altars are separated by the distance of a span; they are not to be contiguous.

Therefore, the two shoulders [of the altar] are one span apart. Upon the northern altar-ground, he throws up the high-altar (*uttaravedi*). The high-altar is indeed cattle; verily, he wins cattle. Moreover, it is for the sake of not interrupting the joints of the sacrifice. These five oblations are indeed accompanied by their respective *brāhmaṇa* explanations. Now, this [oblation] belongs to Indra and Agni. Indra and Agni are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath of the gods; in that there is an offering to Indra and Agni, [it is for the sake of obtaining] out-breath and in-breath.

Verily, he secures for himself the out-breath and the in-breath. Indra and Agni are the vigor and strength of the gods; in that there is an offering to Indra and Agni, he secures vigor and strength. There is a curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) for the Maruts and a curd-mixture for Varuṇa; there is a ewe and a ram. Verily, through this pair, he releases offspring from the noose of Varuṇa. They are hairy for the sake of their sacrificial purity.

He scatters *śamī* leaves; verily, he bestows fodder upon these two. Prajāpati did not obtain food. By means of this oblation with a hundred kindling-sticks, he won food. That there are more than a hundred *śamī* leaves is for the winning of food. Karīra fruits indeed belong to Soma. And the oblation belonging to Soma truly causes rain to fall from heaven. That there are karīra fruits [is for that purpose].

By means of the very gentle oblation, he secures rain from heaven. There is a cake on one potsherd for Ka; it is for the welfare of creatures. There are bowls of groats for each person; thus, he releases the creatures already born from the noose of Varuṇa. One is in excess; thus, he releases the creatures yet to be born from the noose of Varuṇa.

Anuvāka 5: The Varuṇapraghāsa offerings in the Rājasūya sacrifice. {1.6.5.1} He places the other oblations on the northern altar; he places the offering to the Maruts on the southern altar. Thus he yokes her with the pole removed; moreover, he thereby takes away their strength. Therefore, from both the priesthood and the nobility, the common people depart elsewhere. He proceeds first with the offering to the Maruts; thus he expiates the untruth. With the subsequent offering to Varuṇa, he finally expiates Varuṇa for whatever the Adhvaryu has done.

The Pratiprasthātṛ performs that [rite]. Therefore, what the superior one does, the inferior one does. He makes the wife recite [the formula]; he thereby makes her pure for sacrifice. Moreover, he leads her toward austerity. If she were not to declare him who is her lover, she would obstruct a dear kinsman. She should point him out, saying, "This man is my lover. Having pointed him out, he causes him to be seized by the noose of Varuṇa.

With the verse, "We invoke the Praghāsya gods," he leads the wife forward. Even though she has not been previously summoned, he has indeed summoned her. If the wife were to recite the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), the sacrificer would be deprived of his virility; therefore, the sacrificer himself recites it, thereby placing virility within his own self. Both of them recite the offering verse (*yājyā*) for the sake of possessing shared virility. When he says, "What in the village, what in the forest," he thus propitiates Varuṇa according to the injunction. Indeed, the Āhavanīya fire has the sacrificer as its deity.

{1.6.5.4} The southern fire has the rival as its deity. If he were to offer in the Āhavanīya fire, he would cause the sacrificer to be seized by the noose of Varuṇa. He offers in the southern fire; thus he causes the rival alone to be seized by the noose of Varuṇa. He offers with a winnowing basket; thus he propitiates another Varuṇa. Having placed it upon his head, he offers; thus he propitiates Varuṇa from the very head. Standing facing west, he offers. {Editor’s Note:
This verse, located within the square brackets, became eight-line due to an error in the *padapāṭha* or a misplacement of the line break.}

Turning westward, he is indeed released from Varuṇa’s noose. "The doers of the rite have performed the rite," he says; "having paid the debt to the gods, go home free from debt"—this is indeed what he says. That which remains over of what was taken with a *yajus* formula belongs to Varuṇa: namely, the husks and the scrapings. With the husks and the scrapings he goes down to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). By means of that which was seized by Varuṇa, he performs a sacrifice to appease Varuṇa. He goes down to the purificatory bath into the waters.

Varuṇa is indeed in the waters. Thus he propitiates Varuṇa directly. "The noose of Varuṇa is cast off," he says; verily, he is released from Varuṇa’s noose. They return without looking back, for the sake of concealment from Varuṇa. "Thou art fuel; may we prosper," he says; with fuel they approach Agni while paying him homage. "Thou art splendor; bestow splendor upon me," he says; verily, he places splendor within himself.

Anuvāka 6: The Sākamedha in the Rājasūya {1.6.6.1} The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. Agni said, "This body of mine is the Anīkavatī (the 'Possessing-Army'); satisfy it, and then you shall overcome the Asuras. The gods offered a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Anīkavat. Agni Anīkavat, gratified by his own portion, produced fourfold armies. Thereupon the gods prospered, and the Asuras were defeated.

{1.6.6.2} When he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Anīkavat, he gratifies Agni Anīkavat with his own portion. That Agni Anīkavat, gratified by his own portion, generates fourfold armies. Indeed, that Agni Anīkavat is yonder sun; its rays are the armies. He offers [the oblation] together with the rising sun; thus he directly generates armies for him. Those Asuras, being defeated and fleeing, took refuge in heaven and earth.

Those gods offered a pap (caru) to the Maruts, the Sāṃtapanas. They heated it on both sides by means of Heaven and Earth. In that he offers a pap to the Maruts, the Sāṃtapanas, the sacrificer thereby heats his rivals on both sides by means of Heaven and Earth. He offers it at midday; for then the sun shines most intensely. It is a pap; thus he heats them from every side.
Those gods, being about to achieve victory on the morrow, prepared a *caru* offering for the *Gṛhamedhins* in the milk of all [the cows].

"We shall fast today, having already eaten our fill," they said. "To whom does this belong? To whom will it belong tomorrow? That [oblation] was cooked; they did not eat of it while it was still unoffered, for the gods do not eat what has not been offered. They said, "To whom shall we offer this? "To the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhins," they replied. They offered it to the Maruts, the Gṛhamedhins.

{1.6.6.5} Thereupon the gods prospered and the asuras were defeated. For whomsoever, knowing thus, they offer in the house to the Maruts, the householders, he prospers in himself and his rival is defeated. Whatever in the sacrifice is performed in a simple manner is beneficial to cattle; and this [offering] is indeed performed in a simple manner, in that there is neither fuel nor sacrificial grass (barhis), and he does not recite the *sāmidhenī* verses.

{1.6.6.6} No *prayāja* offerings are made; no *anūyāja* offerings are made. He who knows thus becomes possessed of cattle. He offers the two *ājyabhāga* portions; he does not deprive the eyes of the sacrifice. He offers to the Maruts, the householders (*gṛhamedhin*); verily, he satisfies them with their own portion. He offers to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt for the sake of firm standing. It concludes with the *iḍā*. The *iḍā* is indeed cattle; verily, he finds firm standing in cattle at the end.

Anuvāka 7: The Sākamedha in the Rājasūya {1.6.7.1} If the wife were to eat of the Gṛhamedhīya offering, she would indeed become a housewife (gṛhamedhī), but his sacrifice would be frustrated. If she were not to eat, she would not be a housewife, and his sacrifice would not be frustrated. They should cook a meal for a neighbor; she should eat of that. Thus she becomes a housewife, and his sacrifice is not frustrated.

{1.6.7.2} Those gods, having sacrificed with the Gṛhamedhīya offering, became satiated; they anointed themselves and rubbed themselves [with unguents]; they let the calves stay with their mothers. The Asuras sent hunger against them. Having found no place among the gods, it returned again to the Asuras. Having sacrificed with the Gṛhamedhīya, they become satiated; they anoint themselves and rub themselves.

{1.6.7.3} They let the calves stay with their mothers. By this, the sacrificer sends hunger to his rival. Those gods, having sacrificed with the *gṛhamedhīya* offering, deposited the scrapings for Indra, thinking, "Tomorrow Indra will come to us, having received his portion. Indra, having received his portion, came to them. Having sacrificed with the *gṛhamedhīya*, one should deposit the scrapings for Indra. Thus Indra himself comes to him, having received his portion. He offers in the *gārhapatya* fire.

{1.6.7.4} By means of his own portion, he indeed causes him to prosper. He calls upon the bull; that is his *vaṣaṭ*-call. Moreover, by that, the sacrificer appropriates the power and vigor of his rival. Having slain Vṛtra, Indra went to the furthest distance, thinking, "I have committed a fault. He said, "Who will know this? They [the Maruts] said, "O Maruts, let us choose a boon."

{1.6.7.5} "Now let us know: let the oblation be set aside for us first! Thus they mocked him; that is the reason for the name of the Krīḍins (the Mockers). When the first oblation is set aside for the Maruts, the Krīḍins, it is for the sake of victory. He offers it together with the rising sun; for it was in this very world that Indra slew Vṛtra—this is for the sake of prosperity. These five oblations are indeed accompanied by explanatory passages (*brāhmaṇa*). This [passage] regarding the offering to Indra and Agni is the *brāhmaṇa*.

Now, this oblation for Indra takes place. Having slain Vṛtra, Indra indeed set aside this as his special portion (*uddhāra*) above all other deities. In that there is this oblation for Indra, the sacrificer sets aside that very portion above all other offspring. There is a cake on one potsherd for Viśvakarman; by means of it, the sacrificer secures all ritual actions.

Anuvāka 8: The Piṇḍapitṛyajña in the Rājasūya {1.6.8.1} By means of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, Prajāpati created offspring. By means of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, he released them from the noose of Varuṇa. By means of the Sākamedha sacrifices, he established them. By means of the Tryambaka offerings, he appeased Rudra. By means of the Pitṛyajña, he caused them to go to the heavenly world. In that the sacrificer performs the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, he thereby creates offspring. By means of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, he releases them from the nooses of Varuṇa. By means of the Sākamedha sacrifices, he establishes them. By means of the Tryambaka offerings, he appeases Rudra.

{1.6.8.2} By means of the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), he causes [the sacrificer] to go to the heavenly world. He offers from the south while wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*); for the ancestors turn toward the south. Disregarding that, however, he should offer from the north while wearing the cord over the left shoulder (*upavīya*); for both the gods and the ancestors are being worshipped. Moreover, in that he places the oblation on the southern half [of the fire], by that he follows the southern course. He offers a cake on six potsherds (*ṣaṭkapāla*) to Soma accompanied by the ancestors (*pitṛmat*). Soma, indeed, is the year accompanied by the ancestors.

{1.6.8.3} He gratifies the year itself. He offers parched grains (*dhānā*) to the *barhiṣad* fathers; for the months are indeed the *barhiṣad* fathers. He thus gratifies the months. In whichever season a man dies, that [season] becomes his state in yonder world. The parched grains are of many forms for the sake of conquering the days and nights. He offers a stirred drink (*mantha*) to the *agniṣvātta* fathers; for the half-months are indeed the *agniṣvātta* fathers.

He gratifies the half-months themselves. It is [the milk] from a cow that has recently calved; for she yields what belongs to the ancestors. That which is full belongs to humans; the upper half belongs to the gods, and the lower half belongs to the ancestors. He churns one half, for one half belongs to the ancestors. He churns with a single [hand].

For the ancestors have but one [lineage]. He churns toward the south; for the movement of the ancestors is from left to right. He churns without taking hold [of the vessel]; for that goes to the ancestors. He digs up the altar toward this direction; for both the gods and the ancestors are sacrificed to. It has four corners; for the ancestors extend along all the directions. It is not dug out [deeply].

For the gods [dwell] in the sky; Agni is established in the middle, for the gods are established at the end. The fuel becomes larger than the firewood for the sake of distinction. He encloses it; for the world of the fathers is hidden from the world of men. That which is split along the joint belongs to the gods; that which is between [the joints] belongs to men.

{1.6.8.7} That which has roots belongs to the ancestors. The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) has roots for the sake of distinction. He spreads it toward the south, for the movement of the ancestors is toward the south. He goes around three times; for the ancestors are in the third world from here; he thus gratifies them. He goes around again three times; thus they amount to six.

There are six seasons; thus he gratifies the seasons. If he were to take up the *prastara* with a sacrificial formula (*yajus*), the sacrificer would be liable to die prematurely. If he were not to take it up, he would be without a support. He should simply set it down silently; then he does not die prematurely, nor is he without a support. As for the three enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), he should lay them around.

{1.6.8.9} If he were not to enclose [the altar] with enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), Death would seize the sacrificer; the *rakṣases* would destroy the sacrifice. He lays down two enclosing-sticks for the warding off of the *rakṣases*; moreover, he thereby releases the sacrificer from death itself. If they were to bring up three oblations (*havir*) at a time, three of them would die together. They bring them up one by one in succession; thus, one of them dies after the other. [He gives] a cushion (*kaśipu*) to one who desires a cushion.

[He offers] a cushion for Upabarhaṇya, collyrium for Āñjanya, and ointment for Abhyañjanya; thus he gratifies them each according to their respective share. Anuvāka 9: The Pitṛyajña in the Rājasūya. "Recite for Agni, who is being kindled, for the gods and the fathers," he says. For both the gods and the fathers are sacrificed to. He recites one verse; for the fathers have one [share]. He recites three times; for the gods have three [shares]. He pours the two libations (āghāra); this is to avoid the interruption of the joints of the sacrifice. He does not choose an *ārṣeya* (ancestral lineage), nor does he choose a *hotṛ*.

{1.6.9.2} In that he chooses a *ṛṣi*-descendant [as his *ṛtvij*], and in that he chooses a *hotṛ*, the sacrificer might become subject to premature death, and the *hotṛ* might become subject to premature death. Therefore, he does not choose one, for the protection of the sacrificer and the *hotṛ*. He performs the *prayāja* offerings excluding the *barhis*. The *barhis* is indeed offspring; thus he releases offspring from death. He performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings.

He does not let the two eyes of the sacrifice come between [himself and the offering]. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he sacrifices to Soma; for these oblations have the ancestors as their deity. He cuts off five portions, for there are five deities: the two *puro’nuvākyās*, the *yājyā*, the deity, and the *vaṣaṭ*-call. It is these very ones that he gratifies. He cuts off the portions continuously.

{1.6.9.4} For the continuity of the seasons: with the first *puro’nuvākyā* he announces them; with the second he leads them forth; with the *yājyā* he causes them to arrive. Or rather, the ancestors are in the third world from here. With the first *puro’nuvākyā* he brings them across from the day; with the second, from the night. With the *yājyā* he causes them to arrive. Having cut off the portions from the south, he steps across toward the north for the sake of distinction.

He causes the announcement with "Svadhā! The response is "Let there be Svadhā! He utters the *vaṣaṭ* call as "Svadhā namaḥ! For the *svadhā*-utterance belongs to the ancestors (*pitṛs*). He sacrifices to Soma first; for the ancestors have Soma as their *prayāja*. He sacrifices to Soma accompanied by the ancestors; Soma accompanied by the ancestors is indeed the year; thus he sacrifices to the year itself. He sacrifices to the ancestors seated on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣad*).

Those who are indeed performers of sacrifice are the *pitaraḥ* seated on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣadaḥ*); it is them that he worships at that time. He worships the *pitaraḥ* consumed by fire (*agniṣvāttāḥ*). Those who are householders but do not perform sacrifices are the *pitaraḥ* consumed by fire; it is them that he worships at that time. He worships Agni Kavyavāhana; it is that very fire of the *pitaraḥ* which he worships at that time.

{1.6.9.7} Moreover, it is just as when one sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. With the words, "This for thee, O father, and for those who follow thee," he places [the food] on three corners. Therefore, they do not mention the names [of ancestors] beyond the third generation; for only so many are sacrificed to. He says, "O fathers, rejoice here according to your respective portions. For the fathers are modest. They go out toward the north. This is indeed the direction of men; thus they go out following their own direction.

{1.6.9.8} They pay reverence to the Āhavanīya fire. By doing so, they truly satisfy him while the Āhavanīya is still present; then they proceed elsewhere. They continue to pay reverence until the exhaustion [of the breath]. Having made Agni himself their witness, they offer satisfaction to the ancestors. Those who pay reverence until the exhaustion reach the very end of their vital breaths. "Thee, O fair to behold," he says.

The breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed "well-looking" (*susaṃdṛk*). They place the breath within themselves. He says, "Yoke now, O Indra, thy two bay steeds. Thus he yokes the breath again. With the words, "They have eaten, they have rejoiced," they stand in worship before the *gārhapatya* fire. "They have eaten, they have rejoiced—now we stand in worship before thee," is what this means. With the words, "The Soma-loving fathers have rejoiced," they enter [the hall]. "The fathers have rejoiced—now we enter unto thee," is what this means. He sprinkles water around; he thus purifies them.

{1.6.9.10} Moreover, he indeed satisfies [the gods]. He prospers with offspring and cattle—he who knows thus. He performs two after-offerings (*anūyāja*) without the *barhis* grass. The *barhis* is indeed offspring; verily, he releases offspring from death. He performs four fore-offerings (*prayāja*) and two after-offerings; they amount to six. There are six seasons; verily, he gratifies the seasons. The wife does not sit near the altar, nor do they perform the *saṃyāja* offerings. If the wife were to sit near the altar, or if they were to perform the *saṃyāja* offerings, [it would be as follows].
She would be subject to death; therefore, he does not sit behind her, nor do they perform the *saṃyājyā* offerings, for the protection of the wife.

Anuvāka 10: The Tryambaka Oblation in the Rājasūya {1.6.10.1} He offers one cake on a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) for each person. He thereby expiates the Rudras for the offspring already born. One [cake] is in excess; he thereby expiates the Rudras for the offspring yet to be born. They are made from cakes on a single potsherd; thus he expiates the Rudra in a single manner. He does not pour clarified butter over them; for were he to pour butter over them, he would make Rudra a wanderer among the people. They proceed with a single firebrand (they lead the firebrand).

{1.6.10.2} For that is the portion of Rudra. They go toward this quarter; for this indeed is the quarter of Rudra. Thus, he propitiates Rudra in his own quarter. Rudra did not stand by the oblation when it was offered without an animal victim. He should point out a specific animal, saying, "This one is your animal," naming whichever person he hates. It is him whom he hates that he points out as the animal for him. If he should have no one to hate, he should say, "A mole is your animal."

He does not harm domestic animals, nor wild ones. He offers at a crossroads; for this is indeed the "shackle" (paḍbīśa) of the fires. Thus he offers in a place possessed of fire. He offers with the middle leaf, for this [leaf] is a sacrificial ladle (sruk). Now, however, it should be offered with the end [leaf] alone; thus he propitiates Rudra from the very end.

"This, O Rudra, is your portion, together with your sister Ambikā," he says. Autumn, indeed, is his sister Ambikā; with her, he strikes down whomever he strikes down. With her, he pacifies him. "A remedy for the cattle," he says; for as many domestic animals as there are, for them he provides a remedy. "We have appeased Rudra, O Mother," he says; he thus invokes this very blessing.

He says, "We worship Tryambaka," for he thereby says, "May I be released from death, but not from immortality. They scatter [the grains]; they seek to obtain fortune (*bhaga*). Having placed them in a bag, they tie it up; it is just as one provides lodging for a person who is traveling. He says, "This is your portion, O Rudra," for the sake of complete satisfaction. They return without looking back. He sprinkles water around, for the sake of Rudra’s concealment. Indeed, these [priests] fall away from this world.
Those who perform the Tryambaka offerings, having returned, offer a *caru* oblation to Āditya. This earth, indeed, is Aditi; verily, they find firm support upon her.

Prapāṭhaka 7, Anuvāka 1: The Śunāsīra [offering] in the Rājasūya. {1.7.1.1} These five oblations have Brāhmaṇa explanations. Now he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Indra Śunāsīra. Indra Śunāsīra is indeed the year; verily by means of the year he secures food for him. There is milk for Vāyu. Vāyu is the one who causes rain to be bestowed; he himself causes rain to be bestowed upon him. There is a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya.
Or rather, the rain is held by the sun in yonder world; he himself bestows that rain upon him.

A plough drawn by twelve oxen is the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity. The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. Those gods said to Agni: "With you as our hero, we shall overcome the Asuras. He replied, "I will divide myself threefold. He divided himself threefold: one-third as Agni, one-third as Rudra, and one-third as Varuṇa.

He said, "Who is this fourth one? "I am," said Indra. "Let us two unite," he said. They united. That Indra became the fourth part (*turīya*). Because Indra became the fourth part, that is the reason for the name *Indraturīya*. From that, the gods indeed conquered. When the *Indraturīya* is offered, it is for the sake of victory.

{1.7.1.4} A milch-cow that carries [her calf] is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Insofar as she carries [her calf], she belongs to Agni; insofar as she is a cow (*go*), she belongs to Rudra; insofar as she is a milch-cow (*dhenu*), she belongs to Indra; and insofar as she is female and yet self-controlled (*dāntā*), she belongs to Varuṇa for the sake of prosperity. Prajāpati created the sacrifice.

{1.7.1.5} When he had been created, the *rakṣases* sought to destroy him. Prajāpati fashioned these deities from his own self; with them, he drove away the *rakṣases* from the quarters. In that he offers the fivefold oblation, the sacrificer thereby drives away the *rakṣases* from the quarters. He says, "The *rakṣas* is crushed! The *rakṣas* is burnt up!"—verily, he burns up the *rakṣases*. He says, "To Agni, the slayer of *rakṣases*, svāhā!"—verily, he provides a portion for the deities who have been victorious. A chariot drawn by four horses is the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity.

{1.7.1.6} Having slain Vṛtra and defeated the Asuras, Indra could not capture Namuci, the Asura. He seized him with his *śakti* (thunderbolt). The two grappled together. He became more difficult for him to overcome. Indra said: "Let us make a compact; then I shall release you. You shall not strike me with anything dry, nor with anything wet."

{1.7.1.7} "Neither by day nor by night. He poured out this foam of the waters. It was neither dry nor moist; it was when the dawn had broken but the sun had not yet risen. This was neither by day nor by night. In this world, he turned his head upward with the foam of the waters. That followed after him as "the betrayer of a friend" (*mitradhruk*).

He produced these *apāmārga* plants; he offered them as oblations. With them, indeed, he struck away the *rakṣases*. In that there is an offering of *apāmārga*, it is for the striking away of the *rakṣases*. They proceed with a single fire-brand (*ulmuka*), for that is the portion of the *rakṣases*. They go toward this direction; for this is the direction of the *rakṣases*. Thus, he strikes away the *rakṣases* in their own direction.

{1.7.1.9} He offers in a self-made salt-flat or in a cleft; for this is the abode of the Rakṣases. He thus slays the Rakṣases in their own abode. He offers with a ladle made of *parṇa*-wood; for the *parṇa* is the Brahman. By means of the Brahman, he thus slays the Rakṣases. "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he says; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he slays the Rakṣases. "The Rakṣas is slain! We have struck down the Rakṣas! he says, for the destruction of the Rakṣases. Whatever garment he wears, that is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the removal [of the Rakṣases]. They return without looking back, for the concealment of the Rakṣases.

Anuvāka 2: The Devikā Offerings in the Rājasūya {1.7.2.1} He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Dhātṛ. Dhātṛ is indeed the Year; verily by means of the Year he causes offspring to be born for him. Anumati gives her approval after him; Rākā grants him what is given; Sinīvālī brings forth; and when the offspring have been born, Kuhū bestows speech upon them. A pair of cattle is the sacrificial fee for prosperity. He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu;
[he offers] a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Viṣṇu.

{1.7.2.2} A cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu. Agni is indeed vigor; Indra is vigor; Viṣṇu is vigor. He establishes progeny once born upon vigor. Therefore, progeny is vigorous. A dwarf bull that draws [the cart] is the sacrificial fee. In that it is a drawer, it belongs to Agni; in that it is a bull, it belongs to Indra.

By that [offering] it belongs to Indra; because [the sacrificer] is dwarfed, it belongs to Viṣṇu for the sake of prosperity. He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Soma, a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra-Soma, and a pap to Soma. Soma is indeed the placer of seed; Agni is the progenitor of offspring; Indra is the bestower upon those who have grown old. It is Soma alone who places seed in him.

Agni generates offspring; Indra bestows it when grown. A brown animal is the sacrificial fee for prosperity. He offers a *caru* oblation to Soma and Pūṣan, and a *caru* oblation to Indra and Pūṣan. Soma, indeed, is the depositor of seed; Pūṣan is the progenitor of cattle; Indra is the one who causes the grown ones to be bestowed. Verily, Soma deposits seed for him, and Pūṣan procreates cattle.

Indra bestows the elders. There is an oblation of cooked rice for Pūṣan; for Pūṣan is indeed this earth, and thus he finds firm support upon her. A dark-grey animal is the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity. Indeed, a man approaches much that is impure; therefore, he offers an oblation on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara. Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; by means of the year itself, he makes him palatable. Gold is the sacrificial fee.

Gold is indeed a means of purification; it purifies him. A Rājanya indeed commits much untruth: he carries off his sister, he oppresses a Brāhmaṇa, and he speaks falsehood. When untruth is committed, Varuṇa seizes the offender. He offers a sacrificial pap (*caru*) made of barley, dedicated to Varuṇa; thus he releases him from the noose of Varuṇa. A horse is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); for the horse has Varuṇa as its deity. This is for the sake of prosperity.

Anuvāka 3: The Oblations of the Ratnins in the Rājasūya {1.7.3.1} These oblations belong to the Ratnins. They are indeed the bestowers of the kingdom; they are the supporters of the kingdom. Those who are the bestowers of the kingdom and those who are the supporters of the kingdom—they alone bestow the kingdom upon him. He truly becomes the possessor of the kingdom. If he were to offer them after collecting [the materials] together, they would not be "ratnins" (jewels/precious ones). He offers them according to their respective order for the sake of their being ratnins.

{1.7.3.2} If he were to offer [the oblations] all at once, he would obtain only as much blessing as one obtains by means of a single oblation. He offers them day after day; thus he obtains an ever-increasing blessing and approaches more numerous sacrificial rites. He offers a pap for Bṛhaspati in the house of the Brahman priest; verily, he sharpens his spiritual power (brahman) from the very beginning. Moreover, he causes the ruling power (kṣatra) to follow the spiritual power. A white-backed bull is the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity.

{1.7.3.3} An offering on eleven potsherds for Indra is for the house of the Rājanya; verily, he wins power (*indriya*). A bull is the sacrificial fee for prosperity. A pap for Aditi is for the house of the Mahiṣī; Aditi is indeed this earth; verily, he finds support in her. A milch cow is the sacrificial fee for prosperity. A pap for Bhaga is for the house of the Vāvātā; verily, he bestows fortune (*bhaga*) upon him. A four-year-old cow that has miscarried is the sacrificial fee for prosperity.

{1.7.3.4} For the sake of the woman who has been superseded, he offers a *caru* of black rice, crushed with his fingernails, in the house of the *Nairṛta*. He thus expiates evil, even *Nirṛti* herself; a black female goat (*kūṭā*) is the sacrificial fee for prosperity. In the house of the commander of the army, [he offers] a cake on eight potsherds to Agni. He thus shatters his enemy's army; gold is the sacrificial fee for prosperity. In the house of the charioteer, [he offers] a cake on ten potsherds to Varuṇa. He thus secures for himself the *Varuṇasava* sacrifice; a large castrated bull (*mahāniraṣṭa*) is the sacrificial fee for prosperity.
In the house of the village headman, [he offers] a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts.

The Maruts are indeed food; verily, he wins food for himself. A speckled cow is the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity. An offering on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ is performed in the house of the chamberlain for the sake of successful delivery. A soiled horse is the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity. An offering on two potsherds to the Aśvins is performed in the house of the charioteer. The Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods; through them, he provides medicine for him. Two horses born of the same mother are the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity. An oblation of cooked rice to Pūṣan is performed in the house of the tax-collector.

Pūṣan is indeed food; verily, he wins food. A dark-grey animal is the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity. In the house of the grain-gatherer, there is a pap of *gāvīdhuka* grains for Rudra; thus, at the very end, he propitiates Rudra. A dappled bull with a white tail-tip is the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity. These offerings number twelve; the year has twelve months. By means of the year, he wins for him the kingdom; he becomes the very kingdom itself.

{1.7.3.7} If he were not to offer [the oblation] in return, the possessors of jewels would withhold their blessings. He offers in return: a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra the Good Protector (Sutrāman), and for Indra the Deliverer from Distress (Aṃhomuc). Thus he secures the blessings themselves. "He has come to us; this king is our Vṛtra-slayer," he says, "having become king, may he slay Vṛtra. By this he invokes that very blessing. There is an offering to Mitra and Bṛhaspati, prepared with the milk of a white cow that has a white calf.

{1.7.3.8} He places the oblation for Mitra upon that for Bṛhaspati. Thus he provides him with both the spiritual power (*brahman*) and the ruling power (*kṣatra*) in harmony. Moreover, he establishes the ruling power within the spiritual power. He proceeds first with the offering for Bṛhaspati; thus he sharpens the spiritual power for him from the very beginning. Moreover, he causes the ruling power to follow after the spiritual power. The altar is self-made; the sacrificial grass is self-cut; the fuel is self-prepared—for the winning of what has not yet been won.
Therefore, the forest is conquered by kings. That very white cow with a white calf is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the sake of prosperity.

Anuvāka 4: The oblations of the *devasū* in the Rājasūya. These are the oblations of the *devasū*. So many indeed are the *sava*s (impulses/empowerments) of the gods. They themselves bestow those *sava*s upon him; they empower him. Agni empowers him among householders; Soma, among the lords of the forest; Rudra, among cattle; Bṛhaspati, among speeches; Indra, among the eldest; Mitra, among the truthful.

Varuṇa is the lord of the laws. All this indeed comes to pass. "May Savitṛ impel you among those who impel," with these words he takes his hand for the sake of impulsion. "O gods who are the impellers of the gods," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula (*yajus*). "For great sovereignty, for great overlordship, for great royal power over the people," he says; he thus invokes this very blessing. "This one, O Bharatas, is your king; Soma is the king of us Brāhmaṇas," he says; therefore the Brāhmaṇas have Soma as their king. "That name, that kingship, has been established against [the enemy]," he says.

He bestows sovereignty upon him. "Varuṇa has clothed himself in his own body," he says; thus he secures for himself the Varuṇa-consecration. "We have become the followers of the pure Mitra's vow," he says; he thus makes him a pure follower of the vow. "We have meditated upon the name of the great *ṛta*," he says; he thus causes him to understand it. "All the hosts have become [the subjects] of Varuṇa," he says; he thus makes him one whose host is complete. "Mitra has overcome hostility with friendly acts," he says. (TS 1.8.10.f)

He causes him to cross over enmity itself. "The worshipful ones have purified [him] by means of the *ṛta*," he says; thus he makes him palatable. "Trita has driven away our old age," he says; thus he bestows life-span upon him. He wipes [the offering-spoon] with two verses; the sacrificer has two feet—for the sake of stability. From the cake on eleven potsherds for Agni-Soma and from the oblations of the *devasū* sacrifice, he cuts portions together for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Verily, he encloses him on both sides with the deities. He strides the strides of Viṣṇu; having become Viṣṇu himself, he conquers these worlds.

Anuvāka 5: The Taking of Water and the Fetching of Water in the Rājasūya Sacrifice {1.7.5.1} He offers with the formula, "Ye are purposeful. By means of the oblation, he redeems them and then takes [the water]. Moreover, he takes [the water] that has been consecrated by the call to prepare the oblation (*haviṣkṛta*). He takes [the water] from flowing streams; for these indeed are the domain (*rāṣṭra*) of the waters. Verily, he secures the domain for him. Moreover, they carry prosperity toward him. He says, "Thou art the lord of the waters"; verily, he creates a pair. He says, "Thou art the male wave"; [verily, he bestows virility].

He thus makes it possessed of waves. "Thou art Vṛṣasena," he says; he thus sharpens his army. "Ye are dwellers in the fold," he says; these indeed are the subjects of the waters; he thus bestows a subject-people upon him. "Ye are the vigor of the Maruts," he says; the Maruts are indeed food; he thus secures food for himself. "Ye are sun-bright," he says.

He has indeed made the kingdom resplendent. "You are sun-skinned," he says; for this is the truth: when it rains. When it shines and rains, that is untruth. Verily, he secures both truth and untruth; neither truth nor untruth shall harm him who knows thus. "You are the cheering ones," he says; he has indeed made the kingdom possessed of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*).

"You are the submissive ones," he says; thus he makes the kingdom submissive. "You are the powerful ones," he says; the *śakvarī* verses are indeed cattle; thus he wins cattle. "You are the all-sustaining ones," he says; thus he makes the kingdom rich in milk. "You are the people-sustaining ones," he says; thus he makes the kingdom rich in sensory power (*indriya*). "You are the fiery ones of Agni," he says.

He has indeed made the kingdom radiant. "You are the essence of the waters, the essence of the plants," he says; he has indeed made the kingdom sweet. He draws the *sārasvata* cup. Sarasvatī is indeed the back of the waters; he thus makes him the back of his equals. He draws it with sixteen [verses]. Man consists of sixteen parts; in the man, as he truly is, he bestows vigor. He offers with sixteen and draws with sixteen.
They amount to thirty-two. The *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables; speech is the *anuṣṭubh*, and speech is all the meters. Verily, by means of speech, he consecrates him with all the meters.

Anuvāka 6: The Purification of the Water in the Rājasūya "O divine waters, unite with those that are honey-sweet," he says. By means of the *brahman*, he thus unites them. "Sit down, unsubdued," he says. By means of the *brahman*, he thus causes them to settle. He settles them between the *dhiṣṇiya* hearth of the Hotṛ and that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. The Hotṛ indeed belongs to Agni; the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin belongs to Indra. Thus, by means of both brilliance and sensory power (*indriya*), he encompasses the kingdom on both sides.
He purifies with gold. For they purify the oblation with two strainers for the sake of distinction.

It is a *śatamāna* [weight]; man has a life-span of a hundred years and possesses a hundred powers; thus he becomes established in life and power. "Thou art uncrushed," he says, for this is indeed uncrushed. "The kinsman of speech," he says, for this is indeed the kinsman of speech. "Born of heat," he says, for this is indeed born of heat. "Thou art the gift of Soma," he says.

{1.7.6.3} For this is the gift of Soma. He says, "I purify you, the bright ones, with the bright [Soma]," for the waters are bright and gold is bright. He says, "The radiant ones, with the radiant," for the waters are radiant and gold is radiant. He says, "The immortal ones, with the immortal," for the waters are immortal and gold is immortal.

"Swāhā to the Rājasūya! he says; for he purifies them for the sake of the Rājasūya. With the verse addressed to Varuṇa, "These [waters] are the companions at the feast, glorious and free from disease," he draws [the water]; thus he secures the very pressing of Varuṇa. He draws it with a single [verse]; he bestows vigor upon the sacrificer in a single manner. "Thou art the caul of the Kṣatra, thou art the womb of the Kṣatra"—with these words he hands over the linen garment and the turban, for the sake of providing a common origin. He purifies [himself] with one hundred and one bunches of *darbha* grass. Man indeed has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundredfold vigor; the self is the one hundred and first.

{1.7.6.5} As great as man is, into him he places vigor. He causes him to eat curd; verily, he wins sensory power. He causes him to eat udumbara fruit; for the attainment of food. He causes him to eat young grass shoots; verily, he makes him strong with the *surā* offering. These are the "attainments" (*āvid*); verily, they cause him to attain attainment.

Agni protects him with the *gārhapatya* fire; Indra with power (*indriya*); Pūṣan with cattle; Mitra and Varuṇa with out-breath and in-breath. Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra; he scratched the sky; it became the path of Aryaman. He ran to Heaven and Earth with the words, "O Heaven and Earth of unbroken vows, firm in your ordinances. Impelled by these two alone, Indra struck Vṛtra with the thunderbolt.
When he says, "O Heaven and Earth of unbroken vows, firm in your ordinances," [he does so for this reason].

{1.7.6.7} Impelled by these two, the sacrificer hurls the thunderbolt at his rival. "The divine Aditi, all-formed, has been won," he says. This earth, indeed, is the divine Aditi, all-formed; verily, he finds firm support upon her. "This one, so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, has been won for this people, for this kingdom," he says. Verily, he endows him with the people and the kingdom. "For great dominion, for great sovereignty, for great lordship over the people," he says.
He utters this very benediction: "O Bharatas, he is your king; Soma is the king of us Brāhmaṇas," he says. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇas have Soma as their king.

"Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra," with these words he hands over the bow for the sake of victory. "Ye are the harassers of enemies," [with these words] he hands over the arrows; thus they indeed harass his enemies. "Protect me from behind, protect me across, protect me from the front," he says. There are three directions of flight: backward, across, and forward; it is from these that they protect him. "Protect me from the quarters," he says; it is from the quarters that they protect him.

"Protect me from all destructive powers," he says; thus they protect him from the unlimited. With the *triṣṭubh* verse, "The golden-colored [horses] at the dawning of the dawns," he raises his arms. The *triṣṭubh* is indeed power and vigor; verily, he places power and vigor upon himself from above.

Anuvāka 7: Meditation on the Conquest of the Quarters in the Rājasūya [1.7.7.41] He establishes the quarters for the conquest of the quarters. If he were to advance [merely] after [the others], he would conquer the quarters, but he might also become deranged. He advances after [the thought] in his mind; thus he conquers the quarters and does not become deranged. "Mount the fuel-stick," he says; verily, he wins splendor.

"Mount the fierce one," he says; verily, he wins power. "Mount the Virāj," he says; verily, he wins food. "Mount the northern one," he says; verily, he wins cattle. "Mount the upward one," he says; verily, he conquers the world of heaven. He rises up after it for the attainment of the world of heaven.

{1.7.7.3} This [offering] belongs to the Maruts. The Maruts are indeed food; verily, he wins food for himself. It consists of twenty-one potsherds for the sake of stability. That troop which is to be recited in the forest, he places in the middle. By means of the domestic animals, he thus encompasses the wild animals. Therefore, wild animals are encompassed by domestic animals. Pṛthu Vainya was consecrated.

He did not become a sovereign. He saw these *pārtha* offerings; he offered them. By means of them, indeed, he became a sovereign. In that one offers the *pārtha* offerings, one becomes a sovereign. That which belongs to Bṛhaspati is the last of the former [offerings]; that which belongs to Indra is the first of the latter. Thus, it bestows upon him both the spiritual power (*brahman*) and the ruling power (*kṣatra*) in harmony. Moreover, it establishes the ruling power within the spiritual power itself.

{1.7.7.5} He offers six oblations before the consecration and six after it; thus they amount to twelve. Twelve months make a year, and the year is indeed the citadel of the gods. Thus, he enters the very citadel of the gods from the middle; for him, there is no injury from any quarter whatsoever. He offers the *aveṣṭi* (encircling) oblations to the beings. Death is born here and there; wherever death is born, [he offers these].

Therefore, he offers a propitiatory sacrifice for him; thus, one who has performed the Rājasūya reaches a full lifespan, for all his deaths have been warded off. Therefore, one who has performed the Rājasūya must not practice sorcery against anyone; rather, the sorcery recoils upon him and strikes him down.

Anuvāka 8: The Consecration in the Rājasūya {1.7.8.1} "Thou art the brilliance of Soma; may my brilliance be like thine," with these words he spreads out a tiger skin. Whatever brilliance is in Soma and whatever is in the tiger—that very brilliance he secures for himself. Of death, indeed, is this color, namely the tiger; gold is immortality. "Thou art immortality; protect me from death," with these words he places gold [upon it]. Verily, he interposes immortality between himself and death. It is a hundred-māna weight.

A man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred senses; he thus becomes firmly established in life itself and in the senses. With the words, "O lightning, protect me," he places [the stone] on top; he thus bestows protection upon him from both sides. With the words, "The biting serpents have been warded off," he pierces a eunuch with lead; he thereby offers a sacrifice to the biting serpents themselves. Therefore, the biting serpents bite the eunuch. With the words, "The head of Namuci is cast out," he throws away red iron; he thus casts away evil, which is Namuci himself. "The vital breaths of the self were consecrated first," so they say.

"Soma the King, Varuṇa, and those gods who are the impellers of dharma—may they each impel speech for you; may they each impel breath for you," he says. Thus, he consecrates the vital breaths within himself first. If he were to say, "I consecrate you with the splendor of Agni," he would indeed become full of splendor, but he would suffer from skin disease. He says, "I consecrate you with the glory of Soma. For man has Soma as his deity.

{1.7.8.4} He consecrates him with his own deity. "With the brilliance of Agni," he says; verily, he bestows brilliance upon him. "With the luster of Sūrya," he says; verily, he bestows luster upon him. "With the power of Indra," he says; verily, he bestows power upon him. "With the heroism of Mitra and Varuṇa," he says; verily, he bestows heroism upon him. "With the might of the Maruts," he says.

Verily, he bestows vigor upon him. "Thou art the lord of lords among lords," he says; verily, he makes him the lord of lords among lords. "Guard beyond the sky," he says; by this he means, "Guard beyond others. "They have turned together from below toward the north," he says; verily, he makes the kingdom stable for him. He offers with the remnant; Rudra indeed has the remnant as his portion. Verily, by means of his own portion, he propitiates Rudra.

{1.7.8.6} Having gone toward the north, he offers in the *agnīdh*’s station. This, indeed, is the quarter of Rudra. Thus, he propitiates Rudra in his own quarter. "O Rudra, that which is thy supreme name, Krayin"—so he says. For whatever is his supreme name, Krayin, by that indeed he strikes down whomsoever he strikes down; by that very name he pacifies him. "Thou art offered to him, thou art sacrificed to Yama"—so he says. Verily, from Yama he expiates his death.

{1.7.8.7} With the verse, "O Prajāpati, none other than you [possesses] these," he should offer an oblation in the house of her whom he desires, thinking, "May the kingdom be her offspring. Verily, the kingdom becomes her offspring. The Adhvaryu consecrates with a cup made of *parṇa* wood; verily, he bestows spiritual luster and brilliance upon him. With one made of *udumbara* wood, a Rājanya is consecrated; verily, he bestows vigor and food-eating power upon him. With one made of *aśvattha* wood, a Vaiśya is consecrated; verily, he bestows the people and prosperity upon him. With one made of *nyagrodha* wood, a Janya is consecrated; verily, he provides him with friends, and also for the sake of stability.

Anuvāka 9: Victory through the mounting of the chariot in the Rājasūya sacrifice. "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra," with these words he brings down the chariot for the sake of victory. "By the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, the two directors, I yoke thee," he says. Verily, by means of the sacred word (*brahman*) and by means of the two deities, he yokes it. He yokes one drawn by side-horses (*praṣṭivāhin*); for the chariot of the gods is indeed drawn by side-horses; verily, he yokes for him the very chariot of the gods. There are three horses; the chariot is the fourth; there are two charioteers on the left; thus they become six.

There are six seasons; verily, by means of the seasons he yokes him. He strides the strides of Viṣṇu; having become Viṣṇu himself, he conquers these worlds. The Kṣatriya who has been appointed as deputy takes hold of [the horse]; verily, he becomes the kingdom itself. He takes hold with a Triṣṭubh verse; the Triṣṭubh is indeed power; verily, he bestows power upon the sacrificer.

"May I conquer at the impulse of the Maruts," he says. Thus, impelled by the Maruts themselves, he conquers. "The mind has been attained," he says. Whatever he desired with his mind, that has been attained. He overcomes the Rājanya; he steps forward unassailed. He who overcomes a Rājanya is deprived of power and vigor. "I am united with power and vigor," he says.

He bestows sensory power and vigor upon himself. He puts on two boar-skin sandals, thinking, "Thou art the fury of cattle; may my fury be like thine. For the boar is indeed the fury of cattle; by means of it, he bestows the fury of cattle upon himself. This earth desires him when he has been consecrated; she is capable of taking away his sensory power and vigor. He puts on the two boar-skin sandals;
he interposes them from her, so that there may be no taking away of his sensory power and vigor.

"Obeisance to Mother Earth," he says for the sake of non-violence. "So much is your life; give me life," he says; verily, he bestows life upon himself. "Thou art vigor (ūrj); give me vigor," he says; verily, he bestows vigor upon himself. "Thou art a yoke; thou art splendor (varcas); bestow splendor upon me," he says; verily, he bestows splendor upon himself. He offers it to the Brahman priest in a single portion; verily, in a single portion, the sacrificer bestows life, vigor, and splendor. He offers the oblations for unyoking the chariot for the sake of stability.

There are three horses; the chariot is the fourth. Therefore, he offers four times. If both were to stand together, they would go to the same world. He places the chariot on the chariot-stand together with the charioteer; thus, he separates him from the heavenly world. With the verse, "The swan dwelling in purity," he places it; by means of the *brahman*, he brings it down; by means of the *brahman*, he establishes it. He places it with an *aticchandas* meter.

The *aticchandāḥ* (exceeding meter) indeed encompasses all meters. With all the meters, he thus establishes it. The *aticchandāḥ* is indeed the summit of the meters. In that he establishes [the fire] with the *aticchandāḥ*, he makes him the summit among his equals.

Anuvāka 10: The Sacrificer’s Service by All after Victory in the Rājasūya. {1.7.10.1} "Thou art Mitra; thou art Varuṇa," he says. The day belongs to Mitra, and the night belongs to Varuṇa. Verily, by means of day and night, he brings him down [to the service]. "Thou art Mitra; thou art Varuṇa," he says. The right side belongs to Mitra, and the left side belongs to Varuṇa. The *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) belongs to the Viśve Devas. Verily, he brings them down to their own respective portions. "Together with all the gods," he says.

{1.7.10.2} Offspring indeed belong to the Viśvedevas; he thus makes them edible. "Thou art the navel of the kṣatra, thou art the womb of the kṣatra"—with these words he spreads out the upper garment for the sake of providing a womb. "Sit on the pleasant one, sit on the comfortable one," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula. "May she not harm thee, may I not be harmed," he says for the sake of non-injury. "Varuṇa, firm in his vow, has sat down in the dwellings for sovereign rule, he of good wisdom," he says; he thus makes him a sovereign of good wisdom.
"O King, you are Brahmā; you are Savitṛ, of true impulsion," he says. He thus makes him Savitṛ of true impulsion.

"O King, you are a Brahman; you are Indra, possessed of true vigor," he says. He thereby makes him Indra, possessed of true vigor. "O King, you are a Brahman; you are Mitra, the very gracious," he says. He thereby makes him Mitra, the very gracious. "O King, you are a Brahman; you are Varuṇa, whose law is truth," he says. He thereby makes him Varuṇa, whose law is truth. "You are Savitṛ, of true impulsion," he says.

By this he utters the *gāyatrī* itself. "Thou art Indra, of true might," he says; by this he utters the *triṣṭubh* itself. "Thou art Mitra, the kindly one," he says; by this he utters the *jagatī* itself. These deities are truth; these meters are truth; verily, he wins truth. "Thou art Varuṇa, whose law is truth," he says; by this he utters the *anuṣṭubh* itself. The *anuṣṭubh* indeed consists of both truth and falsehood; Varuṇa consists of both truth and falsehood; verily, he wins both truth and falsehood.

Neither truth nor falsehood harms him who knows thus. He hands over the wooden sword (*sphya*) with the formula: "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra. The wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt; by means of the thunderbolt he subjects to him [the enemy] both what is below and what is above. For it is better that these should be subject to him. He hands over five dice with the formula: "This king has come to rule over the quarters. These are indeed all the dice; he thus makes him invincible.

They announce the rice porridge. This rice porridge is indeed Parameṣṭhin; he thus causes him to attain supreme prosperity. "O you of fair fame! O you of auspiciousness! O you whose king is Truth!"—thus he says. He thereby invokes this very blessing. He causes the Śaunaḥśepa story to be recited; he thereby releases him from Varuṇa’s noose. It consists of more than a hundred [verses]. Man has a lifespan of a hundred years and possesses a hundred powers.

He becomes established in life itself and in the vital powers. He makes a single combined portion for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt from the cake on twenty-one potsherds for the Maruts and the curd-mixture (āmikṣā) for the Viśve Devas. Thus, by means of the deities, he encloses him on both sides. He offers three oblations with the formulas: "Svāhā to Apāṃ Napāt! Svāhā to Ūrjaḥ Napāt! Svāhā to Agni Gṛhapati! These are the three worlds; verily, he becomes established in these very worlds.

Prapāṭhaka 8, Anuvāka 1: The Oblation of the Saṃsṛps in the Rājasūya When Varuṇa had pressed the Soma, his sensory power and vigor departed in ten directions. That [power] crept along after him with the *saṃsṛps* (creeping ones). Therefore, the *saṃsṛps* have their name "creeping" (*saṃsṛt*). On the first day, he joined it together with Agni as the deity; on the second, with Sarasvatī as speech; on the third, with Savitṛ as impulsion; on the fourth, with Pūṣan and the cattle; on the fifth, with Bṛhaspati as the sacred formulation (*brahman*);
on the sixth, with Indra as the deity; on the seventh, with Varuṇa by means of his own divinity.

{1.8.1.2} On the eighth day, [he offers] with Soma the King; on the ninth, with Tvaṣṭṛ for form. Through Viṣṇu and the Sacrifice, he obtains [the goal]. In that there are the *saṃsṛp* offerings, the sacrificer thereby obtains sensory power and vigor. Each preceding altar-ground is larger than the one before, for the attainment of sensory power and vigor. Before the *upasad* rites, he proceeds with the offering to Soma. Soma, indeed, is the placer of seed; thus he places the seed. Between [the first and second *upasad*s], he proceeds with the offering to Tvaṣṭṛ. Once the seed is placed, Tvaṣṭṛ fashions its forms.

Above, with the verse addressed to Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus he finds firm support in the sacrifice at the very end. Anuvāka 2: The Procedure for the Daśapeya in the Rājasūya {1.8.2.1}. They commit a repetition (jāmi) when they consecrate [the sacrificer] on the same day and purchase the Soma on the same day. He gives him a lotus-wreath (*puṇḍarisraj*) to avoid repetition. When the Aṅgirases were going to the world of heaven, they caused consecration (*dīkṣā*) and austerity (*tapas*) to enter into the waters. That became the lotus flower. In that he gives the lotus-wreath, he directly obtains consecration and austerity.

He purchases Soma with ten young bulls. The Virāj consists of ten syllables; the Virāj is food. Verily, by means of the Virāj, he secures for himself the eating of food. They are castrated for the sake of companionship with Indra. It is a Daśapeya sacrifice for the securing of food. A hundred Brāhmaṇas drink [the Soma]; man has a life-span of a hundred years and possesses a hundredfold power. Verily, he becomes established in life and power. The chant (stotra) consists of seventeen verses; Prajāpati is seventeenfold.

{1.8.2.3} For the attainment of Prajāpati, he gives two mirrors to the Adhvaryu; by giving two mirrors to the Adhvaryu, he causes him to attain light. He gives a garland to the Udgātṛ; verily, he causes him to shine. He gives a gold plate to the Hotṛ; verily, he raises him up to the sun. He gives a horse to the Prastotṛ and the Pratihartṛ; for the horse belongs to Prajāpati; it is for the attainment of Prajāpati.

Twelve four-year-old heifers to the Brahman; verily, he wins long life. A barren cow to the Maitrāvaruṇa; verily, he makes the kingdom submissive. A bull to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; verily, he makes the kingdom possessed of power. Two garments to the Neṣṭṛ and Potṛ; these two are his means of purification. A single-horse chariot laden with barley to the Acchāvāka; verily, from the very end he offers sacrifice to Varuṇa.

{1.8.2.5} He gives an ox to the *agnīdh*. The ox is indeed a carrier (*vahni*), and the *agnīdh* is a carrier; by means of a carrier, he thus secures for himself the carrier of the sacrifice. When Indra had pressed [the Soma], his power and vigor fell away in three parts: one third became the Bhṛgu, one third the *Śrāyantīya* chant, and one third Sarasvatī. The *hotṛ* is a descendant of Bhṛgu; the *brahman*sāman is the *Śrāyantīya*; the *agniṣṭoma*sāman is the *Vāravantīya*. He takes water from the Sarasvatī.

For the securing of sensory power and vigor, the Śrāyantīya becomes the Brahman-sāman; thus it bestows sensory power and vigor upon him. The Vāravantīya is the Agniṣṭoma-sāman; thus it secures sensory power and vigor for him.

He who is established according to the quarters is liable to go mad. There are offerings to the quarters; he thus finds firm support in the quarters themselves for the sake of avoiding madness. He sacrifices to five deities; there are five quarters; he thus finds firm support in the quarters themselves. Having sacrificed with each oblation, he pours clarified butter over the offering to Bṛhaspati. Bṛhaspati has the sacrificer as his deity; he thus endows the sacrificer himself with splendor.

{1.8.3.2} He sacrifices a pregnant, long-eared ewe to the Ādityas, and a spotted heifer of two years old to the Maruts. He thus bestows upon him both the subjects and the ruling power in harmony. He proceeds first with the offering to the Ādityas and afterwards with that to the Maruts; he thereby binds the subjects to the ruling power. He causes the call for the Āditya offering to be heard aloud, but for the Marut offering in a low voice; therefore the ruling power speaks over the subjects. The ewe to the Ādityas is pregnant.

The embryo is indeed the sense-power (*indriya*); he has thus deprived the kingdom of its sense-power. The offering to the Maruts is without an embryo; the Maruts are indeed the common people (*viś*); he has thus deprived the people of their sense-power. The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. Those gods, having deposited the truth of speech with the Aśvins and Pūṣan, overcame the Asuras by means of untruth. They offered a cake on twelve potsherds to the Aśvins and Pūṣan. Thereupon, they indeed secured the truth of speech.

{1.8.3.4} When he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to the Aśvins and Pūṣan, he overcomes his rivals by means of untruth itself and wins the truth of speech. To Sarasvatī of true speech, he offers a pap; this has already been explained, and he recites the invitatory verse with the subsequent [formula]. To Savitṛ of true impulsion, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds for the sake of instigation; he dispatches messengers. These [verses] are "announcements" (*āvida*); they cause him to reach announcement itself. Moreover, he is not cut off from his messengers. A bow with three arrows and a dry skin-bag is the sacrificial fee for the sake of prosperity.

Anuvāka 4: The Procedure for the Oblations of the Prayuj-offerings in the Rājasūya {1.8.4.1} He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni. Therefore, in the winter, the Kurus and Pañcālas go eastward. He offers a pap to Soma. Therefore, having determined upon the spring, they set out. He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ. Therefore, before the barley is ripened, they are held back by Savitṛ. He offers a pap to Bṛhaspati. Having been held back by Savitṛ, they take up the barley through the Brahman. He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Tvaṣṭṛ.

{1.8.4.2} By means of these, they produce forms: [they offer] a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara. Therefore, during the latter part of the summer, the Kurus and Pañcālas travel westward. He offers a pap for Sarasvatī. Therefore, during the rainy season, all voices speak. They settle their affairs with an offering to Pūṣan; they plow with an offering to Mitra; they remain supported by an offering to Varuṇa; they cause their crops to ripen with an offering to Kṣetrapati; and they store away [the grain] with an offering to Aditi.

{1.8.4.3} "These oblations are to be offered month by month," they say; "thereby one sets the seasons in motion. Now, however, they also say: "Who will live for a year? Only six [oblations] are to be offered on the previous day, and six on the following day. Thereby one sets the seasons in motion. The right horse of the chariot-pole is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the former [six], and the left for the latter [six]. Thus he joins the two ends of the year for the attainment of the heavenly world.

Anuvāka 5: The Procedure for the Sautrāmaṇī Sacrifice in the Rājasūya {1.8.5.1} When Indra was performing the *soma* pressing, his sensory power and vigor fell away in ten parts. What he spat out first became the *kvala* (jujube) fruit; what he spat out second became the *badara* (jujube) fruit; what he spat out third became the *karkandhu* (jujube) fruit. That which [fell] from his nose became the lion; that which [fell] from his eyes...

That which is on the right ear is the tiger; that which is on the left is the wolf; that which is upright is Soma; that which is downward-pointing is Surā. There are three types of groats for the attainment of sensory power; there are three types of hair.

{1.8.5.3} He indeed wins brilliance. There are three cups; he thus wins vigor. The tenth is by name; there are indeed nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, and the navel is the tenth. The vital breaths are power and vigor. Thus the sacrificer places within himself the vital breaths, power, and vigor. He buys the young shoots from a eunuch with lead. This is neither iron nor gold.

{1.8.5.4} That which is lead is neither female nor male; that which is the eunuch is neither *soma* nor *surā*. That which is the *sautrāmaṇī* is for prosperity. "Thee, sweet, with the sweet," he says; verily, he makes it *soma*. "Thou art *soma*; be cooked for the Aśvins; be cooked for Sarasvatī; be cooked for Indra the Good Protector," he says; for it is indeed for these deities that it is cooked. It remains mixed for three nights.

For the purchased Soma remains for three nights. With the *yajus* formula, "May he purify thy flowing juice," he purifies it for the sake of distinction (*vyāvṛtti*). He purifies it with a strainer; for they purify the Soma with a strainer. "With a constant fleece" (*vāreṇa śaśvatā tanā*), so he says; for they purify the Soma with a fleece. He should not purify with the verse, "Vāyu purified by the strainer," for this [verse] is deficient. He should purify with it only when [the Soma] has already been purified. With the undefined, *prājāpatya* verse, "O, indeed... (*kuvid aṅga*), he takes [the draught].

{1.8.5.6} Prajāpati is undefined. This is for the attainment of Prajāpati. He draws [the cup] with a single verse; thus he bestows vigor upon the sacrificer in a single manner. He offers a smoke-colored animal to the Aśvins. The Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods; through them, he provides medicine for him. [He offers] a ram to Sarasvatī. Sarasvatī is indeed speech; through speech itself, he heals him. [He offers] a bull to Indra, for the sake of possessing Indra’s power.

Anuvāka 6: The Sautrāmaṇī Ritual in the Rājasūya {1.8.6.21} If he were to immolate [the animals] at three sacrificial posts, he would place sensory power and vigor outside of himself; he would produce a rival for him. He immolates them at a single post. Thus, he places sensory power and vigor in him all at once. He does not produce a rival for him. There are no *puroḍāśa* cakes for these animals, for they are indeed *graha-puroḍāśas*. "O Aśvins, you two [drink] the *surā*"—these are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses addressed to all the deities. Thus, he gratifies all the deities.

{1.8.6.2} One should hire a Brāhmaṇa who will drink the remnants of the offering; for a Brāhmaṇa is the one who drinks the remnants of the oblation. If one cannot find a Brāhmaṇa, one should pour it into an anthill. That itself is the expiation for that. Whatever in the Sautrāmaṇī is unsuccessful, that becomes successful for her. The animals and the sacrificial cakes belong to different deities for the sake of prosperity. Among the animals, the one dedicated to Indra is the last; among the sacrificial cakes, the one dedicated to Indra is the first.

{1.8.6.3} He bestows upon him the two senses joined together. Before the after-offerings (anūyāja), he proceeds with the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa). The sacrificial cakes are indeed cattle; verily, he wins cattle for himself. He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra; verily, he wins power (indriya). A cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ is for instigation. A cake on ten potsherds to Varuṇa: at the very end, he propitiates Varuṇa. A mare is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

{1.8.6.4} Moreover, this [sacrifice] produces a horse, or a mule, or Soma, or Surā—since the Sautrāmaṇī is for the sake of prosperity. He offers a fourth animal to Bṛhaspati for one who has passed through the purification. Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods; by means of the Brahman, he thus heals whatever in the sacrifice has been unsuccessful. This animal sacrifice includes a cake offering, for they do not draw a cup (graha) for it. Saying, "O Fathers, who have Soma as your face, be satisfied," he pours [the remnants] together into the hundred-holed stone.

A man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers. He thus establishes himself in life-span and power. He offers the oblation in the southern fire to ward off misfortune. He holds gold between [the ladle and the fire]; thus he offers it as something purified. It is a weight of a hundred mānas; for a man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers. He thus establishes himself in life-span and power. Wherever he holds the hundred-holed [vessel], [he gains] that very [life-span].

He places it down for the sake of stability. Indeed, the power and vigor of one whom Soma flows past goes to the ancestors. He pays homage with the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses of the ancestors; whatever power and vigor of his has gone to the ancestors, that he thereby recovers. He pays homage with three verses; for the ancestors are in the third world from here; thus he gratifies them. Moreover, there are indeed three powers of the sacrifice: the Adhvaryu, the Hotṛ, and the Brahman.
They attend upon him; with whatever powers belong to the sacrifice, with those very powers he provides healing for him.

Anuvāka 7: The Ritual for the Purifiers (Pavitrāha), the Ritual for the Consecration (Abhiṣecanīya). {1.8.7.1} He performs the Agniṣṭoma first. The Agniṣṭoma is indeed the mouth of the sacrifice; having commenced at the very mouth of the sacrifice, he ascends to the consecration (sava). Now, this Abhiṣecanīya has a thirty-four-fold Pavamāna stotra. There are thirty-three deities; he thus attains them. Prajāpati is the thirty-fourth; he thus attains him. This is a "crashing together" (saṃśara) of the Stomas, occurring out of their proper sequence, in that the Stomas are unequal.

{1.8.7.2} The sacrifice is indeed as great as the Pavamāna [stotras]. Anything else is merely a means of internal cohesion. Since the Pavamānas are equal, by that it is without fracture; by that it is in proper order. Through the Agniṣṭoma itself, he prospers; through the self, he becomes meritorious. The Ukthas are indeed offspring; the Ukthas are cattle. {The variant reading "prajā vā ukthāni" [offspring are the Ukthas] occurs instead of "paśava ukthāni" [cattle are the Ukthas].} In that there is an Ukthya [stotra], it is for the sake of continuity.
