Anuvāka 8: A specific statement regarding the Sāman and the mantra in the Rājasūya sacrifice {1.8.8.29}. "The sisterly songs [approach] you"—this is the introductory verse (*pratipad*). Vāyu is indeed speech; this is the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of speech itself. He is consecrated for the sake of all creatures; all creatures call him "King. He says, "And him, the ten fingers [consecrate]. The creatures are indeed the Ādityas; by this, he is consecrated for the sake of the creatures. Those who have performed the *sambhāryā* rites depart from the mouth of the sacrifice.

When he says, "Flow on as the leader of speech," by that very means they do not depart from the mouth of the sacrifice. The first [verse] is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter; the last is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter. The *anuṣṭubh* is indeed speech. By speech alone they set out; by speech they rise up. They are ascending [verses]; for the form of the *anuṣṭubh* is ascending, and the Rājanya is of the *anuṣṭubh* nature.

Therefore, they consist of ascending verses. The final verse is an *anuṣṭubh* dedicated to Sūrya; this is for the continuity of the world of heaven. He who departs from the *sava* sacrifice does not find the *sava* returning to him. He who departs from the *sāmans* becomes worse off after having performed the consecration (*suṣuvāṇa*). Indeed, these *sāmans* are the *pṛṣṭhas*; that there are *pṛṣṭhas* [is for this reason].

He does not go with those very *sāmans* which belong to the kings of the gods; by means of them he prospers in that world. With those *sāmans* which belong to the kings of men, he prospers in this world. Thus he prospers in both worlds: in the world of the gods and in the world of men. The twenty-one-fold hymn-form is the last for the consecration (*abhiṣecanīya*), while it is the first for the hair-cutting ceremony (*keśavapanīya*). The ten-soma-draught sacrifice (*daśapeya*) is seventeen-fold.

The twenty-one-fold [stoma] is indeed the peasantry (*viś*); the seventeen-fold is the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*). It is thus from the midst of the peasantry that he is consecrated; therefore, he is dear to the peasantry, for he is consecrated from their midst. When they cause him to stand firm along the quarters there above, he ascends to the heavenly world. If he were not to descend again to this world, he would either pass beyond the people or become intoxicated with pride. In that this [chant] has its stoma directed westward, [he does not do so].
By that very means, he descends again to this world; thus, he establishes himself in this very world so as not to go mad.

Anuvāka 9: Specification of the particulars regarding the consecration in the Rājasūya. {1.8.9.1} This [earth] is indeed the silver one; that [sky] is the golden one. In that there are two gold plates (*rukma*), he thus encompasses him on both sides by means of these two. When Varuṇa was being consecrated, the waters struck away his sensory power and vigor (*indriya-vīrya*). That became gold (*suvarṇa-hiraṇya*). In that he places a gold plate in between, it is for the non-destruction of sensory power and vigor. It is worth a hundred [measures], consisting of a hundred syllables.

A man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers; he thus finds firm support in both life-span and power. Gold is indeed life-span; they pour out for him things that are conducive to life-span. Gold is indeed brilliance; they pour out for him things that are conducive to brilliance. Gold is indeed luster; they pour out for him things that are conducive to luster.

"Unstable, indeed, is he," they say, "who performs the Rājasūya. But when he performs this two-night sacrifice, then there is stability; then he attains the year. As many as are the days and nights of the year, so many are the *stotrīyā* verses of this sacrifice. He thus finds firm footing in the days and nights themselves. The first day is an *agniṣṭoma*; the second is an *atirātra*.

{1.8.10.2} He establishes himself separately in the two days of the day-and-night cycle: the first day falls on the full moon, and the second on the *vyaṣṭakā*. He establishes himself separately in the two half-months: the first day falls on the new moon, and the second on the *uddṛṣṭa*. He establishes himself separately in the two months. However, if there should be two auspicious days within the same fortnight, one should perform the rite on those two for the sake of stability.

{1.8.10.3} "The two-night sacrifice is not conducive to cattle," they say, "for these two are the meters: the Gāyatrī and the Triṣṭubh. They exclude the Jagatī; therefore, they say that the Jagatī has not been employed by it. "When they perform it at the third pressing," [they reply]. "When this [Jagatī] shares in a day of the Ahīna sacrifice, or in a pressing of a single-day sacrifice, then indeed the Jagatī is employed, and then it is conducive to cattle. This two-night sacrifice is indeed a 'dawn-breaker' (vyuṣṭi). He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the two-night rite, [attains that]."
Verily, the light rises for him; moreover, he drives away darkness. He performs the Agniṣṭoma at the end. Agni is all the deities; verily, he finds firm support in the deities.
Book 2, Āraṇyaka Book.

Prapāṭhaka 1, Anuvāka 1: The Introduction to the Agnihotra {2.1.1.1} The Aṅgirases performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*). For them, Pṛśni was the cow that yielded the *gharma* (the hot offering). She lived only on the dregs of the Soma (*ṛjīṣa*). They said, "For what purpose indeed do we perform this sacrificial session, since we do not cause the plants of this [earth] to be born? They released rain from the sky. As many drops as fell, so many plants were produced. Once they were born, the Fathers smeared them with poison.

Having eaten them, they became distressed. They said, "Who has done this? The ancestors replied, "We did it, desiring a share. [The gods asked], "What shall be your share? They replied, "Let there also be for us a share in the *agnihotra*. To them they gave this share: that which one wipes away after making the offering. Thereby, indeed, they caused the plants to become palatable. He who knows thus [causes them to become palatable].

{2.1.1.3} The plants find their relish in him. They let loose a calf [to suckle], saying, "Cause this oblation of ours to be given. He said, "I shall choose a boon: for ten nights after it is born, do not milk me; until the time of the cowherds' return, let me roam with my mother. Therefore, they do not milk a calf for ten nights after it is born; it roams with its mother until the time of the cowherds' return, for that was his chosen boon. Therefore, Rudra is a slayer of the calf that has already begun to suckle, for it sucks beyond the limit of the agreement.

Anuvāka 2: Description of the Agnihotra {2.1.2.1} Prajāpati created Agni. After him, the creatures were created. [Agni] remained without a share and withdrew from him. Prajāpati pursued him, seeking to recover him. He tried to seize him but was unable to do so. He performed austerity. Then Agni desisted, thinking, "Prajāpati has indeed performed austerity."

That became clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Therefore, they say that she whose hair is shaved on the right side possesses the highest fortune belonging to Prajāpati. Because he wiped [the hair] upward from the forehead (*rarāṭa*), there are no hairs on the forehead. He took it up and placed it in the fire. He hesitated: "Shall I offer it? Or shall I not offer it? That was the origin of hesitation. Whoever, knowing this, hesitates, [partakes in that same origin].

He thought only of something better. Speech addressed him, saying, "Sacrifice! He said, "Who are you? "I am your very own speech," she replied. He sacrificed with "svāhā. That was the origin of the *svāhākāra*. Whoever knows thus the origin of the *svāhākāra* performs heroic power through the *svāhākāra*. For one who knows thus, those who sacrifice with the *svāhākāra* perform their work.

{2.1.2.4} His oblation becomes solely for the sake of enjoyment. From that oblation he created the human being. He offered a second oblation; he created the horse. He offered a third oblation; he created the cow. He offered a fourth oblation; he created the sheep. He offered a fifth oblation; he created the goat.

{2.1.2.5} That Agni was afraid, thinking, "They will surely reach me with the oblations. He entered Prajāpati again. Prajāpati said to him, "Be born! He replied, "With what portion shall I be born? [Prajāpati] said, "To you alone shall this be offered. He was born with that as his portion: namely, the Agnihotra.

{2.1.2.6} Therefore, it is called the *agnihotra*. While it was being offered, the Sun said: "Do not offer it! This belongs to both of us. Agni replied: "How will they offer to us? He (the Sun) said: "They shall offer to you in the evening; to me in the morning. Therefore, the offering is made to Agni in the evening and to Sūrya in the morning.

The night belongs to Agni; the day belongs to Indra. If one were to offer the morning oblation before the sun has risen, both [the morning and evening offerings] would belong to Agni. One offers the morning oblation when the sun has risen; thus, it is offered to Agni in the evening and to Sūrya in the morning. Indeed, offspring are born following the night; they find firm support through the day. When one offers the evening oblation...

{2.1.2.11} By that [offering], he is indeed procreated. He offers in the morning when the sun has risen; by that, he is established. Prajāpati desired, "May I be procreated. He beheld this Agnihotra as a pair: one part with the *yajus* formula, the other part silently. Thereupon he was indeed procreated. For him who knows thus, those who offer the Agnihotra when the sun has risen, [he is likewise procreated].

{2.1.2.9} He is indeed born again; moreover, it is just as when one goes about perceiving during the day—such indeed is that. Now, they also say: "If two virtuous men dwell in a house, and one of them he gratifies while the other he does not, he surely comes to grief for both. For the sun enters the fire at evening; therefore, the fire is seen from afar at night, for those two splendors have become united.

{2.1.2.10} Indeed, as the sun rises, Agni ascends after it; therefore, the smoke alone of Agni is seen by day. If one were to offer to Agni in the evening, he would be cut off from Sūrya. If one were to offer to Sūrya in the morning, he would be cut off from Agni. He would create discord among the deities. One should offer in the evening with the formula: "Agni is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā! And in the morning with: "Sūrya is light, light is Agni, svāhā! In this way, the offering is made to both in the evening.

{2.1.2.11} He offers with both [formulas] in the morning. Thus he does not cause strife among the deities. “Agni is light,” he says; Agni, indeed, is the depositor of seed. “Offspring is light,” he says; verily, he procreates offspring for him. “Sūrya is light,” he says; verily, he places seed in the offspring once they have been born. “Light is Agni, svāhā! he says; verily, he establishes the offspring that have been born upon this [earth].

{2.1.2.12} He offers the subsequent oblation silently for the sake of pairing and procreation. If he were to offer the morning oblation after the sun has risen, it would be just as if they were to bring food to a guest who has already departed, leaving an empty dwelling behind; such indeed would that be. "Where then does that [offering] go? they ask. "Since he does not know for whom they bring it," they say. Therefore, when he offers the *auṣasa* (dawn) oblation, that alone is timely. Moreover, it is just as if one serves the *auṣasa* meal at the very moment the guest arrives. Such indeed is that.

Anuvāka 3: The Preparations of the Oblation, such as Placing it on the Fire, in the Agnihotra {2.1.3.1} This Agni is indeed Rudra; the cooking-pot is the wife. If one were to place [the oblation] on the fire in the middle [of the hearth], one would deliver the wife to Rudra, and she would be liable to die prematurely. Having drawn out the embers toward the north, he places [the pot] upon them; this is for the protection of the wife. He makes [the embers] separated [from the main fire]; thus the wife does not die prematurely.

{2.1.3.2} This Agnihotra is indeed an unappeased cauldron that is offered day after day. One should pour water over it for one who desires cattle; for that which is appeased is favorable to cattle. One should not pour water over it for one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); for spiritual luster is like a kindled fire. However, it should indeed be poured over; in that he pours water over it, [he does so].

That which is cooked is fit for cattle; that which he offers as an oblation is conducive to spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Thus he has accomplished both. For that sacrificial food which is cooked but not sprinkled with clarified butter has departed from this world and has not yet reached the world of the gods. He lights it up; he thus sprinkles it with clarified butter. Moreover, he thereby causes it to go to the gods.

{2.1.3.4} He carries fire around [the sacrificial animal]. This is for the purpose of driving away the *rakṣases*. He carries it around three times; for the sacrifice has a threefold structure, and furthermore, it is for the sake of its purity. If he were to remove the fire to the east, he would afflict the sacrificer with impurity. If to the south, it would belong to the ancestors as its deity. If to the west—

He should cause the wife to suffer grief. He carries it out toward the north. This is indeed the peaceful direction among gods and men; he carries it out following that very direction for the sake of peace. He makes a path for the continuity of the sacrifice. He heats it [the vessel] and then spreads [grass] over it. He draws up four times; cattle have four feet.

{2.1.3.6} Verily he wins cattle. He pours out all [the vessels] full; for all [the gods] are meritorious and successful. He pours them out following one after another, for the sake of the continuity of offspring. Thus his offspring becomes productive in succession. He touches [them] together for the sake of distinction. He should not set them down without intending to offer. If he were to set them down without intending to offer, it would be as if he had deposited them for someone else.

If he were to give it to someone else, it would be exactly like that; it would be snatched away from him. When he places it upon the Gārhapatya fire, by that act he gratifies the Gārhapatya. Agni was afraid, thinking, "The oblations will pass me by. He saw this kindling-stick (samidh) and laid it down. From that time on, the oblations were held firm in the fire.

{2.1.3.8} Because he bound him together (*samayacchat*), that is the reason for the name of the fuel-sticks (*samidh*). He places a fuel-stick on the fire; thus he binds him together, for the support of the oblations. Moreover, he thereby makes the Agnihotra itself possess fuel, for the stability of the oblations. The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "Since one offers two oblations after having placed only a single fuel-stick, upon which fuel-stick does one offer the second oblation?"

{2.1.3.} If he were to place two kindling-sticks on the fire, he would produce a rival for himself. Having placed one kindling-stick, he offers another oblation with a sacrificial formula (*yajus*). Thus he offers two oblations, both provided with kindling-sticks; he does not produce a rival for himself. He offers when [the fire] is well-kindled, for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) is, as it were, already kindled. Moreover, it is just as when one serves food after having made the guest bright. He draws out four [portions of ghee] and offers twice.

Therefore, he eats both bipeds and quadrupeds; moreover, he establishes the quadrupeds upon the bipeds. Anuvāka 4: The Preparation of the Oblation Used in the Agnihotra {2.1.4.4} The gods offered their oblation so as to ascend; the Asuras offered theirs so as to descend. Thereupon the gods prospered, while the Asuras were defeated. If one should desire of someone, "May he become more prosperous," he should first offer for him a smaller portion and then offer a larger portion afterwards. This indeed is the ascending oblation. The gods offered it; thereupon they prospered.

{2.1.4.2} For whomsoever they offer in this manner, he indeed prospers. If one should desire of someone, "May he become worse off," one should first offer a larger portion for him and then offer a smaller portion afterward. This, indeed, is the downward-sacrifice (*avācī āhuti*). The Asuras offered it; consequently, they were defeated. For whomsoever they offer in this manner, he is surely defeated.

Having offered, he places [the remains] down for the sake of avoiding sameness (*ajāmitva*), and also for the sake of distinction. He gazes at the *gārhapatya* fire; thus he makes it one that does not look back. Indeed, there is a "stump" (*sthāṇu*) of the *agnihotra*; whoever should step upon it would step upon a sacrificial stump. This, indeed, is the stump of the *agnihotra*: namely, the first oblation. If he were to pour the second oblation over it, [he would step on that stump].

{2.1.4.4} He may encounter a pillar of the sacrifice. He offers the oblation after passing over the previous one; thus he avoids the pillar of the sacrifice. Moreover, having seized his rival, he passes him by. In the evening, he wipes downward; thereby he deposits semen. In the morning, he wipes upward; thereby he brings forth progeny. The exponents of sacred knowledge say: "He draws out four times."

{2.1.4.5} He offers twice. Now, where do these two oblations come to be? One should say: "In Agni Vaiśvānara. For this Brāhmaṇa is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara. Having offered, he eats twice; thus he offers two oblations in Agni Vaiśvānara himself. He offers twice; he wipes [the vessel] twice; he eats twice.

They amount to six; there are indeed six seasons. Thus he gratifies the seasons. The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "To which deity does the *agnihotra* belong? One should reply: "It belongs to the All-gods (*vaiśvadeva*). That which he offers with a sacrificial formula (*yajus*) belongs to Indra and Agni; that which he offers silently belongs to Prajāpati.

{2.1.4.7} That which he wipes away belongs to the plants; that which is the second [wiping] belongs to the ancestors; that which he eats belongs to the embryos; therefore embryos grow without eating. That which he sips belongs to human beings. Having turned toward the north, he sips water.

{2.1.4.8} He washes it for his own protection; he cleanses it for purification; he heats it on the fire to make it palatable. He points it out; thus he gratifies the Seven Seers (Saptarṣis). He turns toward the south; he turns according to his own vigor. Therefore, the right side of the body is more vigorous. Moreover, he turns according to the course of the sun. Having offered the oblation, he adds fuel to the fire.

{2.1.4.9} For the kindling of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). One should not throw the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) into the fire. This sacrifice, namely the *agnihotra*, is indeed unfinished. If one were to throw it into the fire, one would cut off the continuity of the sacrifice. Therefore, it must not be thrown into the fire, for the sake of the continuity of the sacrifice. He pours out water; he has thus performed the form of the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).

Anuvāka 5: Optional Offerings for the Agnihotra {2.1.5.1} The exponents of sacred knowledge say: "Sacrifices have the Agnihotra as their point of departure. What is the point of departure for the Agnihotra? The calf is indeed the point of departure for the Agnihotra; the Agnihotra is [the starting point] of sacrifices. Of that [Agnihotra], the earth is the *sadas* (sacrificial hall), the intermediate space is the *āgnīdhra* (fire-shed of the Āgnīdhra priest), and the sky is the *havirdhāna* (grain-receptacle). The celestial waters are the sprinkling waters, and the plants are the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

{2.1.5.2} The fuel is the trees; the enclosing sticks are the quarters; the sacrificial post is the sun; the victim is the sacrificer; the purificatory bath is the ocean; the year is the utterance of "svaga. Therefore, for one who has established the sacred fires, everything that is offered becomes as if placed upon the sacrificial grass. When he offers in the evening, he thereby makes the night worthy of a sacrificial fee; when he offers in the morning, [he makes the day so].

{2.1.5.3} By that [gift], he makes the day worthy of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇya). Whatever he gives from there is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Indeed, as many gods as ate what was not offered perished. They took portions from everything and offered this Agnihotra. Therefore they say: "The gods indeed saw the Agnihotra as the atonement for the household. When he offers in the evening, it is for the sake of providing food for the night.

{2.1.5.4} For the non-defeat of the sacrificer: that which [is offered] in the morning is for the sake of the day’s being consumed after it has been offered, and for the non-defeat of the sacrificer. That which he eats thereafter is indeed what has been offered. One who desires cattle should offer with milk at both [sessions]. This Agnihotra is indeed a productive pair; he who knows thus is propagated with offspring, cattle, and pairs.

{2.1.5.5} By the first [verse] he milks this [earth]; by the second, that [sky]. Having placed it on the fire, he pours the latter [milk] into it. Thus he pours seed into the womb, into the organ of generation. He should offer with clarified butter for one who desires splendor; for clarified butter is indeed splendor—he becomes possessed of splendor. He should offer with milk for one who desires cattle; for this is indeed the form of cattle. By means of its very form, he wins cattle for him.

{2.1.5.6} He indeed becomes possessed of cattle. For one desiring sensory power, [there is an offering] with curd. Curd is indeed sensory power; he indeed becomes possessed of sensory power. For one desiring a village, [there is an offering] with barley-gruel. Humans are indeed of the nature of plants; by means of his own portion, he wins over his kinsmen for him. He indeed becomes possessed of a village. That which is without the *sāman* is indeed not a sacrifice.

He draws out four times. The *Rathantara* [Sāman] consists of four syllables; this is the characteristic form of the *Rathantara*. He carries it as if above. The *Vāmadevya* [Sāman] is the intermediate space; this is the characteristic form of the *Vāmadevya*. He offers twice. The *Bṛhat* [Sāman] consists of two syllables; this is the characteristic form of the *Bṛhat*. Thus, he makes the Agnihotra itself possessed of the Sāmans.

{2.1.5.8} Or, whoever knows the attendances (*upasada*) of the *agnihotra*, the attendances bow down to him; he finds one who will attend to him. Having drawn [the milk], he sets it down; thus he gratifies the earth. When about to offer, he sets it down; thus he gratifies the intermediate space. Having offered, he sets it down; thus he gratifies the sky. These indeed are the attendances of the *agnihotra*.

{2.1.5.9} He who knows thus—the *upasads* bow down to him; he finds one who attends upon him. Or, he who knows the *āśrāvita* (the call) and the *pratyāśrāvita* (the response) of the *agnihotra*, as well as the *hotṛ*, the *brahmā*, and the *vaṣaṭkāra*—for him alone is the offering truly made. Verily, the breath (*prāṇa*) is the *āśrāvita* of the *agnihotra*; the downward breath (*apāna*) is the *pratyāśrāvita*; the mind (*manas*) is the *hotṛ*; the eye (*cakṣus*) is the *brahmā*; and the winking of the eye (*nimeṣa*) is the *vaṣaṭkāra*.

{2.1.5.10} He who knows thus—for him indeed is the offering truly made. Both the gods who travel in the evening and the gods who travel in the morning come to the house of the one who maintains the *agnihotra*. If he were not to satisfy them, they would spread out [and depart] from his offspring and cattle. If he satisfies them, being satisfied, they shall satisfy him with offspring and cattle. "In harmony with the gods who travel in the evening," he touches [the oblation] in the evening; "in harmony with the gods who travel in the morning," [he touches it] in the morning.
Thus, both those gods who travel in the evening and those who travel in the morning [are honored].

He satisfies both of these [the ancestors and the gods]. They, being satisfied, satisfy him with offspring and cattle. Aruṇa Aupaveśi used to say: "In the very Agnihotra, morning and evening, I hurl the thunderbolt at my rivals. Therefore, my rivals are more wretched than I. He draws out four times; he offers twice. The fuel-stick is the seventh. The Śakvarī metre has seven feet. The thunderbolt is of the Śakvarī nature.
In the very Agnihotra, the sacrificer hurls the thunderbolt at his rival morning and evening; he prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated.

Anuvāka 6: On the running forward [of the fire] in the Agnihotra and the remedy for the absence of an oblation. {2.1.6.1} Prajāpati desired, "May something possessing a self be born from me. He offered an oblation. From it, that which possesses a self was born: Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya. They said, "Prajāpati has offered an oblation, and something possessing a self has been born from him; we have been born from it. Let something possessing a self be born for us. They offered oblations. From the vital breaths (prāṇas), Agni was born; from the body, Vāyu.

{2.1.6.2} From the eye, the Āditya [was born]. From their oblation, the cow itself was born. They strove over her milk, saying, "Mine has been born from the oblation! Mine! They went to Prajāpati with a question. He said to the Āditya and Agni, "Whichever of us two wins, let that belong to both of us together. Prajāpati asked, "Who offered to whom? Who offered to whom? Who offered to whom? Agni replied, "I [offered] to the vital breaths."

"By means of my body, I [am]," thus [says] Vāyu; "By means of my eye, I [am]," thus [says] Āditya. "He who has offered the oblations of the vital breaths—born from that which was offered," "born from the offering of Agni"—this is the reason for the name *agnihotra* (the fire-oblation). Or rather, the cow is the *agnihotra*. He who knows thus, [knowing] "the cow is the *agnihotra*," truly causes Agni to prosper through the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the in-breath (*apāna*). He becomes one who does not fail in his out-breath and in-breath.

{2.1.6.4} He who knows thus—Vāyu said to those two: "Include me in your portion. They replied: "In that you have run toward the Āhavanīya fire after having placed [the offering] upon the Gārhapatya, by that we gratify you. Therefore, when one runs toward the Āhavanīya after having placed [the offering] upon the Gārhapatya, one gratifies Vāyu by that act. Prajāpati, while creating the deities, created Agni first among the deities. Not finding anything else to seize, he [seized Agni].

He turned toward Prajāpati. He was afraid of death. He fashioned that sun from himself. Having offered it, he turned away. Thereby, indeed, he conquered death. He who knows thus conquers death. Therefore, for one who knows thus, even if they do not offer for one day or two days, his offering is indeed considered made; for that sun is the Agnihotra.

Anuvāka 7: Praise of the oblation in the Agnihotra by way of its connection with all the deities. {2.1.7.7} It belongs to Rudra when it is in the cow; to Vāyu when it has been let loose [to the calf]; to the Aśvins while being milked; to Soma when it has been milked; to Varuṇa when placed on the fire; to the Viśvedevas when it is bubbling; to Pūṣan when it begins to overflow; to Sarasvatī while it is trickling; to Mitra when it is curdling; to Dhātṛ when it is removed from the fire; to Bṛhaspati when it is ladled out; to Savitṛ when it has begun to be carried forward; and to Heaven and Earth while it is being carried.
The offering to Indra and Agni is presented; the first oblation is for Agni, the second for Prajāpati, and the one that is offered is for Indra.

Anuvāka 8: The Method of Milking for the Agnihotra {2.1.8.8} He lets [the cow] loose toward the south; by that, he conquers the world of the ancestors. He turns her toward the east; by that, he conquers the world of the gods. Turning her toward the north, he milks; by that, he conquers the world of men. He should milk the two front teats for the eldest son born of the eldest wife, or for one who has already attained prosperity. He should milk the two rear teats for the youngest son born of the youngest wife, or for one who desires to thrive.

He does not touch [the milk], for the sake of averting evil fortune. This [milk] belongs to Vāyu when it is brought near; to the Aśvins while being milked; to Mitra once milked; to Aryaman as it is being placed on the fire; to Tvaṣṭṛ as it is being ladled out; to Bṛhaspati once it has been ladled out; to Savitṛ as it is being carried forward; and to Heaven and Earth as it is being carried away.

{2.1.8.3} The oblation for Indra and Agni has been set forth. Indeed, he who offers the *agnihotra* offers it to all the deities. Just as one satisfies a cow at a watering place, even so does the performer of the *agnihotra* satisfy the sacrificer. He is satisfied with offspring and cattle; he clearly knows the world of heaven; he sees his son; he sees his grandson. He is propagated with offspring, cattle, and pairs of children—he for whom they offer the *agnihotra* knowing this, and he who himself knows it thus.

Anuvāka 9: The two mantras for the unmixed offerings at the Agnihotra {2.1.9.1}. There were three Priyamedhas. One of them offered the Agnihotra thrice; another twice; and another once. Of these, he who offered thrice offered with a *ṛc*; he who offered twice, with a *yajus*; and he who offered once, silently (*tūṣṇīm*).

{2.1.9.2} Both he who offered with the *yajus* and he who offered silently prospered. Therefore, the first oblation should be offered with the *yajus*, and the subsequent one silently. Thus, he secures both forms of prosperity. "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā!"—with these words he offers in the evening; thus he places seed. "Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā!"—with these words he offers in the morning; thus he causes the placed seed to be procreated. For the seed placed by him would otherwise not be procreated.

{2.1.9.3} If the sun rises upon one whose *agnihotra* has not yet been offered, and if this should happen at the end [of the rite], he should pour out the oblation and hasten toward the east. Having approached it, he should sit until he faints. When he faints, he should then offer with "Bhūḥ svāhā! Prajāpati is indeed *bhūta*. He thus resorts to him; he (Prajāpati) raises him up from there. The sacrificer does not meet with misfortune.

Anuvāka 10: The excellence of the *agnihotra* offering according to the specific states of the fire {2.1.10.1}. When he takes out the fire, Agni is then among the Vasus; when one offers into such a fire as that, his *agnihotra* becomes offered into the Vasus themselves. When it has been laid down and lies smoking, Agni is then among the Rudras; when one offers into such a fire as that, his *agnihotra* becomes offered into the Rudras themselves. When the flame first touches the fuel-stick (*idhma*), Agni is then among the Ādityas.

{2.1.10.2} When one offers into such a fire as that, his *agnihotra* offering is indeed offered into the Ādityas. The entire fuel becomes completely ablaze; at that time, Agni is the Viśvedevas. When one offers into such a fire as that, his *agnihotra* offering is indeed offered into the Viśvedevas. The flame descends further and becomes as if reddish; at that time, Agni is Indra. When one offers into such a fire as that, his *agnihotra* offering is indeed offered into Indra.

{2.1.10.3} They become embers. From those embers, a flame rises. At that time, Agni is Prajāpati. When one offers into such [Agni], his Agnihotra is offered into Prajāpati himself. Reeds are placed upon the embers. At that time, Agni is Brahman. When one offers into such [Agni], his Agnihotra is offered into Brahman himself—[namely] into the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Viśvedevas.

In Indra, Prajāpati, and Brahman—thus, for one who knows this and for whom others offer the Agnihotra, as well as for one who himself knows it thus, the oblation becomes offered without omission among these deities.

Anuvāka 11: The sprinkling around [the fire] at different times in the Agnihotra. {2.1.11.1} "I sprinkle thee, the Ṛta, with the Satya"—with these words he sprinkles it in the evening. "I sprinkle thee, the Satya, with the Ṛta"—with these words he sprinkles it in the morning. Agni is indeed the Ṛta; yonder Āditya is the Satya. Thus, in the evening, he sprinkles Agni with Āditya; in the morning, [he sprinkles] Āditya with Agni. As long as day and night exist, so long does this world endure. There is no distress, nor is there injury.
There is neither end nor limit for him who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, or whoever knows this in this way.

*Prapāṭhaka* 2: The *Mantras* beginning with the *Daśahotr*, and their *Brāhmaṇa*. *Anuvāka* 1: Prajāpati desired, "May I create offspring. He beheld this *Daśahotr* [formula]. Having mentally recited it, he offered it upon a clump of *darbha* grass. Thereupon, indeed, he created offspring. Once created, they departed from him. He seized them with a *graha* (libation). That is the reason for the name of the *graha*. Whoever should desire, "May I procreate," [should act accordingly].

Having mentally recited the *daśahotṛ* formula, he should offer it upon a clump of *darbha* grass. Prajāpati, indeed, is the *daśahotṛ*. Having become Prajāpati himself, he procreates. He offers with his mind; for Prajāpati is like the mind. For the attainment of Prajāpati, he offers with a full [ladle]; for Prajāpati is, as it were, full. For the attainment of Prajāpati, he offers with one that is deficient; for from the deficient, Prajāpati created offspring. It is for the creation of offspring.

{2.2.1.3} He offers an oblation upon a clump of *darbha* grass. From this very womb Prajāpati created offspring; from that same womb from which Prajāpati created offspring, from that very womb he himself is born. A Brāhmaṇa sits to the south. The Brāhmaṇa is indeed the overseer of offspring; it is with the approval of the overseer that he is born. There is a cupping (of the fire); it is for the support of the offspring once they have been created. If a Brāhmaṇa who is learned and wise should not attain glory, [this rite ensures it].

{2.2.1.4} Having gone to the forest, having untied a bunch of *darbha* grass, and having seated a Brahmin to his south, he should recite the *Caturhotṛ* formulas. This *Caturhotṛ* [liturgy] is indeed the supreme secret *brahman* of the gods. He causes that very [secret] to become manifest. Once it has become manifest for him, he causes it to become manifest for all creatures. He recites after having untied the bunch of *darbha* grass.

{2.2.1.5} A bunch of *darbha* grass is indeed possessed of fire; thus he recites over that which is possessed of fire. A Brahmin sits to the south. The Brahmin is indeed the overseer of creatures. Fame comes to him together with an overseer. They say, "He is liable to lose his fame," regarding the one for whom he recites this. A boon should be given to him. Whatever approaches him there, that very thing he secures for himself.

{2.2.1.6} One who is establishing the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) should place the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) with the *daśahotṛ* formula. Thus he establishes it as already born. Having churned [the fire] with that very same formula, he should offer the *agnihotra*. Thus he offers it as already born. When about to pour out the oblation-material (*havir*), he should recite the *daśahotṛ* formula. Thus he pours it out as already born. When about to recite the *sāmidhenī* verses, he should recite the *daśahotṛ* formula. Having thus produced the *sāmidhenīs*, he begins and extends the rite. Moreover, the *daśahotṛ* is indeed the sacrifice; he thus extends the sacrifice itself.

{2.2.1.7} One practicing sorcery should offer the *daśahotṛ* formula. There are indeed nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person; the navel is the tenth. Thus, he practices sorcery against him while including his very life-breath. So much indeed is a person's own property: as much as the vital breaths, that which belongs to him. Against that he practices sorcery. He offers [the oblation] in a self-made salt-flat or in a cleft. For this is what is seized by *Nirṛti* (Destruction). Verily, he causes him, already seized by *Nirṛti*, to be further gripped by *Nirṛti*. Whatever is cruel in speech—with that he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call.
4. Verily, he cuts him with the cruel edge of speech. 5. He thereby incurs affliction.

Anuvāka 2 {2.2.2.1} Prajāpati desired, "May I create the New and Full Moon sacrifices. He saw this Caturhotṛ [formula]. Having mentally recited it, he offered it in the Āhavanīya fire. Thereupon, he indeed created the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Once created, they departed from him. He seized them with a *graha* (libation). That is the reason for the name of the *graha*. One who is about to perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices should mentally recite the Caturhotṛ formula and offer it in the Āhavanīya fire.
Having thus created and taken hold of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, he proceeds with them.

{2.2.2.2} It becomes a *graha* (libation) for the support of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices once they have been created. He desired, "May I create the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices. He saw this *pañcahotṛ* [formula]. Having mentally recited it, he offered it in the *āhavanīya* fire. Thereupon, he indeed created the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices. Once created, they departed from him. He seized them with the *graha*. That is the reason for the name of the *graha*. One who is about to perform the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices [should do so].

{2.2.2.3} Having recited the Pañcahotṛ formula mentally, he should offer it in the Āhavanīya fire. Having created and begun the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, he extends them; thus there is a *graha* (libation). This is for the support of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices once they have been created. He desired, "May I create the Paśubandha. He saw this Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula; having recited it mentally, he offered it in the Āhavanīya fire. Thereupon, he indeed created the Paśubandha. Once created, it departed from him. He seized it with the *graha*.

{2.2.2.4} That is the "cup-nature" (*grahatva*) of the cup. One who is about to perform the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) should, having mentally recited the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula, offer it in the *āhavanīya* fire. Having thus brought forth and commenced the animal sacrifice, he extends it; it becomes a "cup. This is for the support of the animal sacrifice once it has been brought forth. He desired, "May I bring forth the Soma-sacrifice (*saumya adhvaram*). He saw this *saptahotṛ* formula. Having mentally recited it, he offered it in the *āhavanīya* fire. Thereupon, he indeed brought forth the Soma-sacrifice.

{2.2.2.5} Once created, it departed from him. He seized it with a *graha* (libation). That is the reason for the name of the *graha*. One who is about to undergo initiation (*dīkṣā*) should recite the *Saptahotṛ* formula mentally and offer it in the *āhavanīya* fire. Having thus created and taken hold of the Soma-sacrifice (*saumya adhvara*), he extends it. It becomes a *graha* for the sake of supporting the created Soma-sacrifice. Indeed, the sacrifice did not suffice for the gods; they collected it in this measure.

{2.2.2.6} Because the ritual materials (*saṃbhārāḥ*) exist, the sacrifice indeed came forth from them. In that there are ritual materials, it is for the sake of the sacrifice’s manifestation. Having set down the *ātithya* (guest-offering), he recites [the formulas]. The *ātithya* is indeed the mouth of the sacrifice; thus, having gathered the sacrifice at its very beginning, he extends it. That which is without a wife is no sacrifice; offspring would not be produced. He recites [the formulas] for the wives; thus he has made the sacrifice itself for the procreation of offspring. He recites [the formulas] during the *upasads*.

This, indeed, is the abode of the wives; he thus settles them in their own abode. Prajāpati desired, "May I procreate. He performed austerity. He created the Trivṛt Stoma. The Pañcadaśa Stoma tore it apart from the middle. These became the bright fortnight (pūrvapakṣa) and the dark fortnight (aparapakṣa). The gods were created following the bright fortnight; the Asuras followed the dark fortnight. Thereupon the gods prospered, while the Asuras perished. For whomsoever one should desire, "May he become more prosperous," [one should proceed in this manner].

{2.2.3.2} One should cause him to sacrifice during the first fortnight; he indeed becomes more prosperous. If one should desire of someone, "May he become worse off," one should cause him to sacrifice during the latter fortnight; he indeed becomes worse off. Therefore, the first fortnight is more auspicious than the latter fortnight. Prajāpati is indeed the Daśahotṛ; [he is] the Caturhotṛ, the Pañcahotṛ, the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ, and the Saptahotṛ. [He is] the seasons and the year.

{2.2.3.3} Offspring, cattle, and these worlds—[these are] Prajāpati. He who thus knows Prajāpati as more than much becomes indeed more than much. Prajāpati created the gods and the Asuras. He did not, however, create Indra. The gods said to him, "Beget Indra for us. He replied, "Just as I have created you through austerity, so must you beget Indra."

{2.2.3.4} They performed austerities. Within themselves, they beheld Indra. They said to him, "Be born! He said, "What portion shall I receive when I am born? They replied, "The seasons, the year, offspring, livestock, and these worlds. He said, "In that case, procreate me by means of an oblation."

{2.2.3.5} They brought him forth by means of the Caturhotṛ formula. He who should desire, "May a hero be born to me," should offer the Caturhotṛ oblation. Prajāpati is indeed the Caturhotṛ; having become Prajāpati himself, he procreates. With the words, "He has generated Indra for power, svāhā! he offers with the *graha* vessel. A hero is born to him, for by this offering the gods brought forth a hero. The Ādityas and the Aṅgirases contended for the world of heaven, saying, "We shall go to the world of heaven first! We shall go first!"

{2.2.3.6} Those Ādityas perceived this Pañcahotṛ [offering]. They offered it in the Āgnīdhra fire before the Prātaranuvāka. Thereupon, they indeed went first to the heavenly world. He who should desire the heavenly world should offer the Pañcahotṛ in the Āgnīdhra fire before the Prātaranuvāka. The Pañcahotṛ is indeed the year; the heavenly world is the year. Having established himself in the seasons within the year, he goes to the heavenly world. Those Aṅgirases said to the Ādityas:

"Where are you? To whom among the virtuous shall we offer the oblation? they asked. "In the meters," they replied—"in the *gāyatrī*, the *triṣṭubh*, and the *jagatī*. Therefore, to the Ādityas who dwell in the meters, the offspring of Aṅgiras offer the oblation. The offspring bring tribute to him; it comes to him unperceived. He who knows thus [attains this]. There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first."
In this [breath], indeed, he is supported; in this, he is established. He who knows him thus as supported and established becomes firmly established himself.

Anuvāka 4: Prajāpati desired, "May I procreate. He saw this Daśahotṛ [formula]. Having divided himself tenfold by means of it, he performed austerity with the Daśahotṛ. His thought (*citti*) was the offering-ladle (*sruc*); his reflection (*citta*) was the clarified butter (*ājya*). Of him, there was only this much speech; such was the sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*). He created the Caturhotṛ [formula]. He rejoiced.

"2.2.4.2" "I have indeed emitted this. For him, Soma was the oblation. He performed austerities by means of the Caturhotṛ formula. He became exhausted. He uttered "bhūḥ. He created the earth, the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, and the Yajus formulas. He performed austerities a second time. He became exhausted. He uttered "bhuvaḥ."

He created the intermediate space, the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, and the Sāman chants. He brooded over the third [world]; he became exhausted; he uttered "Suvar. He created the sky, the Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Atirātra, and the Ṛc verses. These utterances (vyāhṛti) are indeed these worlds. Following these worlds, offspring, cattle, and the meters were born. He who thus knows these first utterances of Prajāpati as they were born [attains them].

{2.2.4.4} He is propagated with offspring, cattle, and pairs. He created the Pañcahotṛ. He did not find an oblation for him. Soma gave him his own body, saying, "This is your oblation. He performed fervor with the Pañcahotṛ; he became exhausted. He pushed back against [the world] from the west; he created the Asuras. That was displeasing to him.

That became gold of inferior color; that is the origin of gold of inferior color. He heated himself a second time. He became exhausted. He pressed forward. He created the gods. That was dear to him; it became gold of excellent color; that is the origin of gold of excellent color. Whoever knows thus the origin of gold of excellent color—

{2.2.4.6} He becomes fair-complexioned in his own self; his rival becomes ill-favored. Therefore, gold should be worn; one becomes fair-complexioned indeed. What is pleasing approaches him, not what is unpleasing. He created the Saptahotṛ. By means of the Saptahotṛ alone, he went to the heavenly world. With the Triṇava Stoma, he drove the Asuras away from these worlds. With the Trayastriṃśa, he established himself. With the Ekaviṃśa, he took hold of splendor.

{2.2.4.7} By means of the seventeenfold [stoma], he was procreated. He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with Soma, goes to the heavenly world by means of the seven Hotṛs. By the twenty-sevenfold stoma, he drives away his enemies from these worlds. By the thirty-threefold, he becomes firmly established. By the twenty-onefold, he bestows luster; by the seventeenfold, he is procreated. Therefore, the seventeenfold stoma must not be omitted. Prajāpati is indeed the seventeenfold; verily, he places Prajāpati in the center for the sake of procreation.

Anuvāka 5 {2.2.5.1}. The gods indeed caused Varuṇa to perform a sacrifice. For whichever deity he brought the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he tore it away from them. They said, "Let us receive [the fee] with a turning away; thus the sacrificial fee will not tear us. They received it with a turning away. Then, indeed, that sacrificial fee did not tear them. He who, knowing this, receives the sacrificial fee with a turning away—him the sacrificial fee does not tear.

{2.2.5.2} "May King Varuṇa lead you, O Goddess," he says regarding gold for Agni. Gold indeed belongs to Agni; thus he accepts it with its own deity. "To Soma, a garment," he says. A garment indeed belongs to Soma; thus he accepts it with its own deity. "To Rudra, a cow," he says. A cow indeed belongs to Rudra; thus he accepts her with her own deity. "To Varuṇa, a horse," he says.

{2.2.5.3} The horse belongs to Varuṇa; he accepts it with its own deity. "To Prajāpati, the man," he says; for the man belongs to Prajāpati; he accepts him with his own deity. "To Manu, the couch," he says; for the couch belongs to Manu; he accepts it with its own deity. "For Utāna Āṅgirasa, the vehicle," he says; for this earth is indeed Utāna Āṅgirasa.

{2.2.5.4} By this very [verse] he accepts it. He accepts the chariot with a verse addressed to Vaiśvānara. For the chariot has Vaiśvānara as its deity; thus he accepts it by means of its own deity. "By that may I attain immortality," he says. Verily, he bestows immortality upon himself. "Vitality to the giver," he says. Having made him [the giver] possess vitality, he causes him to go to the heavenly world. "May there be joy for me, the receiver," he says.

{2.2.5.5} That which is indeed auspicious (*śiva*) is bliss (*maya*). This is a complete exchange with one's very self. "Who has given this? To whom has he given?"—thus he says. *Ka* (Who) is indeed Prajāpati; he thus gives to Prajāpati. "Desire to Desire"—thus he says; for by means of desire one gives, and by means of desire one receives. "Desire is the giver, Desire is the receiver"—thus he says.

"Desire is indeed the giver; desire is the receiver. Enter the ocean of desire," he says. For desire is like the ocean; for there is no end to desire, just as there is none to the ocean. "I receive you with desire," he says. By whatever desire he receives [the gift], that very desire comes to him in the other world. "O Desire, this is for you; O Desire, this is your sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)," he says. Thus, by means of desire itself, the sacrificer seeks the sacrificial fee in the other world.
Not [is it a debt] upon the recipient. He who, knowing thus, accepts the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), accepts it indeed free from debt.

Anuvāka 6 {2.2.6.1}: This tenth day is indeed the end of the sacrifice. On the tenth day they praise with the verses of Sarparājñī. Having reached the very end of the sacrifice, they obtain food. They praise with three [verses]. These worlds are three; from these very worlds they obtain food. They consist of verses containing the word *pṛśni*. Food, indeed, is *pṛśni*.

{2.2.6.2} They indeed obtain food. He intones with the mind; he sings the *udgītha* with the mind; he responds with the *pratihāra* with the mind. For Prajāpati is, as it were, the mind. It is for the attainment of Prajāpati. The serpents are indeed the gods; this earth is their queen. In that they praise with the verses of the Serpent Queen (*sarparājñī*), they find firm support in this very earth.

{2.2.6.3} The Hotṛ recites the Caturhotṛ formulas; he recites the *anuśaṃsana* after the *stotra* for the sake of peace. This tenth day is indeed the end of the sacrifice. The Caturhotṛ formulas are truly the supreme secret *brahman* of the gods. On the tenth day, he recites the Caturhotṛ formulas; having reached the very end of the sacrifice, he wins for himself the supreme secret *brahman* of the gods and causes that very [secret] to become manifest.

Then, having reached the light, he causes the people to go toward the light. He restrains his speech for the support of the sacrifice. The day has the sacrificer as its deity; the night has the rival as its deity. He should meditate on the night through the day; thereby he appropriates the world of his rival. If he were to release his speech during the day, he would leave a remnant of the day for his rival. If he were to release it at night, he would leave a remnant of the night for his rival. Therefore, he releases his speech when the sun is above the trees.
He leaves for him only as much of this world as remains until the sun sets.

Anuvāka 7. Prajāpati created offspring. Once they were created, they clung together. He entered them with form; therefore they say, "Form indeed is Prajāpati. He entered them with name; therefore they say, "Name indeed is Prajāpati. Therefore, even when two enemies meet, if they call out by name, [they recognize one another].

{2.2.7.2} You two are indeed friends. Prajāpati created the gods and the Asuras. He did not, however, create Indra. The gods said to him, "Produce Indra for us. He beheld Indra within himself and created him. The Triṣṭubh, becoming his vigor (*vīrya*), entered into him. A fifteenfold thunderbolt fell into his hand. With it, having risen up, he overcame the Asuras.

{2.2.7.3} He who knows thus overcomes his rivals. Those gods, having conquered the Asuras, went to the heavenly world. In that world they became hungry. They said, "We have lived by means of gifts from there. Having arranged the Saptahotṛ sacrifice, they dispatched Ayāsya Āṅgirasa [with the command]: "By this, provide sustenance there."

{2.2.7.4} Or rather, this is its arrangement: whatever exists here. He who knows thus prospers. This sacrifice among men is the Saptahotṛ; it carries the oblation to the gods who dwell there. He who knows thus, the sacrifice inclines toward him. He thought: "Verily, these [beings] will depart from this world for that world. He uttered, "O Lord of Speech, the heart! Therefore, a son is the heart.
Therefore, people do not desire to depart from this world for that world, for a son is indeed the heart.

Anuvāka 8 {2.2.8.1} The gods indeed performed the sacrifice with the *caturhotṛ* formulas. They were freed from evil and from their rival; they conquered the world of heaven. He who, knowing thus, performs the sacrifice with the *caturhotṛ* formulas, is freed from evil and from his rival; he conquers the world of heaven. He places the *prāyaṇīya* offering with the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula. The *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* belongs indeed to that world. Truly, they slay this Soma when they press it.

{2.2.8.2} By means of the *caturhotṛ* formula, he causes him to go straight to that world. The guest-offering (*ātithya*) is performed with the *caturhotṛ*; the *caturhotṛ* is indeed glory; thus he bestows glory upon himself. With the *pañcahotṛ* formula, he sets down the animal victim. The *pañcahotṛ* leads to heaven; the animal victim is the sacrificer; thus he causes the sacrificer himself to go to the heavenly world. Having drawn the cups (*graha*), he offers the *saptahotṛ* formula. The *saptahotṛ* is indeed vital power (*indriya*).

{2.2.8.3} He indeed bestows the senses upon himself who satisfies the Caturhotṛ formulas at each pressing. He prospers with offspring and cattle; the drinking of Soma comes to him. One should recite the Daśahotṛ at the Bahiṣpavamāna, the Caturhotṛ at the Mādhyandina Pavamāna, the Pañcahotṛ at the Ārbhava Pavamāna, the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ at the Pitṛyajña, and the Saptahotṛ at the Yajñāyajñiya Stotra. Thus, he satisfies them at each pressing.

He prospers with offspring and cattle; the drinking of Soma inclines toward him. The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*) by means of the *caturhotṛ* formulas, desiring glory measured by success. They said, "Whatever glory shall first reach us, let that belong to all of us together. [Thus it was ordained: Soma [is attained] by the *caturhotṛ*; Agni by the *pañcahotṛ*; Dhātṛ by the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ*.

Indra [is associated] with the seven hotṛs; Prajāpati with the ten hotṛs. Among them, glory honored King Soma. He desired that [glory]; he departed by means of it; he wandered away by means of it. The gods sought him through the *praiṣas* (directions); therefore, the *praiṣas* have their name. They announced him by means of the *nivid*s (invocations); therefore, the *nivid*s have their name.

They reached him by means of the *āprī* verses; that is the reason for the name of the *āprīs*. They slew him. His glory they divided among themselves; those became the *grahas* (libation cups). That is the reason for the name of the *grahas*. For one who knows thus, when the *grahas* are drawn, they are truly drawn for him. They said, "He who was indeed the best among us—"

"We have slain him; let us now breathe life into him again! they said. They breathed life into him by means of the *chandas* (metres). That is the reason for the *chandastva* (the nature of being metres) of the *chandas*. They brought him together with the *sāman* (chants). That is the reason for the *sāmatva* (the nature of being a *sāman*) of the *sāman*. They raised him up with the *ukthas* (recitations). That is the reason for the *ukthatva* (the nature of being an *uktha*) of the *ukthas*. He who knows this stands firm indeed.

{2.2.8.8} He attains a full lifespan. Soma is indeed glory (*yaśas*). He who, knowing this, approaches the Soma, glory indeed comes to him. Therefore they say: "Both he who knows thus and he who does not—both approach the Soma; for Soma is glory. But they say of him: "Glory comes to that man alone who has declared 'Soma' at the Soma [sacrifice]. Therefore, one should declare "Soma" at the Soma [sacrifice]; glory indeed comes to him.

Anuvāka 9 {2.2.9.1} In the beginning, indeed, this was nothing at all. There was no sky, no earth, and no intermediate space. That which was non-existent alone made itself the mind, thinking, "May I be. It practiced austerity. From that heated state, smoke was born. It practiced austerity further. From that heated state, fire was born. It practiced austerity further.

From that heating, light was born. It heated itself further. From that heating, radiance was born. It heated itself further. From that heating, rays were born. It heated itself further. From that heating, great sounds were born. It heated itself further. It became condensed like a cloud; it burst its bladder.

{2.2.9.3} It became the ocean. Therefore, people do not drink from the ocean; for they regard it as a source of procreation. Therefore, when an animal is being born, the waters flow out first. Then the *daśahotṛ* was emitted. Prajāpati, indeed, is the *daśahotṛ*. Whoever, knowing thus the potency of austerity, performs austerity, truly comes to be. Now, this world was water, a mere ocean. Prajāpati wept.

Why was it called *ajñi*? Because [it was asked], "What if this were without a foundation? That which fell into the waters became the earth (*pṛthivī*). That which he wiped away became the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). That which he wiped upwards became the sky (*dyauḥ*). Because it wept (*arodat*), that is the reason for the name *rodasī* (the two worlds).

{2.2.9.5} He who knows thus—no one weeps in his house. This, indeed, is the birth of these worlds. He who thus knows the birth of these worlds does not meet with misfortune in these worlds. He found this foundation. Having found this foundation, he desired, "May I procreate. He performed austerity. He became pregnant. From his lower part, he emitted the Asuras.

{2.2.9.6} From them, he milked food into an earthen vessel. That which was his body, he cast it away; it became darkness. He desired, "May I procreate. He performed austerity. He became pregnant. From procreation itself, he created offspring. Therefore, these [beings] are most numerous, for he created them from procreation.

From them he milked milk into a wooden vessel. That which was his body, he cast it away; it became moonlight. He desired, "May I procreate. He performed austerity. He became pregnant. From his armpits alone, he created the seasons. From them he milked clarified butter into a silver vessel. That which was his body, [he cast it away].

He struck it away. It became the junction of day and night. He desired, "May I procreate. He performed austerity. He became pregnant. He created the gods from his mouth. For them, he milked Soma into a green vessel. That which was his body, he struck it away; it became the day.

{2.2.9.9} These indeed are the milkings of Prajāpati. He who knows thus milks forth his offspring. "Day has indeed come to us"—this is the godhead of the gods. He who knows thus the godhead of the gods becomes possessed of gods. This indeed is the birth of days and nights. He who knows thus the birth of days and nights does not meet with misfortune in days and nights.

{2.2.9.10} From the non-existent, the mind was emitted. The mind emitted Prajāpati; Prajāpati emitted the creatures. Indeed, all this that exists here is ultimately established in the mind alone. That is the Brahman named *śvovasīyas* (prospering day by day). For one who knows this, as it dawns again and again, it dawns more and more auspiciously for him. He is procreated with offspring and cattle. He attains the measure of Parameṣṭhin, he who knows thus.

Anuvāka 10 {2.2.10.1} Prajāpati created Indra as the youngest of the gods. He sent him forth, saying, "Go! Become the overlord of these gods. The gods said to him, "Who are you? We are indeed superior to you! He replied, "Who are you? We are indeed superior to you," for thus the gods had spoken to him. Now, at that time, there was still a portion of the sacrificial essence (*hara*) remaining with Prajāpati.

{2.2.10.2} That which was in this Āditya, he said to him: "Give this to me; then I shall become the overlord of these gods. He replied, "Who would I be after giving this? [The other said: "After giving this, you shall be that. "What is this that you say? [He replied: "Who indeed is Prajāpati by name? He who knows thus [becomes Prajāpati]."

They knew him by name. Having fashioned a golden disk (*rukma*) for him, they fastened it upon him. From that, indeed, Indra became the sovereign lord (*adhipati*) of the gods. He who knows thus becomes the sovereign lord of his equals. He thought, "What have I done? and he cried out, "Bring me the moon! That is the reason for the moon's name, *candramas*. He who knows thus [attains that].

He indeed possesses the moon. The gods said of him, "O men, guard him so that he may be full of heroic vigor. That is the *sūryatva* (the solar nature) of Sūrya; whoever knows this is not harmed. [The gods asked], "Who has established this power (*indriya*) within him? That is the *indratva* (the Indra-nature) of Indra; whoever knows this becomes possessed of power.

"This one indeed was the highest here"—that is why Parameṣṭhin is called Parameṣṭhin. He who knows thus reaches the highest pinnacle. The gods surrounded him on all sides: the Vasus from the east, the Rudras from the south, the Ādityas from the west, the Viśvedevas from the north, and the Aṅgirases from behind.

{2.2.10.6} The Sādhyas [placed him] facing away. He who knows thus—his equals submit to him. Having become Prajāpati himself, he caused his offspring to thrive. They did not stand still for him to provide them with food. Looking toward his face from the front, they went around to the south. He turned toward the south. Looking toward his face from the front, [they saw] his face from the south.

{2.2.10.7} She moved around from behind. He turned back from behind. They moved around, looking at his face from the front, from the south, from behind, and from the north. He turned back from the north. They moved around, looking at his face from the front, from the south, from behind, {2.2.10.8} and from the north. They went upward. He turned down from above. Having become one whose face is on all sides, he enveloped them.

Then indeed, creatures submitted to him for the sake of food. He who, knowing this, both turns [the fire] around and settles it down, becomes Prajāpati himself and eats his offspring; creatures submit to him for the sake of food, and he becomes an eater of food.

Anuvāka 11 {2.2.11.1} Prajāpati desired, "May I become more than much. He perceived this Daśahotṛ; he employed it. By its employment, he became more than much. He who should desire, "May I become more than much," should employ the Daśahotṛ. Verily, he becomes more than much. He desired, "May a hero be born to me. From the Daśahotṛ, he fashioned the Caturhotṛ. He employed it.

{2.2.11.2} From its employment, Indra was born. He who desires, "May a hero be born to me," should employ the Caturhotṛ formula. A hero is born to him. He desired, "May I possess cattle. He fashioned the Pañcahotṛ from the Caturhotṛ; he employed it. Through its employment, he became possessed of cattle. He who desires, "May I possess cattle," should employ the Pañcahotṛ formula.

He indeed becomes possessed of cattle. He desired, "May the seasons be arranged for me. He fashioned the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ from the Pañcahotṛ; he employed it. By its employment, the seasons were arranged for him. Whoever should desire, "May the seasons be arranged for me," let him employ the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ; the seasons will be arranged for him. He desired, "May I be a drinker of Soma, a sacrificer of Soma; may a drinker of Soma, a sacrificer of Soma, be born to me."

{2.2.11.4} He fashioned the Saptahotṛ from the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ. He employed it. By its employment, he became a drinker of Soma and a sacrificer with Soma; a drinker of Soma and a sacrificer with Soma was born for him. If one should desire, "May I be a drinker of Soma and a sacrificer with Soma; may a drinker of Soma and a sacrificer with Soma be born for me," let him employ the Saptahotṛ. He becomes a drinker of Soma and a sacrificer with Soma; a drinker of Soma and a sacrificer with Soma is born for him. Indeed, this sacrificial animal stands firm in five ways.

{2.2.11.5} With their feet and their mouths—those gods, having found the cattle, went to the heavenly world. In that world, they became hungry. They said, "We have lived upon what was given from there. Having arranged the Saptahotṛ sacrifice, they dispatched Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, saying, "With this, provide for us there. This is his provision.

{2.2.11.6} Whatever this [world] may be—whosoever knows this, for him it is prepared. Indeed, this sacrifice among men is the Saptahotṛ; it carries the oblation to the gods who abide there. Whosoever knows this, the sacrifice inclines toward him. Whosoever indeed knows the foundation (*nidāna*) of the Caturhotṛ formulas becomes possessed of a foundation. The Agnihotra is the foundation of the Daśahotṛ; the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are the foundation of the Caturhotṛ; the Seasonal sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*) are the foundation of the Pañcahotṛ; the Animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) is the foundation of the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ.

The Soma sacrifice belongs to the *saptahotṛ*. This indeed is the foundation (*nidāna*) of the *caturhotṛ* formulas. He who knows thus becomes possessed of a foundation. Prapāṭhaka 3, Anuvāka 1: The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "What is the reason for the *caturhotṛ* formulas being called *caturhotṛ*? Because in these [formulas] there are fourfold Hotṛ-priests, they are therefore *caturhotṛ*; hence they are called *caturhotṛ*. That is the reason for the *caturhotṛ* formulas being called *caturhotṛ*. Soma is the *caturhotṛ*; Agni is the *pañcahotṛ*; Dhātṛ is the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ*; Indra is the *saptahotṛ*.

{2.3.1.2} Prajāpati is the Daśahotṛ. He who thus knows the prosperity of the Caturhotṛ formulas prospers indeed. He who thus knows their kinship becomes possessed of kin. He who thus knows their arrangement succeeds in his undertakings. He who thus knows their abode becomes possessed of an abode. He who thus knows their foundation [becomes possessed of a foundation].

{2.3.1.3} He stands facing [the fire]. The exponents of the Veda (brahmavādinaḥ) say: "There is the Daśahotṛ, the Caturhotṛ, the Pañcahotṛ, the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ, and the Saptahotṛ. Now, why are they called 'Caturhotṛs'? Indra, indeed, is the Caturhotṛ; for Indra is indeed the most excellent among the deities because of his instruction. He who thus knows Indra as the most excellent among the deities because of his instruction becomes the most excellent among his peers.

Therefore, they recognize him who approaches as the most excellent by his very first arrival, saying, "He has come; he has arrived. His fame precedes him as he approaches the assembly of people; thus, they recognize him by his very first arrival, saying, "He has come; he has arrived."

One who is about to accept a sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) should breathe out seventeen times; thus he kindles his very self for brilliance and vigor. Moreover, becoming Prajāpati himself, he accepts it, so that there may be no injury to his own self. If they should exclude him while he has been chosen for the office of the *ṛtvij* priest, he should offer the *daśahotṛ* formula in the *āgnīdhra* fire with clarified butter taken four times, standing facing west in front [of the fire], reciting it in reverse order and with distinct pauses.

He causes his vital breaths (*prāṇa*) to waste away. If they should train him again, the *Āgnīdhra* alone should offer the *Daśahotṛ* formula with clarified butter taken in four ladlings, sitting behind [the altar] facing east, [reciting it] in the natural order without interruption. Thus he restores the vital breaths for him. At each beginning of the seasons, he offers the *Prāyaścitti-vāghotṛ* formula; thus he makes the seasons favorable for him, and the seasons become favorable for him.

{2.3.2.3} The seasons come to him, prepared for him. Having become the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ*, Prajāpati created all this. He created the mind (*manas*); from the mind he created the *gāyatrī*. Glory (*yaśas*) seized that *gāyatrī*; he took hold of her. From the *gāyatrī* he created the meters (*chandāṃsi*); from the meters he created the *sāman*. Glory seized that *sāman*; he took hold of it.

From the *sāman* he created the *yajus* formulas; from the *yajus* formulas, Viṣṇu. That glory reached Viṣṇu; he seized him. From Viṣṇu he created the plants; from the plants, Soma. That glory reached Soma; he seized him. From Soma he created the animals; from the animals, Indra.

That glory reached Indra; it did not pass him by. He who knows this becomes glorious like Indra; glory does not pass him by. Whatever there is here, all that Uttāna Āṅgirasa received. Since it was received by him, it did not harm him. Whatever one may receive, let him receive it with the thought: "Let Uttāna Āṅgirasa receive all of this. Thus indeed should he receive it.

This [earth] indeed is Uttāna Āṅgirasa; by means of her he accepts it; she does not injure him. He should accept a cow or a horse with sacrificial grass (barhis); for this is the dear abode of cattle; verily, he approaches it with its own dear abode.

He who, being ignorant, causes [the fire] to turn back, becomes headless and full of evil in yonder world. But he who, being wise, causes it to turn back, becomes possessed of a head and free from evil in yonder world. Seven deities, desiring prosperity, turned [the fire] back: Agni and Pṛthivī; Vāyu and Antarikṣa; Āditya and Dyau, and Candramas. Agni turned it back; he prospered with a thousandfold [offspring].

The earth turned back; it flourished with herbs and trees. The wind turned back; it flourished with rays of light. The intermediate space turned back; it flourished with birds. The sun turned back; it flourished with its beams. The sky turned back; it flourished with the constellations. The moon turned back; it flourished with days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, and the year.

He nourishes those nourishments which they formerly nourished. He who, knowing this, both turns [the fire] toward himself and carries it around—{2.3.4.1}—for him, indeed, when he accepted gold from Agni, half of his vital power (*indriya*) departed. He recovered that by means of this very [rite]. By that, he indeed placed half of his vital power within himself. He who, knowing this, accepts gold, places half of his vital power within himself. But he who accepts it without knowing this, half of his vital power departs from him.
When he accepted the garment of that Soma, a third part of his vital power departed.

{2.3.4.2} By means of this very [verse], he accepted it back. By that, indeed, he deposited a third part of his power within himself. He who, knowing thus, accepts a garment, deposits a third part of his power within himself. But he who accepts it without knowing this—of him, a third part of his power departs. When Rudra had accepted the cow, a fourth part of his power departed from him. By means of this very [verse], he accepted her back. By that, indeed, he deposited a fourth part of his power within himself.

He who, knowing this, accepts a cow, takes a fourth part of his sensory power into himself. But he who accepts it without knowing this—of him a fourth part of his sensory power departs. Indeed, when Varuṇa accepted a horse, a fifth part of his sensory power departed from him. He took it back by means of this very [rite]; thereby he took a fifth part of his sensory power into himself. He who, knowing this, accepts a horse, takes a fifth part of his sensory power into himself.

Now, if one who is ignorant accepts [the gift of] a man, the sixth sense departs from him. When Prajāpati accepted a man, the sixth sense departed from him; he accepted him back by means of this very [rite], and thereby he restored the sixth sense to himself. He who, knowing thus, accepts a man, restores the sixth sense to himself. But if one who is ignorant accepts [the gift of] a man, the sixth sense departs from him.

When Manu accepted the bed, the seventh part of his vital power departed from him. He recovered it by means of this very [rite], and thereby he restored the seventh part of his vital power into himself. He who, knowing thus, accepts a bed, restores the seventh part of his vital power into himself. But he who accepts one without knowing this—the seventh part of his vital power departs from him.
When Uttaṇa Āṅgirasa accepted the bed while lying on his back, the eighth part of his vital power departed from him.

{2.3.4.6} He accepted it with this very [formula]. By that, he indeed placed an eighth part of his sensory power within himself. He who, knowing thus, accepts while not breathing, places an eighth part of his sensory power within himself. But he who accepts without knowing, an eighth part of his sensory power departs from him. Whatever there is here, all that Utāna Āṅgīrasa accepted while lying on his back; therefore, having been accepted by him, it did not injure him.

Whatever he may accept, let him accept it all with the formula: "Let Utāna Āṅgirasa accept this. For this earth is indeed Utāna Āṅgirasa; thus he accepts it by means of her, and she does not harm him.

The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "When the *daśahotṛ*s performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*), by what householder (*gṛhapati*) did they prosper? By what means did they create offspring? They prospered indeed with Prajāpati as their householder; by him they created offspring. "When the *caturhotṛ*s performed a sacrificial session, by what householder did they prosper? By what means did they create plants? They prospered indeed with Soma as their householder.

{2.3.5.2} By means of that they created the plants. When the Pañcahotṛs performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*), by what householder did they prosper? By what did they drive away the Asuras from these worlds? By what did they win their cattle? It was by Agni as their householder that they prospered; by him they drove away the Asuras from these worlds; by him they won their cattle. When the Ṣaḍḍhotṛs performed a sacrificial session, by what householder did they prosper?

{2.3.5.3} "By whom did they ordain the seasons? "They prospered by means of Dhātṛ as their householder; by him they ordained the seasons. "When the Saptahotṛs performed the sacrificial session, by which householder did they prosper? By what means did they go to the heavenly world? By what means did they harmonize these worlds? "They prospered by means of Aryaman as their householder; by him they went to the heavenly world; by him they harmonized these worlds."

{2.3.5.4} These indeed are the gods who are the householders (*gṛhapati*). He who, knowing this, undergoes consecration even in the house of another, prospers among the performers of the sacrificial session (*sattra*) in an intermediate way. Or, he who knows Aryaman—for him offspring become desirous of giving. The sacrifice is indeed Aryaman; they call him "one whose dwelling is noble" (*āryā vasatiḥ*) whom they praise. For one who knows thus, his dwelling becomes noble.

{2.3.5.5} Whatever exists here—all that is the Caturhotṛs. From the Caturhotṛs the sacrifice was fashioned. If one who knows thus should dispute, saying, "I alone know more than he who knows the Caturhotṛs," he indeed knows more—namely, he who knows the Caturhotṛs. Verily, he who knows the Hotṛ-priests of the Caturhotṛs eats food among all creatures.

{2.3.5.6} He conquers all the quarters. Prajāpati is indeed the Hotṛ of the Daśahotṛ formulas; Soma is the Hotṛ of the Caturhotṛ formulas; Agni is the Hotṛ of the Pañcahotṛ formulas; Dhātṛ is the Hotṛ of the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formulas; Aryaman is the Hotṛ of the Saptahotṛ formulas. These indeed are the Hotṛs of the Caturhotṛ formulas. He who knows them thus eats food among all creatures and conquers all the quarters.

Anuvāka 6 {2.3.6.1} Prajāpati, having created living beings, became exhausted. He lay down, his heart having become [the seat of his being]. He called out, “Hā! O Self! The waters heard him. They returned to him by means of the Agnihotra sacrifice-rite. They pushed up a clod of earth (*kusindha*). Therefore, for this Agnihotra sacrifice-rite, there is but one officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). He called out four times: Agni, Vāyu, Āditya, and Candramas.

They listened. They returned by means of the very sacrifice-rite of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). They brought back four limbs. Therefore, for the New and Full Moon sacrifice-rite, there are four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); he called out five times; the cattle listened. They returned by means of the very sacrifice-rite of the Four-Monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*). They brought back hair, skin, flesh, bone, and marrow. Therefore, for the Four-Monthly sacrifice-rite...

{2.3.6.3} There were five officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). He called out six times. The seasons (*ṛtu*) responded. They returned by means of the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), a sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*). It was from that [sacrifice] that they brought back the breasts, the testicles, the penis, and the downward breath. Therefore, there are six officiating priests for the animal sacrifice, a sacrificial rite. He called out seven times. The *hotṛ* priests responded. They returned by means of the Soma sacrifice (*saumya adhvara*), a sacrificial rite.

He drew out those seven breaths of the head; therefore, at the Soma sacrifice, the sacrificial rite, the seven officiating priests (hotṛs) utter the *vaṣaṭ* call toward the east. He called out ten times; he heard [the response] as fervor (*tapas*). Through that very action, he returned within the year by means of all the sacrificial rites. He drew out his entire self without remainder. Therefore, within the year, all sacrificial rites are fully accomplished.

Therefore, there is the Daśahotṛ, the Caturhotṛ, the Pañcahotṛ, the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ, and the Saptahotṛ. They bring tribute to the Ekahotṛ; they bring tribute to him who knows this. Offspring come to him unobserved. Whoever knows thus, to him [they come].

Prajāpati created the Puruṣa. He said to Agni, "Let this be my food. Agni was afraid, thinking, "He will surely burn me up entirely. He saw these Caturhotṛ formulas as means for protecting himself; he offered them, and by means of them he protected himself. In that one offers the Agnihotra, one thereby obtains the Ekahotṛ sacrifice-rite of the Agnihotra.

{2.3.7.2} He preserves his own *kusindha* (the vital core) and attains union with the Sun. He draws up four times; thereby he attains the *Caturhotṛ* sacrifice, namely the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). He preserves four limbs of his own body and attains union with the Sun. He draws up four times; the fuel-stick (*samidh*) is the fifth. Thereby he attains the *Pañcahotṛ* sacrifice, namely the Four-Monthly Sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*).
[He preserves] hair, skin, flesh, bone, and marrow.
