This entire world of livestock belongs to you on every side—whatever you behold with the eye of Sūrya. You alone, O Indra, are the lord of cattle. May we enjoy the wealth that you extend to us. O Indra, lead us together with your mind, with cattle, with wise patrons, O Maghavan, and with well-being. Lead us together with the sacred word (*brahman*) that is fashioned by the gods.

{2.8.2.7} Unite us with the goodwill of the gods who are worthy of sacrifice! Drive the enemy far away from us. O Indra, invoked by many, with that fierce *śamba* weapon, bestow upon us wealth consisting of barley and cattle. Grant the singer a prayer rich in booty. [Bring] the ordainer, for he is pure; Bṛhaspati, being born first from the great light in the highest heaven—seven-mouthed and many-born, with his roar and seven reins, he blew away the darkness.

Bṛhaspati has won all treasures; this god has conquered great stalls filled with cattle. Desiring to win the waters and the light, the irresistible Bṛhaspati slays the enemy with his hymns. O Bṛhaspati, protect us! To the father, indeed! From heaven unto us! O daughter of lightning! These offerings we present! That breast of thine, O Sarasvatī, lead us toward it! This one, like a lotus-root-eater, has burst asunder the ridges of the mountains with her powerful waves.
With well-fashioned hymns and inspired thoughts, let us invoke Sarasvatī for our protection—she who reaches as high as the height of a pigeon.

Anuvāka 3 {2.8.3.1} Soma shall give a milch-cow; Soma, a swift steed; Soma, a hero skilled in action. He shall grant one who is a good householder, fit for the assembly, worthy of the council, and a glory to his father—him who has offered oblations to him. Unconquered in battles, O Soma, through thy powers; those stations of thine which they worship with oblation; thou, O Soma, art all these plants; thou hast generated the waters, thou the cattle. Thou hast stretched out the wide mid-air; thou hast dispelled the darkness with light.

{2.8.3.2} Those abodes of yours that are in heaven, those on earth, those in the mountains, in the plants, and in the waters—with all of them, being well-disposed and free from anger, O Soma, accept our offerings as you reign. Now for Viṣṇu’s sake—this is his beloved [abode]. Viṣṇu has stepped forth. Increasing beyond measure with his own body, they do not equal your greatness. We know both your realms upon the earth, O divine Viṣṇu; you alone know the highest.

{2.8.3.3} The god strode out; thrice [he strode], O god! "To thee, the great one," "He who, as soon as born," "Toward the cow-pens. With these [powers], Indra—unharmed—[overcame] the contending rivals; he confounded the fury of the enemy. With these [powers], he scattered all assailants in every direction; he brought down the Dāsa tribes for the Ārya. This one is heard of as conquering and slaying; this one also wins the cattle through battle. When Indra makes his fury true.

The entire firm and trembling world fears him; the waters have flowed according to his self-power (*svadhā*). He grew great in the midst of the navigable rivers. With a concentrated mind and with his most powerful blow, Indra struck him down toward the heavens. We invoke here for new protection that Indra—the bull accompanied by the Maruts, the one who has grown strong, the one whose enemies are not deficient, the divine ruler, the all-conquering, the fierce giver of victory. You were born fierce for victorious power.

{2.8.3.5} Melodious, most powerful, and possessing great pride—the Maruts themselves increased Indra’s strength in this matter, when the most bountiful Mother bore the Hero. Where, O Maruts, was that self-reliance of yours when you left me alone in the slaying of the serpent? For I am indeed fierce, mighty, and powerful; with my weapons, I have bowed down every enemy. Fleeing from the snorting of Vṛtra, all the gods who were your friends abandoned you.
O Indra, let there be friendship between you and the Maruts.

{2.8.3.6} Now, you shall conquer all these hostile armies. O Maruts, with my *indriya* power, I have slain Vṛtra. Having become mighty through my own fury, I, the wielder of the thunderbolt, have made these paths easy for Manu, making them all-glittering. He who is the bull, dwelling together with his virile powers, the sovereign ruler of the great heaven and earth, the one of true strength, to be invoked in battles—he, Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, let him be our protection. Indra overcame Vṛtra in the conquest of Vṛtra.

Invincible is Maghavan, the heroic Indra; the ancient clans rejoiced after him. He is the king of the moving world and of men; he alone is the hero, he indeed is the possessor of valor. He is the sole sovereign, the protector of the world beyond, when the heroic Indra overcame Vṛtra. Then he became the subduer of those with hostile intent. May Indra, the all-knowing, increasing the sacrifice, accept our oblation of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Having struck down Vṛtra the Dānava, the thunderbolt-armed one—

He has made firm the quarters, which were made firm by his firm support; increasing this sacrifice, may Indra, the all-knowing, accept the sacrificial cake. When the heroic Indra overcame Vṛtra, he then became the sole ruler of the people. Indra protected the gods in the slaying of Śambara; Indra became the leader of the gods. Indra, growing strong through the oblation at the sacrifice, the subduer of Vṛtra, shall grant us fearless protection—he who established the seven rivers upon the earth.
May Indra, who created the seven worlds and the quarters, who possesses the oblation and is accompanied by his host of Maruts, the subduer of Vṛtra, come here to this sacrifice.

Anuvāka 4 {2.8.4.1} Indra, the swift, the slayer of the arrogant, the fierce one, with his golden axe, the impetuous, the showerer of rain—may we abide in the favor of that worshipful one, and in his auspicious goodwill. May he, who is golden-hued, grant us fearlessness. Indra, the slayer of the arrogant, victorious in battles, may he extend to us a triple-layered shelter. Do you all protect us always with your blessings. Praise Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, whose back is the hymn (or, O Dyumanta, whose back is the Soma)—may he enjoy our oblation of the sacrificial cake.

Having slain our adversaries and hostile armies, O Victorious One, grant us security from every side. Praise the heroic wielder of the thunderbolt, the peerless Indra, the slayer of adversaries, who is invoked by many. To him, Indra, who alone is the sole lord over all people, offer the oblation. Indra is the sovereign ruler of the gods and their high priest; he has become the lord of the quarters, possessed of great strength. The slayer of adversaries, powerful and mighty, may he grant us wonderful and virile wealth.

{2.8.4.3} Indra, the slayer of the arrogant, who by his greatness and power has firmly established these two, heaven and earth—may he accept our oblation for the sake of bounty. May the divine guardian of the treasures of the gods protect us. Your chariot is unassailable, O Bull, that which belongs to you. Now indeed of Indra’s heroic deeds: he slew the serpent; Indra is the king of what has been settled and what is yet to come. He whose arms wield the thunderbolt is the master of the peaceful and the horned. He, the king, dwells as the ruler of the people; like the felly encompasses the spokes, he has encompassed them all.

{2.8.4.4} He has overcome his enemies; with his sharp bull, he has shattered the fortresses. Indra has struck Vṛtra down with his thunderbolt; exulting, he has furthered his own purpose. Worship Viṣṇu the god, Varuṇa for our protection, and Bhaga—with fat and with the omentum, O gods, perform the sacrifice. May those two come to our sacrifice, providing all nourishment; bestow upon us here wealth accompanied by progeny. Worship Viṣṇu the god and Varuṇa the giver—with fat and with the omentum, O gods, perform the sacrifice.

{2.8.4.5} Driving away our maladies, taking pleasure in this sacrifice, come hither, O Viṣṇu and Varuṇa! Grant great protection to our people and our folk for our sacrifice. Increasing through the oblation, you who are long-extending in worship, burn away the enemies with light as with darkness. By whose power the regions were propped up, most heroic by their manly deeds, most mighty; they who rule with irresistible strength—O Viṣṇu and Varuṇa, come at the first invocation!

O Viṣṇu and Varuṇa, you two are the protectors against imprecation. O gods, worship with oblation and clarified butter. Drive away disease and the demons; then bestow well-being and peace upon the sacrificer. O deliverers from distress, bulls, swift victors, most divine among the gods, most powerful—O Viṣṇu and Varuṇa, take pleasure in this offering presented by us for our protection, O heroes. May the great Heaven and Earth, the eldest, be present here with their splendor and their shining hymns.

When you, building up the two most extensive and lofty [worlds], roared like a bull for those who possess heroes, with your far-reaching movements; then bring forth the two parents born of old at the seat of *ṛta* with newer songs. O Heaven and Earth, come to us with the divine host; great is your protection. He indeed was the skillful craftsman among the worlds, he who brought forth these two, Heaven and Earth—the wide, deep, well-established regions. In the supportless space, the wise one has joined them together by his power.

{2.8.4.8} The two, though footless, carry the many, the moving, the footed embryo; like an eternal son in the lap of his parents, O Heaven and Earth, nourish him who speaks the truth. May this be true, O Heaven and Earth, what I here address to you, O Father and Mother. Be present with your protections, O lowest of the gods. May we find strengthening food, a secure dwelling, and life-sustaining rain. Broad, vast, ample, and far-extending, I address you with reverence at this sacrifice.

May the two who are fortunate and swift-moving bestow [blessings]; O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil. Of all the plants that have been born, which encompass everything—those plants whose king is Soma, which possess horses and which possess Soma—O Mother Plants, may one of you protect the other.

Anuvāka 5 {2.8.5.5} Now [I offer] this pure hymn of praise; [Indra] pierced Vṛtra. O Indra and Agni, both of you, [be] foremost for the people. O slayers of Vṛtra, [come] with songs; the inspired sage [worships]. O Brahmaṇaspati, you are the controller of this; be mindful of the hymn and prosper our offspring. All that which the gods favor is auspicious. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly. He, with his true and radiant friends, with those who seek wealth, pierced through the one who held the cattle.
Brahmaṇaspati [did so] with his bull-like boars.

Through the sweat of his fervor, he has distributed wealth according to his will; he became the lord of sacred prayer (*brahmaṇaspati*). His wrath is true as he performs great deeds; he who drove out the cows distributed them throughout heaven. Like a mighty stream, he has flowed forth with power; kindling the fire, he shall overcome those who attack him. Having performed sacred prayer and offered oblations, he has grown strong.
Born after what is born, he surpasses it; he extends far beyond. Whomever Brahmaṇaspati makes his companion, that one follows him forever, O Brahmaṇaspati, you who are easy to control.

{2.8.5.3} May we be chariot-riders of the wealth of Vivasvat. Bestow heroic strength upon our heroes, you who, being the Lord, come to my invocation through prayer. He indeed, with his people, with his clan, with his kin, with his sons, and with his men, wins booty and riches—he who strives to win the Father of the Gods, Brahmaṇaspati, with a mind of faith and with oblation. O Pūṣan, that which is within your ship; one part of you is bright. Pūṣan [rules] these regions. Pūṣan was born upon the far path of paths.

On the far path of heaven, on the far path of earth, he moves to and fro, knowing the way, toward both most beloved meeting-places. Pūṣan is the good kinsman of heaven and earth; the lord of nourishment, the bounteous one of wondrous luster. Him the gods gave to Sūryā—him who was made by desire, the powerful, the self-moving. He whose horses are goats, the guardian of cattle, the possessor of vigor, the inspirer of prayer, established over all beings. Pūṣan brandishes his supple goad.

Beholding all beings, the god moves along; O Maruts, pure are the oblations for you who are pure. I offer the pure sacrifice to the pure ones. By the *ṛta*, those who are true to the *ṛta* have come, they whose birth is pure, who are pure and purifying. Bring forth a brilliant hymn for the swift host of Maruts, for the self-strong one who sings. They who by force overcome all powers—O Agni, the earth trembles before these mighty ones. Upon your shoulders, O Maruts, are the rings.

{2.8.5.6} Golden ornaments rest upon their chests; they shine like lightnings with their showers of rain. Striving together according to their own nature with their weapons, grant those triple-layered protections which you provide for the one who exerts himself in worship. Extend them to the donor as well. O Maruts, bestow these upon us; O bulls, grant us wealth accompanied by heroic sons. These Maruts bring the swift to a halt; these bend down force against force. They strike down the curse of the one who seeks to harm.

{2.8.5.7} They bestow heavy hatred upon the one who does not give; like spokes, they are never at rest, like days. The bounteous ones multiply with their greatness. The sons of Pṛśni are most excellent and most powerful; by their own will, the Maruts have mingled together. To you was granted for your great Indra-power, all at once in the slaying of Vṛtra, O worshipful one—your sovereignty and your might. Indra, along with the gods, they followed you in the overcoming of men. O Indra, Maghavan, that impetuous strength which is yours—

{2.8.5.8} Teach thy friends, O thou invoked by many, and the men; for thou, O Maghavan, art firm and wise. Open wide the enclosure like a gift of wealth! Indra is the king of the moving world and of the peoples, over all that exists in various forms upon the earth. From thence may he grant riches to the donor. May he, being praised, impel the gift hitherward toward us. Praise him indeed, who possesses surpassing power, Indra, the much-invoked, who conquers unassailed and irresistible. With these [powers], praise the invincible, the fierce, the subduer.

{2.8.5.9} Strengthen the bull of the people with our songs—he who is the lord of abundant and great wealth. Let us praise that Indra in the assemblies, he who conquers with Vāyu for the sake of cattle-rich lands, and who boldly leads us toward better fortune. O Bull, let your fervor come from behind; let it come from above, from below, and from the front. Let it gather from all sides toward us. O Indra, bestow upon us celestial splendor.

May the god Savitṛ, possessor of fine jewels, come forth, filling the mid-air as he is borne by his horses; holding in his hand many benefits for men, settling the world and impelling it. Enveloped in pearls, multiform, with golden pins, great and worthy of worship—Savitṛ of wondrous luster has mounted his chariot, bestowing power upon the dark regions. May that god Savitṛ, the lord of treasures, impel us toward our impulse and bestow riches upon us.

Spreading far and wide, he bestows upon us vast splendor and the food of mortals; let him not withhold it from us. The dark-hued steeds with white-footed hooves have looked out over the people, drawing the chariot with its golden fore-shaft. All the worlds abide within the lap of the divine Savitar, who forever illumines the quarters of space. The fair-winged one has surveyed the mid-air, the Asura of deep vibration and excellent guidance. Where now is the Sun? Who knows? To which heaven has his ray extended itself?

Seeking strength, we pray for fortune, wisdom, and abundance. May Narāśaṃsa and Gnāspati protect us. May we be in the gathering of all desirable wealth and riches; may we be dear to the god Savitṛ. May all the gods come to us, unimpeded—Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa, acting in harmony. So that they all may be our increasers, let them make our strength firm and not wavering. May the gods, the Viśvedevas, be auspicious to us; may Sarasvatī be auspicious along with our prayers.

{2.8.6.4} Peaceful be those who pursue us with malice, and peaceful those who bestow gifts. May the divine ones and the earthly ones be peaceful to us; may the waters be peaceful to us. All those gods who are under the ordinance of Mitra and Varuṇa, whose impulse is truth—O Savitṛ—they, bestow upon us auspiciousness, wealth consisting of heroes and cattle, and manifold riches. O Agni, go on your mission as messenger; you are not to be harmed. Come toward the gods with the host of those who fashion sacred prayers (brahman), to Sarasvatī, the Maruts, the Aśvins, and the Waters.
Sacrifice to all the gods so that they may grant us jewels.

O Father Heaven, O Earth Mother, free from treachery; O Brother Agni, O Vasus, be gracious to us! O all you Ādityas and Aditi, being of one accord, extend to us manifold protection. O All-Gods, hear this my invocation—ye who dwell in the mid-region and ye who are in heaven, ye whose tongue is Agni, or who are worthy of sacrifice—having seated yourselves upon this sacred grass (*barhis*), rejoice! O Gods Mitra and Varuṇa, may I with reverence turn you both toward the enjoyment of the oblation through your favor.

May our sacred prayer be victorious in battles; may the divine rain be easy to cross. You two clothe yourselves in fat garments; your thoughts and your outpourings are flawless. You have struck down all falsehoods; O Mitra and Varuṇa, you abide by the Eternal Law (*ṛta*). That indeed is your greatness, O Mitra and Varuṇa: the cows that stood still have been milked day after day. You cause all the streams of the stall to swell; one single wheel of yours rolls along.

{2.8.6.7} That which is most expansive, O bounteous ones, which is not easily pierced—O guardians of the world, grant us that flawless protection. Through that, O Mitra and Varuṇa, protect us; desiring to win, may we be victorious. O Mitra and Varuṇa, sprinkle our pasture with clarified butter and with nourishing offerings for the sake of our oblation. Fulfill here the desire of the people; bestow upon us the splendor of the heavenly light. Stretch forth your arms so that we may live; sprinkle our pasture with clarified butter.

{2.8.6.8} O youthful ones, make us famous among the people! Hear, O Mitra and Varuṇa, these my invocations. Bring these songs to Rudra, the god of the firm bow, the swift-arrowed, the self-sustained; to the unconquered, the victorious, the bounteous giver; to the one with sharp weapons—bring them and listen! {May he of the radiant splendor hear us!} O Rudra, through the most auspicious medicines granted by you, may I attain a hundred winters. Drive far away from us hostility, drive away distress, and scatter in all directions our diseases.

{2.8.6.9} Worthy one, you bear [the bolt]; do not deprive us of our offspring. O Father of the Maruts, let your favor come to us; do not separate us from the sight of the sun. May the hero be gracious toward our horse. May we procreate, O Rudra, through progeny. Thus, O tawny bull, manifesting yourself, so that as a god you neither grow angry nor slay us. O Rudra, hear our invocation here! May we, with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly. May the missile of Rudra pass us by. Praise the famous one, O most bountiful one—worthy one, you bear [the bolt]. You, O Agni, are Rudra. [I praise] your king.

Sūrya approaches the radiant goddess Uṣas, as a youth approaches a maiden, from behind. Wherein the god-seeking men extend their generations for the sake of auspiciousness after auspiciousness. The auspicious bay horses of Sūrya, the bright, swift-moving ones, worthy of praise, have ascended the back of heaven while paying homage; they traverse heaven and earth in an instant.
That is the divinity of the Sun, that is his greatness: in the midst of his work, he has withdrawn what was spread out.

{2.8.7.2} When he has unyoked his bay horses from their station, then Night spreads her garment over all. This form Sūrya assumes in the lap of heaven for the beholding of Mitra and Varuṇa. One part of his power is endless and green; the other, dark, they gather together when the bays have departed. Today, O gods, at the rising of the sun, deliver us from distress and from blame. May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us this.

{2.8.7.3} The golden ornament of heaven, far-sighted, rises up; he whose goal is distant, the swift traveler, shining brightly. Truly, men impelled by Sūrya come forth to pursue their goals and perform their works. Be auspicious to us with your sight, be auspicious to us with your day; be auspicious with your light, be auspicious with your cold, be auspicious with your heat. So that there may be well-being for this [person] on the road and well-being in his home, O Sūrya, bestow upon us that wonderful wealth. The wonderful face of the gods has risen—the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni.

He has filled the heaven, the earth, and the mid-air; Sūrya is the soul of all that moves and stands. Tvaṣṭṛ bestows upon us that seminal essence; Tvaṣṭṛ [bestows] the hero, he of golden hue. The ten [fingers], unwearied and youthful maidens, brought forth this embryo of Tvaṣṭṛ; they bore him who is radiant. Him of sharp aspect, self-glorious among men, shining brightly, they lead around. He, the lovely one, grows within these [women]; upright in the lap of those who are bent, he is self-glorious.

Both [worlds] were afraid of Tvaṣṭṛ as he was being born; turning toward him, they take pleasure in the lion. Mitra [protects] the people—forward, O Mitra! This Mitra is worthy of homage, most gracious; he has been born as a king of goodly power, a wise ordainer. May we abide in the favor of that holy one, in his auspicious goodwill. Free from disease, rejoicing in nourishment, with measured strides upon the wide expanse of the earth, may we remain observing the ordinance of Āditya.

{2.8.7.6} May we abide in the benevolent favor of Mitra. May Mitra, through our sacred work (*śimī*), [grant us] abundance in cattle—[may he be] rich in cattle for us. With pious intent, they have generated [him] in the assembly within the waters. By his splendor and by song, the two worlds (*rodasī*) were made to tremble. [He is] the beloved, worshipful protection of all beings. The great Āditya is to be approached with homage; he who impels men is most gracious to the singer. To that most praiseworthy one, offer this pleasing oblation in the fire for Mitra. May your chariot, encompassing both heaven and earth, [come hither].

Let him come with golden, vigorous horses, shining with his fellies whose path is ghee; the bearer of nourishments, the lord of men, rich in strength, spreading himself over the five worlds. Let the three-seated chariot, yoked by thought, approach—the one by which you two go to the people seeking the gods, taking your course wherever it may be, O Aśvins. Come hither with your own noble horses; O wonder-workers, drink from the honeyed treasure-vessel. Your chariot, moving together with the bride, shall travel forth.

{2.8.7.8} With your two paths, you drive away the ends of heaven; the maiden, the daughter of the Sun, chose your splendor during the night of Paritakmyā. When you protect the one who seeks the gods with your powers, your mind goes around the heat, and by your protection, your vigor reaches the cow. O chariot-borne ones, that very chariot of yours which, yoked, traverses the path while the dawns shine—by means of it, grant us well-being and peace at the breaking of the dawn.

O Aśvins, bring [the gods] to this sacrifice! You two lifted up Bhujyu, who was cast down into the ocean, with your unerring, winged, tireless, and undaunted [steeds]. O Aśvins, may you deliver us by means of your wondrous deeds! O Agni and Soma, he who honors you today with this speech—to him grant heroic strength, the increase of cattle, and abundance of horses. He who honors Agni and Soma with an oblation, with a mind directed toward the gods, and with clarified butter—protect his sacred vow and save him from distress.

{2.8.7.10} O Agni and Soma, grant great protection to the people. Whoever offers an oblation to you, whoever performs the preparation of the sacrificial gift for you—he shall attain offspring, heroic vigor, and a full span of life. O Agni and Soma, that heroic power of yours is well known: that you stole away the food of Paṇi, the cow; that you struck down the remnant of Prathaya; and that you found the one light for many. O Agni and Soma, [accept] this [offering] of mine; O Agni and Soma, [accept] the oblation that has been set forth.

Anuvāka 8 {2.8.8.1} I am the first-born of Cosmic Order (Ṛta), the navel of immortality before the gods. He who gives me away—he alone shall possess me. I am the food; I devour the one who eats the food. Even before the fire, I consume the food. They two sit watchful {they two sit radiant}; I am among the later ones. His jaws are wide open; his teeth are well-formed. The wise behold this; the simple-minded move about [unaware]. I abandon one, I do not abandon the other. I go at will toward the food.

{2.8.8.2} I encompass the common purpose while enjoying it. What mortal man would grant me food? This food is placed in the world beyond; this food is guarded by all the gods and the ancestors. That which is eaten, that which is lost, and that which is cast away—that has become the hundredth part of my body. With milk drawn once, he filled two great vessels; together with the speckled one, both heaven and earth. Drinking that together, the wise ones do not diminish it; it becomes neither more nor less.

{2.8.8.3} They say that food is the out-breath (*prāṇa*), and food is the in-breath (*apāna*). Food is death, yet they call it life. The wise call food old age; they say food is the procreation of living beings. The thoughtless man obtains food in vain; I speak the truth: it is his own destruction. He nourishes neither the noble nor his friend. He who eats alone becomes the possessor of sin alone. I am the thundering cloud raining down; they eat me, and I eat others.

{2.8.8.4} I become truly immortal. Upon me all the Ādityas shine. They have generated divine Speech—that which they speak as speech—endless, fashioned from the end, vast. In her, the gods have placed their provisions: the one-syllabled, the two-footed, and the six-footed. All the gods subsist upon Speech; all the gods subsist upon Speech. The Gandharvas, the animals, and human beings [subsist] upon Speech. In Speech all these worlds are established.

May she, the consort of Indra, enjoy our invocation—Vāc, the first-born syllable of Ṛta, the mother of the Vedas, the navel of immortality. May she, being pleased, come to our sacrifice; may the goddess, who protects, be easy for me to invoke. That goddess Vāc, whom the seers, the makers of mantras, and the wise sought after with austerity and toil—that goddess Vāc we worship with an oblation. May she establish us in the world of the well-done. Speech has been measured out in four quarters.

{2.8.8.6} Those wise Brahmins know them; three [of the quarters of speech] are hidden in the cave and do not stir. Of speech, humans speak only the fourth quarter. Through faith, the fire is kindled; through faith, the oblation is offered. Faith, upon the summit of fortune, we proclaim with our voice. O Faith, what is dear to the one who gives; O Faith, what is dear to the one who desires to give; what is dear among the liberal patrons and the sacrificers.

{2.8.8.7} Make this my utterance come true! Just as the gods established faith among the fierce Asuras, so too, O gods, establish faith among our generous patrons who perform sacrifice. The gods and the sacrificers, protected by Vāyu, wait upon faith with the intention of their hearts. Through faith the oblation is offered; through faith one finds wealth. We invoke faith in the morning.

{2.8.8.8} Faith around midday; faith at the setting of the sun. O Faith, inspire me here. Faith clothes the gods. Faith is this entire world. We magnify Faith, the mother of desire, with an oblation. The Brahman, first born in the east, Vena has revealed from the radiant horizon; his lowest and highest stations are established.

He has disclosed the source of both the existent and the non-existent; the father of sovereign rulers, the bull of riches, the omniform one has entered the intermediate space. They honor him with hymns, the bearer, increasing him who is Brahman by means of Brahman. Brahman gave birth to the gods; Brahman is this entire world. From Brahman the *kṣatra* was fashioned; Brahman is the Brāhmaṇa by his very self. Within him these worlds abide.

{2.8.8.10} Within is this entire world; Brahman alone is the eldest among all beings. With whom, then, could one dare to rival it? O Brahman, the thirty-three gods are [contained] within you; O Brahman, Indra and Prajāpati are [contained] within you; O Brahman, indeed, all beings are contained within you, like those gathered within a boat. Let the four quarters and the fires move forth; may he, knowing us, lead this sacrifice of ours, pouring out ghee that is ageless and rich in heroes.

{2.8.8.11} The *brahman* is the kindling-stick of the oblations: "The cows have come; they have performed what is auspicious. Let them sit in the cow-pen and take delight with us. May they be here, prolific and many-formed, milking forth abundance for Indra at every dawn. Indra bestows gifts upon the sacrificer who gives; he grants his favor and does not steal from him. Increasing his wealth more and more, he establishes the seeker of the gods in an unbroken pasture. These [cows] are never lost, nor do they perish."

{2.8.8.12} Cattle are Bhaga; cattle have Indra come to me; {dyumaṇṭa has come}. Cattle are the first portion of Soma to be consumed. O people, these cattle that are here are Indra. With my heart and with my mind, I truly desire Indra. You cows, you make even the emaciated fat. You make even the unsightly and unlovely one beautiful of countenance. You make the house auspicious, O you of auspicious speech. Great is your vigor proclaimed in the assemblies.

May you be prolific, grazing on good pasture, radiant with joy; may you drink pure waters at a fine watering-place. Let no thief nor any evil-planner have power over you; may the missile of Rudra avoid you. This is the mingling; let it be mingled among these cows, mingled in the seed of the bull, and mingled, O Indra, in your own heroic vigor.

Those two, Sūrya and Candramas, the greatest sustainers of all, possess great splendor; they rule with wealth in the sky. Moving as the self of the *sāman*, they proceed according to the *sāman*. The ordinance of those two gods has never been measured out. Both traverse the two limits by their own power; like the rays of heaven, they stretch across the ocean. Both are the protectors of the worlds, possessing the wisdom of seers. Like the sun and the moon, they move on, their thoughts destroyed.
Both are lords, radiant and all-knowing; both are Sūryas and both are Candramases, far-seeing.

{2.8.9.2} Viśvavārā and Viribhā are worthy of choice; Dyumna and Oṇṭa are worthy of choice. As such, you two, wise ones of great vows, protect us—O you who encompass all, who further us, who carry us across, who find the light of heaven, and who possess many rays for us to behold. For Sūryā and Candrā are beautiful, brilliant, and lovely to look upon. Both, being mindful, now follow the sky together. The seven rivers bear his glory; Heaven and Earth and the broad world bear his lovely form. So that we may behold Sūrya and Candramas, Indra moves about with faith, moving in various ways.

These two move one after the other by means of their creative power (*māyā*); like two children at play, they pass around the sacrifice. One of them surveys all beings; the other, ordaining the seasons, is born again and again. Golden-hued, pure, and purifying are those [waters] whose king is Varuṇa, and whose gods are the Maruts; look upon me with a gracious eye! O auspicious Waters, I behold you; indeed, I see you. At that time, there was neither non-existence nor existence. There was neither the intermediate space nor the sky beyond it.
What did the world envelop, and where? In whose protection did it abide?

{2.8.9.4} What was the covering? Where was the fathomless deep? Was there death, or was there immortality then? {There was no death, nor was there immortality then;} there was no sign of night or of day. That One breathed, windless, by its own inherent power. Other than that, nothing else existed beyond it. Darkness there was, hidden by darkness in the beginning; all this was an indistinguishable sea.
That which was covered by the unreal, the insubstantial—by that very unreality; from the power of darkness, the One was born through fervor. In the beginning, desire arose within it.

{2.8.9.5} That which was the first seed of the mind, they discovered its bond within the non-existent. Having perceived it in the heart through inspired thought, the seers found the thread stretched across them. Was there below? Was there above? There were seed-bearers; there were powers. Self-sustenance was beneath, effort was beyond. Who truly knows? Who here has declared it? Whence was it born, whence came this creation?
The gods are later than this world’s manifestation.

{2.8.9.6} Now, who indeed knows from whence this creation arose? Whence this diverse world has come into being? Whether he [the Creator] established it, or whether he did not—He who is its overseer in the highest heaven, He truly knows, or perhaps even He does not know. What was the wood, and what was that tree, from which they fashioned heaven and earth? O you who possess wisdom, inquire with your mind regarding that very thing: upon what did He stand while supporting the worlds? Brahman was the wood; Brahman was that tree, from which they fashioned heaven and earth.

{2.8.9.7} Since they fashioned heaven and earth, I, the wise one, declare it to you with my mind: Brahmā stood over the worlds, upholding them. At dawn we invoke Agni; at dawn, Indra; at dawn, Mitra and Varuṇa; at dawn, the Aśvins; at dawn, Bhaga, Pūṣan, and Brahmaṇaspati; at dawn, let us call upon Soma and Rudra. At dawn, let us invoke the fierce Bhaga, the conqueror; we [invoke] the son of Aditi who is the distributor, whom even the weak-minded and even the swift consider [worthy].

{2.8.9.8} Even a king says of him, "May I partake of Bhaga. O Bhaga, leader; O Bhaga, whose gifts are true; O Bhaga, grant us this prayer, bestowing it upon us. O Bhaga, further us with cattle and horses; O Bhaga, may we be rich in men through our heroes. And may we be possessed of Bhaga even now—at the beginning of the day, at its midpoint, and at the rising of the sun, O Maghavan—may we abide in the benevolence of the gods. O gods, let Bhaga alone be the possessor of fortune!

{2.8.9.9} Through him may we become fortunate, O Blessed Ones. You, Bhaga, everyone invokes with fervent calls. May you, Bhaga, be our leader here. May the dawns incline toward our sacrifice, like Dadhikrāvan toward the pure station. May they bring hither to us Bhaga, the finder of wealth, as spirited horses draw a chariot. May our auspicious dawns shine forth forever, rich in horses, rich in cattle, and rich in heroes.
Yielding ghee and swelling from all sides, do you protect us always with your blessings.

Prapāṭhaka 1, Anuvāka 1 May Agni protect us; may the Kṛttikās [protect] us—the divine constellation, the source of sensory power. Offer this discerning oblation into their mouth. He whose rays shine, whose banners [are seen], and to whom all these entire worlds belong—he, Agni, dwelling together with the Kṛttikās, may that god establish us in prosperity. O Prajāpati, may Rohiṇī, the wife, accept [this offering]—she who possesses all forms, who is vast, and of wondrous luster.

May she establish us in the success of the sacrifice, so that we may live for many autumns with our heroic sons. The goddess Rohiṇī has risen in the east, delighting in all forms; increasing Prajāpati with the oblation, may she approach the sacrifice, dear to the gods. King Soma has come with Mṛgaśīrṣa; this constellation is auspicious, his beloved abode. Swelling in many ways among the people, may he bestow seed and progeny upon the sacrificer.

{3.1.1.3} That constellation of yours which is Mṛgaśīrṣa, O King—dear, most dear among all that is dear—to it we pay homage with an oblation, O Soma. Be auspicious to our bipeds and auspicious to our quadrupeds! Accompanied by Ārdrā, Rudra advances, the most excellent of the gods, the lord of the inviolable ones. To his constellation we pay homage with an oblation. May he not harm our progeny nor our heroes; may the missile of Rudra pass us by.
May the constellation Ārdrā be pleased with our oblation.

Releasing us from all evils, may they drive away the malevolent one and the enemy. May the goddess Aditi grant us freedom again; may the two *Punarvasū* bring this sacrifice back to us. May all the gods return to us again and again; we worship you repeatedly with oblations. Thus, may the goddess Aditi, who is unassailable, the sustainer of all and the foundation of the world, and the two *Punarvasū*, increasing us through the oblation, enter the beloved path of the gods.

Bṛhaspati, being born first, came together with the constellation Tiṣya. The best among the gods, victorious in battles—may there be safety for us in all directions. May Tiṣya be before us and also in our midst; may Bṛhaspati protect us from behind. May they drive away hatred and grant us security; may we be masters of heroic vigor. Let this oblation be pleasing to the serpents, whose minds follow the Āśleṣās.

{3.1.1.6} Those serpents who dwell in the atmosphere and upon the earth—may they come most readily to our invocation. Those serpents who are even in the radiant realm of the sun, those who roam along the divine heaven, and whose desires follow the Āśleṣās—to those serpents I offer the honeyed oblation. Invited are the ancestors who are with the Maghās; swift as thought, well-doers, and performers of good deeds—may they come most readily to our invocation at this lunar mansion. May they graciously enjoy the sacrifice presented with the *svadhā* offerings.

Those who have been consumed by fire and those not consumed by fire, the ancestors who dwell in that world—both those whom we know and those whom we do not know—may they enjoy the well-performed sacrifice during the Maghā constellation. You are the lord of cattle, O Phalgunī; this is dear to you, O Aryaman, Varuṇa, and Mitra. As such, may we, while living, enter into the company of you who are the winner of all winnings, you who are alive. By him through whom all these worlds were conquered, whose mind the gods follow.

Aryaman the King, undecaying and mighty, bellows as the bull of the *phalgunī* stars. O Blessed One, you are the most excellent Bhaga among the gods; the *phalgunī* stars know this of you. Grant us that wealth! Bestow upon us here unaging dominion and great heroic strength, together with cattle and horses. Bhaga is indeed the giver, Bhaga is the bestower; Bhaga has entered the goddesses, the *phalgunī* stars. May we go to that impulse of Bhaga where, with the gods, we may rejoice in shared revelry.

{3.1.1.9} May the divine Savitṛ come; may he approach with his golden, well-rolling chariot, bringing the auspicious hand, skillful in action, bestowing abundance and holy merit. May the hand bestow immortality and greater wealth; with our right hand we receive this. May I today find the giver, Savitṛ, who impels the sacrifice for our hand. Tvaṣṭṛ approaches the constellation Citrā—the radiant, youthful maiden of beautiful form.

Establishing both the immortals and mortals, fashioning forms and all worlds—may Tvaṣṭṛ reveal that to us; may that constellation be a great giver to me. May it grant us offspring rich in heroes; may it grace our sacrifice with cattle and horses. Vāyu approaches the Niṣṭyā constellation like a sharp-horned bull bellowing loudly, Mātariśvan stirring the worlds. May he drive away hatreds and hostilities.

May Vāyu hear this, and may Niṣṭyā hear it; may that constellation, the giver of much, be for my benefit. May the gods grant us this desire, so that we may cross over all difficulties. Let our enemies go far away, overcome with fear. May Indra and Agni accomplish this, and may Viśākhā accomplish it; may the gods rejoice in this sacrifice for us. May there be safety for us from behind and from before. Viśākhā is the sovereign lady of the constellations; Indra and Agni are the two best guardians of the world.

Driving away the enemies in all directions, may they drive off hunger and ill-will. Full behind and full before, the Paurṇamāsī has risen victorious from the midst. In her, the gods dwelling together shall rejoice here in the highest firmament. Broad, radiant, youthful, and well-disposed, the Paurṇamāsī has risen shining forth. Swelling up all misfortunes, may she yield for the sacrificer a wide and glorious sacrifice.

May we prosper by our oblations, having approached with reverence. May Mitra the god be ours for friendship. Increasing the Anurādhas with our oblation, may we live a hundred autumns with our heroes. The wondrous constellation has risen in the east; that which they call the Anurādhas—therein Mitra goes by the paths traveled by the gods, spread out with golden [rays] across the mid-air. Indra follows the eldest constellation, in which he overcame Vṛtra in the battle against Vṛtra.

{3.1.2.2} From that [cow], milking out immortality, may we cross over hunger, misfortune, and ill-offered sacrifice. For Purandara, the bull, the bold, the unconquered, the conqueror, the bountiful—may she, the most excellent, milking sweetness, create wide space for the sacrificer. May I obtain a root and offspring rich in heroes. Let Nirṛti go away, far away. May the constellation, joined with cattle and livestock, become a day of prosperity for me, the sacrificer.

{3.1.2.3} May the Day bestow upon us today prosperity; that which they call the Root Constellation—by my speech I drive away Destruction far away. May it be auspicious for my progeny, may it be auspicious for me. Those celestial waters which have come together with milk, those which are in the intermediate space and those which are on earth, those whose will the invincible Aṣāḍhā follows—may those waters be propitious and gentle to us. Those which are in wells and those which are in rivers, those of the ocean and those which are in ponds, and those which flow forth.

{3.1.2.4} May those waters for whom they consume honey during the Aṣāḍhā [constellation] be auspicious and gentle to us. May all the gods hear this; may the Aṣāḍhās favor this sacrifice. May that constellation spread prosperity for our cattle. May agriculture and rain be favorable to the sacrificer. Radiant maidens, young women, well-adorned, performers of rites, doers of good deeds, and full of vigor—may the Aṣāḍhās, increasing all the gods with oblations, approach the sacrifice according to their desire.

{3.1.2.5} In which Brahmā conquered all this—the world beyond and this entire world—may that constellation Abhijit, having triumphed, bestow upon us prosperity that is free from resentment. Both these worlds have been won together by Brahmā; may that constellation Abhijit look upon us. In it may we conquer our enemies. May the gods grant us our desire; they hear Śroṇā, the guardian of immortality. I listen to her auspicious voice.

{3.1.2.6} We worship with an oblation this goddess Mahī, the wife of Viṣṇu, who is undecaying and turned toward us. Viṣṇu, the wide-striding, has stepped out threefold: over the great heaven, the earth, and the intermediate space. Seeking renown, she comes to that fame, creating a holy song for the sacrificer. The eight gods, the Vasus, are worthy of Soma; the four goddesses are ageless and most glorious. May they protect the sacrifice beyond the realm of dust, [granting] the immortal well-being that lasts a year.

{3.1.2.7} May the Vasus protect our sacrifice from the east; may the Śraviṣṭhās come to us from the south. Let us enter under the auspicious constellation; let no hostile or evil-intending person come against us. Varuṇa is the king of the ruling power (*kṣatra*), the sovereign lord; Śatabhiṣaj is the most excellent among the constellations. May those two grant long life to the gods; they bestow a hundred thousand remedies. May King Varuṇa approach our sacrifice; may all the gods gather together around this for us.

May that constellation Śatabhiṣaj, being pleased, extend long life and healing remedies for us. Aja Ekapād has risen in the east, rejoicing in all beings. All the gods follow his impulse; they are the Proṣṭhapadas, the guardians of immortality. Blazing brightly, kindled, and fierce, he has ascended the firmament, the sky. All the Proṣṭhapadas follow that god Sūrya, the unborn Aja Ekapād.

The serpent of the deep (*ahir budhniyaḥ*) goes forth expanding; he is the most excellent among gods and among men. All those Brāhmaṇas who drink Soma, who are worthy of Soma, the Proṣṭhapadas—all of them protect him. These four gods perform a single task; they are those whom they call the Proṣṭhapadas. Praising the serpent of the deep who dwells in the assembly, they protect Ahi by approaching him with reverence. Pūṣan follows the path along with Revatī; he is the lord of prosperity, the protector of cattle, and the possessor of strength.

{3.1.2.10} Accepting these offered oblations, come to our sacrifice by easy paths. May Revatī protect our small cattle; may Pūṣan follow after our cows and horses. Protecting food of many forms, may they win strength and the sacrifice for the sacrificer. May the Aśvins, yoked with their horses, come to that place—those most swift to go on their well-governed steeds, worshipping their own constellation with the oblation, mingled with honey and joined with the *yajus* formula.

{3.1.2.11} Those two who are the physicians of the gods, the bearers of oblations, the messengers of all, and the guardians of immortality—may they, delighting in the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), approach us. We pay homage to the Aśvins, the yokers of horses; may the Bharaṇīs carry away our evil. May King Yama, the blessed one, look upon this; for he is the king of the great world, truly great. May he make for us a path that is easy to traverse and free from fear. In which lunar mansion King Yama goes, in which the gods consecrated him—[in that may we prosper].
Let us worship that wondrous one with an oblation; may the Bharaṇīs carry away our evil. For that which the gods bestowed upon you as a dwelling-place.

He becomes ever new as he is born, that ray which the Ādityas cause to swell. Those two who, though different in form, are of one mind, weave their garments; they extend across the same thread. I invoke from every side the pervasive, the powerful, and the all-encompassing. May those two come to our call at the constellation. We, O Goddesses, being in harmony with the sacred word (*brahman*), possessing fine jewels and offering a feast for the gods, increase Day and Night with our oblation.

May we pass beyond evil, passing through liberation. She has appeared facing us as she approaches; the daughter of heaven shines forth. With her eye, the noble one uncovers the great waters; she makes light out of darkness. The sun follows after the ruddy cows as he rises together with the radiant constellation. O Dawn, at your dawning and that of the sun, may we come together with our portion. May that radiant, shining constellation rise up for us as splendor; may it come here to our sacrifice.

To the divine constellation, to Indra, we call the Soma-drop. May he, as Savitṛ, impel for us gain that bestows prosperity and is most rich in heroes. [Recite] "Upwards that bright one," "May Aditi protect us," "The great Mother," "Viṣṇu has traversed this," "That Viṣṇu," "Agni is the head of the world," "May Anumati favor us today," "O Anumati, you indeed," and "The bearer of oblations, the well-offered."

Anuvāka 4 {3.1.4.1} Agni indeed desired, "May I be the eater of food among the gods. He offered this cake on eight potsherds to Agni and the Kṛttikās. Thereupon, he indeed became the eater of food among the gods. Agni is indeed the eater of food among the gods. Just as Agni is the eater of food among the gods, even so does he become the eater of food among men who sacrifices with this oblation and who knows it thus. He offers here: agnaye kṛttikābhyaḥ svāhā | kṛttikābhyo 'gnaye svāhā || 1 ||
Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to the Kṛttikās! Svāhā to Ambā! Svāhā to Dulā! Svāhā to Nitatnī! Svāhā to Abhrayantī! Svāhā to Meghayantī! Svāhā to Varṣayantī! Svāhā to Cupuṇīkā! Thus.

Prajāpati created offspring. Once they were created, they moved away from him. He set his heart upon Rohiṇī among them. He desired: "May she turn toward me; may she come back to me; may I unite with her. He offered this oblation of cooked rice (caru) to Prajāpati for Rohiṇī. Thereupon, she indeed turned toward him; he united with her. Verily, what is dear turns toward him.
He goes with what is dear: he who sacrifices with this oblation and he who knows it thus. He offers here, saying: "To Prajāpati, svāhā! To Rohiṇī, svāhā! To Rocamānā, svāhā! To the progeny, svāhā!"

{3.1.4.3} Soma, indeed, desired: "May I win sovereignty over the plants. He offered this oblation of millet (*śyāmāka*) cooked in milk to Soma Mṛgaśīrṣa. Thereupon, he won sovereignty over the plants. Verily, one who performs this sacrifice with this oblation, and he who knows it thus, wins sovereignty among his equals. He offers here: "Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to Mṛgaśīrṣa! Svāhā to the Invakās! Svāhā to the plants! Svāhā to sovereignty! Svāhā to victory!"

{3.1.4.4} Rudra, indeed, desired: "May I be rich in cattle. He offered this oblation of *praiyaṅgu* groats cooked in milk to Rudra in the constellation Ārdrā. Thereupon he became rich in cattle. Verily, one becomes rich in cattle who performs this sacrifice with this oblation, and who knows it thus. He offers here: "To Rudra, svāhā! To Ārdrā, svāhā! To the swelling one, svāhā! To the cattle, svāhā!"

{3.1.4.5} This earth was indeed hairless. She desired: "May I be propagated with herbs and trees. She offered this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to Aditi and the two *punarvasu* stars. Thereupon, she was propagated with herbs and trees. He who sacrifices with this oblation, and he who knows it thus, is indeed propagated with offspring and cattle. He offers here: "To Aditi, svāhā! To the two *punarvasu* stars, svāhā! To prosperity, svāhā!
To procreation, svāhā! (Ānandāśrama). Svāhā! Svāhā! Svāhā! Svāhā!

{3.1.4.6} Bṛhaspati indeed desired, "May I be possessed of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*). He offered this oblation of wild rice (*naivāra*) cooked in milk to Bṛhaspati Tiṣya. Thereupon he indeed became possessed of spiritual luster. One who sacrifices with this oblation becomes possessed of spiritual luster, as does one who knows it thus. He offers here: "To Bṛhaspati, svāhā! To Tiṣya, svāhā! To spiritual luster, svāhā!"

{3.1.4.7} The gods and the asuras were arrayed against one another. Those gods offered a *karambha* (barley-meal) oblation to the serpents of the *āśleṣā* constellation. They brought it forward by means of these very deities. Verily, by means of these deities, he who sacrifices with this oblation and he who knows it thus brings his hateful rival under his power. He offers here: "To the serpents, svāhā! To the *āśleṣās*, svāhā! To the biters, svāhā!"

{3.1.4.8} The ancestors indeed desired, "May we prosper in the world of the fathers. They offered this cake on six potsherds to the Maghās, the ancestors. Thereupon they indeed prospered in the world of the fathers. He who sacrifices with this oblation, and he who knows it thus, prospers in the world of the fathers. He offers here: "Svāhā to the fathers! Svāhā to the Maghās! Svāhā to the sinless ones! Svāhā to the disease-free ones! Svāhā to the Arundhatīs! {Ānandāśrama}. Svāhā! {Ānandāśrama}. Svāhā! {Ānandāśrama}. Svāhā! {Ānandāśrama}. Svāhā! {Ānandāśrama}. Svāhā! {Ānandāśrama}. Thus.

{3.1.4.9} Now Aryaman desired, "May I possess cattle. He offered this oblation of cooked rice to Aryaman and the two Phalgunīs. Thereupon he indeed became possessed of cattle. One who sacrifices with this oblation becomes possessed of cattle, as does one who knows it thus. He offers here: "To Aryaman, svāhā! To the two Phalgunīs, svāhā! To the cattle, svāhā!"

{3.1.4.10} Bhaga once desired, "May I be the fortunate one, the most excellent among the gods. He offered this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) for Bhaga with the two *Phalgunī* stars. Thereupon, he indeed became the fortunate one, the most excellent among the gods. Whoever performs this sacrifice with this oblation, and whoever knows it thus, becomes the fortunate one, the most excellent among his peers. He offers here: "Svāhā to Bhaga! Svāhā to the two *Phalgunīs*! Svāhā to the state of being most excellent!"

{3.1.4.11} Savitṛ indeed desired, "May the gods place faith in me; may I be a Savitṛ. He offered this cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, made of fast-ripening rice. Then, indeed, the gods placed faith in him; he became a Savitṛ. Men place faith in him who sacrifices with this oblation and who knows it thus. He offers here: savitre hastāya svāhā || 11 || To Savitṛ, the hand, svāhā!
Svāhā to Savitṛ; svāhā to the hand; svāhā to him who gives; svāhā to him who bestows; svāhā to him who offers; svāhā to him who receives—thus.

{3.1.4.12} Tvaṣṭṛ indeed desired: "May I obtain wonderful offspring. He offered this cake on eight potsherds to Tvaṣṭṛ for the sake of wonderful offspring. Thereupon, he indeed obtained wonderful offspring. Whoever performs this oblation and whoever knows it thus obtains wonderful offspring. He offers here: "Svāhā to Tvaṣṭṛ! Svāhā to Citrā! Svāhā to Caitra! Svāhā to offspring!"

{3.1.4.13} Vāyu indeed desired: "May I win unrestricted movement among these worlds. He offered as an oblation the milk of a young cow that had recently calved, dedicated to Vāyu and Niṣṭyā. Thereupon, he won unrestricted movement among these worlds. Whoever sacrifices with this oblation, and whoever knows it thus, wins unrestricted movement among these worlds. He offers here: "Svāhā to Vāyu! Svāhā to Niṣṭyā! Svāhā to unrestricted movement! Svāhā to victory!"

{3.1.4.14} Indra and Agni desired, "May we win preeminence among the gods. They offered this cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni and to the two Viśākhās. Thereupon, they indeed won preeminence among the gods. He who sacrifices with this oblation, and he who knows it thus, wins preeminence among his equals. He offers here: "Svāhā to Indra and Agni! Svāhā to the two Viśākhās! Svāhā to preeminence! Svāhā to victory!"

{3.1.4.15} Now he offers this clarified butter at the full moon sacrifice. The full moon is indeed desire; clarified butter is desire. By means of desire itself, he brings about the fulfillment of his desire. That desire quickly comes upon him with which he performs the sacrifice. He offers here with the formula: "To the full moon, svāhā! To desire, svāhā! To arrival, svāhā!"

Anuvāka 5 {3.1.5.1} Mitra, indeed, desired: "May I win over friendship among these worlds. He offered this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to Mitra and the Anūrādhas. Thereupon, he won over friendship among these worlds. Verily, one wins over friendship among these worlds who performs this sacrifice with this oblation, and also he who knows it thus. He offers here: "To Mitra, svāhā! To the Anūrādhas, svāhā! To the winning of friendship, svāhā! To victory, svāhā!"

{3.1.5.2} Indra, indeed, desired: "May I attain preeminence among the gods. He offered this cake on eleven potsherds for Indra Jyeṣṭha, made of *mahāvrīhi* rice. Thereupon, he indeed attained preeminence among the gods. Whoever performs this oblation and whoever knows it thus attains preeminence among his equals. He offers here: "To Indra, svāhā! To Jyeṣṭhā, svāhā! To Jyaiṣṭhya, svāhā! To victory, svāhā!"

{3.1.5.3} Prajāpati indeed desired: "May I find offspring at its root. He offered this oblation of cooked rice (caru) for Prajāpati the Root. Thereupon, he indeed found offspring at its root. Verily, one finds offspring at its root who sacrifices with this oblation and who knows it thus. He offers here: "To Prajāpati, svāhā! To the Root, svāhā! To offspring, svāhā!"

{3.1.5.4} The waters indeed desired: "May we conquer the ocean, our desire. They offered this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to the waters, the invincible ones (*aṣāḍhā*). Thereby they indeed conquered the ocean, their desire. Verily, he who sacrifices with this oblation, and he who knows it thus, conquers the ocean, his desire. He offers here: "To the waters, svāhā! To the invincible ones, svāhā! To the ocean, svāhā! To desire, svāhā! To conquest, svāhā!"

{3.1.5.5} All the gods indeed desired, "May we conquer what is unconquerable. They offered this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to the All-Gods (*viśve devāḥ*) and the Invincible Ones (*aṣāḍhāḥ*). Thereupon, they conquered what was unconquerable. He who sacrifices with this oblation, and he who knows it thus, conquers what is unconquerable. He offers here: "To the All-Gods, svāhā! To the Invincible Ones, svāhā! To the unconquerable, svāhā! To victory, svāhā!"

{3.1.5.6} Brahman indeed desired: "May I conquer the world of Brahman. He offered this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to the conquered Brahman. Thereby he indeed conquered the world of Brahman. Whoever performs this sacrifice with this oblation, and whoever knows it thus, conquers the world of Brahman. He offers here: "To Brahman, svāhā! To the conquered, svāhā! To the world of Brahman, svāhā! To the conquest, svāhā!"

{3.1.5.7} Viṣṇu indeed desired: "May I hear a glorious report; may no evil reputation come upon me. He offered this cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu Śroṇā. Thereupon he heard a glorious report, and no evil reputation came upon him. Verily, he who sacrifices with this oblation, and he who knows it thus, hears a glorious report, and no evil reputation comes upon him. He offers here as follows:
Svāhā to Viṣṇu! Svāhā to Śroṇā! Svāhā to Śloka! Svāhā to Śruta! Thus.

{3.1.5.8} The Vasus indeed desired, "May we attain preeminence among the gods. They offered this cake on eight potsherds to the Vasus and the Śraviṣṭhās. Thereupon, they indeed attained preeminence among the gods. He who sacrifices with this oblation and he who knows it thus attains preeminence among his equals. He offers here: "To the Vasus, svāhā! To the Śraviṣṭhās, svāhā! To preeminence, svāhā! To attainment, svāhā!"

{3.1.5.9} Indra, indeed, desired: "May I be firm and not loose. He offered this cake on ten potsherds to Varuṇa Śatabhiṣaj for the sake of medicines, made of black rice. Thereupon, he indeed became firm and not loose. Truly, one becomes firm and not loose who sacrifices with this oblation and who knows it thus. He offers here: "To Varuṇa, svāhā! To Śatabhiṣaj, svāhā! To the medicines, svāhā!"

{3.1.5.10} Aja Ekapād desired: "May I be radiant and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*). He offered this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to Aja Ekapād and the Proṣṭhapadas. Thereupon, he indeed became radiant and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge. Radiant and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge indeed becomes he who sacrifices with this oblation, and also he who knows it thus. He offers here: "To Aja Ekapād, svāhā! To the Proṣṭhapadas, svāhā! To radiance, svāhā! To the splendor of sacred knowledge, svāhā!"

{3.1.5.11} The serpent Budhniya indeed desired, "May I find this firm foundation. He offered this cake on eight potsherds to the serpent Budhniya and the Proṣṭhapadas. Thereupon, he indeed found this firm foundation. Verily, he who sacrifices with this oblation finds this firm foundation; and so does he who knows it thus. He offers here, saying: "Svāhā to the serpent Budhniya! Svāhā to the Proṣṭhapadas! Svāhā to the firm foundation!"

{3.1.5.12} Pūṣan indeed desired, "May I possess cattle. He offered this oblation of cooked rice (caru) to Pūṣan and Revatī. Thereupon he indeed became possessed of cattle. One who sacrifices with this oblation becomes possessed of cattle, as does one who knows it thus. He offers here, saying: "Svāhā to Pūṣan! Svāhā to Revatī! Svāhā to the cattle!"

{3.1.5.13} The two Aśvins indeed desired: "May we be possessed of hearing and free from deafness. They offered this cake on two potsherds to the two Aśvins, the possessors of horses. Thereupon, they indeed became possessed of hearing and free from deafness. One who performs this oblation becomes possessed of hearing and free from deafness, as does one who knows it thus. He offers here with: "Svāhā to the two Aśvins! Svāhā to the two possessors of horses! Svāhā to hearing! Svāhā to the act of hearing!"

{3.1.5.14} Yama indeed desired, "May I win sovereignty over the ancestors. He offered this oblation of cooked rice (caru) to Yama and the Apabharaṇīs. Thereupon, he won sovereignty over the ancestors. Verily, one who sacrifices with this oblation, and one who knows it thus, wins sovereignty over his equals. He offers here: "Svāhā to Yama! Svāhā to the Apabharaṇīs! Svāhā to sovereignty! Svāhā to victory!"

{3.1.5.15} Now, he offers this clarified butter at the new moon (amāvāsyā). The new moon is indeed desire; clarified butter is desire. By means of desire itself, he fulfills his desire. That desire quickly comes upon him for whatever desire he sacrifices with. He offers here [the oblation] with: "To the new moon, svāhā! To desire, svāhā! To arrival, svāhā!"

Anuvāka 6 {3.1.6.1} The Moon indeed desired: "Having attained the days and nights, the half-months, the months, the seasons, and the year, may I attain union with and residence in the same world as the Moon. He offered this cake on fifteen potsherds to the Moon for the sake of being seen in return. Thereupon, having attained the days and nights, the half-months, the months, the seasons, and the year, he attained union with and residence in the same world as the Moon.

Having reached the days and nights, the half-months, the months, the seasons, and the year, he attains union with and residence in the same world as the Moon—both he who sacrifices with this oblation and he who knows it thus. He offers here: "Svāhā to the Moon! Svāhā to her who is being seen! Svāhā to the days and nights! Svāhā to the half-months! Svāhā to the months! Svāhā to the seasons! Svāhā to the year!"

Day and night indeed desired: "May we escape beyond day and night; may day and night not reach us. They offered this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to day and night, made from two kinds of rice—white and black—and prepared in the milk of two cows, one white and one black, that had calved together. Thereby, they were indeed released beyond day and night; day and night did not reach them. Verily, one who performs this is released beyond day and night; day and night do not reach him.
Whoever sacrifices with this oblation, and whoever knows it thus—he offers here: "To Day, svāhā! To Night, svāhā! To liberation, svāhā!"

{3.1.6.3} Uṣas indeed desired: "May I be dear to Āditya and fortunate. She offered this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to Uṣas. Thereupon, she indeed became dear to Āditya and fortunate. He who sacrifices with this oblation, and he who knows it thus, becomes dear to his peers and fortunate. He offers here: "To Uṣas, svāhā! To the dawning, svāhā! To her who has dawned, svāhā! To her who is about to dawn, svāhā! To her who has fully dawned, svāhā!"

{3.1.6.4} Now, for this lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), he prepares a sacrificial pap (*caru*), saying: "As you are among the gods, so may I become among men. For just as this [mansion] is among the gods, so indeed does he become among men who sacrifices with this oblation and who knows it thus. He offers here: "To the lunar mansion, svāhā! To the one about to rise, svāhā! To the one rising, svāhā! To the one risen, svāhā! To the taking away, svāhā! To the bringing, svāhā!"

"Salutation to radiance, svāhā! Salutation to splendor, svāhā! Salutation to heat, svāhā! Salutation to the luster of sacred knowledge, svāhā! (3.1.6.5) Sūrya indeed desired, "May I be the foundation of the constellations. He offered this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to Sūrya and the constellations. Thereupon, he indeed became the foundation of the constellations. He who performs this sacrifice with this oblation, and he who knows it thus, becomes the foundation among his equals. He offers here: "To Sūrya, svāhā! To the constellations, svāhā! To the foundation, svāhā!"

{3.1.6.6} Then he offers this oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) to Aditi. Aditi, indeed, is this earth. Verily, he finds firm support upon her. He makes an offering here with: "To Aditi, svāhā! To the foundation, svāhā!

{3.1.6.7} Then he offers this oblation of cooked rice to Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu, indeed, is the sacrifice. Verily, he finds firm support in the sacrifice at the very end. He makes an offering here with: "To Viṣṇu, svāhā! To the sacrifice, svāhā! To the foundation, svāhā!"

Prapāṭhaka 2, Anuvāka 1. In the third heaven from here, Soma was. Gāyatrī brought him down. A leaf of his was torn off; that became the *parṇa* tree. That is the reason for the name of the *parṇa*. The *parṇa* is indeed Brahman. When one drives away the calves with a branch of the *parṇa*, one drives them away with Brahman itself. The *parṇa* is indeed of the nature of the Gāyatrī; cattle are of the nature of the Gāyatrī.

Therefore, there are three leaflets on each blade of the *parṇa* tree; the *gāyatrī* consists of three feet. When he drives out the cows with a branch of the *parṇa* tree, he drives them out by means of its own deity. If he should desire of someone, "May he be without cattle," he should bring for him a branch that has no leaflets and whose tips are dry; verily, he becomes without cattle. If he should desire of someone, "May he be rich in cattle," he should bring for him a branch with many leaflets and many twigs; verily, he makes him rich in cattle.

{3.2.1.3} If he were to bring [the earth] from the east, he would conquer the world of the gods; if from the north, the world of men. He brings it from both the east and the north for the conquest of both worlds. "For food thee! For strength thee! he says; verily, he bestows food and strength upon the sacrificer. "Ye are winds," he says; Vāyu is indeed the overseer of the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*). Animals have the intermediate region as their deity.

He entrusts them to Vāyu himself; he thus impels them forward. When he says, "You are winds," he says, "You are approaching winds"; he thereby summons the cattle for the sake of the sacrificer. "May the god Savitṛ impel you," he says for the sake of instigation. "For the most excellent rite," he says; for the sacrifice is indeed the most excellent rite; therefore he speaks thus. "Swell, O inviolable ones, the portion of the gods," he says.

{3.2.1.5} Formerly, these [cows] swelled for calves and for humans; [now] he causes them to swell for the gods, for Indra. “Full of vigor, full of milk,” he says; for they gather together vigor and milk. “Possessing offspring, free from disease, free from consumption,” he says for the sake of procreation. “May no thief, may no evil-planner have power over you,” he says for protection. “May Rudra’s bolt avoid you,” he says; verily, he protects them from Rudra.
"May you be many and firm in this lord of cattle," he says; thus he makes them many and firm in him.

"Protect the cattle of the sacrificer," he says, for the protection of the cattle. Therefore, in the evening, the cattle return home. He sets [the vessel] down not on the ground, for the support of the embryos and so they do not fall. Therefore, the embryos of living beings do not fall. He places it as if above, for the world of heaven is, as it were, above. This is for the attainment of the world of heaven.

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ," with these words he takes up the horse's rib for the sake of impulsion. "With the arms of the Aśvins," he says; for the Aśvins were the two *adhvaryu* priests among the gods. "With the hands of Pūṣan," he says for the sake of restraint. He who knows the plants joint by joint does not harm them. Prajāpati indeed knows the plants joint by joint; he does not harm them. He goes toward the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the horse's rib; for the horse belongs to Prajāpati, [and thus he acts] for the sake of common origin.

{3.2.2.2} "For the non-injury of the plants," he says; "Thou art the prosperer of the sacrifice," he says; thus the sacrificer bestows wealth upon himself. "The Rakṣas is burnt up, the enemies are burnt up," he says; for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. "This prayer has gone forth toward the sacrificial grass," he says; knowledge indeed is the prayer; by means of knowledge he approaches it. "Made by Manu, fashioned by Svadhā," he says; for the axe is made of Manu's substance and is fashioned by Svadhā.

“They, the sages, bring [it] from the east,” he says. The sages are indeed those who have heard [the sacred lore]. The sacrifice is in the east. Thus, he begins the sacrifice from the very beginning (the front). Moreover, when he brings [the sacrificial grass] from whatever direction after having said this, it becomes as if from the eastern direction itself. “May you sit here upon the sacrificial grass, which is pleasing to the gods,” he says. This is for the prosperity of the sacrificial grass and for the non-failure of the ritual. “You are chosen by the gods,” he says.

{3.2.2.4} Whatever exists here, all that belongs to the gods as their allotted portion. Furthermore, just as one might announce to a superior, "I shall do this," so does the Adhvaryu, having announced it to the gods, cut the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for his own safety. As many tufts as he might designate, if he were to leave any of them remaining, he would cause that to be redundant for the sacrifice. He should designate only one tuft; he should cut that entirely.

{3.2.2.5} "For the sake of the non-excess of the sacrifice," he says, "Thou art increased by rain. Indeed, plants are increased by rain. "O divine sacrificial grass," he says; he thus prepares it for the gods. "Neither lengthwise nor crosswise [may I harm thee]," he says, for the sake of non-injury. "May I succeed in thy joint," he says, for the sake of success. "May I, thy cutter, not be harmed," he says. He who knows thus is not diminished in his own self.

"O divine sacrificial grass (*barhis*), grow with a hundred shoots," he says. The sacrificial grass is indeed offspring; [he says this] for the procreation of offspring. "May we grow with a thousand shoots," he says; thus he invokes this very blessing. "Guard against contact with the earth," he says for the sake of stability. He cuts the handfuls of grass unevenly; [this is] for the sake of pairing and procreation. "Well-prepared, I prepare you," he says; thus he prepares it with the sacred word (*brahman*).

"Thou art the girdle of Aditi," he says. Aditi is indeed this [earth]. He thus makes for her this girdle. "The binding of Indrāṇī," he says. Indrāṇī was the first among the deities to bind herself; she prospered. He binds himself for prosperity. The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is indeed offspring. It is for the non-exclusion of offspring. Therefore, offspring are born with their sinews continuous.

"Pūṣan shall tie your knot," he says; verily, he bestows nourishment upon the sacrificer. "May it not loosen for you," he says, for the sake of non-injury. He tucks it behind, facing forward; for from behind, facing forward, the seed is deposited. Verily, from behind he deposits the seed for him, facing forward. "I lift you up with the two arms of Indra," he says; verily, he bestows power upon the sacrificer. "I carry you on the head of Bṛhaspati," he says; Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman among the gods.

{3.2.2.9} He carries it with the very *brahman*. "Traverse the wide atmosphere," he says, for the sake of movement. "Thou art the path leading to the gods," he says; verily, he causes it to go to the gods. He sets it down not on the ground, for the support of embryos and so they do not fall. Therefore, the embryos of creatures do not fall. He places it as if above, for the world of heaven is, as it were, above. This is for the attainment of the world of heaven.

Anuvāka 3 {3.2.3.1} On the previous day, he prepares the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*). Having thus commenced and taken hold of the sacrifice, he observes the fast. Prajāpati created the sacrifice; its two *ukhā* vessels fell apart. Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice. In that there are the two *ukhā* vessels for the *sāṃnāyya* offering, he thereby places the two *ukhās* of the sacrifice itself to prevent their falling apart. "Be purified for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods," he says. He purifies these very [vessels] for the sacrifice to the gods. "Thou art the cauldron (*gharma*) of Mātariśvan," he says.

The Gharma of Mātariśvan is indeed the intermediate space; [it serves] for the support of these worlds. "Thou art heaven; thou art earth," he says, for this fire-pan (ukhā) is composed of both heaven and earth; therefore he speaks thus. "Thou art all-sustaining by the highest ordinance," he says; rain is indeed all-sustaining; verily, he secures rain. "Be firm, do not waver," he says for the sake of stability.

"Thou art the purifier of the Vasus," he says. The Vasus are indeed the vital breaths; this purifier is their portion. He thus makes it for them. "Hundred-streamed, thousand-streamed," he says; he thereby bestows life upon the vital breaths for the sake of completeness. It consists of three strands made of darbha grass on a branch of the *palāśa* tree. The vital breath is indeed threefold; he thus places the threefold vital breath in the middle of the sacrificer.

The leafy branch is of Soma for the sake of common origin. Darbha grass is the manifest purifier. He places it facing eastward in the evening; that is the form of out-breath (prāṇa) and in-breath (apāna). He places it crosswise in the morning; that is the form of the new moon (darśa), for this day belongs to the new moon. The moon is indeed food, and the vital breaths are food; he thus attains both, to avoid sameness (ajāmitva).

Therefore, this [wind] blows from every side. "The drop is offered, the spray is offered," he says for the sake of stability and so that the oblation does not spill; for what has been offered with the *svāhā* call does not spill. In heaven there is a fire named Nāka; its portion is the droplets. "To Agni, the great Nāka," he says; thus he endows the fire Nāka with its own portion. "Svāhā to Heaven and Earth," he says; thus he establishes it in Heaven and Earth.

{3.2.3.6} He pours [the milk] with a purifier. He thus mingles the essence of both the waters and the plants; furthermore, he establishes the cattle within the plants themselves. Having taken hold [of the calf], he restrains his speech for the support of the sacrifice. He remains holding [the vessel], for they milk while holding [the calf]. "Whom have you milked? he asks, up to the third time. These worlds are three; thus the sacrificer milks these very worlds.

He utters her name, saying, "So-and-so. He thus makes manifest their auspicious work. He says, "She is all-life; she is all-extensive; she is all-action. This earth is indeed all-life; the intermediate space is all-extensive; yonder sky is all-action. By means of these [names], he milks these very worlds in their proper order. Furthermore, just as one invokes a blessing upon a benefactor, even so does he praise them with this.
Therefore, having drawn the milk while saying "She has given," they milk the cattle while offering salutations and praises.

{3.2.3.8} "O you who yield much milk, [yield] for Indra, for the gods, the oblation!"—with these words he releases his speech. Thus he impels [the cow] according to the respective deity, for the sake of distinguishing between the divine and the human. He says it three times, for the gods are characterized by the number three. Remaining silent and not touching [the vessel], he performs the subsequent acts; thus he secures what is unlimited. One should not milk into a wooden vessel. A wooden vessel is indeed like fire; if one were to milk into a wooden vessel, [it would be as if one were milking into fire].

{3.2.3.9} One should sacrifice with an offering whose *yāma* (course/efficacy) has been exhausted. Now, they also say: "The sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) have the cake (*puroḍāśa*) as their head; there is no course for the cake-offering beyond this. One may certainly milk [the cow] using a wooden vessel, but a *śūdra* must not milk. For a *śūdra* is born from what is unreal (*asat*); they say that what a *śūdra* milks is indeed not a true sacrificial offering (*ahavis*).

{3.2.3.10} A Śūdra indeed should not milk for the Agnihotra; for they do not purify that [milk]. "When it truly passes through the filter, then it becomes an oblation (havis)," so it is said. He says, "Be united, O you who possess the cosmic order (ṛtāvarīḥ)! He thus unites the essence of both the waters and the plants. Therefore, we subsist upon the essence of both the waters and the plants. He says, "The delightful one, for the winning of wealth! He thereby bestows nourishment upon the sacrificer. He says, "I mix you with Soma for Indra, as curd!"

{ 3.2.3.11} He thus makes this very [offering] into Soma. For he who, having consumed Soma, does not drink Soma for a year, his drinking of Soma becomes subject to being drunk again. But the *sāṃnāyya* is indeed Soma. He who, knowing this, drinks the *sāṃnāyya*, his drinking of Soma becomes such that it is not to be drunk again. One should not cover [the vessel] with an earthenware [lid]. If one were to cover it with an earthenware [lid], it would belong to the Pitṛs as its deity.

{3.2.3.12} He covers it with either an iron vessel or a wooden vessel; for that [vessel] is possessed of the gods. It contains water. Water, indeed, is the slayer of Rākṣasas; [he does this] for the driving away of the Rākṣasas. "Thou art uninjured; for Viṣṇu thee! he says. Viṣṇu, indeed, is the sacrifice; verily, he makes it uninjured for the sake of the sacrifice. "O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation! he says for protection. He sets it down not on the ground, for the support of embryos and so they do not fall. Therefore, the embryos of creatures do not fall.
He places it as if above; for the world of heaven is, as it were, above. This is for the attainment of the world of heaven.

"May I be able for you two for the sake of the rite for the gods," he says for the sake of capability. Indeed, following the continuity of the sacrifice, the offspring and cattle of the sacrificer continue; following the interruption of the sacrifice, the offspring and cattle of the sacrificer are interrupted.
