"Thou art the continuity of the sacrifice; I strew thee for the continuity of the sacrifice; for the continuity of the sacrifice, I [strew] thee"—thus saying, he extends [the grass] from the Āhavanīya fire for the continuity of the sacrificer’s offspring and cattle.

He leads forward the waters. The waters are indeed faith; having undertaken faith and having led it forward, he proceeds with the sacrifice. He leads forward the waters. The waters are indeed the sacrifice; having undertaken the sacrifice and having led it forward, he proceeds. He leads forward the waters. The waters are indeed a thunderbolt; having hurled the thunderbolt at his enemies and having led them forward, he proceeds. He leads forward the waters. The waters are indeed slayers of the Rakṣases; for the purpose of striking away the Rakṣases. He leads forward the waters. The waters are indeed the beloved abode of the gods; having led forward the beloved abode of the gods, he proceeds.

{3.2.4.3} He leads forward the waters. The waters, indeed, are all the deities. Having taken hold of the deities and having led them forward, he proceeds with the ritual. "For service thee," he says; for he takes this up for service. "The Rakṣas is burnt away, the enemies are burnt away," he says; for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. "Thou art the pole," he says; for this Agni is indeed the pole-bearer. If he were to pass over him without touching him, [the sacrifice would be lost].

{3.2.4.4} It might burn both the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). He passes by after touching [the fire] for the sake of preventing the burning of the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer. "O Dhūr, injure him who injures us; injure him whom we injure," he says. There are indeed two kinds of persons: he whom one injures, and he who injures one. Both of these he strikes with anguish.

"Thou art the most bountiful, the most fulfilling, the most beloved, the best bearer, the best invoker of the gods among the gods," he says. This is exactly according to the sacrificial formula (*yathāyajus*).

"Thou art unswerving, the vessel for the oblation," he says, to prevent injury. "Be firm, do not waver," he says, for the sake of stability. "I gaze upon thee with the eye of Mitra," he says, for the sake of friendship. "Do not fear, do not tremble, may I not harm thee," he says, to avoid injury. Whatever the wind blows upon, all that belongs to the deity Varuṇa. "Wide open for the wind," he says; thus he makes it free from Varuṇa's power.
"In the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he says, for the sake of instigation. "With the arms of the Aśvins," he says.

For the Aśvins were the two *adhvaryu*s among the gods. "With the hands of Pūṣan," he says; this is for the sake of restraint. "I offer what is pleasing to Agni," he says; thus he offers them as something pleasing specifically to Agni. He does so three times with the sacrificial formula (*yajus*); these worlds are three; it is for the attainment of these worlds. The fourth time he does so silently; thus he wins an unlimited amount. In this very manner, he offers the oblations in their proper sequence.

"This belongs to the gods, and this belongs to us together," he says for the sake of distinction. "For prosperity, not for misfortune, I take you," he says for protection. He who is in the enclosure moves, as it were, within darkness. "May I look upon the light of heaven, the Vaiśvānara light," he says; thus he gazes upon the light of heaven, the Vaiśvānara light. When the oblation has been taken, Heaven and Earth may tremble; "May the dwellings of Heaven and Earth be made firm," he says.

"For the support of the houses of heaven and earth," he says; "traverse the wide mid-region," he says for the sake of movement; "I set thee in the lap of Aditi," he says. Aditi is indeed this [earth]; verily, he sets it in her lap. "O Agni, guard the oblation," he says for protection.

Anuvāka 5 {3.2.5.1}: Indra slew Vṛtra; he [Indra] was overwhelmed by the waters. Whatever in them was pure (*medhya*), fit for sacrifice (*yajñiya*), and possessed of the gods (*sadeva*), that went out from them; they became *darbha* grass. In that he purifies the waters with *darbha* blades, it is with those very waters which are pure, fit for sacrifice, and possessed of the gods that he purifies them. He purifies them with two [verses].

The sacrificer has two feet for the sake of stability. "May the god Savitṛ purify you," he says; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he indeed purifies them. "With a flawless strainer," he says; yonder sun is indeed the flawless strainer; with that very thing he purifies them. "With the rays of the Vasu Sūrya," he says; the waters are indeed the vital breaths—the Vasus are the vital breaths, and the rays are the vital breaths.

{3.2.5.3} By means of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) alone he unites the vital breaths, with a verse addressed to Savitṛ: "May my rite be impelled by Savitṛ. Thus his rite indeed becomes impelled by Savitṛ. He recites a *gāyatrī* verse foot by foot for the sake of triple perfection. "O divine waters, you who flow forward, you who move forward," he says; he thus proclaims their form and their greatness. "Lead this sacrifice forward, lead the lord of the sacrifice forward," he says; they indeed lead the sacrifice forward and lead the lord of the sacrifice forward.

"Indra chose you for the slaying of Vṛtra; you chose Indra for the slaying of Vṛtra," he says. For when Indra was about to slay Vṛtra, he chose the waters; the waters chose Indra. He thus declares their common agreement and harmony. "You are sprinkled," he says; thereby the waters are sprinkled. "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni, [and] to Agni-Soma," he says; he thus sprinkles them according to their respective deities. He sprinkles three times, for the sacrifice has a threefold progression.

{3.2.5.5} Now, for the purpose of striking down the *rakṣases*, he says, "Be purified for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods. Verily, he purifies these very things for the sacrifice to the gods. He sprinkles them three times; for the sacrifice has a threefold turn, and also for the sake of their being fit for the sacrifice (*medhya*). "Shaken off is the *rakṣas*, shaken off are the enemies," he says; this is for the striking down of the *rakṣases*. "Thou art the skin of Aditi," he says; for this earth is indeed Aditi.

{3.2.5.6} He makes this its skin. "May the earth recognize you; may Ānanda recognize you," he says for the sake of stability. He spreads it out with the neck toward the east and the hair upward for the sake of purity. Therefore, animals approach the sacrificial food from the front facing westward. Therefore, offspring seek to seize the wild animal. The sacrifice hid itself from the gods, having assumed the form of a black antelope. When they thresh the oblation upon the black antelope skin, one thereby applies the sacrifice from the sacrifice itself, so that the oblation shall not be spilled.

"Thou art the pressing-stone, made of wood," he says; thus he makes it a pressing-stone. "May the skin of the Ādityas recognize thee," he says for the sake of stability. "Thou art the body of Agni," he says; for plants are indeed the body of Agni. "The release of speech," he says; for when creatures eat of the plants, they then release their speech. "I take thee for the enjoyment of the gods," he says.

He thus causes this [sacrifice] to prosper through the deities themselves. "Thou art a stone, belonging to the trees," he says; he thus makes it a pressing-stone (*grāvan*). "Prepare this oblation well for the gods," he says for the sake of peace. "O preparer of the oblation, come! he says; he thus summons those who are the preparers of the oblation for the gods. He summons three times, for the gods are true to the triad. "Utter food! Utter strength! he says.

He bestows nourishment and vigor upon the sacrificer. "Let us speak with splendor; may we conquer the assembly," he says for the sake of overcoming his rivals. The speech of Manu, the god of faith, the sacrificer, was a slayer of the Asuras; it entered into the sacrificial implements. As many of the Asuras as heard the sound of the sacrificial implements being lifted up perished. Therefore, one should perform the sacrifice after settling among one's own people.
As many rivals as hear the sounding of his sacrificial implements, they perish. He says, "Strike loudly! for the sake of victory.

He takes away their sensory power and vigor; he becomes the most excellent among them. "Thou art increased by rain; let what is increased by rain recognize thee! he says. For plants are indeed increased by rain, and the *iṣīkā* reeds are increased by rain; this is for the sake of prosperity. The Rakṣases entered after the sacrifice. They drove them out from the cattle with the husks, and from the plants with the chaff. "Blown away is the Rakṣas, blown away are the enemies," he says; this is for the smiting away of the Rakṣases.

"Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases," he says; by means of the husks, he indeed expiates the Rakṣases. He touches water for the sake of purity. "May Vāyu separate you," he says; Vāyu is indeed the purifier; he thus purifies them. For those [grains] which fall from the winnowing basket do so as if from the intermediate space. "May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you," he says for the sake of stability and to prevent the spilling of the oblation. "Three times should they be winnowed," he says, for the sacrifice has a threefold turn; furthermore, it is for the sake of purity.

"Shaken off is the Rakṣas, shaken off are the enemies," he says; for the smiting away of the Rakṣases. "Thou art the skin of Aditi," he says; for Aditi is this [earth]. He thus makes this its skin. "May the earth recognize thee," he says, for the sake of stability. He spreads it out with the neck toward the west and the hair upward, for the sake of purity. Therefore, animals from the front approach the sacrificial victim facing westward.
Therefore, people seek to catch wild game. The sacrifice fled away from the gods.

{3.2.6.2} Having assumed the form of Kṛṣṇa, when he grinds the oblation upon the black antelope skin, he thereby employs the sacrifice from the sacrifice itself, so that the oblation shall not be spilled. "Heaven and Earth were together," they say; "they moved apart for a distance of one *śamyā* on one day, and for a distance of one *śamyā* on another day. "Thou art the support of heaven; may the Adityas recognize thy skin" (or "may Ānanda recognize thee"), he says; this is for the separation of Heaven and Earth.
"You are the bowl from the mountain; may the support of heaven recognize you," he says, for the separation of heaven and earth.

"You are the bowl, daughter of the mountain; may the mountain recognize you," he says—[and "may Ānanda recognize you"]—for the support of heaven and earth. "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he says for impulsion. "With the arms of the Aśvins," he says, for the Aśvins were the two *adhvaryu* priests among the gods. "With the hands of Pūṣan," he says for restraint. "I pour upon," he says; thus he pours upon them according to their respective deities. "Thou art grain; satisfy the gods," he says; by the power of this *yajus*.

{3.2.6.4} As many as one deity desires, so many does the oblation expand. For there is nothing that would be limited to just that much. As much as he offers, saying, "For out-breathing thee! For in-breathing thee!"—he thus places the vital breaths in the sacrificer. Saying, "Along a long extension, for life, may I establish [thee]," he thus bestows life upon him. Indeed, those [grains] which fall from the grinding stone seem to leap away from the intermediate space.

"May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you," he says for the sake of stability and to prevent the spilling of the oblation. "Grind without scattering; make them fine," he says for the sake of purity.

"Thou art the bold one; bestow the sacred word (*brahman*)," he says for the sake of firmness. "O Agni, drive away the raw-eating Agni; expel the corpse-eater; bring hither the one who sacrifices to the gods," he says. Having thus struck away that which is raw-eating and corpse-eating, he places a potsherd upon the pure fire. "The *rakṣas*-demon is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away," he says; verily, he burns away the *rakṣas*-demons. He places it upon that which possesses fire; verily, he establishes light in this very world. He turns over a coal.

He places light in the intermediate space itself; he places the sun as light in yonder world. These worlds become full of light for him who knows thus. "Thou art firm; make the earth firm," he says; by this he makes the earth firm. "Thou art the support; make the intermediate space firm," he says; by this he makes the intermediate space firm. "Thou art the foundation; make heaven firm," he says; by this he makes heaven firm.

"Thou art the law; make firm the quarters," he says. By this, he makes firm the quarters. By these [formulas], he makes firm these very worlds. These worlds become firm for him with offspring and cattle, for one who knows thus. At first, he places three potsherds. These are the three worlds; it is for the attainment of these worlds. At first, he places one potsherd. Indeed, at first, only one potsherd comes into being for a person.

Then two; then three; then four; then eight. Therefore, the head of a person consists of eight skull-bones (*kapāla*). In that he thus places the skull-bones, Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice; he thus prepares the sacrifice, Prajāpati. He thereby prepares his own self. That self, being prepared—

{3.2.7.5} He follows after [the sacrificer] in that world. In that he lays down eight [bricks], it is commensurate with the Gāyatrī. In that nine, it is with the Trivṛt. In that ten, it is with the Virāj. In that eleven, it is with the Triṣṭubh. In that twelve, [it is with the Jagatī].

{3.2.7.6} That [is done] with the Jagatī metre. By laying down the potsherds in accordance with the metres, he makes these worlds firm in succession for the sake of supporting the quarters. Thereby he bestows life-span, vital breaths, progeny, and cattle upon the sacrificer; he makes his kinsmen numerous around him. "Ye are piled," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula itself. "Be heated by the heat of the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases," he says; verily, he heats them by the heat of the deities themselves. These [potsherds] are then completed.
With the four-footed verse, "The potsherds which they collect for the heat, O wise ones," he releases [the fire]. Cattle are four-footed; thus he establishes himself among cattle from above.

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he says, for the sake of impulsion. "With the arms of the Aśvins," he says; for the Aśvins were the two *adhvaryu* priests among the gods. "With the hands of Pūṣan," he says, for the sake of restraint. "I mix together," he says; thus he mixes these according to their respective deities. "The waters have united with the waters, the plants with their sap," he says. The waters indeed quicken the plants, and the plants quicken the waters; some of them quicken others.

Therefore he says thus: "O wealthy ones, be united with the moving ones; O honey-sweet ones, be united with the honey-sweet ones. The waters are indeed the wealthy ones (*revatī*); cattle are the moving ones (*jagatī*); plants are the honey-sweet ones. Having thus united the waters, the plants, and the cattle into one for him, he makes them honey-sweet. He causes them to overflow with the words: "You are born from the waters; be united with the waters," just as after a good rain has spread over this earth.

The waters magnify the plants; such indeed is that. "I bind thee for procreation," he says; by this, he supports offspring. "For Agni, for Agni-Soma," he says, for the sake of distinction. "Thou art the head of Makha," he says. Makha is indeed the sacrifice; the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is its head. Therefore, he speaks thus.

"Thou art the cauldron (*gharma*), the life of all," he says; verily, he bestows all life upon the sacrificer. "Spread wide; may the lord of the sacrifice spread wide for thee," he says; verily, he causes the sacrificer to expand with offspring and cattle. "Take up the skin," he says; verily, he makes him whole-bodied. Then, having poured water on it, he wipes it around; verily, he places the flesh within the skin. Therefore, the flesh is covered by the skin. This cauldron is indeed unappeased.

{3.2.8.5} Every half-month, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is offered. It is liable to burn the sacrificer with its heat. He carries fire around it; he thus makes it an animal (*paśu*), for the sake of pacification and to prevent burning. He carries fire around it three times, for the sacrifice has a threefold structure; furthermore, it is for the smiting away of the *rakṣases*. "The *rakṣas* is excluded, the enemies are excluded," he says.

{3.2.8.6} For the sake of concealing from the *rakṣases*. When the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) was being placed on the fire, the *rakṣases* sought to strike it. In heaven there is a fire named *Nāka*, the slayer of *rakṣases*; he indeed drove the *rakṣases* away from it. "May the god Savitṛ cook thee," he says; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he cooks it. "Upon the highest firmament (*nāka*)," he says, for the purpose of driving away the *rakṣases*. "O Agni, do not burn up thy body," he says, so that it may not be over-burnt. "O Agni, protect the oblation," he says, for its preservation.

"Without burning it, cook it!"—with these words he releases his speech. Having thus uttered [the name] of the sacrifice and the oblations, he extends them. He makes the *puroruc* for the sake of non-burning and for the sake of cooking. The cake (*puroḍāśa*) is indeed the brain; if he were not to cover it, the brain would be exposed. He covers it; therefore the brain is hidden. He covers it with ashes; therefore the bone is covered by flesh.

{3.2.8.8} He covers [the sacrificial cake] with the Veda. Therefore the head is covered by hair. He who knows thus does not become bald. The sacrificial cake is indeed the image of the animal; it should not be covered without a formula, for it would be as if done in vain. The cattle of the sacrificer might be liable to perish. "Be united with the *brahman*," he says. The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed the *brahman*.

The vital breaths are the cattle; by means of the vital breaths, he unites the cattle with [the sacrificer]. They do not become liable to die prematurely. The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is indeed the sacrificer; offspring and cattle are the loose soil (*purīṣa*). In that he thus covers it over, he causes the sacrificer himself to prosper with offspring and cattle. The gods, having become the oblation and having died, said: "Upon whom shall we smear this? Agni said: "Upon me."

"Place your bodies within me; I shall bring forth that [offspring] for you in whom you shall find delight. Those gods placed their bodies within Agni. Therefore they say: "Agni is all the deities. He [Agni] cast [a spark] into the waters with a coal. From that, Ekata was born. He cast [a second spark] into the waters a second time.

{3.2.8.11} From that, Dvita was born. He struck down a third [time]. From that, Trita was born. Because they were born from the waters (*adbhyaḥ*), that is the "watery" (*āpya*) nature of the Āpyas. Because they were born from the selves (*ātmabhyaḥ*), that is the "self-born" (*ātmya*) nature of the Ātmyas. Those gods purified themselves in the Āpyas; the Āpyas purified themselves when the sun had risen; those purified by the rising sun purified themselves when the sun had set.

{3.2.8.12} One who has been overtaken by the setting sun [is excluded]; one with deformed nails [is excluded]; one with black teeth [is excluded]; one whose younger brother marries before him [is excluded]; one who has married before his elder brother [is excluded]; one who kills a hero [is excluded]; and one who kills a Brahmin [is excluded]—that killing of a Brahmin does not pass away. He pours [the water] within the sacrificial altar for the sake of securing [the result]. He grasps it with a firebrand for the sake of cooking; for the gods, as it were, desire what is cooked.

"By the impulse of the god Savitṛ," with these words he takes up the wooden sword (sphyá) for the sake of impulsion. "With the arms of the Aśvins," he says; for the Aśvins were the two *adhvaryú* priests among the gods. "With the hands of Pūṣan," he says for the sake of restraint. "I take thee; thou art the right arm of Indra," he says; verily, he bestows power (*indriya*) upon the sacrificer. "Thousand-edged, hundred-fold brilliant," he says; he thus proclaims its form and its greatness.
"Thou art Vāyu, of sharp brilliance," he says; Vāyu is indeed brilliance.

{3.2.9.2} He bestows radiance upon him. There was once an Asura named Viṣa. He was afraid, thinking, "The gods will overcome me with the sacrifice. He fled down into the earth; thus it became unfit for the Soma-sacrifice. Furthermore, when Indra slew Vṛtra, his blood flowed along the earth; thus it became unfit for the Soma-sacrifice. "O Earth, place of divine worship! he says.

He thus makes this very [spot] pure and fit for sacrifice. "I shall not harm your root, O plant," he says; this is for the non-injury of plants. "Go to the fold, the cow-pen," he says; the meters are indeed the fold and the cow-pen; he thus provides the meters as a fold and a cow-pen for him. "May the sky rain for you," he says; the sky is indeed rain; he thus secures rain for himself. "Bind [it], O God Savitṛ, in the furthest distance," he says.

{3.2.9.4} There are indeed two persons: he whom one hates and he who hates him. He binds both of them with a hundred fetters in the furthest distance. "He who hates us and whom we hate—do not release him from this," he says for the sake of non-release (or, as Ḍyumoṇṭa says, for the sake of non-liberation). Now there was an Asura named Araru; he lay hidden upon the earth. The gods struck him away from the earth with the words, "Araru is driven away from the earth.
Araru is indeed the rival. When he says, "Araru is driven away from the earth," [he drives away his rival].

{3.2.9.5} He strikes away the rival from the earth. They thought, "He will surely fall from here into the sky. Araru [the adversary] said to him, "Do not leap up to the sky! and they hemmed him in from the sky. Araru is indeed the rival. When he says, "May Araru not leap up to the sky," he thus hemming in the rival from the sky. He carries away the *stambayajus* (the sacrificial grass-stalk). He strikes away the rival from the earth itself. He carries it away a second time.

{3.2.9.6} From the intermediate space itself he drives him away; he carries [the earth] a third time; from the sky itself he drives him away; he carries it a fourth time silently; from the unlimited itself he drives him away. This earth belonged to the Asuras in the beginning, as far as one can see while sitting; that much belonged to the gods. Those gods said, "Let there be a share for us in this as well."

“Nor will we give [it] back,” they said, “until you yourselves take possession of it. With the words, “The Vasus [take] you,” they enclosed it from the south; with “The Rudras [take] you,” from the west; and with “The Ādityas [take] you,” from the north. By means of Agni they conquered toward the east, by the Vasus toward the south, by the Rudras toward the west, and by the Ādityas toward the north. This is the case for one who, knowing thus, has his altar enclosed.

He prospers in himself; his rival is defeated. "In the impulsion of the god Savitṛ," he says, for the sake of instigation. "The wise perform their work," he says, for work is performed when impelled. The pure and the impure separated from the earth: the pure went toward the east and the north; the impure went toward the west and the south. He makes [the ground] sloping toward the east and the north; thus he makes it pure, fit for sacrifice to the gods.

He raises the two shoulders of the altar facing east, for the sake of enclosing the Āhavanīya fire. He makes the two hips face west, for the sake of enclosing the Gārhapatya fire; furthermore, it is for the sake of forming a pair. He digs up [the earth]; whatever in it is impure, that he strikes away. He digs up; therefore plants perish.

He cuts the root. He cuts the very root of his rival. For if he were to leave the root remaining, the *rakṣases* would spring up after it. If he were to cut with his hand, offspring would be born with deformed nails. He cuts with the wooden sword (*sphya*). The wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt; with the thunderbolt itself he strikes away the *rakṣases* from the sacrifice. A hole dug too deep belongs to the Pitṛs. He digs it to this [proper] extent.

{3.2.9.11} Equalized by Prajāpati, the mouth of the sacrifice, the altar (vedi) vanished from the gods. They found it at a depth of four finger-breadths; therefore, it should be dug to a depth of four finger-breadths. He digs to a depth of four finger-breadths, for at four finger-breadths the plants find their firm foundation. He digs for the sake of a foundation; he thus causes the sacrificer himself to reach a firm foundation. He makes [the altar] higher on the south side; he has thereby produced the form of the sacrificial ground.

He makes it possessed of loose soil (*purīṣavat*). Loose soil is indeed offspring and cattle; verily, by means of offspring and cattle, he makes him possessed of loose soil. He performs the second tracing around. So great indeed is this earth as is the altar; having thus excluded his rival from just so much of it, he performs the second tracing around for himself. "Thou art the Truth, thou art the seat of Truth, thou art the glory of Truth," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula.

{3.2.9.13} Indeed, he performs a cruel act when he prepares the altar. He smooths it with the words, "Thou art *dhā*, thou art *svadhā*," for the sake of pacification. He says, "Thou art wide, thou art wealthy"; thus he makes it both wide and wealthy. He says, "Before the creeping of the cruel one, O mighty one," for the sake of sacrificial purity. He says, "Lifting up the earth, the life-giving one, which they sent forth in the moon with *svadhā*-offerings. Having struck away whatever in it is impure, and having made it pure and fit for sacrifice, [he proceeds].

"That which is pure in the moon, he causes that to enter into her; 'Beholding her, the wise perform sacrifice,' so he says for the sake of making her manifest. 'Set down the sprinkling waters! Place the fuel and the sacrificial grass! Wipe the dipping-spoon and the offering-ladles! Gird the wife! Come forth with the clarified butter!'—so he says for the sake of establishing the proper sequence. He sets down the sprinkling waters; for the waters are indeed slayers of the Rakṣases."

{3.2.9.15} For the sake of driving away the *rakṣases*, he places [the water] in the track of the wooden sword (*sphya*). This is for the continuity of the sacrifice. Asita Daivala said: "In that world, there were as many waters as there are sprinkling-waters (*prokṣaṇī*). Therefore, many [sprinkling-waters] should be placed down. While throwing away the wooden sword, he should meditate upon whomsoever he hates; thus he strikes him with affliction.

The wooden sword (*sphya*) is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*). If he were to hold it lengthwise, the Adhvaryu would be struck by the thunderbolt. He holds it crosswise in front; for the wooden sword is a thunderbolt. With the thunderbolt, he drives away the Rakṣases from the south of the sacrifice. With the two fires, [he drives them away] from the east and the west. With the wooden sword, [he drives them away] from the north and the south. Having struck away evil and the rival from this earth with the wooden sword as a thunderbolt, he cuts off [the grass] upon the rubbish heap (*utkara*).

{3.2.10.2} Just as they cut [the wood] after having placed it [on the fire], so [he acts]. He washes his hands; he thus purifies himself. He washes the wooden sword (*sphya*) for the sake of purity; moreover, he cuts off the very limb of his evil rival. He places the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*idhmābarhis*) down for the sake of yoking; for the sake of providing a pairing for the sacrifice; and moreover, he thereby establishes this *puroruc* (introductory verse) for the purpose of illuminating the subsequent rite. He should not place them down from the front toward the back.

{3.2.10.3} If he were to place [the sacrificial grass] in front and facing westward, he would have to set down the fuel (idhma) elsewhere than on the path of the oblations. The sacrificial grass (barhis), indeed, is offspring; he would thus cause the procreation of offspring to fail by means of the sacrificial grass. He places it behind, facing eastward; he sets down the fuel on the path of the oblations. In this way, he truly attains the procreation of offspring through the sacrificial grass. The fuel is on the south, the sacrificial grass on the north. The fuel, indeed, is the self (ātman); the sacrificial grass is offspring.

For offspring is higher than oneself at the place of sacrifice; having thereby brought it to the state of sacrificial vigor (*medha*), he establishes it according to its respective deity. The sacrificer becomes firmly established through offspring and cattle.

Prapāṭhaka 3, Anuvāka 1 "Scorched is the Rakṣas, scorched are the enemies," he says, for the purpose of driving away the Rakṣases. "With the most brilliant splendor of Agni, I scorch [thee]," he says, for the sake of purity. He cleanses the offering-spoons (*sruk*), beginning with the *sruva* ladle; he thus sharpens the male among them for the sake of pairing. Then the *juhū*; then the *upabhṛt*; then the *dhruvā*. The *juhū* is indeed yonder [heaven].

The *upabhṛt* is the intermediate space; the *dhruvā* is the earth. These worlds are indeed the offering-spoons (*sruk*). The sprinklings are the rain. Rain, indeed, prepares these worlds in due order. Once they have been prepared, they flourish. These worlds flourish for him with offspring and cattle, for one who knows thus. If he should desire, "May Parjanya be rich in rain," he should sprinkle [the spoons] beginning from the front.

He brings down rain itself; for rain indeed comes with its tips directed downward. If he should desire, "May it not rain," he should sweep from the root upward; thus he holds back the rain. Regarding this, they say: he should sweep from the tip downward and from the root upward; thus it is performed in proper sequence, and he becomes one who causes rain.

{3.3.1.4} [He places them] facing eastward, with the tips inward; for food is eaten in this very manner. Moreover, from the tips of plants, creatures derive their vital energy (*ūrj*); [this is done] for the attainment of that vital energy and of food. Below, [he places them] facing westward, with the handle at the top. With the root [of one] against the root [of another], it is for stability. Therefore, on the forearm, the hairs are directed forward above and backward below.

{3.3.1.5} This *sruk* is indeed the body. The *sruva* is the breath; the *juhū* is the right hand; the *upabhṛt* is the left hand; the *dhruvā* is the self; and the *saṃmārjana* (cleansing-brushes) are food. The breath (*prāṇa*), having become the downward breath (*apāna*), enters the self as food from the mouth and purifies the external body. Therefore, one cleanses the *sruva* first. For the breath, having become the downward breath, enters the self as food from the mouth.
These two are the out-breath and the in-breath. He who knows this becomes undivided from the out-breath and the in-breath.

"From heaven the craft has descended; it rests upon the peak of the earth. By means of that which has a thousand branches, we destroy the rival—*svāhā*! With these words, he throws the *sruksaṃmārjana* (grass used for wiping the ladle) into the fire. The *darbha* grasses are indeed water. Thus he proclaims their form and their greatness. [He does so] with an *anuṣṭubh* verse. Prajāpati is of the *anuṣṭubh* nature; the Veda belongs to Prajāpati. The *sruksaṃmārjana* grasses are the very tip of the Veda.

{3.3.2.2} He causes these [strewings] to prosper by means of their own respective meters and their own respective deities. Moreover, the *ṛc* is indeed the female and the *darbha* grass is the male; that constitutes a couple. Thus he creates a couple for him at the sacrifice for the sake of procreation. The sacrificer is propagated with offspring and cattle. Some, however, discard them as something useless; that should not be done. It is the milking of that sacrificial rite which has already been undertaken.

{3.3.2.3} If cattle were to step upon these [remnants], it would not be for the benefit of the cattle. Having sprinkled them with water, he should throw them onto the rubbish heap (*utkara*). For whatever part of a sacrificial rite is concluded elsewhere than in the oblations, the rubbish heap is indeed its foundation. For the gods gathered that foundation together for it. In that he sprinkles them with water, by that they are pacified; in that he throws them onto the rubbish heap, he thereby causes them to reach their foundation.

The sacrificer becomes firmly established through offspring and cattle. Moreover, these wiping-cloths for the *sruva* and *sruk* ladles are the very form of a grass-clump (*stamba*). Plants grow in clumps; cattle do not delight in withered grass, for withered grass is unpleasant to them. As much as withered grass is unpleasant to cattle, so much does he become unpleasant to cattle who has these cloths placed elsewhere than in the fire. Indeed, cattle delight in fresh wild plants.

{3.3.2.5} For a new fire-pit (*navadāva*) is dear to them. As dear as a new fire-pit is to cattle, so dear does he become to cattle for whom they cast these [embers] into the fire. Therefore, one should cast these into the fire itself. Whichever [fire] one should sweep [them onto], it is for the support of cattle. "He who is the overlord of beings, Rudra, the wanderer of the threads, the bull—do not harm our cattle."

"Let this be offered to you, svāhā!"—with these words he throws the fire-cleansing brushes into the fire. This, indeed, is their source; this is their foundation. He thus causes them to go to their own source and their own foundation. The sacrificer becomes firmly established through offspring and cattle.

This is indeed no sacrifice which is without a wife. Offspring would not be produced. The wife sits down; she thus completes the sacrifice for the procreation of offspring. If she were to gird herself while standing, she would obstruct her beloved kinsman. She girds herself while sitting, for it is while sitting that she performs her creative power (*vīrya*).

{3.3.3.2} If she were to sit behind him facing eastward, she would create discord; she would create discord with the wives of the gods. She sits behind him facing northward from the south for her own protection. "Seeking favor," he says; having thus made her pure and exclusive, he fulfills her with a blessing. "Becoming devoted to Agni, I gird myself for the sake of good deeds," he says. This, indeed, is the introduction to the vow for the wife.

{3.3.3.3} By means of that very [yoke-tie], he leads her to the vow. Therefore they say: "Whether one knows thus or not, he yokes her with the yoke-tie; she rests upon him, and through that yoke-tie, she comes to be with him in yonder world. That which is the yoke-tie is the acquisition (yoga); that upon which she rests is security (kṣema).

{3.3.3.4} "For the securing of well-being (*yogakṣema*). [The thought is: "May he perform what is joined; may he unite his desire with the blessing. This is for the fulfillment of the blessing. He ties a knot. Thus, he secures the blessings within this [wife]. The knot is indeed male, and the wife is female; that is a pair. He thus creates a pair for him at the sacrifice for the sake of procreation. The sacrificer is propagated with offspring and cattle.

{3.3.3.5} Now, the wife is indeed half of one's own self. For the support of the sacrifice and to prevent its loosening, he says: "With good offspring and good husbands, we have approached thee. He thereby makes the sacrifice itself a couple. [He does this] so that what is deficient may be made complete for the sake of procreation. "Thou art the milk of the great ones, the sap of the plants," he says; he thereby declares its form and its greatness. "Of thee, who art undecaying, I take a portion for the sacrifice to the gods," he says; he thereby invokes this very blessing.

Anuvāka 4 {3.3.4.1} Ghee and honey were Prajāpati. From that which was honey—from that which was bliss—he created offspring. Therefore, there is, as it were, procreation in honey. For this reason, they do not perform the ritual with honey; for it is exhausted. They perform the ritual with clarified butter (ājya). Clarified butter is indeed the sacrifice. Thus, by means of the sacrifice itself, they perform the sacrifice so that it may not be exhausted. The wife gazes upon it.

{3.3.4.2} For the sake of pairing and procreation. Whatever the wife does for the sacrifice, that constitutes a pair. Moreover, this is the wife’s taking hold of the sacrifice so that it may not be interrupted. Indeed, she makes something impure when the wife looks [at the oblation]. She places it over the *gārhapatya* fire for the sake of purity. She moves toward the *āhavanīya* fire for the continuity of the sacrifice. "Thou art brilliance; follow after brilliance," he says.

Agni is indeed brilliance; the clarified butter is brilliance. By means of brilliance, he causes brilliance to prosper. "May Agni not take away thy brilliance," he says for the sake of non-injury. He places [the butter] in the track of the wooden sword (sphya) for the continuity of the sacrifice. "Thou art the tongue of Agni, the well-being of the gods," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula itself. "Be present for every domain of the gods, for every sacrificial formula," he says; thus he invokes this very blessing.

{3.3.4.4} Now, for this reason, he purifies [the clarified butter] by means of the two strainers. The clarified butter is indeed the sacrificer; the two strainers are the out-breath and the in-breath. Thus, he bestows the out-breath and the in-breath upon the sacrificer himself. He does so with repeated scooping, for in this very manner the out-breath and the in-breath move. "Thou art pure, thou art light, thou art brilliance," he says; he thereby declares its form and its greatness. He does so three times with the sacrificial formula (*yajus*); these worlds are three.

{3.3.4.5} This is for the attainment of these worlds. Three times [he does so], for the sacrifice has three stages; moreover, it is for the sake of its purity. Then, with two verses containing the word *ājya*, he pours water. He thereby bestows upon them this form and this color. Furthermore, they say: "Just as a woman sits, wearing beautiful, well-fashioned gold ornaments, displaying her beauty, so do these [waters] appear at this time. Indeed, the waters are all the deities.

{3.3.4.6} For this clarified butter (*ājya*) is indeed the body of all the gods. Regarding this, there is a deliberation concerning both [the butter and the water]: there might be a repetition (*jāmi*). If one were to purify the butter with a sacrificial formula (*yajus*) and the water with a sacrificial formula, there would be a repetition. Therefore, he purifies the water with a *chandas* (verse) to avoid repetition and for the sake of forming a couple. He does so with a verse addressed to Savitṛ, thinking, "May my ritual act be impelled by Savitṛ. Thus his ritual act becomes indeed impelled by Savitṛ. He does so foot by foot with a *gāyatrī* verse for the sake of triple perfection. By means of the waters, he thus unites the plants.

"By means of plants, [he protects] the cattle; by means of cattle, the sacrificer. 'The bright thee in the bright, light thee in the light, flame thee in the flame,' he says for the sake of wholeness, for attainment, and for the absence of interruption."

Anuvāka 5 {3.3.5.1}: The gods and the asuras were engaged in conflict. Indra perceived this opening of the clarified butter (*ājya*). He gazed upon it with it; thereupon the gods prospered, and the asuras were defeated. Whoever, knowing thus, gazes upon the clarified butter, prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated. The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "In that he sprinkles the other oblations (*havīṃṣi*) with clarified butter..."

{3.3.5.2} Now, with what does one sprinkle the clarified butter? One should say, "With truth. For sight is indeed truth; thus he sprinkles it with truth itself. He who looks at the clarified butter with his eye is liable to become blind. He should look at it while closing his eyes; thus he preserves his own sight. He pours the clarified butter over [the oblation], and he takes up the clarified butter.

The *ājya* is indeed the meters; he thus gratifies the meters. He takes four [spoonfuls] in the *juhū*; cattle have four feet; he thus wins cattle. He takes eight in the *upabhṛt*; the *gāyatrī* has eight syllables; breath is of the nature of the *gāyatrī*; he thus places breath in the cattle. He takes four in the *dhruvā*.

{3.3.5.4} Animals have four feet; thus he finds support among animals themselves at the conclusion. The *juhū* ladle has the sacrificer as its deity; the *upabhṛt* ladle has the rival as its deity. When taking four portions in the *juhū*, one should take more; when taking eight in the *upabhṛt*, one takes less. Thus, one makes the rival a subordinate attendant for the sacrificer. The ladles are indeed cows; he takes four portions in the *juhū*. Therefore, she [the cow] has four feet.

Eight portions are taken in the *upabhṛt* ladle; therefore, [the cow] has eight hooves. Four are taken in the *dhruvā* ladle; therefore, she has four udders. Thus he prepares the cow herself; from her, thus prepared, he milks out food and strength. That which he takes in the *juhū* ladle is for the *prayāja* offerings. That which is in the *upabhṛt* is for the *prayāja* and *anūyāja* offerings. Indeed, that clarified butter which is in the *dhruvā* ladle is taken for the sake of the entire sacrifice.

"O divine waters, you who flow first, you who move first," he says. He thus declares their form and their greatness. "Lead this sacrifice forward; lead the lord of the sacrifice forward," he says. They indeed lead the sacrifice forward at the beginning; they lead the lord of the sacrifice forward at the beginning. "Indra chose you for the slaying of Vṛtra; you chose Indra for the slaying of Vṛtra," he says. For when Indra was about to slay Vṛtra, he chose the waters; the waters chose Indra. He thus declares their common agreement and harmony. "You are sprinkled," he says.

{3.3.6.2} By that [sprinkling], the waters are consecrated. Agni hid himself from the gods; having assumed the form of a black antelope, he entered the trees. "Thou art black, dwelling in the lairs; for Agni, svāhā!"—thus he says. Verily, he makes him acceptable to Agni; moreover, he wins the sacrificial essence (*medha*) of Agni himself. "Thou art the altar; for the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), svāhā!"—thus he says. The sacrificial grass is indeed offspring; the earth is the altar.

He establishes offspring upon the earth. "Thou art the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); for the ladles (*sruc*), svāhā! he says. The sacrificial grass is indeed offspring; the ladles are the sacrificer. Thus, he establishes the sacrificer among his offspring. Having placed the sacrificial grass down, he sprinkles it with water, saying, "For heaven thee! For the atmosphere thee! For the earth thee! He thus sprinkles it for these very worlds. Then, together with the ladle, he sprinkles the knot from the front toward the west.
The sacrificial grass is indeed offspring. Just as at the time of birth the waters flow from the front [toward the child].

{3.3.6.4} It is just so. He says, "Svadhā to the fathers," for the utterance of *svadhā* belongs to the fathers. With the words, "Become strength for those seated on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)," he pours [the water] from the southern hip of the altar up to the northern one for the sake of continuity. The months are indeed the fathers seated on the sacrificial grass; thus he gratifies the months. The months cause the plants to grow; the months ripen them for the sake of prosperity. Parjanya rains without skipping over the places where this rite is performed in this manner.

"Go to the earth with strength," he says. Thus he places strength in the earth; therefore, people enjoy the strength of the earth. He loosens the knot; thereby he causes procreation. He draws it upward, forward, and upward again, then pulls it back toward the west. Therefore, seed is deposited facing eastward, and offspring are born facing westward. "Thou art the tuft of Viṣṇu," he says. Viṣṇu, indeed, is the sacrifice.

{3.3.6.6} For the support of the sacrifice, he takes up the *prastara* (grass-bundle) in front. He thereby makes it the principal part. He takes it to this extent: it is commensurate with Prajāpati, the mouth of the sacrifice. He takes it to this extent: it is commensurate with a joint of the sacrifice. He takes it to this extent: for such is the vigor in a man; thus it is commensurate with vigor.

He takes an unlimited [amount]. This is for the attainment of the unlimited. He inserts the two strainers into it. The sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) is indeed the sacrificer; the two strainers are the out-breath and the in-breath. Thus, he bestows out-breath and in-breath upon the sacrificer himself. "I spread thee, the wool-soft," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula. "A good seat for the gods," he says; he thus makes it a good seat for the gods.

{3.3.6.8} He spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). The sacrificial grass is indeed offspring; the altar (*vedi*) is the earth. Thus, he establishes offspring upon the earth. He spreads it so that it is not visible through. By means of offspring and cattle, he makes him invisible. Holding the *prastara* bundle, he lays down the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). The *prastara* is indeed the sacrificer; thus, the sacrificer himself lays down the enclosing sticks. "Thou art the Gandharva Viśvāvasu," he says.

He bestows the full span of life upon the sacrificer. "Thou art the right arm of Indra," he says; verily, he bestows power upon the sacrificer. "May Mitra and Varuṇa enclose thee from the north," he says; Mitra and Varuṇa are out-breathing and in-breathing; verily, he bestows out-breathing and in-breathing upon him. "May Sūrya protect thee from the east," he says, for the smiting away of the Rākṣasas. "From every curse," he says; verily, he protects him from the unlimited.

"O thou who art the recipient of the oblation, [I approach] thee," he says; verily, he thus endows Agni with the office of the Hotṛ-priest. "We kindle thee, the radiant one," he says for the sake of kindling. "O Agni, the great one at the sacrifice," he says for the sake of growth. "Ye two are the supports of the people," he says for the guidance of the people. He places them with their tips pointing northward for the sake of firm establishment. "Sit on the seat of the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas," he says; verily, he places the *prastara* grass-bundle on the seat of the deities. "Thou art the ladle, dripping with ghee by name," he says.

{3.3.6.11} The *juhū* is indeed this [earth]; the *upabhṛt* is the intermediate space; the *dhruvā* is the earth. This is their dear name: "the butter-dripping" (*ghṛtācī*). When he says, "the butter-dripping," he settles them by their own dear name. He says, "These have settled in the world of good deeds. The world of good deeds is indeed truth; he thus settles them in the very truth, the world of good deeds. He says, "O Viṣṇu, protect them! Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; [he does this] for the support of the sacrifice.

"Protect the sacrifice, protect the lord of the sacrifice, protect me, O mistress of the sacrifice," he says; for the sake of the sacrifice, for the sake of the sacrificer, and for his own self—he thus invokes a blessing upon them all for the sake of freedom from harm.

Anuvāka 7 {3.3.7.1}. By means of Agni as the Hotṛ, the gods overcame the Asuras. "Recite for Agni being kindled," he says, for the sake of overcoming one's rivals. There are twenty-one pieces of fuel-wood; man indeed consists of twenty-one parts. This is for the attainment of the person. He places fifteen pieces of fuel-wood on the fire; there are fifteen nights in a half-month. Thus the year is attained by way of half-months. He lays down three enclosing-sticks.

{3.3.7.2} He places two fuel-sticks upright. He leaves over a fuel-stick for the after-offerings (*anūyāja*). Thus they amount to six. There are indeed six seasons; he thus gratifies the seasons. He fans [the fire] with the *veda*-grass-bundle. The *veda* belongs to Prajāpati; breath belongs to Prajāpati; the Āhavanīya fire is the sacrificer. Thus, he bestows breath upon the sacrificer himself.

He fans [the fire] three times. There are indeed three vital breaths (*prāṇa*); he thus places the vital breaths within him. Having approached with the *veda*-grass-bundle, he pours the *āghāra* libation for Prajāpati using the *sruva*-ladle. Prajāpati is indeed the sacrifice; he thus seizes the sacrifice, Prajāpati, from the very beginning. Moreover, Prajāpati is all the deities; he thus gratifies all the deities. "O Agnīdh, cleanse the fire three times each," he says. For the sacrifice has a threefold turn.

{3.3.7.4} Moreover, for the sake of driving away the *rakṣases*, he cleanses the enclosing-sticks (*paridhis*). He thus purifies them. He cleanses each three times; for the sacrifice has a threefold structure. Moreover, it is for the sake of making them fit for the sacrifice (*medhya*). Furthermore, these are indeed the horses of the gods; he thus cleanses the horses of the gods for the attainment of the heavenly world. Sitting down, he pours the other *āghāra* libation.

{3.3.7.5} Standing, he yokes the other [fire], just as one would yoke a cart or a chariot; in this very way the Adhvaryu yokes the sacrifice for the sake of ascending to the heavenly world. Domestic animals carry him who knows thus. "Thou art the world; spread out! he says. The sacrifice is indeed the world; verily, through the sacrifice, he causes the sacrificer to expand with offspring and cattle. "O Agni, O Sacrificer, this homage! he says.

{3.3.7.6} Agni, indeed, is the sacrificer among the gods; he who is the sacrificer among the gods—to him alone he pays homage. He says, "O *juhū* ladle, come! Agni calls you for the sacrifice to the gods. O *upabhṛt* ladle, come! The god Savitṛ calls you for the sacrifice to the gods. The *juhū* belongs to Agni, and the *upabhṛt* belongs to Savitṛ; impelled by these two, he takes them up. He says, "O Agni and Viṣṇu, may I not step between us. Agni is in front, and Viṣṇu, the sacrifice, is behind.

Having addressed those two [the two wooden posts] with those very words, he steps across them, saying: "Part asunder; do not burn me. He says this for the sake of non-injury. "O makers of the world, create a world for me," he says; he thus invokes this very blessing. "Thou art the station of Viṣṇu," he says. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice. That which is the sacrifice is truly the unconquered abode of the gods. Thus he stands in the unconquered abode of the gods themselves. "From here Indra performed his heroic deeds," he says.

He bestows sensory power (*indriya*) upon the sacrificer. "Having taken hold, may the sacrifice rise up, touching the sky," he says for the sake of growth. Having taken hold while the *āghāra* libation is being poured— at this very time the gods went to the heavenly world (*suvarga loka*). Thus, the sacrificer goes directly to the heavenly world; moreover, by means of a successful sacrifice, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world. "The sacrifice of the lord of the sacrifice is unharmed," he says to prevent injury.

"O Indra, the possessor of food, svāhā! he says; thus he bestows power (*indriya*) upon the sacrificer. "Great light! he says; for the great light is indeed the heavenly world. This serves for the attainment of the heavenly world. The *juhū* ladle has the sacrificer as its deity; the *upabhṛt* ladle has the rival as its deity. The *āghāra* libation is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). If he were to let them touch, he would place his vital breath in his rival. Without letting them touch, he strides across; thus he places the vital breath in the sacrificer himself. "Protect me, O Agni, from evil conduct; grant me a share in good conduct," he says.

{3.3.7.10} Agni, indeed, is the purifier. Crookedness, falsehood, and evil conduct [are what must be purified]. Straightforward action, truth, and good conduct [are what remain]. Agni alone protects him from crookedness, falsehood, and evil conduct; he bestows him upon straightforward action, truth, and good conduct. Therefore, one makes this aspiration for the protection of oneself. The *āghāra* libation is indeed the head of the sacrifice; the *dhruvā* ladle is the body.

{3.3.7.11} Having poured the *āghāra* libation, he anoints the *dhruvā* ladle. He thus restores the head of the sacrifice to its own place. He anoints it twice; for there are two vital breaths, out-breath and in-breath. Regarding this they say: "He should anoint it three times, for the head consists of three parts. Indeed, this [ladle] is like the head of the sacrifice. Moreover, there are three vital breaths; he thus places the vital breaths in him. "Thou art the head of Makha; may light anoint with light," he says. He thus places light above him, for the purpose of illuminating the world of heaven.

These are indeed the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths that are established: namely, the Brahman, the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Āgnīdhra, and the Sacrificer. If one were to pass between them, he would draw together the vital breaths of the sacrificer; he would be liable to die. Therefore, the Adhvaryu moves about while holding the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

{3.3.8.2} He leaves that world for the sacrificer alone; he does not draw away his vital breaths, nor does he become liable to die prematurely. Sitting facing westward from the east, he places the *iḍā* of the *iḍā* into the hand of the Hotṛ. The *iḍā* is indeed cattle, and man is cattle; thus he establishes cattle within cattle. This is indeed the procreation of the *iḍā*.

The sacrificer procreates after that procreation. He anoints the two fingers twice at the joints; the sacrificer has two feet, for the sake of stability. He spreads [the butter] once, he places [the offering] twice, and he pours [the butter] over it once; thus it becomes fourfold. There are indeed four supports of the animal; as great as the animal is, so he invokes it.

{3.3.8.4} One should invite [the *iḍā*] as if toward one's own face. Thus, one invites the cattle facing oneself. The *iḍā* is indeed cattle; therefore, it should be touched by both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer. "May I, being invited, become possessed of cattle," he says, for the Hotṛ invites these two. At the invitation of the deities of the *iḍā*, he who knows thus becomes possessed of cattle when he is invited.

That *iḍā* which he places on the hand is the portion of speech; that which he invokes belongs to the vital breaths. Thus, he secures both speech and the vital breaths. Now, at this point when the *iḍā* has been invoked, there arises a deliberation concerning the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) resting upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). The gods said to the sacrificer, "Offer an oblation to us. He replied, "I will not offer it without a share [for myself]."

{3.3.8.6} Speech said, "You shall not recite the invitatory verses (*puro'nuvākya*) without me having a share. The invitatory verse replied, "I shall not be without a share. The offering verse (*yājyā*) replied, "I shall not be without a share. The *vaṣaṭ*-call replied, "You shall not utter the *vaṣaṭ* without me having a share. When, having set aside the sacrificer's portion, he places the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he thereby makes those very deities partakers. He divides it into four parts; there are four quarters. Thus he finds firm support in the quarters. He places it upon the sacrificial grass.

The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is indeed the sacrificer; the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is the offspring. He thus establishes the sacrificer among his offspring. Therefore, some offspring are established by means of bone, and others by means of flesh. Now, they also say: "These very sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) of the *haviryajña* are secured within the altar when he places the sacrificial cake upon the sacrificial grass. He divides it into four parts, for there are these four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) of the *haviryajña*.

{3.3.8.8} The Brahman, the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Agnīdhra—[the sacrificer] should touch them [saying]: "This is for the Brahman; this is for the Hotṛ; this is for the Adhvaryu; this is for the Agnīdhra. Just as in that Soma sacrifice the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) are led forth to the officiating priests according to their assignment, even so is it here. He first bestows [the fee] upon the Agnīdhra.

{3.3.8.9} Prosperity indeed has Agni as its mouth; thus the sacrificer prospers through prosperity that has Agni as its mouth. Having spread [the underlayer of ghee] once, he takes [the portions] twice. Having spread [the underlayer], he pours [the ghee] over them twice. These amount to six. There are six seasons; verily, he gratifies the seasons. With the *veda*-grass-bundle, he carries the Brahman’s portion to the Brahman priest. The *veda* belongs to Prajāpati; the Brahman priest belongs to Prajāpati.

Savitṛ [is invoked] for the impulsion of the sacrifice; then, according to one's desire, by another [priest]. Then [the offering is made] to the Hotṛ. The Hotṛ is indeed the middle of the sacrifice; thus he gratifies the sacrifice from its very center. Then [the offering is made] to the Adhvaryu. The Adhvaryu is the foundation of the sacrifice; therefore, in the case of the Haviryajña, one follows this very sequence.

{3.3.8.11} Other sacrificial gifts are led forth for the firm establishment of the sacrifice. "O Agnīdh, cleanse the fire once, once," he says; for at this point the sacrifice has turned away, as it were. "The divine Hotṛs are impelled," he says; for an impelled rite is performed. "The human [Hotṛ] is sent forth for the auspicious speech; recite the Sūktavāka," he says; thus he invokes this very blessing. "Go happily to the divine Hotṛs," he says; thereby he makes the sacrifice go happily.
"May there be well-being for men," he says; thus he invokes this very blessing. "Recite the *śaṃyu* formula," he says; he thereby gratifies Śaṃyu Bārhaspatya with his own portion.

Anuvāka 9 {3.3.9.1} Now, with two verses in the *anuṣṭubh* meter containing the word *vāja*, he separates the two offering-spoons (*sruc*). The *anuṣṭubh* is indeed a firm foundation, and *vāja* is food; [this serves] for stability and for the attainment of food. He moves the *juhū* spoon eastward; thus he drives away those rivals who have already been born. He moves the *upabhṛt* spoon westward; thus he repels those who are yet to be born. Having thus driven his enemies in all directions, the sacrificer establishes himself firmly in this world.

{3.3.9.2} With two [verses]. For he has a twofold support. "For the Vasus thee! For the Rudras thee! For the Ādityas thee!"—he says this according to the sacrificial formula. He anoints the *prastara* (grass-bundle) upon the offering-spoons (*sruk*). These worlds are indeed the spoons; the sacrificer is the *prastara*. Thus, he anoints the sacrificer himself with splendor. He anoints it threefold; for these worlds are three.

{3.3.9.3} He anoints him for these very worlds. He anoints him from front to back; thus he anoints the sacrificer with splendor from front to back. "Licking that which has been anointed," he says. Ghee is indeed splendor, and the *prastara* is the sacrificer; verily, he anoints the sacrificer with splendor. "Let the birds disperse," he says; having made him a bird, he causes him to go to the heavenly world.

"May I not destroy offspring and the womb," he says; this is for the protection of offspring. "May the waters and the plants swell," he says; he thus causes the waters and the plants to swell. "You are the spotted mares of the Maruts," he says; the Maruts indeed rule over rain; verily, he secures rain. "Go to heaven, from there send down rain for us," he says; heaven is indeed rain; verily, he secures rain.

{3.3.9.5} For as long as the Adhvaryu throws the *prastara* (grass-bundle) into the fire, for so long is his life-span measured away. "O Agni, protector of life, protect my life! he says; thus he bestows life upon himself. For as long as the Adhvaryu throws the *prastara* into the fire, for so long is his sight measured away. "O Agni, protector of sight, protect my sight! he says; thus he bestows sight upon himself. "Thou art firm," he says, for the sake of stability. "The enclosing-stick which thou didst place around," he says.

{3.3.9.6} This is according to the sacrificial formula (*yajus*). "O divine Agni, being carried away by the Paṇis," he says; thus he makes him acceptable to Agni. "I bring this to you according to your pleasure," he says; thus he makes his kinsmen favorable toward him. "May he not think otherwise than this from you," he says for the sake of making him mindful. "Come together to the path of the sacrifice," he says; thus he attains abundance. He throws the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) into the fire for the completion of the sacrifice.

{3.3.9.7} He pours the remnants from the two *sruva*-ladles together. Whatever in that [offering] was harsh, he thereby pacifies it. He pours the *upabhṛt* into the *juhū*. The *juhū* indeed has the sacrificer as its deity; the *upabhṛt* has the rival as its deity. Thus, he makes the rival a subordinate attendant for the sacrificer. "You are sharers of the remnants," he says. The Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas are indeed the sharers of the remnants; that is their allotted portion.

{3.3.9.8} He gratifies them with that very [verse], with a verse addressed to the Viśvedevas; for these are indeed the Viśvedevas. It is in the *triṣṭubh* meter; the *triṣṭubh* is indeed power (*indriya*). Verily, he bestows power upon the sacrificer. "I set you two in the seat of Agni, whose house is secure," he says. This earth, indeed, is Agni whose house is secure; verily, he sets them two in her seat. "For the sake of bliss, O ye two blissful ones, bestow bliss upon me," he says.

Offspring indeed are cattle, and happiness is offspring; verily, he bestows upon himself offspring and cattle. "O two who bear the yoke, protect the yoke-bearer," he says; this is for the protection of husband and wife. "O Agni, of unimpaired life-force, of cool body," he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula itself. "Protect me today from heaven; protect me from bondage; protect me from ill-sacrificed rites; protect me from bad food; protect me from evil conduct," he says; verily, he invokes this very blessing.

"Make our food poisonless; make our seat easy to sit upon—svāhā! Having thus added the wood-shavings to the Anvāhāryapacana fire, he offers the oblation of the husks. Alternatively, there may be extra wood-shavings.

The husks are redundant; the remnants of the clarified butter are redundant. In redundancy he places redundancy. Thus, by means of redundancy itself, having obtained the redundant, he secures it. "The altar hid herself from the gods; they found her with the *veda*-grass-bundle. By the *veda* they discovered the altar, the earth. That earth spread out over all earthly things; she bears the germ within the worlds. From her the sacrifice is born, the giver of all.
With these words, before the *stambayajus*, he sweeps the altar with the *veda*-bundle for the sake of finding [the altar].

{ 3.3.9.11} Now, as for the fact that there is both the *veda* (the sacrificial grass-bundle) and the *vedi* (the altar): it is for the sake of pairing and procreation. Indeed, this *veda* is the beard of Prajāpati. He places it upon the lap of the wife; thus he creates a pair and obtains offspring. The *hotṛ* priest goes forth from the *āhavanīya* fire, spreading out the *veda*; thereby he extends the sacrifice until the next half-month. Upon that continuous [sacrifice] in the subsequent half-month, he offers.

{3.3.9.12} When the proper time has arrived, he performs that sacrifice. The exponents of the Veda say: "He indeed should be the *adhvaryu* who initiates the sacrifice from its source; thus he establishes it. The *adhvaryu* initiates the sacrifice from the wind (*vāta*). He says, "O gods who know the way (*gātuvidas*), having found the way, go upon the way. From whatever source he initiates the sacrifice, from that very source he establishes it. The sacrificer becomes firmly established through offspring and cattle.

He who performs the sacrifice not according to its deity is cut off from the deities and becomes worse off; he who performs it according to the deity is not cut off from the deities and becomes more prosperous. The noose belongs to Varuṇa. "I loosen this noose of Varuṇa," he says; thus he releases her from Varuṇa’s noose. Impelled by Savitṛ, he acts according to the deity.

{3.3.10.2} He is not cut off from the deities; he becomes more prosperous. "In the womb of the Ordainer, in the world of good deeds," he says. Agni indeed is the Ordainer (dhātṛ); meritorious action is the world of good deeds. Thus Agni the Ordainer places her in meritorious action, in the world of good deeds. "I make it pleasant for myself together with my husband," she says, for the non-deprivation of herself and the sacrificer, for their union. "United in life, united in offspring," he says.

{3.3.10.3} He utters this very blessing over the full vessel with an *anuṣṭubh* verse at the end. This four-footed metre is established in the full vessel for the sake of the wife; [it serves] so that she may be firmly established in this world. Thus she becomes firmly established in this very world. Furthermore, the *anuṣṭubh* is indeed speech (*vāk*), and speech is a productive couple. Water is seed and procreation. From this very couple, flashing and thundering, he pours down rain, emitting seed.

{3.3.10.4} Producing offspring: whatever in the sacrifice is joined with the *brahman*, its release is indeed by means of the *brahman*. Its pacification is by means of water. Now, the thong has been released by the *brahman*; taking it, the wife holds it along with water for the sake of pacification. She pours the full vessel into her joined palms; verily, she places seed and offspring within her. For by offspring a man is made full. She wipes her face; having thus assumed the form of the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), she rises.

The Upaveṣa is indeed the trimming-knife of the trees. He who knows thus finds one to trim for him. [He places it] on the rubbish-heap: "That Upaveṣa which the gods established among men—those who are less wise than we, them bring here to us. O Upaveṣa, serve us!"

"May offspring, nourishment, and wealth—both bipeds and quadrupeds—be ours; make them firm and not depart," he says as he hides [the fire-stick] from the front toward the west. Therefore, Śūdras wait from the front toward the west. He hides it from the thicker end. Thus he makes them non-disputants. The *upaveṣa* (fire-stick) is indeed a bold one; it is a thunderbolt sharpened by the sacred word (*brahman*). "Whatever heat is in the *upaveṣa*, let it reach him whom we hate."

{3.3.11.3} Then, having taken his name, he strikes [the sacrificial cake] for him: "Drive that rival away from his home, who attacks us in battle! With the oblation that drives away, may Indra cast him out. Go to the three distant realms; go beyond the five peoples; go beyond the three luminous spheres, as far as the sun is in heaven. To the furthest distance, I send you."

"May Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, lead [him] away, so that we shall not return for eternal years," he says. This thunderbolt is indeed threefold, sharpened by the sacred word (*brahman*). Having pierced him with its very heat, having driven him out from these worlds, he strikes him down with the thunderbolt and the sacred word. "He is slain! We have struck so-and-so! he says for the sake of striking him down. He should meditate upon whomever he hates; thus he pierces him with its very heat.

Prapāṭhaka 4, Anuvāka 1: One sacrifices a Brāhmaṇa for Brahman; a Rājanya for Kṣatra; a Vaiśya for the Maruts; a Śūdra for Tapas; a thief for Darkness; a slayer of a hero for Hell; a eunuch for Sin; a juggler for Deceit; an unchaste woman for Lust; and a Māgadha for Excessive Cursing.

Anuvāka 2 {3.4.2.1}: To song, a bard; to dance, an actor; to dharma, one who frequents the assembly hall; to jesting, a singer; to the *nariṣṭhā* (a type of ritual vessel), a terrifying man; to laughter, a maker of ornaments; to bliss, one devoted to women; to delight, the son of an unmarried girl; to intelligence, a chariot-maker; to fortitude, a carpenter.

For toil, the potter; for illusion, the smith; for form, the jeweler; for beauty, the weaver; for the arrow-case, the arrow-maker; for the weapon, the bow-maker; for action, the bowstring-maker; for destiny, the rope-maker; for death, the hunter; for the ender, the dog-keeper.

To *saṃdhi* (reconciliation), a paramour; to the house, an adulterer; to *nirṛti* (destruction), one who has superseded his younger brother in marriage; to *ārti* (distress), one who has been superseded; to *arādhī* (failure), the husband of a woman whose elder sister is still unmarried; to the purifier, a physician; to discernment, one who observes the stars; to expiation, a female artisan; to strength, a female slave; to appearance, one who conceals her thighs.

From the rivers, the Pauñjiṣṭha; from the Ṛkṣīkās, the Naiṣāda; for the man-tiger, the Durmada; for the Prayus, the Unmatta; from the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the Vrātya; from the serpents and divine hosts, the Apratipad; from the sheep (or from the *ḍyumoṇṭa* and *ayebhyaḥ*), the Kitava; from Irjatā, the Akitava; from the Piśācas, the Bidalakāra; from the Yātudhānas, the Kaṇṭakakāra.

For the causes of collapse, a hunchback; for joy, a dwarf; for the doors, one who is lame; for sleep, one who is blind; for unrighteousness, one who is deaf; for consciousness, a female fortune-teller; for the attainment of desires, an attendant; for instruction, an inquirer; for further instruction, one who asks back; for the boundary, a judge of legal disputes.

For the ritual act, the thief-hearted man; for the slaying of enemies, the slanderer; for discernment, the steward; for the overseer, the charioteer; for strength, the attendant; for abundance, the messenger; for what is dear, the sweet-spoken man; for safety, the horse-tamer; for wisdom, the washerwoman; for desire, the dyer.

For Bhā (Splendor), the wood-bearer; for Prabhā (Radiance), the fire-kindler; for the back of the firmament (*nākasya pṛṣṭha*), the consecrator; for the summit of the sun (*bradhnasya viṣṭapa*), the cleanser of the vessels; for the world of the gods, the fashioner; for the world of men, the scatterer; for all worlds, the blesser; for the unreturning slaughter, the churner; for the heavenly world, the tax-collector; for the highest firmament, the server.

To the *armans* (fortresses), the elephant-keeper; to speed, the horse-keeper; to nourishment, the cowherd; to brilliance, the goat-keeper; to virility, the sheep-keeper; to refreshment (*irā*), the plowman; to the sweet drink (*kilāla*), the brewer of *surā*; to prosperity, the house-guardian; to excellence, the steward of wealth; to the overseer, the charioteer (*anukṣattṛ*).

To fury, the iron-smelter; to wrath, the one who goes forth; to grief, the one who follows after; to the *utkīla* and the *vikūla*, the one with three bones; to union, the yoker; to security, the unyoker; to beauty, the fashioner of forms; to character, the applicator of collyrium; to destruction, the weaver of baskets; to Yama, the female messenger.

Anuvāka 11 {3.4.11.1}: To Yami, the female offspring of Yama; to the Atharvans, the woman who has miscarried; to the Saṃvatsara year, the woman who has been pregnant for a full year; to the Parivatsara year, the woman whose child has not yet been born; to the Idāvatsara year, the woman who has had a miscarriage; to the Idvatsara year, the woman whose pregnancy has passed away; to the Vatsara year, the worn-out woman; to the Sarvavatsara year, the grey-haired woman; to the Forest, the forest-guardian; to the remote wilderness, the forest-fire guard.

From the lakes, [he takes] the Dhaivara; from the pools, the Dāśa; from the standing waters, the Bainda; from the reed-beds, the Śauṣkala; for the far shore, the Kaivarta; for the near shore, the Mārgāra; from the fords, the Ānda; from the uneven places, the Maināla; from the sounds, the Parṇaka; from the caves, the Kirāta; from the ridges, the Jambhaka; from the mountains, the Kimpuruṣa.

Anuvāka 13 {3.4.13.1}: To the echo, one who is like the seasons; to the sound, a barker; to the end, one who speaks much; to the endless, a mute; to the great, a lute-player; to the cry, a fletcher; to the shouting, a drummer; to the distant and near, a conch-blower; to the Ṛbhus, one who sews skins; to the Sādhyas, a leather-worker.

Anuvāka 14 {3.4.14.1} To Bībhatsā, a Paulkasa; to Bhūti, a watchman; to Abhūti, a sleeper; to Tulā, a merchant; to Varṇa, a goldsmith; to the Viśve Devas, one afflicted with white leprosy; to Paścāddoṣa, a glāva; to Ṛti, a gossip; to Vyṛddhi, a coward; to Saṃśara, a cutter.

For laughter, he sacrifices a harlot; for song, a lute-player and an accountant; for aquatic sport, a female diver; for jesting, a woman of auspicious appearance; for dancing, a flute-player, a village headman, and a hand-clapper; for mirth, a mimic; for joy, a cymbalist.

Anuvāka 16 {3.4.16.1} To the King of Dice, the gambler; to the Kṛta age, the courtier; to the Tretā age, the one who perceives faults; to the Dvāpara age, the one who sits outside the assembly; to the Kali age, the pillar of the assembly hall; to Evil Deeds, the wandering teacher; to the Path, the religious student; to the Piśācas, the mountain-dweller; to Thirst, the cow-killer; to Destruction, the cow-slayer; to Hunger, the butcher of cows;
to Hunger and Thirst, him who stands begging for meat from one who is slaughtering a cow.

Section 17 {3.4.17.1}: One sacrifices a floor-crawling creature to the Earth; a shoulder-muscle-bound one to Agni; a *cāṇḍāla* to Vāyu; a bamboo-dancer to the Atmosphere; a bald man to Heaven; a yellow-eyed beast to Sūrya; a squinting man to the Moon; a leper to the Nakṣatras; a white-and-tawny beast to the Day; and a black-and-tawny-eyed beast to the Night.

Anuvāka 18 {3.4.18.1}: He immolates a man for Speech; he offers breath, out-breath, diffused breath, up-breath, and middle breath to Vāyu. He immolates sight for Sūrya; mind for Candramas; hearing for the Quarters; and a man for Prajāpati.

Now he sacrifices these to the Formless Ones: one that is too short and one that is too long; one that is too thin and one that is too stout; one that is too white and one that is too black; one that is too smooth and one that is too hairy; one with too many horns and one with too many teeth; one that blinks excessively and one that keeps its eyes wide open; a sister for Āśā (Hope), and a maiden for Pratīkṣā (Expectation).

Prapāṭhaka 5, Anuvāka 1 {3.5.1.1} I take refuge in Truth. I take refuge in Cosmic Order. I take refuge in Immortality. I take refuge in the dear, unharmed body of Prajāpati. With this fifteenfold thunderbolt, I trample down my hateful rival—him who hates us and whom we hate. Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ! Him!

Anuvāka 2 {3.5.2.1} Forward go your strengths, seeking heaven, rich in oblations, with the butter-dripping ladle; he goes toward the gods, desiring their favor. O Agni, come for the feast, being praised for the giving of the oblation; sit down as the Hotṛ-priest upon the sacred grass. We strengthen you, O Aṅgiras, with fuel-sticks and with clarified butter. Blaze forth mightily, O youngest one! May that [glory] of yours be wide and worthy of renown for us.

{3.5.2.2} O God, you invite us toward great heroic power, O Agni. Worthy of praise, worthy of worship, and worthy of homage, you are visible even through the darkness. Agni, the bull, is kindled; Agni, the bull, is fully kindled like a horse that carries the gods. Those possessing oblations praise him. We, the bulls, kindle you, the bull, O Bull.

{3.5.2.3} O Agni, shine forth mightily! We choose Agni as our messenger, the invoker, the all-knowing, the one of excellent wisdom for this sacrifice. Being kindled at the rite, Agni the purifier is worthy of praise; we seek him whose hair is flame. O Agni, kindled and invoked with oblations, worship the gods at this well-performed sacrifice, for you are the bearer of the offerings. Offer the oblation, serve him; invoke Agni as the rite proceeds. Choose him as the carrier of the offerings. You, O Agni, are Varuṇa and Mitra.
The Vasiṣṭhas magnify you with their prayers; may all wealth be easily won through you. Do you ever protect us with your blessings.

Anuvāka 3 {3.5.3.1} O Agni, you are great, O Brāhmaṇa of the Bharatas—so-and-so, so-and-so. Kindled by the gods, kindled by the mind, praised by the seers, rejoiced in by the sages, lauded by the poets, sharpened by the sacred word (*brahman*), and offered with clarified butter. You are the leader of sacrifices, the charioteer of the rites, the unassailable invoker, the swift bearer of oblations, the vessel of the mouth, and the ladle of the gods.

{3.5.3.2} The cup is the drink of the gods. Like the rim, O Agni, encompasses the spokes, so do you encompass the gods. Bring the gods for the sacrificer. O Agni, bring Agni; bring Soma; bring Agni; bring Prajāpati; bring Agni and Soma; bring Indra and Agni; bring Indra; bring Mahendra; bring the gods who drink the clarified butter; bring Agni for the office of the Hotṛ; bring your own majesty. And, O Agni, bring the gods hither; and perform the sacrifice well, O Jātavedas.

Agni is the Hotṛ; let him partake. Let Agni partake of the office of the Hotṛ; let him partake of the protection. We are here. O sacrificer, may the deity be well-disposed toward you. O Adhvaryu, take up the butter-sprinkled ladle, which seeks the gods and contains all boons. Let us praise the gods worthy of praise; let us honor those worthy of honor; let us sacrifice to those worthy of sacrifice.

Anuvāka 5 {3.5.5.1} May the *samidhs* partake of the clarified butter, O Agni! May Tanūnapāt partake of the clarified butter, O Agni! May the *iḍas* partake of the clarified butter, O Agni! May the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) partake of the clarified butter, O Agni! *Svāhā* to Agni! *Svāhā* to Soma! *Svāhā* to Agni!
