You are the dwellers of the waters, the embryos of the Cosmic Order (*ṛta*), the guardians of the world, the falcons, the guests, the summits of the mountains, the sons of the one who sends forth. With your voice, call upon Indra; with your roar, drive away the malevolent spirits.

{3.7.9.2} "You are harnessed; draw [the stone]! Thus they have spoken to the divine pressing-stones: "The drop belongs to Indra. They have caused Indra to come from the highest distance, from this common dwelling place, from the wide mid-air. They have pressed out what is auspicious; they have pressed out spiritual luster for me. In battle they have struck down the demons; the power of the one who oppresses the Brahmins has been repelled. May both speech and mind attend to you.

{3.7.9.3} May out-breath and in-breath cook you; may sight and hearing cook you; may skill and strength cook you; may vigor and power cook you; may life-span and old age cook you; may the self and the body cook you. You are cooked, you are made cooked. For the cooked one, for the cooked ones, you! Him whom they call Indra, him whom they call Varuṇa, him whom they call Mitra, and him whom they call Truth.

{3.7.9.4} He who among the gods is the most divine, born of ascetic fervor—to him [I offer] you; to them [I offer] you. In me be that great power (*indriya*); in me be skill (*dakṣa*), in me be will (*kratu*). In me has been placed heroic vigor (*suvīrya*). May the three-pointed *gharma* shine for me, together with intention and mind, with the *virāj* and light, with sacrifice and milk. May we partake of its outpouring.

{3.7.9.5} May we obtain his favor; may we obtain his portion. May Speech, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma. Mitra [is] the people; forward, O Mitra! He than whom no other has been born superior; he who has entered into all beings; Prajāpati, in harmony with his offspring—he, the sixteenfold one, attends upon the three lights. This is the Brahman who is timely; he is the famous Indra in the host.

{3.7.9.6} I have proclaimed your two bay steeds at the great assembly; I win for you the timely exhilaration that is desirable to the conqueror. He who is named Indra, like clarified butter, pours forth what is beautiful with his bay steeds. O famous host, may my songs enter you, whose form is golden-brown. O Indra, sovereign lord, you are the overlord of the gods; make me an overlord among men, long-lived and full of splendor.

Indra the sovereign and Varuṇa the king—those two first made this your portion. Following their consumption, I consume it. May Speech, being pleased, be satisfied with the Soma. Prajāpati Viśvakarman—may I succeed through sacrifice with his divine mind. His purpose is not abandoned; his bliss is not abandoned. O Lord of the resting place, find a resting place for me. Homage to Rudra, the Lord of the Dwelling, at the approach and the departure.

{3.7.9.8} In the garden, in the place of ultimate resort, in the turning back and the turning away—he who guards it, him I invoke. Those debts to water which have not been repaid, those joys (*ānanda*) which have not been experienced, by which I move as a tribute to Yama—while remaining right here, let us discharge that; as living beings, let us bring this out from the living. Debtless in this world, debtless in the next, may we be debtless in the third world. [May we follow] those paths leading to the gods and those leading to the fathers.

{3.7.9.9} May we pass through all paths free from debt. To this very better dwelling have we now come. May both these, Heaven and Earth, be auspicious to us—rich in cattle, rich in wealth, rich in horses, and full of vigor. With brave sons, may we move along with heroes. The hymn (*arka*), the purifier, the measurer of the mid-region, sanctifies all the worlds of the gods. Heaven and Earth, in harmony, yielding milk, pour forth clarified butter and swell with nectar. The hymn, the purifier, is the measurer of the mid-region.
He purifies all the worlds of the gods: the light of heaven, great glory. May we attain a firm footing and a secure foundation.

Anuvāka 10 The Sun has risen—Savitṛ, Mitra, and Aryaman. With his yoke-pole he has struck down all enemies. He has made me great and full of heroes. Rest in the *Rathantara*, Svāhā! On earth! Rest in the *Vāmadevya*, Svāhā! In the intermediate space! Rest in the *Bṛhat*, Svāhā! In the sky! I support you with the *Bṛhat*. I take hold of you for glory and for heroism.
O inviolable ones, you have bestowed upon us sensory power and milk—whatever drop of yours there is, whatever surge of yours.

The divine banner has entered the entire world. May he protect us for our safety; *svāhā*! May this entire sacrifice follow after me—the *viśve devāḥ*, the Maruts, the Sāmans and Ārkas, the *āprīs*, the meters, the *nivids*, and the *yajus* formulas—whatever on this earth is worthy of sacrifice. Follow the path of Prajāpati! May we prosper through heroes, through cattle, through horses, and through all forms of nourishment; may we prosper through progeny and through sensory power.

{3.7.10.3} May the gods lead our sacrifice in a straight path. I establish myself in sovereign power, I establish myself in the kingdom; I establish myself in horses, I establish myself in cattle; I establish myself in offspring, in what is to be. One [of these two] has grown beyond the universe; that is resting upon the other. To Dyaus Viśvakarman and to Pṛthivī, I have paid homage. Heaven has settled upon the earth; the young bull has settled upon the cows.

{3.7.10.4} All these beings have been emitted; may the emitted sacrifice procreate. It has been emitted, it has been born, it has procreated. From the emitted is born the bull; from the emitted may we procreate. To those gods whose portion this has become, for whom there are the *prayāja*s and the *anūyāja*s—to the gods who have Indra as their chief and Varuṇa as their king, who maintain the fire-offering, *svāhā*! And may that prayer of ours reach them by day.

Aditi has come with her aid; may she, the bringer of peace, grant us well-being and joy. May she drive away our enemies. And may those two divine physicians, the Aśvins, grant us well-being; may they ward off evil from us and drive away our enemies. May Agni grant us well-being through his fires; may Sūrya warm us pleasantly; may the wind blow auspiciously and free from harm.

{3.7.10.6} Away with failures! The wise man does not doubt that very step, when the dead man returns again to the living. That which is the triple wheel of the world, the chariot’s course—the living embryo, not dead, shall live. Bring all things to him who desires to drink, to the one who knows, who comes readily, who has gone his way, the hero whose path is never behind. The drop has gone to the drop (Indra); Indra has drunk of the drop.
Of you, O drop, drunk by Indra, full of sweetness, invited, I partake as one who is invited.

Brahman is the foundation of the mind; Brahman is that of speech; Brahman is that of sacrifices, oblations, and clarified butter. Whatever in the ritual is redundant and whatever is deficient, may the sacrifice go on, knitting together its joints and restoring them. May the offering consecrated with *svāhā* reach the gods. Whatever has been called for (*āśrāvita*), whatever has been responded to (*atyāśrāvita*), whatever has been accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ*-call, and whatever has been recited in the sacrifice—whatever in the ritual is redundant and whatever is deficient—may the sacrifice go on, knitting together its joints and restoring them.
May the offering consecrated with *svāhā* reach the gods.

{3.7.11.2} Whatever offense we may have committed against you, O gods, even through speech, an offering intended for the gods but gone astray; or the stingy enemy who seeks to bring us misfortune—O Maruts, cast that away from us elsewhere! This has been performed by me, O Waters, and it is performed again. The sweetest prayer is recited as a hymn of praise. This is the ocean, the all-healing medicine. O Ṛbhus, satisfy yourselves with this which is consecrated with *svāhā*! "Out of the darkness we have risen," "Up that one," "The bright one."

{3.7.11.3} "This for me, O Varuṇa," "That I entreat of thee," "Thou, O Agni, art our [leader]," "So thou, O Agni, art our [leader]," "Thou, O Agni, art the messenger," "O Prajāpati," "I set up this boundary for the living; let none of these go to the further side of it. May they live a hundred abundant autumns, keeping death away by means of this mountain. Svāhā to the beloved! Vaṣaṭ to the unbeloved! Svāhā to the remedy for ill-sacrificing! Svāhā to the expiation! Svāhā to the removal of misfortune! Svāhā to the divine bodies!"

Hail to prosperity! Hail to complete prosperity! From whatever we fear, O Indra, from that grant us freedom from fear. O Maghavan, be gracious; let that be for our protection. Strike down our enemies, strike down those who oppose us. The giver of well-being, the Lord of the people, the slayer of Vṛtra, the dispeller of adversaries, the self-controlled one—may the Bull Indra go before us, the giver of well-being and the creator of fearlessness. Whatever is lacking of ours through these songs, [may he fulfill it].

{3.7.11.5} Swell forth, O Lord of the Bay Steeds, growing strong; when you burst open the great cow-pens for those who praise you, may we then be the ones who receive the greatest portion. Whatever in the sacrifice is done incorrectly, whether through lack of knowledge or through ignorance—O Agni, make that right, for you indeed know it exactly as it is. The sacrifice is commensurate with man; the sacrifice is commensurate with man—O Agni, make that right, for you indeed know it exactly as it is. Whatever is done by a mind that is simple yet weak in resolve...
Mortals deliberate upon the sacrifice; Agni, the wise Hotṛ who knows the rite, shall discern it. As the best of sacrificers, may he worship the gods according to the seasons.

Anuvāka 12 {3.7.12.1} O Gods, whatever offense against the gods we have committed, O Ādityas, release me from that! By the truth of Truth, and by the desire for life, O Gods, whatever untruth we have uttered with our speech—may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin; may he make me free from transgression for all the misdeeds we have committed. May he make me sinless.

By the *ṛta* (Cosmic Order), O Heaven and Earth; by the *ṛta*, O Sarasvatī. By the *ṛta*, deliver me from distress. Deliver me from the sin committed [by others]. Whatever wrong we have done, whether through the censure of a kinsman or the censure of a relative, whether through the censure of one who is superior or one who is inferior—whatever unknown sin has been committed against the gods, from that, O Jātavedas, release us! Whether by speech, or by mind, or by the two arms, or by the two thighs, or by the two knees.

Whatever untruth we have committed with our genitals, may Agni deliver me from that sin. Whatever offenses I have committed with my two hands, while suppressing the sound of the dice—may Dūrepaśyā and Rāṣṭrabhṛt, those two Apsarases, remit those debts. Whatever debt I incurred while not gambling, or whatever I consumed from people without intending to repay it—may Agni deliver me from that sin. Whatever [debt] was incurred by my mother while I was still in the womb...

Whatever sin my father has committed, may Agni release me from that sin. When as a joyful son, while sucking, I pressed against my mother or my father, may both parents remain unharmed by me; through this, O Agni, may I become free from debt. Whatever [sin] we have committed against the mid-region, the earth, or the sky, or against our mother or our father—may Agni release me from that sin. Whatever [sin] was committed through a wish, through a command, or through a prohibition...

Whatever sin we have committed, whether new or old—may Agni deliver me from that sin. May I pass beyond misfortune and whatever guilt there is; I cast off defilement in the highest dwelling-place, where the doers of good go, and not the doers of evil. I ascend now to that world of the righteous. The gods wiped away this sin upon Trita; Trita wiped it away among men. If anything has reached me from that, may Agni deliver me from that sin.

May the Gārhapatya fire release us from whatever misfortunes we have committed. May he make me free from sin. Those waters born in heaven, born in the waters, those born from the plants, and those waters born from fire—may those purifying waters cleanse us. Whatever evil we have done at night, O Waters, or by day, whether new or old, O golden-colored ones, purify us from that. "Hear this my cry, O Varuṇa," "That I implore of you," "O Agni, do thou protect us," "So do thou, O Agni, protect us," "O Agni, thou art the unswerving one."

O King Soma, whatever of your dear limbs or your well-hewn joints the pressing-stones have severed, heal that with clarified butter and cause it to grow. Free from sin, may we dwell together in peace. Whatever the stone, moving from the arms, has caused to fall, or whatever the men have milked from you with their right hands—let that swell for you, let that be restored for you, O divine Soma. Whatever of your skin they have pierced, or your source, and whatever you feel as if displaced from your station by yourself.

O Soma, let that be protected by you for us. May this bond of ours be established in the highest heaven. Having come together with milk, the body has emerged from the day; its color becomes one after another. In that [bond], we are invited; we are yours. Grant us a share in the assembly of all forms. O Soma, the beholder of men, may you hear us. Do not abandon our songs as you choose them; increasing the bodies of those who are sinless, may he, being born, bring form to us.

The ladles flow with clarified butter, increasing your beloved limbs. To you, O Soma, be homage and *vaṣaṭ*! Summon me, O King, for the sake of good deeds. Be united with out-breath and in-breath, and with bliss; be united with sight, O King Soma, and with hearing. May that which has entered you be well for you. May they recognize us at the meeting of the paths. May he recognize this one in the highest heaven. The wolves, the vigorous ones, dwell together; they know his form.

When he comes by the paths traveled by the gods, make his sacrificial offerings and pious works manifest to him. O King, go forth unharmed and free from disease; let there be homage to your swift-glancing eye. Ascend to the firmament together with the sacrificer; go to the sun in the highest heaven. Now indeed has the god Savitṛ become worthy of praise for us; he is now to be invoked by men at the beginning of the day—he who distributes treasures among the descendants of Manu.

May it bestow upon us here the most excellent wealth. O Mitra and Varuṇa, protect us here; as friends, look upon us here. The noose of the Ādityas is a fierce weapon; may that hundred-jointed, deadly snare pass us by. Swell, [O Soma]! May [your] strength gather together!

Whatever I have consecrated myself with in mind, and whatever with speech; or whatever with the vital breaths, with sight, and with hearing; or whatever with semen, with the couple, and even with the self—from the waters the worlds have received luster and sensory power. The bright waters are the releasers from consecration and from austerity; may the waters release luster and sensory power within me. Whatever I have consecrated myself with through the *ṛc*, the *sāman*, and the *yajus*; on the skin of animals, with the oblation; or with the meters, with the plants, and in the tree—from the waters the worlds have received luster and sensory power.

{3.7.14.2} Bright, releasing from consecration and from austerity; waters that release—may splendor and sensory power be in me! By which [power] Brahman [attains its state], by which Kṣatra, by which Indra and Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, and King Varuṇa, by which the All-gods, the seers, and the vital breaths; from the waters the worlds received splendor and sensory power—bright, releasing from consecration and from austerity; waters that release—may splendor and sensory power be in me! You are the flower of the waters, the essence of the plants, the beloved abode of Soma.

{3.7.14.3} This is the most beloved oblation of Agni; Svāhā! You are the flower of the waters, the essence of the plants, the dear abode of Soma, the most beloved oblation of Indra; Svāhā! You are the flower of the waters, the essence of the plants, the dear abode of Soma, the most beloved oblation of the Viśve Devas; Svāhā! O Soma, in your sacred law, may we, filling our minds and bodies with you, possessing offspring, attain [fulfillment].

Svāhā to the gods, to the fathers! Svāhā to the Somya fathers! Svāhā to the Kavya fathers! O gods, rejoice here! O Somyas, rejoice here! O Kavyas, rejoice here! May the Somya fathers not be excluded from the drinking of the Soma. Let death depart; immortality has come to us. May Vaivasvata grant us freedom from fear, like the leaf of a tree.

May wealth fall upon us; may the Lord of Power attend us. O Death, depart along your own path, which is other than the way of the gods. To you who have eyes and hear, I say this: do not harm our progeny, nor our heroes. We have now come to this most excellent dwelling, which wins cattle, wins wealth, and wins horses—like the leaf of a tree. May wealth fall upon us; may the Lord of Power attend us.

Prapāṭhaka 8, Anuvāka 1: He performs the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice with the thought, "May I win over this community. The girdle consists of twelve cubits; the year has twelve months; verily, he wins the year. It is made of Muñja grass; Muñja grass is indeed strength; verily, he wins strength. The constellation Citrā is used; for this rite is indeed wonderful.

{3.8.1.2} Since the Aśvamedha leads to prosperity, he settles at a sacrificial ground with an auspicious name; thereby he wins auspicious fame. He causes the officiating priests to arrive on foot until the Subrahmaṇyā litany, for the attainment of the heavenly world. He shaves his hair and beard, clips his nails, cleanses his teeth, and bathes. He puts on a new, unwashed garment for the removal of evil. Having restrained his speech, he observes the fast.

For the protection of the heavenly world, they remain awake through the night; for the attainment of the heavenly world. Anuvāka 2. There are four kinds of water, for the horse belonging to Prajāpati has four hooves; it is for the sake of prosperity. They are brought together from the quarters, for water is in the quarters. Water is indeed food; from water food is born. Whatever food is born from water, that he secures for himself. In them he cooks the *brahmaudana* (the rice-mess for the Brahman); verily, he thereby places seed.

It consists of four *śarāva* measures; thus he finds firm support in the quarters. There are gold plates on both sides; thus he bestows radiance upon him from both sides. He takes it out for the sake of being thoroughly cooked. It is provided with clarified butter for the sake of purity. Four descendants of seers (*ārṣeya*) consume it; thus he offers into the light of the quarters. He gives four pieces of gold; thus he wins the lights of the quarters.

{3.8.2.3} Whatever ghee remains, he moistens the cord in it. The cooked rice is indeed Prajāpati; the ghee is seed. In that he moistens the cord in the ghee, he provides Prajāpati with seed. The cord is made of darbha grass. For this horse wanders much and approaches what is impure; darbha grass is indeed a means of purification.

{3.8.2.4} In that the girth-rope is made of *darbha* grass, it purifies him; he sacrifices him as one who is purified and fit for the sacrifice. When the horse was sacrificed, its greatness (*mahiman*) departed; it entered the *mahartvijas*. That is why they are called *mahartvijas*. In that the *mahartvijas* eat [the portions], they thereby bestow greatness upon him. When the horse was sacrificed, its seed departed; it became gold.
In that he gives gold, he bestows seed. He gives it with cooked rice; for cooked rice is seed, and gold is seed. Thus, by means of seed, he bestows seed upon him.

He who binds a horse fit for sacrifice without having announced it to the *brahman*, to the gods, and to Prajāpati, is cut off from the deities and becomes worse off. He who has announced it is not cut off from the deities and becomes more prosperous. When he says, "O *brahman*, I shall bind the horse fit for sacrifice for the gods and for Prajāpati; may I prosper through it,"—the *brahman* is indeed the *brahman*.
Having thus announced it to the *brahman*, to the gods, and to Prajāpati, he binds the horse fit for sacrifice.

{3.8.3.2} He is not cut off from the deities; he becomes more prosperous. With the words, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he takes up the halter for the sake of impulsion. "With the arms of the Aśvins," he says, for the Aśvins were the two *adhvaryu* priests among the gods. "With the hands of Pūṣan," he says for the sake of restraint. That which is performed without a sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is indeed unsuccessful in the sacrifice. "They have grasped this halter of Order," he recites over it for the sake of providing a sacrificial formula and for the success of the sacrifice.

Regarding this, they say: "Should the girdle be twelve cubits long, or thirteen cubits? This horse is indeed the bull of the seasons, just as the year is. Of that [year], the thirteenth month is the hump; and this Aśvamedha is the bull of sacrifices. Just as the hump belongs to a bull, so does the hump belong to this [sacrifice]. He thus adds a thirteenth cubit to the girdle.

"Just as one prepares the summit of a bull, so indeed is that. 'In former times, at the assemblies, he was a sage,' he says; verily, he bestows life upon him. 'With that, the gods attained the pressed [Soma],' he says; verily, he turns toward prosperity. 'Uttering the course of the Truth,' he says; the Truth is indeed reality (*ṛta*); verily, by means of reality and truth, he seizes him. 'Thou art the bond,' he says."

Therefore, the performer of the horse sacrifice overcomes all beings. He says, "Thou art the world"; verily, he attains abundance. He says, "Thou art the controller"; verily, he makes him a controller. He says, "Thou art the supporter"; verily, he makes him a supporter. He says, "Him, Agni Vaiśvānara"; verily, he offers him in Agni Vaiśvānara. He says, "The far-extending."

Verily, he causes him to expand through progeny and cattle. "Svāhā! he says; this is his oblation. "On the earth," he says; verily, he establishes him upon this very earth. "Controller, sovereign; thou art controller, thou art restrainer; thou art supporter, thou art sustainer," he says; thus he proclaims his form and his greatness. "For cultivation thee, for security thee, for wealth thee, for prosperity thee," he says; verily, he invokes this very blessing. "To the gods, go happily," he says.

He thus sends him back safely to the gods. "Svāhā! To Prajāpati, thee! he says. For the horse belongs to Prajāpati; to whichever deity the animal is offered, with that very deity he makes him prosper.

The son of the father’s younger wife leads in front; the son of the mother’s younger wife leads behind. Thus they tear away evil from him in every direction. He incites the four-eyed dog with the words, "He who seeks to kill the courser, him Varuṇa strikes. They strike the four-eyed dog with the words, "Away, mortal! Away, dog! For the rival, the evil one, is indeed like a dog. Thus he strikes away his rival, the evil one. The pestle is made of *saidhraka* wood.

{3.8.4.2} It accomplishes for him exactly what he intends to do. A son of an unchaste woman kills [the enemy]. For the gods deposited their impurity in the unchaste woman; it is with that very impurity that he strikes away his [enemy's] impurity. "Evil indeed seeks him," they say, "who sacrifices with the horse-sacrifice. He throws down the horse's footprint. The horse belonging to Prajāpati is indeed a thunderbolt; with the thunderbolt itself, he tramples down his evil rival. He causes the sacrificial fee to float away.

He causes evil and impurity to float away from him. The carriage-pole is made of *aiṣīka* reeds; the *iṣīkā* reeds are indeed life-force (*āyus*). Verily, they bestow life-force upon him. The *iṣīkā* reeds are indeed immortality (*amṛta*). Verily, they bestow immortality upon him. It is bound with a branch of the cane (*vetasa*); for the horse has its origin in the waters, and the cane grows in the waters. Verily, he fashions him from his own source. He raises it up from the front toward the west; verily, he places immortality within him from the front toward the west.

With the words, "I and you, O slayer of Vṛtra," the Brahman priest takes the hand of the sacrificer; thus he unites the spiritual power (brahman) with the ruling power (kṣatra). With the verse, "O Indra, through wisdom you have become great upon the earth," the Adhvaryu makes the sacrificer recite for the sake of victory.

The four officiating priests sprinkle him. They impel him from these very four directions. The Adhvaryu, together with a hundred princes, standing in front facing west, sprinkles [him], saying: "Having sacrificed with this horse fit for the sacrifice, may this king slay Vṛtra. For the Adhvaryu is the kingdom, and the prince is the ruling power (*kṣatra*); verily, by means of the kingdom he bestows the ruling power upon him. The Brahman priest, together with a hundred fierce non-kings, [sprinkles him].

{3.8.5.2} Standing to the south, facing north, he sprinkles [the horse], saying: "Having sacrificed with this sacrificial horse, may this king be unassailable. The Brahman is indeed strength; the fierce non-king is strength. By means of strength, he thus bestows strength upon him. Standing behind [the horse], facing east, together with a hundred charioteers and village headmen, the Hotṛ sprinkles, saying: "Having sacrificed with this sacrificial horse, may this king [be master] of this people."

"To her who has many cows, many horses, many goats and sheep; to her who has much rice and barley, much beans and sesame; to her who has much gold, many elephants; to her who has many male and female slaves, who is possessed of wealth, possessed of prosperity, and possessed of abundant increase of riches—may she be a queen! The Hotṛ is indeed abundance; the charioteers and village headmen are abundance. By means of abundance, he bestows abundance upon him. The Udgātṛ, together with a hundred attendants and collectors, stands to the north and sprinkles from the south.

"Having sacrificed with this sacrificial horse, may this king attain a full lifespan"—for the Udgātṛ is indeed life, and the Kṣattṛ and Saṃgrahītṛ are life. Verily, by means of life he bestows life upon him. There are one hundred each; man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundredfold sensory power. Thus he becomes established in life and sensory power. There are four hundred; there are four quarters. Verily, he becomes established in the quarters.

Just as indeed a portion of an oblation that has been taken spills over, even so does this [portion] of the horse spill over, when they release it after it has been washed but not yet sacrificed. In that he recites the *stokyā* verses, he makes it a complete offering so that nothing may be spilled; for what spills from that which has been offered is not truly spilled. He recites a thousand [verses]; the heavenly world is commensurate with a thousand. This is for the conquest of the heavenly world.

{3.8.6.2} If he were to recite a limited number [of verses], he would obtain only a limited amount. He recites an unlimited number; for the world of heaven is unlimited. This is for the attainment of the world of heaven. He offers with drops of water; thus he obtains those waters which fall from the sky. He offers upon this earth; for this earth is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara.

{3.8.6.3} He establishes these very [offerings] upon this [earth]. Prajāpati indeed said: "I establish the Aśvamedha in the *stokyās*; with it, once established, I move about. He says, "To Agni, svāhā!"—he thus offers it to Agni. He says, "To Soma, svāhā!"—he thus offers it to Soma. He says, "To Savitṛ, svāhā!"—he thus offers it to Savitṛ.

"To Sarasvatī, svāhā! he says; thus he offers it to Sarasvatī herself. "To Pūṣan, svāhā! he says; thus he offers it to Pūṣan himself. "To Bṛhaspati, svāhā! he says; thus he offers it to Bṛhaspati himself. "To the joy of the waters, svāhā! he says; thus he offers it to the waters themselves. "To Vāyu, svāhā! he says; thus he offers it to Vāyu himself.

"To Mitra, Svāhā!"—thus he says; to Mitra alone he offers it. "To Varuṇa, Svāhā!"—thus he says; to Varuṇa alone he offers it. To these very deities he offers it. He offers in sets of ten. The Virāj consists of ten syllables; the Virāj is food. Through the Virāj, he wins the enjoyment of food. Indeed, he who offers oblations that go away from him falls away from this world. Therefore, he offers them again and again, turning back toward himself.

He finds firm support in this very world. This indeed is what he told Askaṇḍa regarding the completion of the Aśvamedha; for that which spills from the sacrifice once it has been completed is not truly spilled.

"Obeisance to Prajāpati, I sprinkle thee, who art dear to him," saying this, he sprinkles [the horse] from the front while standing facing west. Prajāpati is indeed the eater of food and the most vigorous among the gods; verily, he bestows upon it both food and vigor. Therefore, among animals, the horse is the greatest eater of food and the most vigorous. "To Indra and Agni, thee!"—saying this, [he sprinkles] from the south. Indra and Agni are indeed the most powerful and strongest among the gods; verily, he bestows upon it both might and strength.
Therefore, the horse is the most powerful and the strongest among animals. With "For Vāyu, thee," [he offers] from behind; for Vāyu is indeed the swiftest and the most fleet-footed among the gods.

{3.8.7.2} He bestows speed upon him; therefore the horse is the swiftest of animals, the most fleet-footed. With the words, "For all the gods, thee," he places it on the north side. All the gods are indeed the most glorious among the gods; he thus bestows glory upon him. Therefore the horse is the most glorious of animals. With the words, "For the gods, thee," he places it below. The gods are indeed the most honored among the gods; he thus bestows honor upon him. Therefore the horse is the most honored of animals.

{3.8.7.3} "For all the gods, thee!"—thus [he sprinkles] above. All the gods are indeed possessed of brilliance (*tviṣi*) and heat (*haras*). Verily, he bestows brilliance and heat upon him. Therefore, among animals, the horse is the most brilliant and the most full of heat. "For heaven thee! For the atmosphere thee! For earth thee!"—so he says. He thus sprinkles it for these very worlds. "For what exists thee! For what does not exist thee! For the waters thee! For the plants thee! For all beings thee!"—so he says.

Therefore, all beings subsist upon the performer of the horse sacrifice. The exponents of the Veda say: "Since the horse belongs to Prajāpati, why then does one sprinkle it for other deities as well? Indeed, all the deities are dependent upon the horse. When one sprinkles it with the words, "For all beings, thee!", one causes the deities themselves to become dependent upon it. Therefore, all the deities are dependent upon the horse.

Just as indeed a portion of an oblation that has been taken spills out, even so does this spill out of the horse: when they sprinkle it with water and then release it without having sacrificed it. In that he offers the "horse's ways" (aśvacaritāni), he makes it a complete offering to prevent spilling; for that which spills from what has been offered is not truly spilled. He says, "To the sound *īm*, svāhā! To that which has been made with *īm*, svāhā! These indeed are the horse's ways; by means of these ways, he brings the horse to fulfillment.

Regarding this, they say: "The practices of the horse are indeed not oblations; these should not be offered. But then they also say: "They must certainly be offered. For it is here that one who knows thus completes the Aśvamedha sacrifice—namely, when he offers the horse-practices. Therefore, they should be offered. [If he were not to offer them], he would place him outside his own abode and produce a rival for him.

{3.8.8.3} If one offers oblations elsewhere than in the proper place, other than in the *āhavanīya* fire, he should offer the "horse's deeds" (*aśvacaritāni*) in the *āhavanīya* prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the sacrifice to Savitṛ. Thus he offers his oblations in their proper place; he does not thereby produce a rival for himself. Regarding this they say: "They should be offered at every opening of the sacrifice, for the sake of the sacrifice’s proper arrangement and for the manifestation of the heavenly world. Furthermore, they also say:

If one were to offer [the oblations] at every opening of the sacrifice, he would deprive the sacrificer of his cattle; he would fall away from the heavenly world and become worse off. Therefore, they should be offered only once. Thus, he does not deprive the sacrificer of his cattle; he conquers the heavenly world and does not become worse off. He offers forty-eight forms of the horse. The *jagatī* meter consists of forty-eight syllables, and the horse belongs to Prajāpati; this is for the sake of prosperity. He offers one extra [oblation]; therefore, one among offspring is preeminent.

"Vast through my mother, powerful through my father," he says. This earth is indeed the mother; yonder sky is the father. Verily, by means of these two, he entrusts him [the horse] to them. "Thou art a steed, thou art a courser," he says; he thus instructs him. Therefore, offspring are born well-instructed. "Thou art a racer," he says; therefore the horse surpasses all other animals. Therefore the horse attains preeminence among all animals.

He who knows thus attains glory and preeminence. "Thou art a man; thou art a courser; thou art a prize-winner," he says. This is his very form; he thereby proclaims his greatness. "Thy name is Yayus," he says. This indeed is the horse's beloved name. He addresses him by his beloved name. Therefore, even when two enemies meet and call each other by name, they become friends.

"Follow the path of the Ādityas," he says; thus he causes him to go to the Ādityas. "Svāhā to Agni, svāhā to Indra and Agni"—with these words he offers the preliminary oblations. Thus he transcends his hateful rival right from the beginning. "Thou art the earth; for the past thee, for the present thee, for the future thee"—with these words he releases [the horse] for the sake of its wholeness. "O gods, guardians of the quarters, protect this horse sprinkled for sacrifice for the gods," he says.

There are indeed a hundred royal princes, the gods who guard the quarters; it is to them that he entrusts him. For the horse, once released, is liable to go to the furthest distance. He offers oblations at its four feet with the words: "Here is stability, svāhā! Here is support, svāhā! Here is delight, svāhā! Here is pleasure, svāhā!"

{3.8.9.4} These indeed are the fetters of the horse; with them he binds it. Therefore, when the horse is released, it returns to its tethering place; therefore, when the horse is released, it does not abandon its tethering place. The Aśvamedha is indeed the kingdom. Verily, those who guard the sacrificial horse strive for the kingdom. Of them, those who reach the completion go from the kingdom to the kingdom itself. But those who do not reach the completion—

{3.8.9.5} They are indeed cut off from their kingdom; he who, being weak, performs the Aśvamedha is cast away. If enemies were to capture his horse, his sacrifice would be destroyed. Four hundred men guard [the horse] so that the sacrifice may not be struck down. Then, having brought another [horse], they should sprinkle it with water; that is the atonement for that.

Prajāpati desired, "May I sacrifice with the Aśvamedha. He performed austerity. As he was performing austerity, seven deities, his own selves, emerged from him; she became the *dīkṣā*. He saw these Vaiśvadeva offerings; he offered them. By means of them, he indeed obtained the *dīkṣā*. In that the sacrificer offers the Vaiśvadeva oblations, it is the *dīkṣā* itself that he obtains by means of them.

He offers seven oblations, for seven were those deities who went forth. He offers them day by day; verily, day by day he secures the consecration (*dīkṣā*). He offers three Vaiśvadeva oblations and four Audgrahaṇa oblations; they amount to seven. Seven indeed are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in the head. The consecration is the vital breaths. By means of the vital breaths, he secures the vital breaths, the consecration.

He offers twenty-one oblations to the Viśvedevas. There are indeed twenty-one worlds of the gods: the twelve months, the five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun as the twenty-first. This is the world of heaven; this is the divine *kṣatra*, this is prosperity, this is the summit of the radiant one (*bradhna*), and this is called self-sovereignty (*svārājya*).

He offers thirty *audgrahaṇa* oblations. The *virāj* consists of thirty syllables; the *virāj* is food. Verily, by means of the *virāj*, he secures for himself the eating of food. He offers to the deity after dividing [the offering] into three parts. The gods are indeed thrice-returned (*tryāvṛt*); these worlds are thrice-returned. This is for the attainment of these worlds, for the establishment of these worlds. Indeed, the vital breaths depart from this person.

{3.8.10.5} He who exceeds the consecration (*dīkṣā*) [should act thus]: they proceed for seven days. There are indeed seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in the head; the consecration is the vital breaths. By means of the vital breaths, he wins the vital breaths, the consecration. He offers the final full-offering (*pūrṇāhuti*). The full-offering is indeed everything; verily, he obtains everything. Moreover, this earth is the full-offering; verily, he finds firm support upon this very earth.

Prajāpati created the Aśvamedha. Once created, nothing at all could sustain it. The Vaiśvadeva offerings alone sustained it. In that one offers the Vaiśvadeva oblations, it is for the sake of sustaining the sacrifice. "Svāhā to the mental effort (ādhi) for what has been mentally resolved; svāhā! Svāhā to the mental resolve for the mind; svāhā! Svāhā to the mind for Prajāpati; svāhā!"—"To Ka svāhā, to Kasmai svāhā, to Katamasmai svāhā"—these two [formulas] belong to Prajāpati and are primary.

He raises him up by means of those deities who have Prajāpati as their mouth. He says, "To Aditi, svāhā! To Aditi the Great, svāhā! To Aditi the Compassionate, svāhā! Aditi, indeed, is this earth; it is for her support that he raises him up. He says, "To Sarasvatī, svāhā! To Sarasvatī the Vast, svāhā! To Sarasvatī the Purifying, svāhā! Sarasvatī is indeed speech; it is by means of speech that he raises him up.

"To Pūṣan, svāhā! To Pūṣan who goes on the paths, svāhā! To Pūṣan who observes men, svāhā!"—so he says. Pūṣan is indeed cattle; verily with cattle he raises him up. "To Tvaṣṭṛ, svāhā! To Tvaṣṭṛ the seminal, svāhā! To Tvaṣṭṛ of many forms, svāhā!"—so he says. Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the fashioner of the forms of paired cattle; verily he bestows form upon the cattle. Moreover, verily with forms he raises him up.

"To Viṣṇu, svāhā! To Viṣṇu, the protector of the furrow, svāhā! To Viṣṇu, the protector of the furrows, svāhā!"—so he says. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; it is for the sake of the sacrifice that he raises him up. He offers the final full-offering (pūrṇāhuti) for the sake of support and stability.

Anuvāka 12 {3.8.12.1} In the morning, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Savitṛ. The Gāyatrī has eight syllables; the morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī. Verily, from the morning pressing and from the Gāyatrī metre, he fashions him. Moreover, by this means he attains the morning pressing and the Gāyatrī metre. At midday, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Savitṛ, the Impeller. The Triṣṭubh has eleven syllables; the midday pressing belongs to the Triṣṭubh. Verily, from the midday pressing and from the Triṣṭubh metre, he fashions him.

{3.8.12.2} Moreover, by this [offering], he obtains the midday pressing; the *triṣṭubh* is the metre. In the afternoon, [he offers] a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ Āsavitr. The *jagatī* has twelve syllables; the third pressing belongs to the *jagatī*. Verily, from the third pressing and from the *jagatī* metre, he fashions him forth. Moreover, by this, he obtains the third pressing; the *jagatī* is the metre. Indeed, a horse that is let loose is liable to go to the furthest distance.

He offers four oblations with the formulas: "Here is support, svāhā! Here is separation, svāhā! Here is delight, svāhā! Here is delight, svāhā! There are four quarters; verily by means of the quarters he encloses him. The enclosure is made of *aśvattha* wood. Prajāpati hid himself from the gods; having assumed the form of a horse, he stayed for a year in an *aśvattha* tree. That is the reason for the *aśvattha*'s name (*aśvattha*). In that the enclosure is made of *aśvattha* wood, he establishes him in his own womb.

"May a Brāhmaṇa, endowed with Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcas*), be born in this sacred word (*brahman*)," he says. Verily, he bestows Vedic splendor upon the Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, in former times, a Brāhmaṇa was born endowed with Vedic splendor. "In this kingdom, may a Rājanya be born, skilled in archery, a hero, and a great chariot-warrior," he says. Verily, he bestows heroism and greatness upon the Rājanya. Therefore, in former times, a Rājanya was born skilled in archery, a hero, and a great chariot-warrior. "May there be a cow that yields milk," he says.

"He places milk in the cow itself; therefore, in former times, the milch-cow was born. 'The draught-ox,' he says; he places vigor in the ox itself; therefore, in former times, the draught-ox was born. 'The swift steed,' he says; he places speed in the horse itself; therefore, in former times, the swift horse was born. 'The fortunate woman,' he says; he places beauty in the woman herself; therefore, a young woman is naturally beloved. 'The victorious one standing on the chariot,' he says; indeed, a victorious one standing on the chariot is born there."

"Where they sacrifice with this sacrifice, [the priest] says, 'May a youth fit for the assembly be born. He who is indeed in the prime of his life is a youth fit for the assembly; therefore, a young man is beloved. [The priest says,] 'May a hero be born to this sacrificer! Indeed, a hero is born to the sacrificer where they sacrifice with this sacrifice. [The priest says,] 'May Parjanya rain for us according to our desire! Indeed, Parjanya rains there according to their desire."

"Where they sacrifice with this sacrifice, may our plants bear fruit," he says. Indeed, where they sacrifice with this sacrifice, the plants there bear fruit. "May security and prosperity be prepared for us," he says. Indeed, where they sacrifice with this sacrifice, security and prosperity are prepared for the people.

Prajāpati assigned the sacrifices to the gods; he kept the Aśvamedha for himself. The gods said to him, "The Aśvamedha is indeed the sacrifice; let there be a share for us in it as well. He gave them these food-oblations (annahoma). They offered them. By means of those, he indeed gratified the gods. In that he offers the food-oblations, he gratifies the gods.

{3.8.14.2} By these [offerings], the sacrificer gratifies the gods. He offers with clarified butter (*ājya*). Clarified butter is indeed the form of Agni; in that he offers with clarified butter, he gratifies Agni himself. He offers with honey (*madhu*). Honey is indeed the form of the Great Deity (*mahatī devatā*); in that he offers with honey...

{3.8.14.3} Thus he gratifies that very great deity. He offers with rice grains; for rice grains are indeed the form of the Vasus. In that he offers with rice grains, he gratifies the Vasus. He offers with flattened rice (pṛthuka); for flattened rice is indeed the form of the Rudras. In that he offers with flattened rice...

{3.8.14.4} Thus he gratifies the Rudras. He offers with parched grains (*lāja*); for parched grains are the form of the Ādityas. In that he offers with parched grains, he gratifies the Ādityas. He offers with groats (*karamba*); for groats are the form of the Viśvedevas. In that he offers with groats, [he gratifies the Viśvedevas].

{3.8.14.5} By this, he gratifies all the gods. He offers with parched grains (*dhānā*). Parched grains are indeed the form of the constellations (*nakṣatra*); in that he offers with parched grains, he gratifies the constellations. He offers with groats (*saktu*). Groats are indeed the form of Prajāpati; in that he offers with groats, [he gratifies Prajāpati].

{3.8.14.6} Thus he gratifies Prajāpati. He offers with *masūṣya* grains; for these *masūṣya* grains are indeed the form of all the deities. In that he offers with *masūṣya* grains, he gratifies all the deities. He offers with *priyaṅgu* rice grains; for these are indeed called "dear-limbed" (*priyaṅga*). By means of these, the gods restored the limbs of the horse. In that he offers with *priyaṅgu* rice grains, he restores the very limbs of the horse. He offers ten kinds of food; the Virāj consists of ten syllables. The Virāj is for the attainment of complete food.

Prajāpati created the Aśvamedha. Once it was created, the Rakṣases sought to destroy it. Prajāpati saw these nocturnal oblations (naktaṃhomās); he offered them. By means of them, he indeed drove the Rakṣases away from the sacrifice. In that he offers the nocturnal oblations, the sacrificer thereby drives the Rakṣases away from the sacrifice. He offers with clarified butter (ājya). Clarified butter is indeed a thunderbolt (vajra); by the thunderbolt itself he drives the Rakṣases away from the sacrifice.

{3.8.15.2} He makes the *ājya* the opening verse. The *ājya* is indeed breath; thus he places breath in his mouth. He offers oblations of food; verily, he secures for himself a body. He offers them alternately; this is for the securing of both. He offers at night; this is for the striking away of the *rakṣases*. At the end, he offers with *ājya*.

The clarified butter (*ājya*) is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*). He thus bestows the vital breath upon him from both sides—both before and after. "Svāhā to one! he says; verily, he finds firm support in this world. "Svāhā to two! he says; verily, he finds firm support in yonder world. Verily, he finds firm support in both worlds—both in this one and in yonder one. "Svāhā to a hundred! he says. Man has a lifespan of a hundred years and possesses a hundredfold vigor; verily, he secures for himself both life and vigor.
"To a thousand, svāhā! he says. A thousand is indeed life; thus he secures life for himself. "To all, svāhā! he says. Thus he secures the unlimited.

Regarding this, they say: "He who sacrifices with the Aśvamedha seeks Prajāpati. And they also say: "He seeks all beings. He says, "Svāhā to one! Prajāpati is indeed the one; he attains him. He offers oblations in successive order, saying, "Svāhā to one! Svāhā to two! Thus he goes to the heavenly world in successive order. He offers one more each time.

{3.8.16.2} He goes to the heavenly world as one alone. He offers continuously for the continuity of the heavenly world. "To the hundred, svāhā! he says. Man indeed has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundredfold vigor; thus he secures both life-span and vigor. "To the thousand, svāhā! he says. A thousand is indeed life-span; thus he secures life-span. "To the ten-thousand, svāhā! To the hundred-thousand, svāhā! To the million, svāhā! he says.

{3.8.16.3} "These are the three worlds. He thereby wins these very worlds. "To Arbuda, svāhā! he says. Arbuda is indeed speech; he thereby wins speech. "To Nyarbuda, svāhā! he says. That which is the abundance of speech is Nyarbuda; he thereby wins the abundance of speech. "To Samudra, svāhā! he says.

He obtains the ocean itself. He says, "Svāhā to the middle!"—he obtains the middle itself. He says, "Svāhā to the end!"—he obtains the end itself. He says, "Svāhā to the highest limit (parārdha)!"—he obtains the highest limit itself. He says, "Svāhā to the dawn! Svāhā to the breaking of light! Dawn is indeed night; the breaking of light is day. Thus he wins both day and night, and moreover, he finds firm support in day and night. If he were to offer those two [sets of oblations] either by day or by night, [he would not obtain them].

He should cause confusion regarding day and night. He offers before sunrise with the formulas: "To the Dawn, svāhā! To the breaking forth, svāhā! To that which is about to rise, svāhā! To that which has risen, svāhā! He offers after sunrise with the formulas: "To that which has risen, svāhā! To the heavenly world, svāhā! To the world, svāhā! This is for the sake of avoiding confusion between day and night.

He offers the names of the Aśvins with the verses, "Vibhū with his mother, Prabhū with his father. He thus causes him to attain the name in both worlds. He offers the "running-forth" oblations with the formulas, "To the coming, svāhā! To the departure, svāhā! He thus causes him to go to the heavenly world entirely without spilling. He offers the preliminary oblations with the formulas, "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! He thus overcomes his hateful rival even before [the main sacrifice].

"To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā!"—thus he says; this is exactly according to the sacrificial formula (*yajus*). "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā!"—with these words he performs the preliminary consecration (*pūrvadīkṣā*); he thus passes over his hateful rival beforehand.

{3.8.17.2} "To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the twenty-one-fold initiation. There are indeed twenty-one worlds of the gods: twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first; this is the world of heaven. It is for the attainment of the world of heaven. With "Obeisance to the gods through [this] rite," he offers the seasonal initiation; thus he prepares the seasons for him. He offers with "To Agni, svāhā! To Vāyu, svāhā! for the sake of non-interruption.

{3.8.17.3} "May the sacrifice come hither," with these words he offers the *āpti* oblations, for the attainment of the heavenly world. "The past, the present, and the future," with these words he offers the *paryāpti* oblations, for the full acquisition of the heavenly world. "May my houses be [prosperous]," with these words he offers the *ābhū* oblation, for the prosperity of the heavenly world. "By means of Agni he experienced fervor," with these words he offers the *anubhū* oblation, for the experience of the heavenly world.
With "Svāhā to the one who intends [evil], svāhā to the one who has intended," he offers all the Vaiśvadeva oblations together; thus, he completely overcomes his hateful rival.

"To the teeth, svāhā! To the jaws, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the oblations to the limbs. For evil is clung to every single limb of a person; by means of this, he releases him from evil limb by limb. "To the speckled one, svāhā! To the black one, svāhā! To the white one, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the forms of the horse. Verily, he thus endows him with his forms. "To the plants, svāhā! To the roots, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the oblations to the plants. For plants are of two kinds.
Some take fruit from the flowers; others from the roots. Thus he secures both kinds.

With the formula, "To the lords of the forest, svāhā! he offers the oblations to the lords of the forest, for the sake of securing wild food. With the formula, "May the ram protect thee with cooked offerings," he offers the *apāvya* oblations; the gods who are the *apāvya*s are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*s). Verily, he secures the vital breaths. With the formulas, "To the well-water, svāhā! To the waters, svāhā! he offers the oblations to the waters. Indeed, the waters are in the waters; the waters are food; from the waters food is born. Whatever food is born from the waters, that he secures.

He offers the *ambhāṃsi* (waters). These waters are indeed this world; the Vasus are its overlords, and Agni is its light. In that he offers the *ambhāṃsi*, he wins this very world; he attains union with the Vasus; he wins Agni as light. He offers the *nabhāṃsi*. These *nabhāṃsi* are indeed the intermediate space.

{3.8.18.2} Of that [world], the Rudras are the overlords; Vāyu is the light. When he offers the *nabhas* oblations, he wins the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) and attains union with the Rudras. He wins Vāyu as the light. He offers the *mahaḥ* oblations. The sky (*asau lokaḥ*) indeed is the *mahaḥ*; of that [world], the Ādityas are the overlords; Sūrya is the light.

{3.8.18.3} When he offers the *mahas* oblations, he wins that very world; he attains union with the Ādityas; he wins the light of the sun. He offers the *yavya* oblations with the words, "Homage to the King! Homage to Varuṇa! for the sake of winning food. He offers the *gavya* oblations with the words, "May the wind blow pleasantly upon the cows," for the sake of winning cattle. He offers the continuous oblation (*saṃtatihoma*) with the words, "To breath, svāhā! To out-breath, svāhā! for the continuity of the heavenly world.

"To the white one, svāhā! To the black one, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the *pramukti* oblations for the sake of liberation from the world of heaven. "To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā!"—thus he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula itself. "To the toothed one, svāhā! To the toothless one, svāhā!"—with these words he offers the *śarīra-homa* oblations; by means of them, the sacrificer wins the world of the fathers. "Who yokes you? Let him yoke you"—with these words he yokes the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*). These enclosing-sticks are indeed the worlds;
verily, he yokes these worlds for him, for the attainment of the world of heaven.

He offers the two *mahiman* oblations with the verses, "He who [gives] breath" and "He who gives the self. The *mahaḥ* (great) world is indeed the heavenly world (*suvarga*); by means of these two, the sacrificer secures the heavenly world for himself. He offers all the *brahmavarcasa* (spiritual splendor) oblations with the formula, "O Brahman, may a Brāhmaṇa be born endowed with spiritual splendor"; by means of these, the sacrificer secures spiritual splendor for himself. He offers with the verse, "The seed has been produced," for the sake of non-interruption.

He offers the *saṃnati* oblations with the formulas, "To Agni he has bowed," "To the Earth he has bowed," for the sake of bowing to the heavenly world. He offers the two oblations to the past and the future with the formulas, "To the past, svāhā! To the future, svāhā! For this world is indeed the past.

He will become that. He finds firm support in these very two worlds. For the attainment of all; for the securing of all. With the verse, "When you first neighed at birth," he offers the *Aśvastomīya* oblation. For the attainment of all; for the conquest of all. By means of this, he attains everything and conquers everything—he who sacrifices with the Horse Sacrifice (*Aśvamedha*).

And whoever knows this: when the *rakṣases* sought to destroy the sacrifice, Prajāpati saw these night-oblations (*naktaṃhomāḥ*) and offered them. By means of them, he drove the *rakṣases* away from the sacrifice. In that the sacrificer offers the night-oblations, he drives the *rakṣases* away from the sacrifice by means of them. He offers at the end, saying, "Svāhā to the Dawn! Svāhā to the Breaking of Dawn! for the attainment of the heavenly world.

Anuvāka 19 {3.8.19.1} Either there is a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*) or a set of eleven. The sacrificial posts of other sacrifices are different; for the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), there is a set of twenty-one, for the conquest of the heavenly world. It is made of *bilva* wood, or *khadira*, or *palāśa*. The sacrificial posts of other sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) are different; for the horse sacrifice, there is one of *rājjudāla* wood, twenty-one cubits long, for the attainment of the heavenly world. They do not cut portions from the limbs of other animals; they do cut portions from the horse.

The splinter is indeed evil; it serves for the removal of evil. They cut portions of other animals on a branch of the *plakṣa* tree, but that of the horse on a branch of the *vetasa*. For the horse has its origin in the waters, and the *vetasa* grows in the waters; thus he cuts it upon its own source. They tie domestic animals to the sacrificial posts, while they keep the wild animals on the pegs; this is for the separation of the animals. They obtain the domestic animals [for sacrifice] and let loose the wild ones; this is for the removal of evil.

He erects a pillar of *rājjudāla* wood at the site of the fire-altar (*agniṣṭha*) for the removal of the sin of killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*). On both sides there are two pillars of *pautudrava* wood for the acquisition of a holy fragrance. Having removed the sin of killing an embryo from him, he encloses him on both sides with a holy fragrance. There are six pillars of *bilva* wood for the acquisition of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). There are six pillars of *khadira* wood for the acquisition of brilliance (*tejas*).

{3.8.20.2} There are six made of *pālāśa* wood, for the attainment of the drinking of Soma. They amount to twenty-one. Twenty-one, indeed, are the worlds of the gods: twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first. This is the world of heaven; [it serves] for the complete attainment of the world of heaven. There are a hundred animals.

A man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred faculties; he thus becomes firmly established in life and in his faculties. Indeed, one obtains everything through the Aśvamedha. They are unlimited in number, for the sake of securing the unlimited. The exponents of sacred knowledge (brahmavādinaḥ) say: "By what truth do they cut portions from the other animals on the right side, but from the horse on the left? For the horse belongs to Varuṇa.

{3.8.20.4} This, indeed, is the quarter of Varuṇa. He cuts the portions for him in his own quarter. When he cuts the portions for the other animals, he thereby secures that which belongs to a hundred deities. Upon the piled fire-altar, on a mat of *vetasa* reeds, he piles the horse. For the horse has its origin in the waters, and the *vetasa* reed is born from the waters; thus he establishes it in its own womb. To the east, facing westward, he piles the hornless goat; to the west, facing eastward, the wild ox.

He places the out-breath and the in-breath together within him. He offers these as a complete oblation (*sarvahuta*): the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal; this is for the conquest of these worlds. He offers them with his own self; he thus makes him possessed of a self and possessed of a body. He who knows thus becomes possessed of a self in yonder world. Moreover, by that [offering], he wins the stream of wealth itself. "To the plow-ox, svāhā! To the draft-ox, svāhā! so he says. The plow-ox, indeed, is the year.

The *parivatsara* is the ox. From the *parivatsara*, which is indeed the *saṃvatsara*, he secures long life; verily, he bestows long life upon him. Therefore, the sacrificer of the horse-sacrifice, when worn out by old age, goes to that world.

Anuvāka 21 {3.8.21.1}: The fire-altar consists of twenty-one parts; the Stoma is twenty-onefold; there are twenty-one sacrificial posts. Just as horses, bulls, or stallions might clash together, so do these Stomas clash when they are twenty-onefold. If they were to collide, his sacrifice would be destroyed. "The fire-altar should consist of twelve parts," they say; the Stoma is twelvefold.

There are eleven sacrificial posts. In that the fire-altar becomes twelvefold, the year consists of twelve months; verily, by means of the year, he secures food for him. In that there are ten sacrificial posts, the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and the *virāj* is food; verily, by means of the *virāj*, he secures the eating of food. That which is the eleventh is its teat.

{3.8.21.3} By that very means, he indeed milks her. Regarding this they say: "If there were twelve fires, the twelvefold *stoma*, and eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), it would be as if one were traveling with a wagon-pole; such would that be. They say: "The fire should be twenty-onefold; the *stoma* twenty-onefold; the sacrificial posts twenty-one. It is just as if one travels with side-horses (*praṣṭi*); such indeed is that."

{3.8.21.4} Or, whoever knows the three peaks (*kakubh*) in the Aśvamedha becomes a peak among kings. The fire-altar is twenty-onefold; the *stoma* is twenty-onefold; there are twenty-one sacrificial posts. These indeed are the three peaks in the Aśvamedha. Whoever knows thus becomes a peak among kings. Or, whoever knows the three heads in the Aśvamedha becomes a head among kings. The fire-altar is twenty-onefold; the *stoma* is twenty-onefold; there are twenty-one sacrificial posts.
These indeed are the three heads in the Aśvamedha; he who knows thus becomes the head of kings.

In the *Aśvamedha*, when the *Pavamāna* [laud] was being performed, the gods did not know the world of heaven. The horse knew it. Therefore, in the *Aśvamedha*, when they proceed northward for the *Bahispavamāna* with the sacrificial horse, it is for the sake of knowing the world of heaven. Indeed, a human does not know the world of heaven directly; the horse indeed knows the world of heaven directly. If the *Udgātṛ* were to chant the *Udgītha*, it would be just as if one who does not know the field were to lead someone along another path—that is how it would be.

{3.8.22.2} Having excluded the *udgātṛ*, he chooses a horse for the *udgītha*. Just as one who knows the terrain leads directly, even so does the horse lead him directly to the heavenly world. They grasp the tail; this is for the attainment of the heavenly world. He utters "hiṃ"; this is the *sāman* itself. He utters "hiṃ"; that is his *udgītha*.

Mares stand around [the horse], for the sake of pairing and procreation; moreover, it is just as when singers join in with their singing. "The sacrificial horse has sung aloud," he says. The horse belongs to Prajāpati, and the *udgītha* is Prajāpati; thus he secures the *udgītha* itself. Moreover, he finds firm support in both the *ṛc* and the *sāman*. He dedicates [the horse] with gold. Gold is indeed light; he thus places light at the very beginning, both for the sacrificer and for his offspring. Moreover, with gold as his light, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world.

The sacrifice is indeed man; the sacrifice is Prajāpati. In that they yoke the animals to the horse, he thereby sets the sacrifice in motion from the sacrifice itself. [The animals are] the horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal; he immolates them at the post standing nearest the fire. He thus sharpens the very front of the army. Therefore, the face of a king is prone to be formidable. [He offers] one for Agni with a black neck in front, upon the forehead; he thereby establishes the eastern fire.

Therefore, they place the *pūrvāgni* (the eastern fire) in front, and the *pauṣṇa* cake behind it. Pūṣan is indeed food; therefore, they bring the food to be served at the *pūrvāgni*. The *aindrāpauṣṇa* cake is placed above. The *rājanya* is indeed connected with Indra, and Pūṣan is food; thus he encloses him on both sides with food. Therefore, the *rājanya* is destined to be an eater of food. Two black-necked [goats] dedicated to Agni are for the two arms; verily, he bestows strength upon the two arms.

Therefore, a *rājanya* is destined to be strong of arm. Two [goats] for Tvaṣṭṛ with hairy thighs are offered at the two thighs; verily, he bestows vigor upon the thighs. Therefore, a *rājanya* is destined to be strong of thigh. Two [goats] for Bṛhaspati with white backs are offered at the back; verily, he bestows spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) above. Moreover, he thus places these two as armor on both sides. Therefore, a *rājanya*, when armored, performs heroic deeds. A speckled-bellied [goat] for Dhātṛ is offered below.

He thus establishes this very foundation. Moreover, this earth is indeed Dhātṛ; he thus finds firm support upon her. He places a white-spotted [brick] dedicated to Sūrya at the tail; he thus creates a swelling. Therefore, when there is fear, living beings seek refuge in a swelling.

Prapāṭhaka 9, Anuvāka 1. Prajāpati created the Aśvamedha. Once created, it departed from him. He pursued it with sets of eighteen [animals] and caught it. Having caught it, he secured it by means of the sets of eighteen. In that the sets of eighteen are sacrificed, the sacrificer secures the sacrifice itself by means of them. These sets of eighteen are indeed a counterpart of the year: twelve months and five seasons.

The year is eighteenfold. When eighteen-month-old animals are sacrificed, the sacrificer, having attained the year through them, secures it for himself. He dedicates the other animals at the central post; he dedicates the eighteen-month-old ones at the other sacrificial posts to avoid monotony. Nine are sacrificed at each [post] to ensure they possess equal strength. If he were to conclude with wild animals, father and son would fall out; their paths would diverge, and the boundaries of the two villages would become far apart.

{3.9.1.3} There may be born in the forests ṛkṣīkas, man-tigers, robbers, hunters, and thieves. Regarding this they say: "These wild animals are indeed no cattle. If he were to conclude the sacrifice with wild animals, they would soon carry off the sacrificer dead to the forest, for wild animals have the forest as their abode. If he were not to immolate the animals, his cattle would remain unacquired. If he were to release them after the fire has been carried around them...

He would cause a desecration of the sacrifice (*yajñavaiśasa*) were he to slaughter the animals. By [the fact that] he slaughters the animals, he thereby wins the cattle. In that he releases them after they have been carried around with fire (*paryagnikṛta*), it is to avoid the desecration of the sacrifice (*ayajñavaiśasa*). His cattle become secured; there is no desecration of the sacrifice, nor do they carry the sacrificer dead to the forest. He establishes [the sacrifice] with domestic animals. These indeed are the cattle called "peace" (*kṣema*).

Father and son seek protection together; their paths run together; the boundaries of two villages become contiguous. Neither *ṛkṣīkas*, nor man-tigers, nor robbers, nor murderers, nor thieves are born in the forests.

Anuvāka 2 {3.9.2.1} Prajāpati desired, "May I win both worlds. He saw these two kinds of animals: those of the village and those of the forest. He sacrificed them. By means of them, he indeed won both worlds. By the village animals he won this world; by the forest animals, that world. In that he sacrifices the village animals, he wins this very world by them; in that [he sacrifices] the forest animals— [He wins] that world by them.

{3.9.2.2} "With these [animals], that one. They say, "The year is indeed not secured for him who employs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices here and there [without following the proper order] throughout the year. The year is indeed as much as the Cāturmāsyas. When these Cāturmāsya animals are sacrificed, the sacrificer directly secures the year through them. He is indeed deprived of offspring and cattle who employs the year [in this manner]. The year is the world of heaven.

{3.9.2.3} But he does not fail to reach the heavenly world. The set of eleven animals is indeed offspring and cattle. In that these eleven animals are sacrificed, the sacrificer directly secures for himself offspring and cattle. Prajāpati created the Virāj; once created, she entered the Aśvamedha. He impelled her with sets of ten [animals] and attained her. Having attained her, he secured her by means of sets of ten. In that sets of ten are sacrificed, [it is for this reason].

{3.9.2.4} By means of these, the sacrificer attains and secures the Virāj. Eleven sets of ten animals are sacrificed; the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, and cattle are of the nature of the Triṣṭubh. Thus he secures cattle. The horse belongs to the Viśvedevas; the other animals have various deities, for the sake of the completeness of the horse. They are of various forms; therefore cattle are of various forms. They are of many forms; therefore cattle are of many forms, for the sake of prosperity.

For this world, domestic animals are sacrificed; for that [other] world, wild animals. In that he sacrifices domestic animals, he thereby wins this very world. In that [he sacrifices] wild animals, he [wins] that [world]. He sacrifices both kinds of animals—both domestic and wild—for the winning of both worlds. He sacrifices both kinds of animals.

{3.9.3.2} Both domestic and wild [animals]. This is for the attainment of both kinds of food. He sacrifices both domestic and wild animals; this is for the attainment of both kinds of livestock. There are three of each. These worlds are three; it is for the attainment of these worlds. The exponents of sacred knowledge (brahmavādinaḥ) say: "By what truth?"

{3.9.3.3} "There are many desires in this world"—this refers to the fact that different animals are sacrificed to the same deities. By this, he bestows desires upon this very world; therefore, there are many desires in this world. He offers the omenta of three animals together at a time. The gods are indeed thrice-repeated; these worlds are thrice-repeated. This is for the attainment of these worlds, for the establishment of these worlds. They release the wild animals after they have been carried around the fire, for the sake of non-injury.

“He yokes the ruddy one,” he says. Yonder sun, indeed, is the ruddy one; verily, he yokes the sun for him. “The red one,” he says. Agni, indeed, is the red one; verily, he yokes Agni for him. “Moving about,” he says. Vāyu, indeed, is moving about; verily, he yokes Vāyu for him. “Standing around,” he says.

"These worlds indeed stand around. He thus yokes these very worlds for him. "The luminaries shine in heaven," he says; the luminaries in heaven are indeed the constellations (*nakṣatra*); he thus causes the constellations to shine for him. "They yoke his two beloved ones," he says; he thus yokes desires for him. "The two bay steeds on either side," he says; the two bay steeds on either side are indeed these two [worlds]; he thus yokes these very two for him.

"Red, bold, carrying heroes"—so he says. Day and night, indeed, are those that carry heroes; verily, he yokes day and night for him. He yokes these very deities for him, for the attainment of the heavenly world. "Making a banner for those who have no banner," with these words he fastens the standard; verily, he causes him to attain glory among kings. "His appearance is like that of a thundercloud," so he says; this is according to the sacrificial formula.
"Those paths of yours, O Savitṛ, which are ancient," with these words the Adhvaryu makes the sacrificer recite for the sake of victory.

The sacrifice of him indeed goes away, whose animal, once brought forward, goes elsewhere than to the sacrificial altar. "O singer, turn this horse back by this path for us," he says. Vāyu is indeed the singer; he thus places Vāyu at its rear for the sake of turning it back. Just as the oblation spills when it has been taken up, so does the horse spill [its essence] when the hair falls from it once it has been brought forward. When they weave glass beads into the tail-hairs, they thereby gather back its very hair.

{3.9.4.5} With the formulas "Bhūḥ! Bhuvaḥ! Suvaḥ! they cause [the horses] to descend by means of the verses addressed to Prajāpati. The horse, indeed, belongs to Prajāpati; thus they endow it with its own deity. "Bhūḥ" is for the chief queen (mahiṣī); "Bhuvaḥ" is for the favorite wife (vāvātā); "Suvaḥ" is for the discarded wife (parivṛktī). This is for the conquest of these worlds. There are golden ornaments; gold is indeed light, and the Aśvamedha is sovereignty.

He bestows upon him both light and sovereignty in unison. There are a thousand [oblations]; the heavenly world is commensurate with a thousand; it is for the conquest of the heavenly world. Indeed, brilliance, sensory power, cattle, and prosperity depart from him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice. "May the Vasus anoint you with the Gāyatrī metre," [with these words] the queen anoints [the horse]. Clarified butter is indeed brilliance, and the Gāyatrī is brilliance; thus, by means of brilliance, he secures brilliance for him.

"May the Rudras anoint you with the Triṣṭubh metre," [with these words] the favorite wife anoints him. Clarified butter is indeed brilliance, and the Triṣṭubh is power; verily, by means of brilliance he secures power for him. "May the Ādityas anoint you with the Jagatī metre," [with these words] the discarded wife anoints him. Clarified butter is indeed brilliance, and the Jagatī is cattle; verily, by means of brilliance he secures cattle for him. The wives anoint him; this is indeed the form of prosperity.

{3.9.4.8} As for the wives: they thereby bestow prosperity upon him; from him brilliance, sensory power, cattle, and prosperity do not depart. They present extra food to the horse, saying, "O you who win parched grain, O you who win the prize, glory be mine, mine! Thus they make offspring eaters of food. He says, "The gods ate this food; eat this food, O Prajāpati! Thus they place the eating of food within offspring. If he should not smell it, one should make him smell it while reciting, "Agni was the animal."

He indeed smells [the horse]. He consecrates the horse with the mantra: "The steed has stepped forth; the steed has stepped across. Heaven is your back, earth your seat. This is for the conquest of these worlds. "Kindled, anointing the vessel of thoughts"—these are the *āprī* verses for the horse, for the sake of uniformity.

He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice is indeed deprived of splendor and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). The Hotṛ and the Brahman priest engage in a theological debate (*brahmodya*); thus they endow him with both splendor and spiritual luster. The Brahman priest stands on the south side; for the Brahman has his station on the south. The Brahman belongs to Bṛhaspati; he thus bestows spiritual luster upon him from the south. Therefore, the right side is more endowed with spiritual luster. The Hotṛ stands on the north side.

{3.9.5.2} The Hotṛ priest has his seat to the north. The Hotṛ is indeed related to Agni; Agni is brilliance. Thus he bestows brilliance upon him from the north. Therefore, the northern half is more brilliant. They both speak around the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). The post is indeed the deity of the sacrificer; thus they endow the sacrificer himself with brilliance and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). He says: "What was the first thought? The sky, indeed, is the rain; the sky is the first thought.

{3.9.5.3} He secures rain from heaven itself. "What was the great bird? he asks. The horse, indeed, is the great bird; verily, he secures the horse. "What was Piśaṅgilā? he asks. Night, indeed, is Piśaṅgilā; verily, he secures the night. "What was Pilippilā? he asks. Prosperity, indeed, is Pilippilā; verily, he secures food.

{3.9.5.4} "Who indeed wanders alone? he asks. "The sun, yonder, indeed wanders alone. He secures splendor (*tejas*) for himself. "And who, indeed, is born again? he asks. "The moon, indeed, is born again. He secures life-span (*āyus*) for himself. "What is the remedy for the cold? he asks. "Fire, indeed, is the remedy for the cold. He secures spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) for himself. "What is the great receptacle? he asks.

This world, indeed, is a great receptacle; verily, he finds firm support in this very world. "I ask you about the furthest end of the earth," he says. The altar, indeed, is the furthest end of the earth; verily, he wins the altar. "I ask you about the navel of the world," he says. The sacrifice, indeed, is the navel of the world; verily, he wins the sacrifice. "I ask you about the seed of the stallion," he says. Soma, indeed, is the seed of the stallion.
Verily, he wins the drinking of Soma. "I ask for the highest heaven of speech," he says; the Brahman is indeed the highest heaven of speech. Verily, he wins spiritual luster.

The vital breaths indeed depart from him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice. While the horse is being slaughtered, he offers oblations with the words: "To the out-breath, svāhā! To the diffused breath, svāhā! Thus, he places the vital breaths back into it; the vital breaths do not depart from him. He says: "You are protectors; may you protect me. You are dear among the dear, the most excellent among kinsmen. We invoke you, the lord of treasures, as the treasure-lord, O Vasu, mine. By this, he indeed causes the vital breaths to flow back toward him.

{3.9.6.2} Moreover, they indeed shake him; moreover, they humiliate him. They go around three times; these worlds are three. It is from these very worlds that they shake him. They go around again three times; thus they amount to six. The seasons are six. It is by means of the seasons that they shake him. Indeed, the vital breaths depart from these [who do not perform this rite].

{3.9.6.3} Those who perform the *dhuvana* (shaking) at the sacrifice go around nine times. There are indeed nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person; they thus place the vital breaths within themselves, so that the vital breaths do not depart from them. He leads the wife forward with the words, "O Mother! O Ambālī! O Ambikā!"—he has truly called her. "O fortunate one, dweller of Kāmpīla! he says; he thus brings her near through austerity. "In the world of heaven, may you two cover yourselves together," he says.

He causes her to go to the heavenly world itself. "I have conceived the embryo-bringer; may you conceive the embryo-bringer," he says. The embryo is indeed offspring and cattle; verily, he places offspring and cattle within himself. At the Aśvamedha, when the Pavamāna chant was being performed, the gods did not know the heavenly world; the horse knew it. In that they prepare the sword-paths with needles, it is for the sake of knowing the heavenly world. "Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī," he says.

{3.9.6.5} This is exactly according to the sacrificial formula (*yajus*). There are three kinds of needles: iron, silver, and golden. The iron ones are the form of this world; the silver ones, of the intermediate space; and the golden ones, of the sky. Or rather, the iron ones are the quarters; the silver ones, the intermediate quarters; and the golden ones, the upward directions. Thus, he prepares the quarters for him. He says, "Who cuts you? Who dissects you? for the sake of non-injury.

From him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice, prosperity and sovereignty depart. [The priest] says, "Raise this one upward!
