For the Aśvamedha is indeed prosperity and sovereignty; he thus raises prosperity and sovereignty upward for him. [He says,] "Like a load of bamboo on a mountain. For a load is indeed sovereignty; he thus piles sovereignty around him. [He says,] "And may its center prosper! For the center of sovereignty is indeed prosperity.

He indeed wins prosperity. "When the cold wind blows, as if purifying," he says. The cold wind is indeed the security of the kingdom; he thus wins security. "That the spotted deer eats the barley," he says. The spotted deer is the people (*viś*), and the barley is the kingdom. He thus bestows both the people and the kingdom upon him in harmony. "He does not consider the cattle to be well-fed," he says. Therefore, a king does not let his cattle become fat.

{3.9.7.3} "When a Śūdra woman, being the paramour of an Ārya, does not seek nourishment nor wealth," he says; therefore they do not consecrate the son of a Vaiśya woman. "This little bird," he says; the little bird is indeed the common people (viś), and the Aśvamedha is the kingdom (rāṣṭra). Thus he bestows both the people and the kingdom upon him in harmony. "It crawls about, saying 'āhalam'," he says; therefore the people crawl toward the kingdom. "The embryo in the womb is struck," he says; the embryo is indeed the common people.

The kingdom is the foot. He strikes the kingdom itself into the people; therefore, the kingdom is destructive to the people. "Both your mother and your father," he says. This earth is indeed the mother, and yonder sky is the father. Verily, by means of these two, he entrusts him [the sacrificer] to them. "Climb to the top of the tree," he says. The top of the tree is prosperity (*śrī*). Verily, he attains prosperity.

"‘I am about to impel,’ [with these words] his father thrust his fist into the womb; thus he says. The womb, indeed, is the people (*viś*); the fist is the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*). He strikes the kingdom into the people; therefore, the kingdom is destructive to the people. The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) depart from those who speak what is unpurified at the sacrifice. They recite the fragrant verse: ‘I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan. The fragrant ones, indeed, are the vital breaths. Thus they place the vital breaths within themselves; the vital breaths do not depart from them."

With the verse, "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss," they purify themselves with water. The waters, indeed, are all the deities; thus, by means of the deities themselves, they purify their own selves.

Prajāpati, having created the creatures, entered into them with his vital breath (*preṇā*). He was unable to reconstitute himself from them. He said, "He shall indeed prosper who shall gather me back together from here. The gods gathered him back together by means of the Aśvamedha alone. Thereupon, they indeed prospered. He who sacrifices with the Aśvamedha gathers Prajāpati himself and prospers. He immolates a human being.

{3.9.8.2} Man is indeed the *vairāja*. He thus sacrifices to the *vairāja* itself. Moreover, the *virāj* is food; he thus secures food for himself. He sacrifices a horse. The horse belongs to Prajāpati; he thus sacrifices to Prajāpati himself. Moreover, the one-hoofed animal is prosperity (*śrī*); he thus secures prosperity for himself. He sacrifices a cow.

The cow is indeed the sacrifice; verily, he seizes the sacrifice itself. Moreover, the cow is food; verily, he wins food for himself. He seizes goats and sheep for abundance; moreover, abundance is indeed prosperity; verily, he wins prosperity for himself. Having carried fire around the man and the wild animals, they release them for the sake of non-injury. Both these kinds of animals are seized: those that are domestic and those that are wild. Both of these are bound for his sacrifice; they are sacrificed to and gratified.

They are conquered and offered in sacrifice. Neither do fanged beasts, when bound at the sacrifice, harm him; for they are sacrificed to and gratified. Indeed, neither those who conquer nor those to whom offerings are made harm the one who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice, nor him who knows this thus.

Having succeeded by means of the first *stoma*, the fourfold *stoma*, on the previous day, he establishes himself on the twenty-one-fold *stoma* as a firm foundation on the following day. From the twenty-one-fold foundation, he ascends to the seasons. The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed the seasons; the seasons are the year. Having established himself in the seasons, that is, in the year, he ascends to the deities. The *śakvarī* verses constitute the *pṛṣṭha*;
there are various different meters, for these animals are sacrificed one after another.

{3.9.9.2} Both those that are domestic and those that are wild—[the sacrificer] thus makes them prosper by means of the form of the day. Moreover, this tribute is offered to the day itself. Regarding this, they say: "These are indeed not cattle—namely, goats, sheep, and wild animals. Only those belonging to the cow are truly all cattle. Therefore, on the final day, he immolates cattle belonging to the cow.

By that very means, he wins both kinds of cattle. They belong to Prajāpati; it is for the winning of what has not yet been won. There are nine white barren cows as *anūbandhya* victims; thus, at the very end, he wins spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). He sacrifices pairs of animals, such as two oxen used as draft animals for Soma the Self-Ruler; this is for the winning of days and nights. Indeed, he who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice is deprived of cattle.

He immolates the goat, the brindled one, the peacock, and the *vidīgaya*—these are the animals belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ. By means of these animals, he indeed makes himself prosper. He who performs the Aśvamedha becomes deprived of the seasons; therefore, he immolates the seasonal animals, saying, "Three tawny ones for spring," and so forth. By means of the seasons, he indeed makes himself prosper. He who performs the Aśvamedha is indeed cut off from cattle; they release them after the fire has been carried around them, so that there may be no injury.

Anuvāka 10 {3.9.10.1} Prajāpati desired, "May I become great, a consumer of food. He saw these two *mahiman* cups in the Aśvamedha; he took them. Thereupon, indeed, he became great, a consumer of food. He who desires, "May I become great, a consumer of food," should take these two *mahiman* cups in the Aśvamedha. He becomes great, indeed, a consumer of food. The omentum (*vapā*) has the sacrificer as its deity, while the *mahiman* cup has the King [Soma] as its deity. In that he sacrifices on both sides of the omentum with the *mahiman*, [he unites the two].

He encloses the sacrificer on both sides with sovereignty. Some gods have the *svāhā*-utterance before [the offering], others have the *svāhā*-utterance after. Both these types of gods are indeed secured within the sacrificial horse itself. When he sacrifices on both sides with the omentum and the *mahiman* cup, he gratifies all those gods.

The horse belongs to the All-gods (*vaiśvadeva*). If one were to make it belong to Prajāpati, he would deprive those deities who have no share of their portion; he would cause strife among the deities. [With the words] "The *stega* snakes with his two tusks, the frogs with his teeth," having made an oblation of clarified butter as a portion, he offers the oblations while enumerating them. Thus, he satisfies with their respective portions those very deities who have no share; he does not cause strife among the deities.

He offers these fourteen *anuvākas* for the sake of non-interruption. "To *prayāsa*, svāhā!"—with this he offers the fifteenth. There are indeed fifteen nights in a half-month; by [offering] half-month by half-month, the year is attained. The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict. They said, "O Agnis Sviṣṭakṛts, let us take out a portion from the sacrificial horse; then we shall overcome them. They took out the blood. Thereupon, the gods prevailed.

The Asuras are driven away. In that he offers blood to the Sviṣṭakṛts, it is for the sake of overcoming his rivals; he prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated. He offers the first oblation with the neck of a Gomṛga. The Gomṛga is indeed cattle, and Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is Rudra. Thus, he interposes the cattle from Rudra. Moreover, wherever this oblation is offered, there Rudra does not harm the cattle.

{3.9.11.4} With a horse’s hoof he offers the second oblation. The one-hoofed animal is indeed cattle; Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is Rudra. Thus, from Rudra himself, he interposes the cattle. Moreover, wherever this oblation is offered, there Rudra does not aim his wrath at the cattle. With an iron water-pot he offers the third oblation. Mankind is indeed of iron; Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is Rudra. Thus, from Rudra himself, he interposes mankind. Moreover, wherever this oblation is offered, there Rudra does not aim his wrath at mankind.

Anuvāka 12 {3.9.12.1}: When the horse was being immolated, its sacrificial essence (*medhas*) departed; that became the *Aśvastomīya* [offering]. In that he offers the *Aśvastomīya*, he immolates it with its very essence. He offers with clarified butter (*ājya*); clarified butter is indeed essence, and the *Aśvastomīya* is essence. Thus, by means of essence, he bestows essence upon it. He offers thirty-six times; the *Bṛhatī* meter has thirty-six syllables.

The cattle belong to the *bṛhatī* [meter]. That is the measure of cattle. He thus causes cattle to prosper by means of their proper measure. If he were to offer more or fewer than that, he would deprive cattle of their measure. He offers thirty-six [oblations]. The *bṛhatī* consists of thirty-six syllables; cattle belong to the *bṛhatī*. That is the measure of cattle. He thus causes cattle to prosper by means of their proper measure.

{3.9.12.3} Having offered the Aśvastomīya oblation, he offers with two-footed verses. Man indeed has two feet and is established on two supports; thus he endows him with a firm foundation. Regarding this they say: "Should the Aśvastomīya be offered first, or the two-footed verses? The Aśvastomīya is the horse, and the two-footed verses are man. He offers the two-footed verses after having offered the Aśvastomīya; therefore, the biped eats the quadruped. Moreover, he establishes the quadrupeds upon the biped. [He does so] after having offered the two-footed verses.

One should not offer another subsequent oblation. If one were to offer another subsequent oblation, one would fall away from a firm foundation. One offers the two-footed verse at the end for the sake of stability.

Prajāpati created the Aśvamedha. Once created, it departed from him. He sought it with sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*); he did not find it with the sacrificial rites. He sought it with *iṣṭi*-offerings; he found it with the *iṣṭi*-offerings. That is why the *iṣṭis* are called *iṣṭis*. When one sacrifices with *iṣṭis* for a year, one is thereby seeking the horse itself. There are [oblations] to Savitṛ.

This earth, indeed, is Savitṛ. Whatever perishes or hides upon her, it is on her that they find it; for they say, "No one at all can escape this earth," whether by going sideways or upwards. In that there are oblations to Savitṛ, he seeks him out only when impelled by Savitṛ. Now, a horse that has been let loose is liable to go to the furthest distance; in that he offers the *dhṛti* oblations in the evening, it is for the restraint and the holding back of the horse.

When he sacrifices with the morning offerings (*iṣṭi*), he seeks the horse itself. When he offers the evening *dhṛti* oblations, it is for the sake of the horse’s restraint and stability; therefore, creatures are at peace in the evening. When he sacrifices with the morning offerings, he seeks the horse itself; therefore, it goes about searching by day. In that he sacrifices with the morning offerings and offers the evening *dhṛti* oblations, he seeks it by means of both day and night; moreover, he thereby provides security and prosperity (*yogakṣema*) for him through both day and night.

Prosperity and the kingdom indeed depart from him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice. Two Brāhmaṇas, lute-players and singers, sing. The lute is the very form of prosperity; thus they bestow prosperity upon him. Indeed, when a man attains prosperity, a lute is played for him. Regarding this, they say: "If both should be Brāhmaṇas, what then?"

Fortune might fall away from him; indeed, fortune does not delight in a Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, let one be a Brāhmaṇa and the other a Rājanya. The Brāhmaṇa is indeed the *brahman*, and the Rājanya is the *kṣatra*. In this way, his fortune becomes encompassed on both sides by both the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*. Regarding this, they say: "If both were to sing during the day, the kingdom would depart from him."

"Or rather, the kingdom does not rest upon a Brāhmaṇa. Indeed, when the king desires [to take], then he overcomes the Brāhmaṇa. The Brāhmaṇa should sing by day; the Rājanya, by night. Day is indeed the form of the *brahman*, and night is that of the *kṣatra*. Thus his kingdom becomes encompassed on both sides, by means of both the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*. "You have given," "you have sacrificed," "you have cooked"—thus should the Brāhmaṇa sing. For the *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial and charitable merit) belongs to the Brāhmaṇa.

{3.9.14.4} "By means of his sacrifices and meritorious works (*iṣṭāpūrta*), he indeed makes him prosper," [he says]. "Thou art clad in antelope skin," "thou hast fought," "thou hast slain that enemy in battle"—thus [he addresses] the *rājanya*. Battle, indeed, belongs to the *rājanya*; by means of battle, he indeed makes him prosper. "The seasons of him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice are unestablished," they say. One [priest] sings three [verses], the other sings three; thus they amount to six. There are six seasons; verily, they establish the seasons for him.

He gives them at the conclusion; and he gives them when a hundred [cows] have been yoked. A man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred faculties. Verily, he becomes established in life-span and in faculties.

In all these worlds, indeed, deaths are inherent. If one were not to offer oblations to them, death would find him in every single world. [Therefore,] he offers the oblations in successive order, saying, "To Death, svāhā! To Death, svāhā! Thus, from every world, he propitiates death; death does not find him in any world. If, while offering, he were to look about, thinking, "To such-and-such, svāhā! To such-and-such, svāhā!", he would make death his many enemy.
With the formula, "To Death, svāhā! one should offer a single oblation to Death alone; for Death is indeed singular in that world.

Hunger is indeed death; he thus expiates that very [death] in yonder world. With the words, "Svāhā to the killing of a learned Brahmin (bhrūṇahatyā)," he offers an oblation at the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha); he thereby expiates the killing of a learned Brahmin. Regarding this they say: "Since the killing of a learned Brahmin is a sin from which there is no vessel [of atonement], why is it performed even in the sacrifice? They reply: "There is indeed another [form of] death distinct from the killing of a learned Brahmin; the killing of a learned Brahmin itself is death. Thus, when he offers the oblation at the avabhṛtha with the words, "Svāhā to the killing of a learned Brahmin," [he expiates it].

Having satisfied Death itself with the oblation and having made it a protection, he provides a remedy for the slayer of a learned Brāhmaṇa (*bhrūṇahan*). Muṇḍibha Audanyava indeed discovered this expiation for the killing of a learned Brāhmaṇa. He provides a remedy for anyone among his offspring who kills a Brāhmaṇa. At the final bath (*avabhṛtha*), he offers the last oblation with the words: "To Jumbaka, Svāhā!"

Varuṇa is indeed Jumbaka. Thus, he propitiates Varuṇa right at the end. He offers on the head of a bald, moist, white, and yellow-eyed [animal]. This is indeed the form of Varuṇa; by means of that very form, he propitiates Varuṇa.

The horse belongs to Varuṇa; he deprives it of its deity when he makes it belong to Prajāpati. "Homage to the King! Homage to Varuṇa! he says. The horse belongs to Varuṇa; verily, he endows it with its own deity. "Homage to the Horse! Homage to Prajāpati! he says. The horse belongs to Prajāpati; verily, he endows it with its own deity. "Homage to the Overlord! he says.

Dharma is the overlord; he wins dharma itself. "You are the overlord; make me the overlord; may I become the overlord of creatures," he says. He thus makes him the overlord among his equals. "Place me; place me in me," he says; he thereby invokes this very blessing. "To the one brought near, svāhā!"—thus he offers when [the victim] has been brought near. "To the one seized, svāhā!"—thus he offers when it has been assigned. "To the one offered, svāhā!"—thus he offers when the offering has been made. This is for the conquest of these worlds.

{3.9.16.3} He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice indeed falls away from these worlds. He offers those animals—the one for Agni, the one for Indra-Agni, and the one for the Aśvins—for the sake of firm establishment. In that there is an animal for Agni: Agni is all the deities; thus he wins the deities themselves. Agni is indeed the *brahman*; Indra is the *kṣatra*. In that there is an animal for Indra-Agni...

He secures both the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*. In that there is an offering to the Aśvins, it is for the securing of blessings. There are three [offerings]; these worlds are three; verily he finds firm support in these very worlds. He performs a sacrifice consisting of ten oblations, beginning with "To Agni, the deliverer from distress, [an offering] on eight potsherds. The *virāj* has ten syllables; the *virāj* is food. Verily, by means of the *virāj*, he secures the eating of food. "I meditate upon Agni, the first, the wise," are the invitatory and offering verses, for the sake of completeness.

Anuvāka 17 {3.9.17.1} If a disease should befall a horse, he should offer an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni, a pap to Soma, and an oblation on eight potsherds to Savitṛ. In that there is an offering to Agni—Agni is all the deities—it is by means of the deities themselves that he heals it. In that there is an offering to Soma—Soma is indeed the king of plants—it is from those very [plants] from which the disease finds him that he heals it.

{3.9.17.2} By means of these very [verses] he heals him. In that there is an offering to Savitṛ, he heals him indeed with the impulse of Savitṛ. By means of these very deities he heals him; he becomes truly free from disease. He should offer a pap to Pūṣan if he should be lame. Pūṣan is indeed the physician of the lame; he himself heals him. He becomes truly not lame.

{3.9.17.3} He should offer a *caru* oblation to Rudra if he should be afflicted by a great deity; for the horse belongs to that deity. Thus, he heals it with its own deity, and it indeed becomes free from disease. He should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara at the lair of a wild beast if [the horse] does not return. For this earth is Agni Vaiśvānara; she alone brings him back from all sides with her flames. Thus he surely reaches the day of the Soma-pressing, provided he continues his study.

{3.9.17.4} To Agni, the Deliverer from Distress, an offering on eight potsherds; milk for Sūrya; a portion of clarified butter for Vāyu. The horse is indeed the sacrificer. He whose horse, consecrated for sacrifice, wanders away is seized by distress. In that he offers to the Deliverer from Distress, he is thereby released from distress. The horse is indeed the sacrificer; he is deprived of his seed.

{3.9.17.5} If the horse consecrated for sacrifice strays away, [the priest] offers to Sūrya. That which is the milk for Sūrya is seed; thus he endows it with seed. The horse is indeed the sacrificer; he is deprived of his embryos when the horse consecrated for sacrifice strays away. The embryos belong to Vāyu; since there is an *ājyabhāga* offering to Vāyu, he thereby endows him with embryos. Moreover, for whomsoever this expiation is performed in the Aśvamedha, having sacrificed, he becomes more prosperous.

Regarding this, they say: "One should offer twelve *brahmaudana* oblations once the sacrifice is completed; one should perform twelve *iṣṭi* sacrifices. If he were to perform the *iṣṭis*, the sacrifice would come to him readily, but he would become worse off. For the meters have already been attained by him who has sacrificed; who could employ them again so soon? Indeed, all speech is attained when the sacrifice is completed.

{3.9.18.2} That [milk] becomes exhausted and its vital energy spent; for it has become harsh and turned ruddy. They say that it must not be used again. One should offer twelve *brahmaudana* oblations once the sacrifice is completed. The *odana* (boiled rice) is indeed Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice. Thus the sacrifice inclines toward him; he does not become worse off. There are twelve [oblations]; the year consists of twelve months. He thus finds firm support in the year itself.

This sacrifice is indeed named Vibhū (the Pervasive). Everything there becomes pervasive where they sacrifice with this sacrifice. This sacrifice is indeed named Prabhū (the Abundant). Everything there becomes abundant where they sacrifice with this sacrifice. This sacrifice is indeed named Ūrjasvān (the Full of Vitality). Everything there becomes full of vitality where they sacrifice with this sacrifice. This sacrifice is indeed named Payasvān (the Full of Milk).

{3.9.19.4} Everything indeed becomes full of milk there where they sacrifice with this sacrifice. This sacrifice is indeed named "The Sustained" (*vidhṛta*); everything indeed becomes sustained there where they sacrifice with this sacrifice. This sacrifice is indeed named "The Separated" (*vyāvṛtta*); everything indeed becomes separated there where they sacrifice with this sacrifice. This sacrifice is indeed named "The Established" (*pratiṣṭhita*); everything indeed becomes established there where they sacrifice with this sacrifice.

{3.9.19.5} Wherever they sacrifice with this sacrifice, this sacrifice is indeed called "The Radiant" (*tejasvin*); everything there becomes radiant where they sacrifice with this sacrifice. This sacrifice is indeed called "The Endowed with Spiritual Splendor" (*brahmavarcasin*); a Brahmin endowed with spiritual splendor is surely born there where they sacrifice with this sacrifice. This sacrifice is indeed called "The Piercer" (*ativyādhi*); a Kshatriya who is a piercer is surely born there where they sacrifice with this sacrifice.

Where they sacrifice with this sacrifice—this is indeed the sacrifice named Dīrgha (the Long). Men there become long-lived, where they sacrifice with this sacrifice. This is indeed the sacrifice named Klṛpta (the Arranged). Welfare and security are indeed arranged for the subjects there, where they sacrifice with this sacrifice.

Anuvāka 20 {3.9.20.1}: They quiet the horse with a *tārpya* garment. The *tārpya* is indeed the sacrifice; thus they cause him to prosper through the sacrifice. The *prastotṛ* priest stands by it with the *yāma* *sāman*; he causes him to go to the world of the twins (*yamaloka*). They quiet the horse upon both a *tārpya* garment and a *kṛtyadhīvāsa* garment; this is indeed the form of cattle; verily by means of their form he wins cattle. There is a golden cushion; it is for the attainment of splendor.

{3.9.20.2} There is a golden plate; it serves to illuminate the world of heaven. There is a horse; it serves for the attainment of Prajāpati. The garment of silk-cotton (*tārpya*) is the form of this world; the woollen mantle (*kṛtyadhīvāsa*) is that of the intermediate space; the golden cushion (*hiraṇyakaśipu*) is that of the sky; the golden plate is that of the sun; the horse is that of Prajāpati. By means of the silk-cotton garment, he attains this very world.

{3.9.20.3} By means of the *kṛtyadhīvāsa* he attains the intermediate space; by the golden *kaśipu* the sky; by the gold plate (*rukma*) the sun. Through the sacrificial horse itself, he attains union with and residence in the same world as Prajāpati. He attains union with, equal power, and residence in the same world as these very deities—whoever performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice and whoever knows it thus.

Anuvāka 21 {3.9.21.1} The Ādityas and the Aṅgirases contended for the world of heaven. Those Aṅgirases brought to the Ādityas that white horse, the sun, as a sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*). They said, "That which they have not given us has become the prize (*vara*). Therefore, they call the horse *savarya*. Therefore, the prize is given at the sacrifice. Because Prajāpati, when seized, became a horse, therefore it is called "horse" (*aśva*).

Because that which was swelling (*śvayat*) became wounded (*aru*), therefore it is called *arvan*. Because he immediately (*sadyas*) won the prize (*vāja*), therefore it is called *vājī*. Because he took away the worlds of the Asuras, therefore it is called *āditya*. Agni is the womb and the abode of the Aśvamedha; Sūrya is the womb and the abode of Agni. When, in the Aśvamedha, he scatters the high altar (*uttaravedi*) upon the built-up fire-altar (*agni citya*), he thereby makes it possessed of a womb and possessed of an abode.

He who knows this becomes possessed of a womb and a dwelling place. These two, the Arkā and the Aśvamedha, are indeed the out-breath (prāṇa) and the in-breath (apāna) of the gods; he truly secures for himself out-breath and in-breath. These two, the Arkā and the Aśvamedha, are indeed the vigor (ojas) and the strength (bala) of the gods; he truly secures for himself vigor and strength. Fire is the womb and the dwelling place of the Aśvamedha; the Sun is the womb and the dwelling place of Fire. When, at the Aśvamedha, he piles the high altar (uttaravedi) upon the fire-altar that has been built up (citya), [he establishes the Sun within Fire].
Those two are the Arka and the Aśvamedha; verily he wins the Arka and the Aśvamedha. Moreover, he finds firm support in the Arka and the Aśvamedha themselves.

Anuvāka 22 The gods, having made Prajāpati their father into a sacrificial animal, immolated him for the sacrifice. Having immolated him, they waited upon him, thinking, "We shall sacrifice tomorrow morning. Now, a year is indeed one day of the gods. Therefore, the horse is immolated before the end of the year. Because Prajāpati, once immolated, became a horse, therefore it is called *aśva*. Because he became the sacrificial essence (*medha*) immediately, therefore it is called *medhya*.

Therefore, it is the Aśvamedha. He who knows this becomes a knower of the Vedas and possesses swift horses. For when Prajāpati was sacrificed, he became a horse; therefore, among animals, the horse is most similar to Prajāpati. A son resembling him is born to one who knows this. Having gathered all beings together, he sacrifices them. The gods bring him together for splendor and Brahman-splendor—he who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice.

And whoever knows this thus—the gods indeed then took that deity, having become an animal, for the sacrificial offering; [they took] the sacrifice itself. "By means of the sacrifice, the gods sacrificed with the sacrifice"; they made the sacrifice a fulfiller of desires. They desired immortality; they attained immortality. Whoever sacrifices with the Aśvamedha goes by the very path of the gods.

{3.9.22.4} He sacrifices with the sacrifice belonging to Prajāpati, which fulfills all desires. He indeed goes to a state from which there is no return to death. In accordance with the form of this [sacrifice], he first offers a hornless bull of many colors to Prajāpati. It is for the sake of all desires, for the attainment of everything, for the conquest of everything. He who performs the Aśvamedha and he who knows it thus attains everything and conquers everything by means of it.

Anuvāka 23 {3.9.23.83} He who knows the two hairs of the sacrificial horse offers hair by hair of the sacrificial horse itself. Day and night are indeed the two hairs of the sacrificial horse; when he offers in the evening and in the morning, he offers hair by hair of the sacrificial horse itself. Following this very model, they used in ancient times to offer hair by hair of the sacrificial horse. He who knows the two feet of the sacrificial horse offers at every step of the sacrificial horse itself. The New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa) are indeed the two feet of the sacrificial horse.

{3.9.23.2} When one performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices, it is as if one offers at every step of the sacrificial horse. Indeed, in ancient times, they used to offer at every step of the sacrificial horse in imitation of this. Furthermore, he who knows the turning of the sacrificial horse offers at every turning of the sacrificial horse. Verily, that sun is the horse; he comes to the Āhavanīya fire, and there he turns. When one offers the Agnihotra, it is [an offering] at that turning.
At each turning of the sacrificial horse, he offers an oblation. Indeed, in accordance with this very model, in former times they used to offer oblations at each turning of the sacrificial horse.

Prapāṭhaka 10, Anuvāka 1: The Sāvitra Fire-altar Construction {3.10.1.1} Consciousness, discernment, wisdom, knowing, and fully knowing; intending, planning, and arranging; well-arranged and arranged; better, more excellent, extending, becoming, and being; the wonderful banner, shining, illuminating, and radiating; luminous, brilliant, glowing, heating, and intensely heating; radiant, shining, beautiful, gleaming, and auspicious.

The New Moon (Darśā), the seen (Dṛṣṭā), the beautiful (Darśatā), the multiform (Viśvarūpā), the fair to behold (Sudarśanā); the swelling (Āpyāyamānā), the swelling forth (Pyāyamānā), the swelling one (Pyāyā), the source of true joy (Sūnṛterā); the waxing (Āpūryamāṇā), the being filled (Pūryamāṇā), the filling (Pūrayantī), the full (Pūrṇā), the Full Moon (Paurṇamāsī); the giver (Dātā), the bestower (Pradātā), bliss (Ānanda), joy (Moda), and supreme delight (Pramoda).

Causing to enter, causing to settle, the one who causes to rest, the thoroughly pacified, the peaceful; becoming manifest, arising, coming into being, that which has come into being, the existent; the commenced, the praised, the fully lauded, the auspicious, the multiform; the pure, the immortal, the radiant, the light, the kindled; the ruddy, the luminous, the possessed of rays, burning all around, the ascetic; the progenitor, the impeller, the shining, the illuminating, the blazing; flaming, the causer of flame, heating, warming, thoroughly scorching.

The radiant one, the shining one, the beautiful one, the beautifying one, the lovely one; the pressed one, the pressing one, the well-pressed one, the being-pressed one, the being-poured-out one; the drinking, the drinking-place, the shared-drinking, the satisfaction, the satisfying one.

The beloved, the desirable, born of desire; long-lived, the fulfiller of desires. The accuser, the consenter; bliss, joy, and delight. Causing to sit down, causing to settle, the one who settles, the settled, the firmly seated. The pervasive, the all-pervasive, the pre-eminent, the source of well-being, the world. The purifier, about to purify, the purified, the fit for sacrifice. Glory, glorious; life, the immortal. The living, about to live; the heavenly world. The powerful, more powerful; possessed of vigor, the subduer.
Conquering, completely conquering; possessing excellent wealth, the giver of wealth. With pure filter, golden-haired; joy and delight.

Aruṇa, Aruṇarajas, Puṇḍarīka, Viśvajit, Abhijit; Ārdra, Pinvamāna, Annavat, Rasavat, Irāvat; Sarvauṣadha, Sambhara, Mahasvat; Ejatkā, Jovatkā; Kṣullakā, Śipiviṣṭakā; Sarisrarā, Suśerava; Ajirāsa, Gamiṣṇava; Idānīm, Tadānīm, Etarhi, Kṣipram, Ajiram; Āśu, Nimeṣa, Phaṇa, Dravat, Atidravat.

Speeding, hastening, swift, rapid, impetuous—Agniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Atirātra, Dvirātra, Trirātra, Catūrātra; Agni is the season, Sūrya is the season, Candramas is the season; Prajāpati is the year, the Great Who.

Anuvāka 2: The Sāvitra Fire-altar Construction {3.10.2.1} Bhūḥ! May Prajāpati settle you—the fire and the earth, myself, the three worlds, and the year—with that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit firm. Bhuvaḥ! May Prajāpati settle you—the wind and the intermediate space, myself, the three worlds, and the year—with that deity, in the manner of the Aṅgirases, sit firm. Svaḥ! [May Prajāpati settle you]—the sun and the sky, and myself.

The three worlds and the year—may Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ—the moon and the quarters, me, the three worlds, and the year—may Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras!

Anuvāka 3: The Sāvitra Piling {3.10.3.1} You alone know yourself; who you are, that you are. You alone have piled yourself. You are both piled and completely piled, O Agni. You are both as much as this and more than this, O Agni. Whatever of yours is deficient, O Agni, and whatever of yours is redundant—let the Ādityas and the Aṅgirases pile that up for you. Let all the gods fill out your piling. You are both piled and completely piled, O Agni. You are both as much as this and more than this, O Agni.

O Agni, let me not, through deficiency or through excess, diminish your lifespan. That light which rises when it has been kindled—the light of all lights, the unassailable vigor born of austerity—that is your light, O brick. With that, heat yourself for me; with that, blaze for me; with that, shine for me, as long as the gods endure, as long as the sun remains visible, and as long as the sacred word (*brahman*) persists.

Anuvāka 4: The Sāvitra Piling {3.10.4.1} You are the *saṃvatsara* (the full year), you are the *parivatsara* (the recurring year), you are the *idāvatsara* (the year of this present time), you are the *iduvatsara* (the year of the moon), you are the *idvatsara* (the year of the sun), you are the *vatsara* (the year). Of you, the spring is the head; the summer is the right wing; the rainy season is the tail; the autumn is the left wing; the winter is the middle. The bright fortnights are the layers (*citayaḥ*); the dark fortnights are the loose soil (*purīṣam*).

The days and nights are the bricks. You are the bull, the heavenly world. From whichever direction you are magnified, from that bring us greatness. Having become Vāyu, blow through all the directions; blow along all the directions; blow together through all the directions. Fill the layer with consciousness; fill the layer with non-consciousness. You are consciousness, whose source is the ocean.

{3.10.4.3} Indu, the skillful, the falcon, the observer of cosmic order; the golden-winged bird, the swift mover; the great one, firmly seated in his dwelling—homage be to you! Do not harm me. *Ā*, *pra*, *vī*, *sam*, *ud*. Grant me heaven! Grant me the intermediate space! Grant me the earth! Grant me the earth! Grant me the intermediate space! Grant me heaven! Spread out by day; contract by night. Spread out by night; contract by day. Spread out according to desire; contract according to desire.

Anuvāka 5: The Sāvitra Fire-altar {3.10.5.1} Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Ojas, bala, brahman, kṣatra, glory, greatness, truth, austerity, name, form, immortality, sight, hearing, mind, life, all-glory, majesty, equanimity, austerity, Hara, light—whether you are Jātavedas or Pāvaka, whether you are Vaiśvānara or Vaidyuta, grant welfare to the subjects and a world to the sacrificer; bestowing strength and nourishment, turn toward us (turn toward us with bliss)!

Anuvāka 6: The Piling of the Sāvitra Fire {3.10.6.1} Rājñī, Virājñī, Samrājñī, Svarājñī; Arcis, Śocis, Tapas, Haras, Bhās; Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati; the Viśve Devas, the guardians of the world—may they all endow me with glory.

Anuvāka 7: The Sāvitra Fire-altar Construction {3.10.7.1} To Asu, svāhā! To Vasu, svāhā! To Vibhu, svāhā! To Vivasvat, svāhā! To Abhibhū, svāhā—to the Overlord, svāhā! To the Lord of Heaven, svāhā—to the Lord of Misfortune, svāhā! To the Lord of Sight, svāhā—to the Lord of Light, svāhā! To the King, svāhā! To the Virāj, svāhā! To the Saṃrāj, svāhā! To the Svarāj, svāhā! To Śūṣa, svāhā! To Sūrya, svāhā! To Candramas, svāhā! To Jyotis, svāhā! To Saṃsarpa, svāhā! To Kalyāṇa, svāhā! To Arjuna, svāhā!

Anuvāka 8: The Sāvitra Fire-altar {3.10.8.1} Sing to the wise Pavamāna; like a great stream, the flowing juice rushes forth. Like a serpent, he sloughs off his worn-out skin; like a playful horse, the tawny bull has flowed. You are taken with a support; I take you, who are pleasing, for Death. This is your womb; I take you for Death. Away with death! Away with hunger! Drive away the curse from here! And then, O Agni, bring to us thousandfold abundance of wealth.

{3.10.8.2} Those thousand and ten thousand nooses of yours, O Death, intended for the slaying of mortal man—those we all expiate with the creative power (*māyā*) of the sacrifice. You are the portion; you are the drink of immortality. Of you, who have been drunk by Death, who possess the nectar of immortality, who have been made ready with the cry of *svagā*, who are full of sweetness, and who have been invited—I, being invited, partake. You are the delightful, overpowering banner of sacrifices, the Voice. Come here, [O] So-and-so!

{3.10.8.3} Blind yet watchful is the *prāṇa* (out-breath). Come here, O so-and-so! Deaf yet crying out is the *apāna* (in-breath). Come here, O so-and-so! Handless yet hurling is the *cakṣus* (eye). Come here, O so-and-so! Footless yet devouring is the *manas* (mind). Come here, O so-and-so! O sage of far-reaching intellect, come here, O *śrotra* (ear)! {3.10.8.4} Well-handed and well-clothed, you are named *śūṣa*, the immortal among mortals. As such I know you; come here, O so-and-so! Agni has taken refuge in my speech; speech in the heart; the heart in me; I in the immortal; the immortal in Brahman. Vāyu has taken refuge in my breath (*prāṇa*).

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. The sun is established in my eye; the eye is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. The moon is established in my mind; the mind is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. The quarters are established in my hearing; the hearing is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. The waters are established in my semen.

{3.10.8.7} Semen is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. The earth is supported in my body; the body is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. The plants and trees are supported in my hairs. {3.10.8.8} The hairs are in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. Indra is supported in my strength; the strength is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. Parjanya is supported in my head.

{3.10.8.9} The head is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. Īśāna is established in my *manas*; the *manas* is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. The Self (*ātman*) is established in my self.

{3.10.8.10} The Self is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. My self has returned; life has returned; breath has returned; intention has returned. Vaiśvānara, increasing with his rays, let him stand within as the guardian of the immortal.

Anuvāka 9: The Sāvitra Fire-altar {3.10.9.1} Prajāpati created the gods. They were born fettered by evil. He split them apart. Because he split them apart (*vyadyat*), therefore it is called lightning (*vidyut*). He cut him [the evil] off. Because he cut him off (*avṛścat*), therefore it is called rain (*vṛṣṭi*). Therefore, wherever these two deities reach [him], his evil is indeed split apart there.

{ 3.10.9.24} And [regarding] the two who cut: this very inquiry has been established in relation to the *agnihotra* itself; [it is] established [as being] bliss (*ānanda*). Now they say: "In all sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*). One who is about to offer should touch water, saying: "Thou art lightning; strike away my evil. Then, having offered, he should touch water, saying: "Thou art rain; cut away my evil. Whether one is about to sacrifice or has already sacrificed, these two deities indeed cut away his evil.

{3.10.9.3} And [the story] of Vṛścata and Atyaṃha Āruṇi. Having posed questions to a religious student (*brahmacārin*), he sent him away, saying: "Go; ask Plakṣa Daiyāmpāti: 'Do you know the Sāvitra verses? Or do you not know them? Having returned, the student asked him: "The teacher has sent me; he said: 'Do you know the Sāvitra verses? Or do you not know them? He replied: "I know them."

"On what is he established? "In that which is beyond the dust. "What is that which is beyond the dust? "He who shines yonder is indeed that which is beyond the dust," he said. "And this one here [on earth] is that which is below the dust. "On what, then, is he established? "On truth. "What is that truth? "Heat."

"3.10.9.5] 'In whom, then, does austerity [rest]? 'In strength. 'What is that strength? 'In breath. 'Do not ask beyond breath,' said the teacher; so spoke the religious student (brahmacārī). Plakṣa Daiyāmpāti said to him: 'O religious student, had you asked beyond breath, you would have asked beyond bliss (*ānanda*). Your head would have fallen off! I shall indeed become superior to your teacher, who instructed me regarding the Sāvitra [mantra].'"

Therefore, one should not converse with one who belongs to Savitṛ. For whoever converses with one who knows the [mantra] belonging to Savitṛ regarding that which belongs to Savitṛ, he bestows prosperity upon him. Indeed, yonder sun, while shining, regards him as possessing prosperity; prosperity regards him as possessing heat; heat regards him as possessing strength; and strength regards him as possessing vital breath. When he says, "Consciousness, discernment, the new moon, the full moon," this very thing is what is meant.

Now, as to what he says: "The one who has begun the praise, the one who has completed the praise, the pressed one, the one pressing"—this indeed is that; for this [Sun] is those days, and this is the nights. And as to what he says: "The bright banner, the giver, the bestower, the impeller, the prompter, the commander, the consenter"—this indeed is that; for this is the moments (muhūrta) of the day, and this is the moments of the night.

{3.10.9.8} Now, as for what he says: "The purifier, about to purify; the powerful one, more powerful; the ruddy one, with ruddy dust"—this indeed is that. For this alone is those half-months; this is the months. Then, as for what he says: "The Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, Agni, the season, Prajāpati, the year"—this indeed is that. For this alone is those sacrificial rites (yajñakratu); this is the seasons.

This is the year. Now, as to what one says, "Now" and "then"—this is indeed that. For this [year] is the very moments (*muhūrta*) of those moments. Janaka of Videha once met with him by means of days and nights. They said to him: "Whoever knows us, he goes forth, casting off evil."

He reaches a full lifespan; he conquers the heavenly world; his food does not fail him in yonder world. Indeed, casting off evil, he goes; he reaches a full lifespan; he conquers the heavenly world; his food does not fail him in yonder world—he who knows thus. Ahīna Āśvatthya indeed discovered the Sāvitra [rite].

{3.10.9.11} Having become a golden swan, he went to the heavenly world, to union with the Sun. Indeed, having become a golden swan, one who knows this goes to the heavenly world, to union with the Sun. Devabhāga Śrautarṣa learned the Sāvitra [hymn]. To him, Speech, remaining invisible, spoke.

"Surely Gautama knows everything, he who knows the Sāvitra"—thus [the other] spoke. He replied, "What is this speech of yours? "I am this Sāvitra, the highest world of the gods, bearing the secret greatness. At these words, Gautama, having placed his sacred thread over his shoulder, prostrated himself, saying, "Homage! Homage!"

He said: "Do not fear, Gautama; your world has indeed been won. Therefore, whoever knows the Sāvitra [mantra], they have all won their worlds. He who knows the eight-syllabled foot of the Sāvitra consecrated with glory (*śrī*) is indeed consecrated with glory. "Ghṛṇi" consists of two syllables; "Sūrya" consists of three; "Āditya" consists of three.

{3.10.9.14} This indeed is the eight-syllabled foot of the Sāvitra [mantra], consecrated by glory. He who knows this is indeed consecrated by glory. This has been declared in a Ṛgvedic verse: "In the imperishable syllable of the Ṛcs, in the highest heaven, wherein all the gods have taken their seat—what will he do with the Ṛc who does not know that? But those who know it, they sit together here. Indeed, for him who knows the Sāvitra, there is no need for the Ṛc, nor for the Yajus, nor for the Sāman.

{3.10.9.15} This very thing is that which encompasses the wheel of the gods; moist and swelling, it goes to the world of heaven, leaving behind all beings while beholding them. Indeed, one who knows this goes to the world of heaven, moist and swelling, leaving behind all beings while beholding them. Śūṣa Vārṣṇeya once came to Āditya. He said to him: "Come, learn the Sāvitra [fire]. This is indeed the heavenly fire, the deliverer, born from the immortal."

This indeed is that Sāvitra [fire], which shines yonder. "Come, know me!"—this is what he said to him. *Anuvāka 10: The Piling of the Sāvitra Fire* This earth is indeed the honey-bee; its honey is Agni himself. Those nights of the waxing and waning fortnights are the honey-makers; those days are the honey-drones. Verily, he who knows these honey-makers and honey-drones—these [bees] produce honey for him in the fire, and his merit from sacrifice and good works (*iṣṭāpūrta*) is not consumed. But he who does not know this... [is consumed].

{3.10.10.2} They do not make these [offerings] honey for him in the fire; they consume his merit from sacrifices and charitable works. He who knows the names of the days and nights does not meet with misfortune during the days and nights. "Saṃjñānam" (unification), "vijñānam" (discernment), "darśa" (the new moon), "dṛṣṭā" (seen)—these two sections are the names of the days and nights of the first fortnight. "Prastutam" (proclaimed), "viṣṭutam" (celebrated), "sutā" (pressed), "sunvatī" (pressing)—these two sections are the names of the days and nights of the second fortnight.
He who knows thus does not meet with misfortune during the days and nights.

{3.10.10.3} He who indeed knows the names of the *muhūrtas* does not meet with misfortune during the *muhūrtas*. [The names are: Citra, Ketur, Dātṛ, Pradātṛ, Savitṛ, Prasavitṛ, Abhiśāstṛ, Anumantṛ. These sections are the names of the *muhūrtas*. He who knows thus does not meet with misfortune during the *muhūrtas*. And he who indeed knows the names of the half-months and the months does not meet with misfortune during the half-months nor during the months.
"Purifier, about to purify; powerful, more powerful; ruddy, ruddy-rayed"—these are the names of the half-months and the months.

He who knows thus does not suffer misfortune in the half-months nor in the months. Indeed, he who knows the names of the sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*), of the seasons (*ṛtu*), and of the year (*saṃvatsara*) does not suffer misfortune in the sacrificial rites, nor in the seasons, nor in the year. "The *agniṣṭoma*, the *ukthya*, Agni, the season, Prajāpati, the year"—these sections are the names of the sacrificial rites, of the seasons, and of the year.

He who knows thus does not meet with misfortune in sacrifices, in the seasons, or in the year. Indeed, he who knows the moments of the moments does not meet with misfortune in the moments of the moments.

"‘Now’ and ‘then’—these indeed are the moments (*muhūrta*) among moments. He who knows this does not meet with misfortune within the moments of the moments. Furthermore, just as one who is a knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), having entered [the body], eats food, even so, having become a knower of the field, he enters these and eats food. He attains co-residence (*salokatā*) and union (*sāyujya*) with these very ones. He who knows this conquers renewed death."

Anuvāka 11: The Piling of the Sāvitra Fire {3.10.11.1} Indeed, some person, having departed from this world, knows himself: "I am this one. Another does not recognize his own world; being deluded by the fire, he is confounded by its smoke and does not recognize his own world. But he who knows this Sāvitra fire—he, having departed from this world, knows himself: "I am this one."

He recognizes his own world. And this very Sāvitra [Agni] indeed carries him to the heavenly world. For by means of days and nights joined together, this [sacrifice] is performed. "They have consecrated themselves for the rātri-sattra; they have undertaken the vow for the rātri-sattra"—these [merits] belong to one who does not know thus. They store up a treasure in yonder world. He indeed follows after that stored-up treasure. Now, he who knows this Agni Sāvitra—

{3.10.11.3} Indeed, for him, the days and nights do not consume his treasure-store in that world. He indeed goes forth following after the treasure-store of what he has studied. Bharadvāja lived as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*) for three lifetimes. To him, when he was decrepit, aged, and lying down, Indra approached and said: "Bharadvāja, if I were to grant you a fourth lifetime, what would you do with it? He replied: "I would simply practice the life of a student of sacred knowledge with it."

He showed him three forms resembling mountains that were, as it were, unrecognizable. From each of them, he took a handful. He said, addressing him by name, "Bharadvāja! These are indeed the Vedas; the Vedas are truly infinite. By means of these three lifetimes, you have only recited this much. Yet, the rest of them remains entirely unrecited by you. Come, learn this: this, indeed, is all knowledge."

To him he taught this Agni Sāvitra. Having understood it, he became immortal and went to the heavenly world, attaining union with Āditya. Indeed, whoever knows this becomes immortal and goes to the heavenly world, attaining union with Āditya. This indeed is the threefold knowledge.

{3.10.11.6} Indeed, as great a world as one conquers through the threefold knowledge, so great a world does he conquer who knows this. These are indeed the names of Agni; he who knows this attains union with Agni and residence in the same world as him. These are indeed the names of Vāyu; he who knows this attains union with Vāyu and residence in the same world as him. These are indeed the names of Indra.

He who knows this attains union with Indra and residence in the same world as him. These are indeed the names of Bṛhaspati; he who knows this attains union with Bṛhaspati and residence in the same world as him. These are indeed the names of Prajāpati; he who knows this attains union with Prajāpati and residence in the same world as him. These are indeed the names of Brahman; he who knows this attains union with Brahman and residence in the same world as him. He who knows this [attains these].

2. This very Agni is indeed Vāyu, without wings or tail. 3. Fire is his mouth. 4. Yonder sun is his head. 5. That which is between these two deities, 6. he sews all that together. 7. Therefore, it belongs to Savitṛ.

Prapāṭhaka 11, Anuvāka 1: The Piling of the Nāciketa Fire {3.11.1.1} You are the world; you are heaven. You are infinite; you are boundless. You are undecaying; you are imperishable. You are the foundation of austerity. Within you is this universe: every spirit, every being, and every good thing. You are the sustainer of all, the progenitor of all. As such, I place you here—the inexhaustible cow of plenty. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras!

{3.11.1.2} You are austerity, resting upon the world; you are the foundation of splendor. Within you is this all: every spirit, every being, every well-being. You are the sustainer of the universe, the progenitor of the universe. As such, I place you here—yielding desires, imperishable. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

{ 3.11.1.3} You are brilliance; you rest upon heat. You are the foundation of the ocean. Within you is this: every spirit, every being, everything well-being. You are the sustainer of all, the progenitor of all. As such, I place you down—yielding desires, imperishable. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

You are the ocean, resting in splendor; you are the foundation of the waters. Within you is all this: every spirit, every being, everything that is well-being. You are the sustainer of the universe, the progenitor of the universe. As such, I place you here—the inexhaustible cow of plenty. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

{3.11.1.5} You are the waters, resting in the ocean; you are the foundation of the earth. Within you is this entire world: every spirit, every being, and every well-being. You are the sustainers of all, the progenitors of all. As such, I place you down—yielding desires, imperishable. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

The earth is supported in the waters; it is the foundation of Agni. Within you is all this: every mystery, every being, and every well-being. You are the sustainer of all, the progenitor of all. As such, I place you here—the inexhaustible cow of plenty. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

{3.11.1.7} You are Agni, resting upon the earth; you are the foundation of the intermediate space. Within you is all this: every Yakṣa, every being, everything well-being. You are the sustainer of all, the progenitor of all. As such, I place you here—the inexhaustible cow of plenty. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

The intermediate space is yours; it rests in Agni. It is the foundation of Vāyu. Within you is all this: every spirit, every being, and every well-being. You are the sustainer of the universe and the progenitor of the universe. Therefore, I place you here, the inexhaustible cow of plenty. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

Vāyu is seated in the intermediate space; he is the support of heaven. Within you is all this: every spirit, every being, everything well-being. You are the sustainer of all, the progenitor of all. As such, I place you here—the inexhaustible cow of plenty. May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

You are the sky, resting in the wind; you are the support of the sun. Within you is all this: every spirit, every being, everything well-being. You are the sustainer of all, the progenitor of all. As such, I place you here—the inexhaustible cow of plenty. May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

You are Āditya, resting in heaven; you are the foundation of the moon. Within you is all this: every Yakṣa, every being, everything well-being. You are the sustainer of the universe, the progenitor of the universe. As such, I place you here—the inexhaustible cow of plenty. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

The moon is situated in the sun; it is the foundation of the stars. Within you is all this: every spirit, every being, and every well-being. You are the sustainer of the universe, the progenitor of the universe. As such, I place you here—you who are the inexhaustible cow of plenty. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

{3.11.1.13} You are the constellations, resting in the moon. You are the foundation of the year. This is within you: the entire Yakṣa, the entire being, the entire well-being. You are the sustainers of the universe, the progenitors of the universe. As such, I set you down—yielding all desires, imperishable. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

You are the year, resting in the lunar mansions; you are the foundation of the seasons. Within you is all this: every spirit, every being, everything that has come into existence. You are the sustainer of the universe, the progenitor of the universe. As such, I place you down, the inexhaustible cow of plenty. May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

{3.11.1.15} You are the seasons, resting in the year. In you is the foundation of the months. This is within: the whole Yakṣa, the whole being, the whole well-being. You are the sustainers of the universe, the progenitors of the universe. As such, I lay you down—those inexhaustible, wish-fulfilling ones. May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

{3.11.1.16} You are the months, resting in the seasons; you are the foundation of the half-months. This is within you: every spirit, every being, everything well-being. You are the sustainers of all, the progenitors of all. I place you down as inexhaustible wish-fulfilling cows. May Prajāpati settle you. With that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

{ 3.11.1.17} You are the half-months; you are resorted to by me. In you is the foundation of day and night. This is within: the entire Yakṣa, the entire being, the entire well-being. You are the sustainers of all, the progenitors of all. As such, I place you down—those who yield desires, the imperishable. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

{3.11.1.18} You two abide in day and night, resting within the half-months. You are the foundation of what has been, the foundation of what is to be. Within you two is all this: every spirit, every being, and every good thing. You two are the sustainers of the universe, the progenitors of the universe. As such, I place you two here, O inexhaustible ones who yield all desires. May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

The full moon, the eighth day, and the new moon—be you givers of food, milkers of food for us. Within this [altar] are all power, all being, and all prosperity. You are the sustainers of the universe, the progenitors of the universe. As such, I place you down as inexhaustible wish-fulfilling cows. May Prajāpati settle you; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

{ 3.11.1.20} You are the sovereign; you are the lofty glory, the wife of Indra, the wife of Dharma. You have pervaded all that has come into being. Within you is this [all]. All that is mystical, all that has come into being, all that is well-being. You are the sustainer of all, the progenitor of all. As such, I place you here, the inexhaustible cow of plenty. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.

{3.11.1.21} You are vigor; you are endurance. You are strength; you are splendor. You are the immortal abode of the gods. You are the immortal one, born of ascetic heat. Within you is all this: every mystery, every being, every well-being. You are the sustainer of the universe, the progenitor of the universe. As such, I place you here—the wish-fulfilling, inexhaustible one. May Prajāpati settle you. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras!

Anuvāka 2: The Piling of the Nāciketa Fire-altar {3.11.2.1} O Agni, you are Rudra, the Asura of the great heaven; you are the host of Maruts; you rule over nourishment. You travel with the ruddy winds, O friend of the house; as Pūṣan, you yourself protect those who worship you. O gods, take your place among the gods! Take your place as the first among the second! Take your place as the second among the third! Take your place as the third among the fourth! Take your place as the fourth among the fifth! Take your place as the fifth among the sixth!

{3.11.2.2} Rest upon the seventh [bricks] as the sixth! Rest upon the eighth [bricks] as the seventh! Rest upon the ninth [bricks] as the eighth! Rest upon the tenth [bricks] as the ninth! Rest upon the eleventh [bricks] as the tenth! Rest upon the twelfth [bricks] as the eleventh! Rest upon the thirteenth [bricks] as the twelfth! Rest upon the fourteenth [bricks] as the thirteenth! Rest upon the fifteenth [bricks] as the fourteenth! Rest upon the sixteenth [bricks] as the fifteenth!

O sixteenfold ones, rest upon the seventeenfold ones! O seventeenfold ones, rest upon the eighteenfold ones! O eighteenfold ones, rest upon the nineteenfold ones! O nineteenfold ones, rest upon the twentyfold ones! O twentyfold ones, rest upon the twenty-onefold ones! O twenty-onefold ones, rest upon the twenty-twofold ones! O twenty-twofold ones, rest upon the twenty-threefold ones! O twenty-threefold ones, rest upon the twenty-fourfold ones! O twenty-fourfold ones, rest upon the twenty-fivefold ones! O twenty-fivefold ones, rest upon the twenty-sixfold ones!

{3.11.2.4} Rest upon the twenty-sixfold [stomas] in the twenty-sevenfold; rest upon the twenty-sevenfold in the twenty-eightfold; rest upon the twenty-eightfold in the twenty-ninefold; rest upon the twenty-ninefold in the thirtyfold; rest upon the thirtyfold in the thirty-onefold; rest upon the thirty-onefold in the thirty-two-fold; rest upon the thirty-two-fold in the thirty-threefold. O gods, you who are thrice eleven and thrice thirty-three, be superior!

Those who follow the northern path, those who are superior beings—whatever desire I have for which I offer this oblation, may that be fulfilled for me. May we be masters of riches. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā!

Anuvāka 3: The Piling of the Nāciketa Fire {3.11.3.1} O Agni and Viṣṇu, being of one accord, may these songs of praise increase you both. Come hither with splendors and with strengths. Rājñī, Virājñī, Samrājñī, Svarājñī; Arcis, Śocis, Tapas, Haras, Bhās; Agni, Soma, Bṛhaspati; the All-Gods, the guardians of the world—may they all come together and protect this speech of mine. May we be masters of riches. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā!

Anuvāka 4 {3.11.4.1} O Lord of food, give us food—food that is free from disease and full of vigor. Bless the giver with long life. Grant strength to our bipeds and our quadrupeds. O Agni, Lord of the earth! O Soma, Lord of the plants! O Tvaṣṭṛ, Lord of the kindling woods! O Viṣṇu, Lord of the quarters! O Mitra, Lord of the truthful! O Varuṇa, Lord of the laws!

{3.11.4.2} O Maruts, you who are sources of bliss! O Maruts, lords of the hosts! O Rudra, lord of cattle! O Indra, lord of vigor! O Bṛhaspati, lord of sacred knowledge (*brahman*)! May I myself shine with radiance. Shining, may I shine forth with radiance. Having transcended this world, bring the light here! In that womb, as a progenitor, may I be procreated. May we be masters of riches! *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā!*

Anuvāka 5: The Piling of the Nāciketa Fire-altar {3.11.5.1} Seven, O Agni, are your fuel-sticks; seven your tongues; seven the seers; seven your beloved abodes. You who know the seven priestly offices, fill the seven wombs with clarified butter. The eastern direction; Agni is its deity. May that god Agni reach the deity among the deities of the directions, whoever seeks to harm me from this direction. The southern direction; Indra is its deity.

{3.11.5.2} May he who seeks to harm me from this direction reach Indra, the god of the quarters, among the deities. The western quarter; Soma is its deity. May he who seeks to harm me from this direction reach Soma, the god of the quarters, among the deities. The northern quarter; Mitra and Varuṇa are its deities. May he who seeks to harm me from this direction reach Mitra and Varuṇa, the gods of the quarters, among the deities.

The upward direction; Bṛhaspati is its deity. May he reach Bṛhaspati, the god of the directions among the deities, who seeks to harm me from this direction. This is the downward direction; Aditi is its deity. May he reach Aditi, the goddess of the directions among the deities, who seeks to harm me from this direction. The person is the direction; may the person fulfill my desires.

The blind one who is wakeful is the out-breath (*prāṇa*). Come hither, O so-and-so! The deaf one who cries out is the in-breath (*apāna*). Come hither, O so-and-so! May I attain every dawn. May I attain the light. May I attain the waters. May we be masters of riches. *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā*.

Anuvāka 6: The Piling of the Nāciketa Fire-altar {3.11.6.1} O Agni, that which of yours was un-piled and that which was piled; that which of yours was deficient and that which was redundant—let the Ādityas and the Aṅgirases pile that up for you. Let all the gods fill your layer. You are both piled and completely piled, O Agni; you are both this much and more, O Agni. Fill the space, fill the gap; and so, sit down, you who are auspicious. Indra, Agni, and Bṛhaspati have seated you in this womb.

{3.11.6.2} By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! These dappled cows, yielding milk for the libation, mix the Soma; they are the clans at the birth of the gods, in the three luminous realms of heaven. By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! O Agni, being born, bring the gods here for him who has spread the sacrificial grass; you are our Hotṛ-priest, worthy of praise. We have approached the youngest one with a great mind.

{3.11.6.3} He who has shone forth, kindled in his own dwelling, with brilliant luster between the two wide worlds—he who is well-invoked from every side, facing all directions, the creator of wisdom, the accomplisher of the sacrifice, Agni the Hotṛ, the most pervasive thought. You alone, the same for all, do men choose for their small oblation; they choose you for the great, none other than you. Like Manu, we establish you; like Manu, we kindle you. O Agni, O Aṅgiras, like Manu!

Sacrifice to the gods for the one who seeks the gods; for Agni, the observer of all people, bestows a prize-winning steed upon the clan. May Agni grant us wealth that is self-sustaining; being well-pleased, he goes toward what is desirable. Bring nourishment to those who praise you! Agni is sought in heaven, Agni is sought on earth; sought, he has entered into all plants. Agni Vaiśvānara is sought with power; may he protect us from harm by day and by night.

Anuvāka 7: The Piling of the Nāciketa Fire-altar {3.11.7.1} This very one who purifies (the wind) is the Nāciketa fire-altar. When he purifies toward the east, that is its head. Then when [he purifies] toward the south, that is the right wing. Then when [he purifies] toward the west, that is the tail. When [he purifies] toward the north, that is the left wing.

{3.11.7.2} Now, when it blows, that is its contraction and expansion; moreover, that is its attainment. Truly, whatever desire one has when sacrificing who piles the Nāciketa fire, or who knows it thus—that desire is attained for him. Verily, he who knows the abode and the foundation of the Nāciketa fire becomes possessed of an abode and attains a firm foundation.

Gold, indeed, is the abode and the foundation of the Nāciketa fire. He who knows this becomes possessed of an abode and goes to a firm foundation. Verily, he who knows the body of the Nāciketa fire goes to the heavenly world with his very body. Gold, indeed, is the body of the Nāciketa fire. He who knows this goes to the heavenly world with his very body. Moreover, it is just as a gold ornament would shine when heated.

In this very way, he shines with splendor and glory both in this world and in the next. Indeed, these worlds that are below the sun are called "wide" (*uravaḥ*). But those worlds that are beyond the sun are even more extensive (*varīyāṃsaḥ*). He who [attains] what is below the sun wins a world that has an end and is perishable. But he who [attains] what is beyond the sun wins a world that is infinite, shoreless, and imperishable.

He who builds the Nāciketa fire-altar, and he who knows it thus, wins an infinite, shoreless, and inexhaustible world. Moreover, just as one standing on a chariot looks out at the two sides as they turn, so does he look out at day and night; day and night do not reach his world—he who builds the Nāciketa fire-altar, and he who knows it thus.

Anuvāka 8: The Piling of the Nāciketa Fire-altar {3.11.8.1} Uśanas Vājaśravasa, it is said, gave away all his possessions as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). He had a son named Naciketas. While he was still a youth, faith entered him as the sacrificial fees were being led away. He said, "To whom will you give me? A second time, and a third time. Being overcome with grief, his father said to him, "I give you to Death. As he stood up, a voice addressed him.

"O Gautama, [bring] the boy," he said. He replied, "Go to the house of Death; indeed, I have given you to Death. He said, "When he has gone away on his journey, you shall go [to him]. "He must stay in your house for three nights without eating," he said. "If he should ask you, 'Boy, how many nights have you stayed? you should answer, 'Three. And if he asks, 'What did you eat on the first night?'"

"Thine offspring," [he said]. "What about the second? "Thine cattle. "What about the third? "Thine good deeds. He indeed went away while he was traveling abroad. For three nights, he stayed at home without eating. When [the father] returned, he asked him: "Boy, how many nights have you spent here? "Three," he replied.

"What did you eat on the first night? "Your offspring. "What on the second? "Your cattle. "What on the third? "Your good deeds. "Homage be unto you, O Blessed One," he said. "Choose a boon," [the other] replied. "May I go back to my father while still alive. "Choose a second boon," [the other] said.

"Tell me of the imperishability of my sacrifices and charitable works," he said. To him, he spoke of this Nāciketa fire-altar. From that time on, his sacrifices and charitable works did not perish; nor do the sacrifices and charitable works of one who builds the Nāciketa fire-altar perish, or of one who knows it thus. "Choose a third boon," [the god] said. "Tell me of the conquest of repeated death for me," he replied. To him, he spoke of this Nāciketa fire-altar. From that time on, he indeed conquered repeated death.

{3.11.8.6} He conquers recurrent death who piles the Nāciketa fire-altar, and he who knows it thus. Prajāpati, desiring offspring, performed austerities. He cast out gold; he threw it into the fire. It did not conceal itself from him. He threw it a second time; it did not conceal itself from him even then. He threw it a third time.

That [gift] did not please him at all. He cast it into his own heart, into the Vaiśvānara fire within himself; that pleased him. Therefore, gold is the smallest of riches, yet it is the most beloved when enjoyed, for it is born from the heart. He indeed could not find anyone to whom he might have brought that sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā). He brought it to his own right hand and accepted it.

"By means of skill (*dakṣa*), I accept you as the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*). Having accepted the sacrificial gift, he became skilled (*adakṣata*). Indeed, one becomes skilled after accepting the sacrificial gift, if he knows thus. Knowing this, the Vājaśravasa Gotamas used to accept even a designated sacrificial gift, thinking, "By both means we shall become skilled—by accepting the sacrificial gift and by [this formula]. They became skilled after accepting the sacrificial gift. Indeed, one becomes skilled after accepting the sacrificial gift, if he knows thus. He, however, causes another to perish.

Anuvāka 9: The Piling of the Nāciketa Fire-altar {3.11.9.1} Some indeed pile this very fire-altar on the *uttaravedi* at the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), saying, "This fire is commensurate with the *uttaravedi*. One should not do so. He would deprive this fire of its desire; being deprived of its desire, it would deprive him of his desire. Rather, one should pile this fire at the Soma sacrifice, or wherever the greatest number of oblations are offered. Thus he endows this fire with its desire; being endowed with its desire, it endows him with his desire.

He fulfills one's desires. Now, in ancient times, the seers piled this very fire on the high altar (*uttaravedi*) for the sake of a sacrificial session (*sattra*). Thereby, they indeed obtained offspring and conquered the heavenly world. He who piles the *Nāciketa* fire, and he who knows it thus, obtains offspring and conquers the heavenly world. Now, Vāyu, desiring prosperity, [piled it].

He laid them down exactly as they were sown. From that, indeed, he attained that prosperity which Vāyu has attained here. He attains that very prosperity which Vāyu has attained here—whosoever piles the Nāciketa fire-altar, and whosoever knows it thus. Now Gobala Vārṣṇa, desiring cattle, piled it in the fivefold manner: five in the east.

{3.11.9.4} Five [bricks] to the south; five to the west; five to the north; one in the middle. Verily, he obtained a thousand cattle; he obtains a thousand cattle who piles the *Nāciketa* fire-altar, and he who knows it thus. Then Prajāpati—desiring preeminence, desiring glory, and desiring progeny—piled it as the *Trivṛt*.

Seven in the east, three in the south, seven in the west, three in the north, and one in the middle. Thereby he indeed attained glory and preeminence; he brought forth this procreation which all creatures here bring forth. Preeminence is indeed threefold: mother, father, and son.

The *trivṛt* is procreation; the womb is the middle layer. He attains glory and preeminence; he is born with this same procreative power that these creatures are born with. This applies to him who piles the *nāciketa* fire-altar and he who knows it thus. Now, Indra, desiring preeminence, piled it upwards; from that, indeed, he attained preeminence.

He attains preeminence who piles the Nāciketa fire-altar, and he who knows it thus. Now, that sun, desiring heaven, piled [the bricks] facing eastward; from that, indeed, he conquered the heavenly world. He conquers the heavenly world who piles the Nāciketa fire-altar, and he who knows it thus. If he should so desire:

"May I be radiant, glorious, and possessed of the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*)," [thinking thus], he should creep forward toward the *dhishnya* of the Hotṛ priest. [He should say: "This glory that has come forward—may it envelop me with radiance, glory, and the splendor of sacred knowledge. Thus, he indeed becomes radiant, glorious, and possessed of the splendor of sacred knowledge. Now, if he should desire: "May they have the greatest faith in me; may they bring the most abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)," [he should proceed accordingly].

When the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) are being led forward, he should take a portion with the dipping-spoon (sruva) from the clarified butter while reciting, "O East, come! O East, come! and offer it into the Āhavanīya fire with the formula: "May the East, being pleased, partake of the clarified butter; Svāhā!"

{3.11.9.9} They place the greatest faith in him; they bring the most abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Having spread the loose earth (*purīṣa*), having touched it with the *citiklṛpti* formulas, having led forward the fire and kindled it, he offers these four oblations: "Thou, O Agni, art Rudra"—this is the form of the *Śatarudrīya*; "O Agni and Viṣṇu"—this is for the *Vasordhārā*; "O Lord of Food"—this is the food-oblation (*annahoma*); "Seven are thy fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven thy tongues"—this is the *Viśvaprī*.

Anuvāka 10: The Piling of the Nāciketa Fire-altar {3.11.10.10} The first brick which he lays down—with that he conquers this world. Moreover, he attains union with and residence in the same world as those deities who are in this world. The second brick which he lays down—with that he conquers the intermediate world. Moreover, he attains union with and residence in the same world as those deities who are in the intermediate world. The third brick which he lays down—with that he conquers yonder world.

{3.11.10.2} Moreover, he attains union with and residence in the same world as those deities who are in that world. Furthermore, regarding those other eighteen [bricks]—those very worlds which are both wide and more extensive—he conquers them by means of those [bricks]. Indeed, for him who piles the Nāciketa fire-altar and he who knows it thus, there is freedom of movement within those wide and more extensive worlds. The Nāciketa fire is indeed the year; of it, spring is the head.

Summer is the right wing; the rainy season is the left wing; autumn is the tail; the months are the workmen; day and night are the Śatarudrīya; Parjanya is the Vasordhārā. Just as Parjanya, having sent down good rain, fulfills all desires for living beings, even so he fulfills all his desires who piles the Nāciketa fire-altar.

And whoever knows this thus: The Nāciketa fire-altar is indeed the year. Of it, spring is the head; summer is the right wing; the rainy season is the tail; autumn is the left wing; winter is the middle. The bright fortnights are the layers (*citayaḥ*); the dark fortnights are the loose soil (*purīṣam*); days and nights are the bricks (*iṣṭakāḥ*). This, verily, is that fire-altar consisting of fire, ever renewed. Having become an altar consisting of fire, ever renewed, one goes to the heavenly world.
One attains union with Āditya—he who builds the Nāciketa fire-altar, and he who knows it thus.

Prapāṭhaka 12, Anuvāka 1: The Cāturhotra Fire-piling and the Vaiśvasṛja Fire-piling {3.12.1.1} To thee, O best of Aṅgiras, may we attain that desire, O Agni! Thee, the Lord of all quarters; all the quarters [are thine]. May Anumati favor us today; indeed, O Anumati, thou art favorable. Desire was the first of what has come into being. The Brahman was born, the father of the Virājs. This sacrifice is wealth; this is the sacrifice. Auspicious are the waters; then indeed do I behold them. To thee they bring [oblations], who art the giver of bodies. The gods were before, by means of the later [sacrifice]; [thou art] Prāṇa and Apāna. The bearer of oblations, the well-offered [sacrifice].

Anuvāka 2: The Cāturhotra Fire-altar Piling; The Vaiśvasṛja Fire-altar Piling {3.12.2.1} The heavenly world had indeed become hidden from the gods. They said to Prajāpati: "O Prajāpati, the heavenly world has become hidden from us; seek it out. He sought it out by means of sacrificial rites (yajñakratu). He did not find it by means of the sacrificial rites. He sought it out by means of offerings (iṣṭi). He found it by means of the offerings. That is the reason for the name of the offerings (iṣṭi).
They are indeed called *iṣṭayas*; they are referred to as *iṣṭayas* cryptically, for the gods, as it were, love the cryptic.

Hope said to him: "O Prajāpati, you toil indeed because of hope. I am indeed Hope. Sacrifice to me; then your hope will become true, and you shall find the heavenly world. He offered this cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kāma, a pap to Hope, and a pap to Anumati. Then, indeed, his hope became true, and he found the heavenly world. Truly, his hope becomes true.

He who sacrifices with this oblation, and he who knows it thus, finds the heavenly world. He offers here as follows: "To Agni Kāma, svāhā! To Āśā, svāhā! To Anumati, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! To the heavenly world, svāhā! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā!"
